stories.Headline: Job concerns rise as AI-generated actors take roles
stories.Summary:
AI-generated actors are moving from online short dramas into advertising and other commercial work in China, offering production teams a cheaper and more controllable option than human performers. Li Xiaolong, a young actor and student at the Shanghai Theatre Academy who stars in the short play My Dual Control, said this shift could further narrow job opportunities for human actors as productions face tighter budgets. He recounted that a friend in Hengdian, Zhejiang province, a major film and television hub, reported fewer actors working there, with some leaving the profession or taking costumed jobs at tourist sites. Li described the account as anecdotal, but it reflects the uncertainty some performers feel.

AI performers let producers control expressions and movements through text instructions, and they generally cost less than human actors, Li said. Producers can also revise scenes by changing prompts, which reduces the need for repeated filming. Actors without a strong personal following find work harder to get, and Li said even day-rate jobs that once paid more than 1,000 yuan ($150) have become difficult to secure. Despite these pressures, he believes human performance keeps qualities AI has not fully matched, such as the slow building of a character through research and emotional exploration. Some viewers, he noted, still prefer the realism and nuance of human acting.

The commercial rise of AI actors is visible in Fang Taozi, an AI-generated actress whose recognizable look and growing following have made her a fixture of AI short dramas. Her breakout role in The Laid-off Girl, which debuted on Douyin on June 12, brought her to a wider audience, and her Douyin account had more than 510,000 followers by August 25. On August 27, fashion magazine Cosmo Crush previewed her on its official Weibo account. Rates listed for her on Douyin's Xingtu influencer marketing platform have reportedly ranged from 168,000 yuan for videos up to 20 seconds to 258,000 yuan for videos longer than 60 seconds, though the articles caution that listed rates may not reflect actual transaction values.

Industry figures cited in the reporting suggest the economics are attractive, with some reports putting AI short drama costs at around 80,000 yuan per minute, depending on complexity and methods. The DataEye Research Institute estimated that China's AI short drama market, including animated dramas, could exceed 40 billion yuan in 2026, up about 138 percent year on year, after passing 22 billion yuan in the first five months. Hou Wenjie, secretary-general of the Shanghai-based Yu Ce Think Tank, argued that AI actors have moved past proof of concept into real monetization. He pointed to Fang's independent account, which posts everyday lifestyle content and recreates the companionship audiences associate with human influencers. The articles stress that these market figures cover AI short dramas broadly and are industry estimates, not official statistics.

Hou said AI actors offer brands greater control, predictable scheduling and fewer risks tied to personal scandals, and he expects AI characters to expand into lifestyle content and longer-term brand partnerships. He also called for more attention to labeling of virtual-person advertising, likeness rights and content authenticity. The articles note that popularity does not guarantee lasting value, and the reported removal of an advertisement featuring Fang over concerns that its claims could mislead consumers shows the risks. Questions about whether AI characters resemble existing performers too closely are also likely to grow as the technology improves. Li expects stage work to be less affected than screen work, and he anticipates closer integration of AI and human actors as the technology develops.

stories.Headline: Tracking AI adoption in North Korean threat actor tradecraft
stories.Summary:
Microsoft Threat Intelligence reports that North Korean threat actors are expanding their use of generative and agentic AI across their operations, with varying levels of adoption. Jade Sleet launched campaigns through three front companies in a single week, Onyx Sleet produced dozens of tailored lures in minutes, and Coral Sleet quickly built a capability to trojanize private source code repositories. Onyx Sleet and Pearl Sleet have also used the open-source agentic AI penetration testing framework ARTEX in their operations. Microsoft says these operations remain human-directed and have not become fully autonomous.

The adoption is assessed across four stages: emerging, expanding, accelerating, and operationalized. Jade Sleet, Coral Sleet, and Jasper Sleet are rated as operationalized, meaning AI is built into their routine workflows across entire operations. Diamond Sleet, Onyx Sleet, Pearl Sleet, and Sapphire Sleet are rated as accelerating, and Emerald Sleet is rated as expanding. Microsoft has not assessed any North Korean actor as merely emerging. The report also observes that the use of AI supports existing goals, such as revenue generation for the regime and intelligence collection, rather than marking a change in motivation.

The main uses include reconnaissance on target organizations, research into cryptocurrency and blockchain workflows, and the creation of fake digital personas for job-themed social engineering. Microsoft describes a June 8 to June 12, 2026 campaign in which Jade Sleet posed as recruiters for a spoofed AI-powered blockchain intelligence company using tailored domains and social media profiles. Jasper Sleet is described as using AI-assisted resume workflows to scale fake personas, and Diamond Sleet has returned to targeting the oil and gas sector since August 2026 while building fake communications technology companies. Microsoft notes that these shifts suggest AI is improving the efficiency of existing workflows.

A Seoul Economic Daily editorial, dated October 28, 2026, links the threat to a separate wave of suspected North Korean hacking against South Korea. It reports more than 4.4 million attempts to access South Korean financial firms from North Korean IP addresses, following a banking sector breach earlier that month. The editorial argues that individual companies cannot stop sweeping attacks alone and that the response should be framed as a national security matter. It calls for chief executives to take responsibility for security reviews and for the government to reorganize its cybersecurity response around a central control tower. The editorial also states that the lazarus group quickly tried to exploit a PHP vulnerability once it was found.

stories.Headline: AG Uthmeier announces 100 felony counts against Kissimmee man, lawsuit against AI company over child abuse images - Florida’s Voice
stories.Summary:
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier announced charges and a civil lawsuit tied to the sexual exploitation of children, with the criminal case filed against Jerry Jesus Reyes, 26, of Kissimmee. Prosecutors with the Office of Statewide Prosecution brought 100 felony counts against him for possessing and transmitting child sexual abuse material and for possessing images of sexual activity involving animals. The case began when the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children sent a CyberTipline report about a Snapchat account. Osceola County Sheriff's Office detectives used subpoenas and search warrants to tie the account to Reyes and found multiple files showing the sexual abuse of young children. Some of the possession counts were reclassified as first-degree felonies because of the number of images involved.

The charges carry serious penalties, including a second-degree felony count for transmitting child pornography through an electronic device that carries a mandatory minimum of five years in prison. Reyes remains in the Osceola County Jail on a $100,000 bond, with conditions barring internet access and contact with minors. If convicted on all counts, he could face decades in state prison. Senior Assistant Statewide Prosecutor Lauryn Day is handling the case in Florida's Ninth Judicial Circuit, and the investigation is still ongoing. The charges against Reyes have not been proven in court.

In a separate action, Uthmeier filed a civil lawsuit against Rengstorff Consulting Ltd., which operates the A2E artificial intelligence platform and related mobile applications. The complaint alleges that the platform lets users upload photos and videos of real people, including children, and generate nude or sexually explicit images without consent. It also says the platform offers tools to digitally alter adults to look like minors in sexual content. State attorneys argue that despite terms of service that ban such activity, the company did not put adequate safeguards in place, such as monitoring users, verifying consent, terminating accounts, or reporting violations to law enforcement. The lawsuit points to earlier criminal cases in Tampa and Tallahassee in which A2E was allegedly used to create illegal sexual images of minors.

Uthmeier is asking a court for a permanent injunction that would stop the company from offering AI products that create, store, view, or share child sexual abuse material or non-consensual sexualized images. The lawsuit also seeks recovery of profits allegedly gained through unlawful practices and civil penalties of up to $10,000 per violation under the Florida Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act. Uthmeier said anyone who possesses, shares, or creates such images takes part in that abuse, and he said companies that build AI tools making it easier to generate such material, while claiming to prohibit it, will be held accountable. His office said it will keep working with local police and the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children on child exploitation cases and on legal action against companies whose technology allegedly enables illegal activity. The allegations against the company have not been proven in court.

stories.Headline: Bank asks people to, please, not share passwords with AI agents
stories.Summary:
Bank of America has sent customers an email titled "Protecting your finances in the AI world," asking them not to share their banking username and password with anyone, including an AI tool or agent that offers to act on their behalf. A bank spokesperson confirmed to TechCrunch that the email, which was posted on social media, is genuine. TechCrunch reported on the message on October 27, 2026, and ZDNET followed on October 29. The warning arrives as personal AI assistants grow more popular and more people hand over their log-in details to them.

The email lays out the risks and the stakes. An assistant could do something with a customer's money without their knowledge, or the bank might think the account is under attack and lock the owner out. A security flaw in an assistant could also leak the credentials elsewhere and give hackers a way in. The bank also says that anyone who shares credentials is responsible for activity that results from that access. TechCrunch notes that account agreements at most banks hold customers accountable for anyone they give their log-in to.

The reaction across the industry goes beyond one bank. ZDNET reports that Bank of America, the second-largest bank in the US, is following a trend in which Citi, Morgan Stanley and Wells Fargo are restricting third-party AI agent access. Axios reported last week that AI agents are gaining unauthorized access to users' bank accounts and acting outside their instructions, which sent some of the biggest US banks into a frenzy. JPMorgan has already blocked the Muse and Instinct agents from reaching bank accounts. Its chief executive, Jamie Dimon, said on the company's earnings call that the bank will not let just any outside agent inside because it is too risky for clients and for the bank.

The broader picture is that banks are still working out how AI tools fit into finance. TechCrunch says banks, payment providers and processors are trying to figure out how to let customers reach their accounts through AI, including for agentic payments, where an agent buys things at the best price or the right time. ZDNET points to Meta's Muse as an example of the privacy worry. It asks for contacts, calendar, email and logins during setup, and can also gather photos, videos, financial and health data, with a privacy policy saying the data may be used or shared. Muse launched in September and has passed 10 million users in 40 days, and neither article says what the banks will do next.

stories.Headline: Trump pushes new name for AI in executive branch
stories.Summary:
President Donald Trump announced on social media that he planned to officially ban the term "artificial intelligence" and replace it with "SI" or "super intelligence." He made the post on Truth Social, the platform he uses for announcements, and he described the current label as a poor fit. The articles also note that in late September Trump had signed an executive order directing the executive branch to use SI instead of AI. Reports on the announcement were published on October 27, 2026, by several local NonStop Local news stations. The sources say the change would apply to all relevant documents.

Trump said the current name is inaccurate and bad, and he also asked when The Wall Street Journal would begin using the new term. The articles do not say which documents the order covers beyond the executive branch, nor do they describe any deadline for the switch. They also do not report any formal rule that would force private companies to change their language. Still, the wording in the post suggests the change is meant to affect government records and communications. The articles provide no further detail on how the change would be carried out.

Trump is the person responsible for the announcement, and the articles present his remarks as his own words and his own stated position. He called the name "very bad and inaccurate." The articles do not include any response from federal agencies or independent experts. They do note that most AI companies, including Anthropic and OpenAI, still call themselves artificial intelligence companies and continue to use "AI" in their branding. This means the executive branch's preferred term and the industry's common term now differ.

The context shows a gap between the White House's stated preference and the way the private AI sector describes itself. The articles do not say whether any companies have indicated they will change their naming in response. They also do not report any legal challenge or congressional reaction. Based on the material provided, the next steps are unclear, and the articles offer no timetable for when the term change would take effect in federal documents.

stories.Headline: Pa. law doesn’t regulate AI-generated candidates in election ads, but some hope to change that
stories.Summary:
On October 27, 2026, WPSU reported that Republican gubernatorial challenger Stacy Garrity had released an AI-generated video depicting her Democratic opponent, incumbent Josh Shapiro, with the midterm elections less than a week away. The ad opens with a figure resembling Shapiro at the governor's office, flanked by American and Pennsylvania flags, and the artificial Shapiro refers to sexual harassment scandals. The video also shows a real New York Times headline about a harassment complaint against an aide. The ad includes no watermark or on-screen notice that it was artificially produced, and the fake Shapiro does not reveal he is not the real candidate until about 45 seconds in.

A spokesperson for the real Shapiro called the ad "cheap" and "dishonest" in a statement to Axios. Garrity told KDKA-TV that she stands by the ad. The reporting notes that Pennsylvania currently has no law prohibiting deepfakes in political ads and no requirement for a disclaimer. Sen. Lisa Boscola has said she plans to introduce legislation barring AI-generated or AI-altered video, audio or images of a candidate during the 90 days before an election, though that bill had not yet been introduced. A separate bill on deepfakes in campaign ads passed the state House last year but did not clear the state Senate.

The reporting places Pennsylvania among states that lag behind its neighbors. Delaware, Maryland and New York have laws that either prohibit election deepfakes or require a disclaimer that content is AI-generated. The WPSU story also points to earlier coverage of AI and election misinformation, including a 2024 article on experts fighting back and reports on U.S. Senate committee action and state efforts to counter AI threats to elections. The articles do not say whether Boscola's bill will be introduced before the election or whether any proposal will become law.

stories.Headline: From AI Pilots to Accountable Operations: How Companies Can Build Technology That Earns Trust - Global Banking & Finance Review
stories.Summary:
Global Banking & Finance Review published an article on October 29, 2026, arguing that companies moving AI from pilot projects into daily operations need to design for accountability, security and customer trust. The piece, written by Barnali Pal Sinha, does not report a single incident or event; it is an advisory analysis. It starts from the premise that the question for boards is no longer whether to experiment with artificial intelligence, but how promising demonstrations can become dependable services. It separates low-consequence uses, such as drafting marketing emails, from higher-stakes ones, such as summarising loan applications or influencing insurance responses, where the same underlying technology carries very different risks.

The article sets out a sequence of practical steps. It advises organisations to begin with a defined operational decision rather than a model, and to record the decision being supported, the information required, the people affected and the cost of a wrong answer. It treats data quality and access permissions as governance matters, warning that connecting more documents to a system does not make its outputs more reliable. It also calls for measuring operational gains alongside corrections, escalations and failure modes, and for human oversight that is realistic about volume and gives reviewers authority to challenge the system. On regulation, it notes that the European Union's AI Act applies obligations in stages, so firms should keep an inventory of their systems and avoid assuming every application falls into the same legal category.

The article attributes its guidance to recognised frameworks and points to several sources. It cites the US National Institute of Standards and Technology's AI Risk Management Framework, describing AI risk management as a continuing organisational discipline rather than a one-off approval, and its Generative AI Profile, which flags unreliable output and privacy and security concerns. It refers to the European Commission's implementation guidance for the AI Act and to a 2025 OECD survey on SME digitalisation, which it uses to argue that technology purchases must be matched by changes in roles and procedures. The author's conclusion is that boards should ask which processes depend on AI, how failures were handled and whether the benefits still justify the exposure.

stories.Headline: Ohio schools set guardrails for AI use in classrooms
stories.Summary:
Ohio school districts are now required to have artificial intelligence policies in place, following a state law that took effect this year. As of late October 2026, the statewide framework is in its third official month, and districts must either adopt the state's model policy or write their own. The article, published October 29, 2026, reports that the requirement creates a statewide baseline for how schools use the technology safely and ethically in classrooms. Districts had already spent the past couple of years setting their own boundaries for AI, so the state rules build on work that was underway.

Chris Yaluma, an AI ethics professor at Ohio State University, said the right guardrails can help AI support personalized learning and reinforce student skills. He noted that the state model gives districts flexibility because the tools students use can change within weeks. Yaluma warned that policies will vary in how they are carried out, and he suggested smaller districts may struggle with staffing, oversight committees and other implementation needs. He also said families should understand how students use AI tools and how to limit risks while still gaining benefits. A statewide policy, he added, gives researchers a way to track the effects of these rules.

Christopher Lockhart, who works in the information technology department of Columbus City Schools, described his district's safeguards, including teaching older students how to use AI safely and avoiding the entry of personal information. He said Columbus has used specialized apps and tools to address cheating and computer-generated work, and that revision history in online document programs lets teachers see how long a student spent creating work. According to Lockhart, the district is responding to concerns while also planning ahead, guided by three principles: student safety, student privacy and academic integrity. He also argued that classroom AI use can help students build college readiness and compete more effectively as they enter careers.

Some districts moved before the state requirement. The article reports that in September 2024, Cincinnati Public Schools became the first of Ohio's four largest districts to draft its own AI policy, and Columbus followed soon after. The reporting makes clear that the state mandate now sets a common floor, while individual districts still decide how closely to follow it. The article does not say what enforcement or review the state will apply to these policies.

stories.Headline: Livermore Unified School District Forms AI Workgroup
stories.Summary:
The Livermore Valley Joint Unified School District, known as LVJUSD, has set up an Artificial Intelligence Workgroup to help decide how AI should be used in its classrooms. The group was formed at the start of the school year and includes teachers from all levels, students from Granada and Livermore high schools, school counselors, district administrators, and parents. It also has a board member and AI experts from Quest Science Center and Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory. Since beginning its work in September, the group has focused on building a shared understanding of AI, assessing district readiness, and reviewing privacy and security concerns.

The workgroup has been asked to develop an approach that supports teaching and learning while addressing academic integrity, student privacy, security, and equitable access. Its findings will guide the LVJUSD Board of Directors as it adopts a districtwide AI policy. As the school year continues, the group will run a limited AI pilot involving educators and students. It will also review guidance and a model AI policy being developed by the state Department of Education, along with approaches taken by other districts. Staff, students, families, and the community will have a chance to review and comment on the findings before the board considers a policy for implementation before the 2027-28 school year.

Chris Connor, the district's director of TK-12 Education, said that the district's job is to determine thoughtfully how AI can support learning while keeping students at the center of decisions, rather than simply reacting to the technology. Michelle Pechette, assistant superintendent for Educational Services, said that AI offers major opportunities but also raises important questions that the district intends to answer together with the community. She said the goal is guidance that prepares students for an AI-influenced future while protecting critical thinking, creativity, relationships, and human judgment. The district is also partnering with Quest Science Center on a Workforce Development Planning Initiative. That effort brings together Bay Area tech leaders, educators, higher education institutions, and community members to shape guidelines linking STEM classroom learning to future careers.

The move comes as schools across the country and the state wrestle with how students should use generative AI tools, both as learning aids and as possible shortcuts that undermine academic work. The article does not say how the pilot will be structured, which schools will take part, or when the pilot results will be published. It also does not give a date for the board's vote beyond the target of a policy before the 2027-28 school year. Those details, along with the outcome of the state guidance, are likely to shape the district's final policy.

stories.Headline: US Federal Trade Commission targets airline ticket pricing as scrutiny of AI and personal data intensifies
stories.Summary:
The US Federal Trade Commission has ordered nine companies, including three major American airlines, to provide information about how they set prices. The orders, announced on October 28, 2026, cover Delta Air Lines, United Airlines and JetBlue, alongside Uber, Lyft, DoorDash, Instacart, Target and Walmart. The agency wants to learn whether businesses use personal data such as browsing history, location, purchasing behaviour or loyalty-programme participation to offer different prices to individual customers. The FTC has not found that any of the airlines has broken the law.

The orders were issued under Section 6(b) of the FTC Act, which lets the agency run broad market studies and demand information even when no specific violation is under investigation. Each company has 45 days from receiving its order to respond, and the FTC can seek federal court enforcement if a company does not comply. The agency is asking for details on the data, algorithms and tools used to set prices and, where relevant, how gig workers are paid. The distinction at the centre of the inquiry is between dynamic pricing, which airlines already use to adjust fares for demand, seat availability and booking timing, and personalised pricing, which would use information about a specific customer to set that customer's fare. FTC Chairman Andrew N. Ferguson said the agency intends to examine methods that could affect how much consumers pay for the same product.

The airlines have been drawn into this debate by earlier controversies. In 2025, Delta faced questions from US lawmakers about its work with Fetcherr, an AI pricing technology provider, and in an August 2025 response to senators the airline said it had never used or planned to use fares targeted to individuals based on personal data. In April 2026, JetBlue apologised after a social-media reply suggested that clearing browser cookies or using incognito mode might help a customer whose fare had risen by $230, saying the reply was wrong and that its fares were not set using cached or personal data. A proposed class-action lawsuit has since alleged that JetBlue used customer data to raise fares, but those allegations are unproven and the airline denies them. The FTC's wider work includes a study launched in July 2024 into third-party firms that sell personalised pricing tools, and in August 2026 it invited public comment on a proposed enforcement policy on the subject.

Responsibility for the pricing decisions rests with the airlines themselves, and each has denied using personal data to set individual fares. The reporting says the immediate effect is likely to be closer scrutiny of pricing systems, data governance and customer communications rather than an instant change to how tickets are sold. Airlines may need to document which customer data they collect and how it is used, establish controls on pricing algorithms, make clear to customers how fares are determined, and review their arrangements with outside AI providers. The FTC will use the responses to inform policymakers, and the outcome of the inquiry will depend on what the companies disclose in the coming weeks.

stories.Headline: The Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act: A 10^25-Operation Pause, a Department of AI, and 20 Years in Prison
stories.Summary:
On 3 September 2026, Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Representative Greg Casar of Texas publicly announced the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act. The announcement was a press release describing forthcoming legislation, not a bill. The formal texts followed later: S. 5493 was introduced in the Senate on 23 September and H.R. 10538 in the House on 24 September. Neither bill has had a hearing, markup or vote since.

If enacted, the bill would make it unlawful to develop or deploy superintelligence and any system showing a listed precursor trait. It sets a compute threshold of 10^25 operations for advanced AI, adjusted yearly by the Secretary, and imposes a pause on advanced systems until a new Department of Artificial Intelligence is staffed and has issued safety rules. Violators who act recklessly could face up to 20 years in prison, and a charter holder that violates the rules could lose its charter and its intellectual property. The bill also requires discoverers of such systems to notify the Secretary within 24 hours.

The sponsors' release and the bill texts are the primary sources for these provisions. The House version has eleven cosponsors, all Democrats, added between 24 September and 13 October. The findings section cites statements from Geoffrey Hinton, Elon Musk, Sam Altman, Mustafa Suleyman, Max Tegmark and Stuart Russell, along with a July 2026 open letter signed by more than 1,300 AI scientists. The articles present those citations as the sponsors' case, not as verified findings.

The Machine Intelligence Research Institute endorsed the bill on 23 September, calling it the first legislation with a real chance of stopping the threat, while also saying it lacks chip tracking and may over-classify some narrow systems. The National AI Association's Caleb Max told NBC News that the bill would be dead on arrival with industry and in Washington, calling it a de facto ban. The Congressional Research Service status for the House bill, refreshed 14 October, still listed the 24 September introduction as its latest action. More to follow.

Articles.Title: The Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act: A 10^25-Operation Pause, a Department of AI, and 20 Years in Prison - OrcaRouter

stories.Headline: AssemblyAI Ships AssemblyAI-TTS-1: A $15 per 1M Character Text-to-Speech API for Voice Agents
stories.Summary:
AssemblyAI has released AssemblyAI-TTS-1, its first text-to-speech model, and made it generally available. The model is aimed at voice agents handling live phone calls, where response speed and correct pronunciation affect whether a caller stays on the line. It is priced at $15 per 1M characters, with no annual contract and no concurrency tier to purchase. Developers who already use AssemblyAI's speech-to-text service can now handle both sides of a voice conversation with a single vendor. The model runs only on AssemblyAI's cloud, in the US (us-east-1) or EU (eu-north-1) regions, and no open weights or on-premises option is offered.

It can be reached through an HTTP API, a WebSocket API, or an OpenAI-compatible route, and the WebSocket session supports a cancel message for interrupting speech mid-reply. Output comes as mono PCM, mu-law or A-law at rates from 8 kHz to 48 kHz, with 24 kHz PCM as the native format. The launch includes a library of more than 4,000 voices and instant voice cloning, which requires a short recording and confirmation that the speaker has given permission. Six languages are supported at launch: English, Spanish, French, German, Italian and Portuguese.

AssemblyAI's own tests, dated October 28, 2026, show the model matching ElevenLabs v4 on entity accuracy, with a 93.7% score against 93.6%, at under a fifth of that model's price. The company reports a median time to first byte of 47 ms, the fastest of the models it tested. Independent results are more mixed, with a Cekura benchmark placing the model's median streaming latency at 159 ms and ranking it eighth of 19 timed models. Under the same benchmark, Inworld TTS-2 Flash posted 45 ms and 93.2% reading accuracy at the same price.

AssemblyAI also says the model lacks SSML, speed control, pronunciation dictionaries and emotion tags for now. AssemblyAI describes the model as a streaming system trained on millions of hours of audio, including real conversational data, that works on continuous audio representations rather than the discrete tokens used by most TTS models. The company says this approach improves realism and shortens the wait before speech begins. The launch was covered by MarkTechPost on October 29, 2026, and the article includes LiveKit and Pipecat reference agents that AssemblyAI has published for developers.

stories.Headline: AI in Cell Factories: Is the Highly Anticipated Big Payoff for Capital Investors and Stakeholders Just Around the Corner?
stories.Summary:
AI is now being applied in cell factories, the synthetic biology field that once drew heavy capital before losses and failed pilot tests cooled investor enthusiasm. The article, published by 36Kr on October 30, 2026 and written by Liu Lingguo, asks whether a long-awaited financial payoff for investors is close at hand. It notes that on October 14 David Baker's team published two papers in Nature showing AI can design proteases from scratch, and that Claude and Gemini 4 have since claimed similar enzyme design abilities. Investors interviewed say a recovery is underway this year, though not a return to the 2021 peak.

The most concrete example given is Xinbeile's lactulose project, where AI screened 100 sequences from more than 30,000 enzyme sequences, and about 20 of them showed catalytic activity. Through successive rounds of AI-guided design, the best mutant reached roughly five times the original activity and about three times the stability, moving from wild-type enzyme to industrial enzyme in three months. Liu Huatao, the company's CTO, concluded that AI cuts the R&D cycle by about 80% compared with blind screening. The article also describes AI helping a dapoxetine intermediate project avoid equipment modifications that could have cost hundreds of thousands or even millions of yuan, and a Bluepha pilot whose unstable output was traced to its cause in about a week.

Several industry figures are quoted describing these gains. Luo Xiaozhou, founder of Senris, says the recovery is driven by AI and the 15th Five-Year Plan policies, and that an AI analysis flagged a valve problem later confirmed as a roughly 10% deviation. Li Yingjie of Inno Kechuang Fund evaluates projects on several criteria, including scaled production experience and sufficient market size. Luo Hongzhen of Bailun Bio explains that scale-up changes in dissolved oxygen, pH and substrate concentration cause problems that small tests do not reveal. The article stresses that AI mainly predicts risks and troubleshoots bottlenecks, while experienced technicians still make decisions on feeding, stirring, ventilation and contamination.

The article identifies market demand as the area AI helps least and where past failures were most painful. It cites Danimer Scientific, whose capacity expansion to 55 million pounds in 2022 left plants idle and led to bankruptcy protection in March 2025, and erythritol, where domestic capacity reached 380,000 tons by May 2023 and the price fell from 40,000 yuan to 9,500 yuan per ton. Companies are now choosing products either along clear downstream demand or by replacing existing supply with cheaper methods. The article's account of how these product choices are playing out continues beyond the portion available to this summary.

stories.Headline: 2027: Govs, experts call for ethical journalism, AI regulation
stories.Summary:
Governors Abba Yusuf of Kano and Uba Sani of Kaduna, along with media experts and other stakeholders, called for responsible journalism, stronger measures against misinformation and clear guidelines on artificial intelligence ahead of Nigeria's 2027 general elections. The call was made at the launch of a book, Digital Shift in Nigeria's Newspaper Industry, written by Leadership Newspapers Group News Editor Sunday Isuwa, in Abuja on Thursday. The speakers warned that hate speech, personal attacks and unverified information could weaken democratic institutions and erode public confidence in the electoral process. Yusuf, represented by his Commissioner for Information and Internal Affairs, Ibrahim Waiya, said the rising use of hate speech during campaigns was unhealthy for democracy and urged politicians to focus on issues rather than opponents. Sani, represented by his Commissioner for Information, Ahmed Maiyaki, urged journalists to look beyond campaign events, investigate claims, establish facts and consider how their reports could affect national stability.

Archbishop Sunday Onuoha, president of Vision Africa and a former special assistant to President Olusegun Obasanjo on privatisation, urged media organisations to adopt clear policies on the use of artificial intelligence in journalism. Presenting a paper at the event through Methodist Bishop of Kubwa Diocese, Bishop Frederick Onoja, Onuoha also urged newsrooms to work with reputable fact-checking bodies, saying they would struggle to counter disinformation alone. He further recommended specialised training for political reporters in electoral law, data journalism, digital investigations, AI detection, conflict-sensitive reporting and hate-speech monitoring. In his welcome address, Isuwa warned journalists against sacrificing accuracy, professional ethics and public trust in the rush to publish. He named the spread of misinformation, shifting business models and declining public confidence as major challenges facing the newspaper industry.

Isuwa said his book examines how digital platforms have changed the production, distribution and consumption of news, and it aims to improve media literacy while encouraging journalists to adopt new tools without abandoning core principles. He stressed that technology alone cannot guarantee good journalism, which still depends on ethical practice, careful verification, fairness and service to the public. The debate comes as AI-generated fake news has spread across social media platforms in Nigeria ahead of the presidential election scheduled for January 16, 2027. The articles do not report any specific measures that have been adopted, and the speakers' recommendations were made at the event without a stated timetable for implementation.

stories.Headline: AI Beyond Speech Capability: Stopping Unwanted Interruptions – How Omni AI Revolutionizes Real-Time Interaction
stories.Summary:
A survey paper released on October 29, 2026 by researchers from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Carnegie Mellon University, and Columbia University argues that AI systems must do more than speak; they must also know when to hold back and when to interrupt. The review, which covers 349 related works, is framed as a survey of real-time interactive systems that combine multiple types of input, such as text, images, audio, and video. The authors say that being able to listen, see, and reply does not by itself give a system natural conversational behavior. The article presents the paper as a response to a practical problem: a model that is asked to analyze a chart and then receives the follow-up "wait a minute, look at the curve on the right" must stop its current answer, update its target, and check whether its earlier calculations still hold. The paper splits real-time omni-modal intelligence into two linked parts, which it calls omni intelligence and omni interactivity.

Omni intelligence covers cross-modal understanding, reasoning, and generation, while omni interactivity covers timing of responses, turn management, interruption handling, and dynamic adjustment. The authors describe three defining features: streaming input, an internal state that keeps changing, and online control over when to respond, wait, or revise output. The review also sorts existing approaches into two technical paths. One adapts pre-trained language or multi-modal models by adding streaming processing, modality modules, post-training, and external orchestration, which reuses existing abilities but struggles with latency and state synchronization. The other builds native interactive models that embed continuous processing, timing structure, and interaction control into the architecture and training, which tightens perception and interaction but demands more training data and greater care in preserving capabilities.

On interruptions, the review lists six recovery steps: detect whether the user truly interrupted and separate real instructions from background sound, yield by stopping or reducing speech promptly, roll back to what the user actually heard, revise intent and tasks based on the new instruction, and resume from the updated state. It also names an "intelligence-interactivity trade-off," in which responding too early can leave a model with insufficient information while waiting for a slow calculation harms the interaction. To manage this, the authors discuss multi-rate interactive intelligence, in which a fast front end handles continuous perception and quick replies while a back end asynchronously runs heavier reasoning, retrieval, and tool calls, with state synchronization to prevent stale results from being used. The paper further proposes evaluating systems across six dimensions: latency, timing quality, content quality, robustness, long-conversation quality, and recovery capability. The authors list future directions including coordination across time scales, persistent memory, active and social interaction in multi-person settings, and safety and efficiency in open environments.

Articles.Title: AI Beyond Speech Capability: Stopping Unwanted Interruptions – How Omni AI Revolutionizes Real-Time Interaction - eu.36kr.com

stories.Headline: Time Is Running Out for Embodied Intelligence: Urgent Action for the Next Era of AI
stories.Summary:
The embodied intelligence sector, which builds AI-driven robots that operate in the physical world, is described in an October 29, 2026 commentary on eu.36kr.com as having fallen into a deadlock of what the author calls narrative involution. According to the piece, capital, demonstrations, and press exposure have come to matter more than real-world deployment, so startups burn through funding and large enterprises invest heavily without achieving large-scale industrial rollout. The author argues that the track is not simply suffering from overwork or talent shortages but has been structured around staged demos from the start. The article also says the sector needs to pivot toward tangible, real-world implementation.

The commentary attributes the problem to how projects are judged, saying that presentation effects, financing totals, media coverage, and demonstration videos serve as the main measures of success for teams and investors alike. It describes ultra-long development cycles, demonstration iterations that go nowhere, and prototypes that linger in exhibition halls. Ordinary projects, the author says, lack time to build deep industry scenarios, polish reliable engineering solutions, or gather large volumes of real-world data, and many end up with polished but interchangeable demo results. The article cites an industry survey and states that projects capable of stable commercial operation make up less than 5 percent of all humanoid robot projects. It also points to high failure rates, costly maintenance, and weak robustness in harsh environments.

The article places responsibility with the screening systems used by capital markets and with the industry's own evaluation habits, which it says reward stories rather than engineering. It argues that conferences, pilot programs, and technical iterations have changed surface features without altering the underlying logic of demonstration first and financing first. Resource gaps between large manufacturers and startups are described as widening, with the largest players controlling computing power, supply chains, and customers. The author contends that traditional automation companies with long experience on production lines are better positioned for industrial needs, and that real competitiveness will depend on stability, long-term reliability, and low-cost mass production. The piece does not present a concrete timetable or specific policy measures for the changes it calls for.

stories.Headline: How Ropes & Gray is developing AI for transactional diligence
stories.Summary:
Law firm Ropes & Gray is developing a transactional diligence AI tool in partnership with OpenAI, as described in an OpenAI customer story dated October 29, 2026. The firm is an enterprise in the North American services industry, and it uses ChatGPT in the project. The work is aimed at speeding up the investigation buyers must carry out before an acquisition to check a seller's financial and legal claims. That process uncovers risks and liabilities, and it has traditionally demanded a large team of lawyers working through many documents on short deadlines.

The new tool takes a first pass through thousands of pages, identifies relevant documents, and groups them by themes and issues. It also produces summaries and a completed report in the firm's own format, and it inventories and categorizes a data room so reviewers can examine full relationships rather than isolated files. Lawyers can inspect the grouping and categorization to confirm nothing is missed. Early development has focused on material commercial contracts, with the firm comparing test outputs against human-written diligence reports from completed deals and refining the rubric and format accordingly. The firm describes the tool as comparable to the work of a capable junior-to-mid-level associate.

Howard Glazer, Partner and Head of Practice AI at Ropes & Gray, says the tool frees lawyers to make judgments rather than simply review contracts. Josh Lichtenstein, Partner and Head of ERISA Fiduciary Practice, says lawyers must still review everything because the firm needs to stand behind any work it delivers to a client. The firm has publicly described an ambition to produce a detailed, issue-level diligence report in hours rather than weeks. The article also says the firm uses GPT-6 Astra alongside the proprietary tool, and that it has solved client problems faster than before.

Looking ahead, Glazer believes the next stage of AI will help build collective knowledge across the firm, which has 340 partners and 1,500 lawyers. The aim is to give people access to knowledge from client meetings and past projects so the firm can better solve client problems. Glazer frames this as a way to create value directly, beyond saving time and money. The article does not give a launch date for the diligence tool or describe its availability to clients beyond the firm.

stories.Headline: AI smart-glasses exam cheating could bring criminal charges and multiyear retest bans, Education Ministry warns
stories.Summary:
South Korea's Ministry of Education announced on Thursday, October 29, 2026, that students who wear AI-powered smart glasses to cheat on the state-administered College Scholastic Ability Test (CSAT) could face police investigations and criminal trials. The ministry said such cheating would be treated as a deliberate, premeditated attempt to disrupt a national examination, which warrants a law enforcement probe and judgment. Offenders could be charged with obstructing official duties through fraud. The announcement came as the ministry prepares for this year's CSAT, scheduled for November 19.

The ministry is also seeking to amend the Higher Education Act to bar students caught cheating from retaking the CSAT for up to three years, up from the current one-year ban. It plans to strongly recommend that universities adopt stronger anti-cheating measures for their own entrance exams, including essay tests and interviews. In July, education authorities added smart glasses to the list of prohibited items at CSAT sites for the 2027 academic year and issued guidelines on handling violations. Starting with this year's exam, 1,312 specialists will be stationed at all 1,312 testing sites nationwide, one at each location, to determine whether suspected devices are smart glasses. If a device cannot be identified on site, emergency response teams at regional education offices, the ministry and the Korea Institute for Curriculum and Evaluation will provide immediate help.

The ministry is also meant to ease the burden on proctors, who would otherwise have to judge for themselves whether a device counts as prohibited equipment. It will expand liability insurance coverage for incidents during examinations and extend the period in which proctors can file claims, starting this year. From the CSAT for the 2028 academic year, it plans to seek improvements to proctor working conditions, including adjustments to compensation. The ministry is also weighing radio-frequency detectors, now being developed by a specialized institution, to find advanced electronic devices. Depending on the assessment, these could be distributed to testing centers nationwide as early as next year.

The article attributes the measures to the Ministry of Education, which made the announcement, and does not report any specific reaction from other parties. Beyond the examples given, the article does not say how many students have been caught using smart glasses this year. Its context is that organized cheating with electronic devices has previously led to criminal convictions, including an eight-month suspended prison sentence for a 2005 scheme in which students swapped answers by mobile phone. The article does not describe further steps beyond the planned legal amendment, the detector assessment and the proctor measures.

Articles.Title: AI smart-glasses exam cheating could bring criminal charges and multiyear retest bans, Education Ministry warns

stories.Headline: New AI tool helps scientists identify bacteria hidden in soil
stories.Summary:
A new artificial intelligence tool called BBERT, developed by researchers at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem and partner institutions, helps scientists identify bacterial DNA hidden in soil samples. The study was published on October 29, 2026, in the journal Nucleic Acids Research. It was led by Dr. Amir Erez of the university's Racah Institute of Physics and Dr. Omri M. Finkel of its Department of Plant and Environmental Sciences. Dmitry Alekhin, Dr. Moshe Alon and Dr. Tomer Sidi contributed equally, working with colleagues from the University of Haifa and the Volcani Institute of the Agricultural Research Organization.

The problem the tool addresses is that a single soil sample yields millions of short DNA fragments from many organisms, and many soil bacteria are missing from reference databases. Existing tools match fragments against stored sequences, so unmatched DNA often stays unidentified or is labeled incorrectly. BBERT takes a different approach by learning patterns in bacterial DNA, which lets it assess unfamiliar fragments without finding a match. It can recognize bacterial fragments only 100 DNA letters long. The researchers say this makes the tool useful for analyzing the so-called microbial dark matter that earlier methods could not explain.

In benchmark tests, BBERT distinguished bacterial from nonbacterial DNA with about 90% accuracy, and it identified protein-making fragments with about 88% accuracy. When applied to 1,969 publicly available soil DNA data sets, it classified a substantial share of fragments that a widely used comparison tool had left unclassified. The team also found that fragments that could not be linked to known functions were more likely to contain nonbacterial DNA. In simulated mixtures, filtering with BBERT cut genome reconstruction time from about 66 hours to 25 hours per data set, with fewer errors and about 96% of bacterial genome coverage retained.

The tool has limits that the researchers acknowledge. It can miss some bacterial fragments and can confuse chloroplast DNA from plants with bacterial sequences, and it can struggle to separate bacteria from archaea. It can run on a personal computer with a suitable graphics card, and the team demonstrated it on a laptop, which could help laboratories without large computing facilities. The articles do not say when the tool will be widely available, but they suggest researchers may use it to revisit existing environmental DNA collections.

Articles.Title: New AI tool helps scientists identify bacteria hidden in soil

stories.Headline: Your AI Chats May Be Discoverable: Preservation and Privilege Considerations for Generative AI Prompts and Outputs - The National Law Review
stories.Summary:
Generative AI prompts, outputs and conversation logs are generally treated as electronically stored information under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 34, according to an advisory by attorneys Bruce G. Vanyo, Christina L. Costley and Jamie N. Noonan of Katten, published October 29, 2026. The authors say courts have begun to define when AI interactions may be shielded as irrelevant or privileged, and when that protection can be lost. In In re OpenAI, Inc. Copyright Infringement Litigation, Magistrate Judge Wang ordered OpenAI on May 13, 2025 to preserve and segregate output log data that would otherwise be deleted, and the district judge upheld the order over OpenAI's objection. In United States v. Heppner, decided February 17, 2026, the court held that a criminal defendant's search prompts were not protected by attorney-client or work product privilege.

The advisory says a duty to preserve attaches to relevant AI prompts, outputs and related account settings, and that litigation hold notices should expressly cover generative AI tools, both enterprise and consumer. It says most platforms retain histories a court will consider within a party's control, and that failure to preserve is analyzed under Rule 37(e). It recommends routing litigation-related AI use through counsel and approved enterprise tools, and avoiding confidential or privileged information in open consumer AI tools. It also says a party should weigh the risk of waiver before relying on AI outputs in a pleading or filing. The authors say prompts drafted by counsel may be protected work product under Rule 26(b)(3)(B) if they reflect counsel's mental impressions, conclusions, opinions or legal theories about litigation.

They cite Tremblay v. OpenAI, Inc., where the district judge reversed a magistrate judge and found the prompts were queries crafted by counsel containing counsel's mental impressions and opinions. They also cite Concord Music Group, Inc. v. Anthropic PBC, which reached a similar result for undisclosed attorney-generated prompts. In both cases, however, the authors say the courts held protection was waived because the parties placed the prompts and outputs at issue in the complaint or other court filings.

The advisory notes that in January 2024 the DOJ Antitrust Division and the FTC updated standard preservation letters, second requests and compulsory process, including grand jury subpoenas, to address collaboration tools and ephemeral messaging platforms. The DOJ said it expects counsel to preserve and produce all responsive documents, including data from ephemeral messaging applications, and warned that failure to produce such documents may result in obstruction of justice charges. The authors say the release does not mention AI tools by name, but its reasoning seems consistent with AI tools that may be described as ephemeral. They add that whether a task is protected turns on a standard work-product analysis, and that business use by non-attorneys with no anticipation of litigation will likely receive no protection at all.

Articles.Title: Your AI Chats May Be Discoverable: Preservation and Privilege Considerations for Generative AI Prompts and Outputs - The National Law Review

stories.Headline: Horses, Typewriters, and AI: Are You Practicing Law in the Past?
stories.Summary:
Steve Fretzin wrote in a LawFuel.com article published on October 30, 2026, that lawyers who refuse to embrace artificial intelligence are like an attorney today insisting on a typewriter instead of a computer. He compared them to farmers who once relied on horses to plow fields and writers who used pens before typewriters and typewriters before computers. He said every advancement changed how people worked, and those who embraced the improvements generally became more productive than those who resisted. He said AI is changing the legal profession at an extraordinary pace and that lawyers who are not learning to use it will find themselves falling behind.

Fretzin described himself as a legal business development coach and author, not an AI technology specialist, and said his expertise is helping attorneys build books of business through marketing, branding, relationships and time management. He said most lawyers he coaches are overwhelmed with billable hours, client demands and administrative work, and he suggested AI could free up five or ten hours each week. He said some lawyers spend four to six hours a day on email, and that even saving an hour a day creates five additional hours a week. He encouraged lawyers to use AI to interview them about their practice and differentiators, to help draft a 30-second introduction or improve a LinkedIn profile, and to research prospective clients and suggest questions before meetings. He said he uses AI in his own business, turning podcast conversations into transcripts, articles and books, and he advised starting small with one repetitive task, one branding opportunity and one business development activity.

Fretzin said lawyers must use approved tools, protect confidential information, verify outputs and apply their own professional judgment. He said AI will not replace the trust developed between two people, and that relationships still win business. He said he was not suggesting that failing to use ChatGPT constitutes malpractice, but that technological competence, efficiency, confidentiality and quality of representation are already important professional obligations, and that ignoring AI may create increasingly serious risks. He said that if two attorneys deliver equally strong legal work but one communicates faster and operates more efficiently, that lawyer will have the advantage. He said AI saves time and relationships create business, and that lawyers who leverage both will build stronger practices.

Articles.Title: Horses, Typewriters, and AI: Are You Practicing Law in the Past? - LawFuel.com

stories.Headline: Yongsan opens English library for kids combining AI tech, interactive exhibits
stories.Summary:
Yongsan District opened the Dongbinggo English Library for Children in central Seoul on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, and announced the opening on Thursday. The library sits on the first floor of the Onnuri Youth Center in Dongbinggo Neighborhood Park and gives children a dedicated space for reading, language development and hands-on learning. The 389.74-square-meter facility includes a children's reading room, program rooms, a waiting area for parents, a digital aquarium and interactive content meant to carry children's experiences beyond the pages of books. About 80 people, including Yongsan District Mayor Kim Gyeong-dae and local residents, attended a ceremony that included a project briefing, congratulatory remarks, the unveiling of the library sign and a facility tour.

The library offers English-language books and programs grouped by reading level, with activities meant to build reading habits, comprehension and confidence. Children can read picture books, take part in follow-up activities, move through structured reading levels and explore new subjects through monthly book selections. One AI-based activity, called Be a Talkie!, lets children listen to English and practice repeating words and phrases. Other offerings introduce children to different cultures, encourage creative projects tied to their reading, and include an exploration program called Dongbinggo Library Explorers, in which children complete missions throughout the facility. The library will also host lectures for parents featuring experts from various fields, aimed at helping families support reading at home.

Mayor Kim framed the library as a place where children can discover new worlds through English books and naturally develop a love of reading. He said the district will keep operating and supporting the library so that children can take part in a wide range of reading and cultural activities. The district plans to run trial programs throughout November before starting its regular schedule in December. The Korea Times noted that its article was published with the assistance of generative AI and edited by its staff.

Articles.Title: Yongsan opens English library for kids combining AI tech, interactive exhibits

stories.Headline: [INTERVIEW] Fines won't fix problem: Korea needs new playbook as AI changes hacking paradigm
stories.Summary:
Suspected AI-assisted cyberattacks have spread through Korea's financial sector, reaching commercial banks, brokerages and cryptocurrency exchanges. On Wednesday, brokerage firm Daishin Securities, cryptocurrency exchange Bithumb and asset manager Mirae Asset Global Investments reported hacking incidents, adding to a string of similar cases involving 16 financial firms earlier this month. On Thursday, virtual asset exchange Prabang reported losses of 100 million won ($75,000), the first reported case of actual asset losses in the recent hacking spree. Financial authorities have also detected large-scale scanning attempts against financial systems from IP address ranges associated with North Korea, for the first time.

Lim Jong-in, chair of the AI committee at Soongsil University and a former presidential special adviser on cybersecurity, argued that fines alone will not solve the problem. He said that humans cannot keep pace with AI agents and that the whole paradigm of cybersecurity has changed, so both government and industry must rethink their defenses. He warned that companies that suffer attacks are also victims, and that they vary widely in their security capabilities and budgets. He added that the threat reaches beyond finance, since a breach at a major semiconductor company could spread across the broader economy.

Lim called for a task force led by the presidential office to develop a Korean version of a cognitive zero-trust architecture (CZTA). The task force would bring together the National Intelligence Service, the Ministry of Science and ICT, and the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources. Under the proposed design, the CZTA would use AI to continuously assess user behavior and emerging threats, flag suspicious activity and adjust access privileges in real time. Lim also cautioned against assuming who is behind the attacks, since attackers can use proxy IP addresses to hide their origins, and he said identifying perpetrators is growing harder because AI agents leave few traces.

Articles.Title: [INTERVIEW] Fines won't fix problem: Korea needs new playbook as AI changes hacking paradigm

stories.Headline: GitHub Octoverse 2026: AI agents drive developer activity surge
stories.Summary:
Developers pushed code to GitHub 17.9 billion times in the 12 months ending September 2026, surpassing the combined activity of 2024 and 2025. The surge became sharp around June 2026, when AI agents moved from experimental tools to integral parts of developer workflows. Repositories configured with an AI agent logged eight times more commits than those without, which points to a faster pace of work. The findings come from GitHub's Octoverse 2026 report, published in late October 2026. Many of the same figures appear in coverage by TechGig, which reported them on October 29, 2026.

By September 2026, more than 40 per cent of pull requests on GitHub were started by an agent, up from 17 per cent in March. This shift means that directing an agent is becoming the first step for a growing share of development tasks. GitHub Copilot users are also spreading their work across models, with 61 per cent of users who manually selected a model using more than one in September 2026. The report also notes that the language an agent picks, when a developer does not specify one, is starting to shape language choice. TypeScript remained the most used language on GitHub, followed by Python and JavaScript.

TypeScript, Python, and Rust, the fastest-growing language communities, show merged pull requests with detected AI involvement at rates between 40 and 44 per cent. The United States, with 38.3 million developers, and India, with 32 million, remain the two largest developer communities on GitHub. Each country added more than 10 million developers over the past year. India has closed 28.3 per cent of its projected growth toward 57.5 million developers by 2030. AI adoption is also reaching beyond traditional software sectors, as public repositories serving mining, construction, health care, and agriculture have grown several times over since 2022.

Construction repositories show the highest share of agent-opened pull requests of any sector, at about 9 per cent. GitHub is responsible for the report and the platform data behind it. The company has also made GitHub Copilot Fusion, a tool for model orchestration, generally available, and it automatically selects the appropriate model for each step of the development process. The system checks whether a task is ready, runs the coding agents, verifies the results, and handles failed checks and review feedback along the way. Engineers keep control over what gets built and what ships.

The software is model-agnostic, so teams can connect their own model accounts and API keys. It is released under the Apache 2.0 open-source license, and teams can self-host it on their own infrastructure. According to the article, SuperPlane is meant to coordinate routine work around coding agents rather than replace engineers. Its design encourages a shared environment in which skills, setup steps, tools, and context are available to the whole team, so one person's improvements benefit later runs for everyone.

It also supports a single set of standards, with readiness checks and verification rules established once for the team. A Kanban board gives visibility into running tasks, failures, costs, and the points where human intervention is needed. stories.Headline: Meta eyes record US$95 billion equity raise to fund AI expansion
stories.Summary:
Meta Platforms said on Oct 26 that it plans to raise up to US$95 billion, or S$121.63 billion, in its largest-ever equity fundraising, to fund its costly AI infrastructure expansion. The Facebook parent has launched public offerings worth about US$35 billion in common and preferred stock. It also plans a separate at-the-market share sale programme worth up to US$60 billion. The larger programme will launch after its new non-voting Class C shares begin trading, which is expected in the first quarter of 2027, though Meta said it has not finalised the timing and terms.

Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom have shown interest of up to US$5 billion in total for Class A shares. Meta has committed to spend about US$825 billion in the future, mainly on data centres, AI-related infrastructure and cloud computing power. It reported a US$2.12 billion cash burn in the third quarter, its first negative free cash flow in over a decade, compared with positive cash flow of US$10.63 billion a year earlier. As of Sept 30 it had cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities of US$82.45 billion and long-term debt of US$80.92 billion.

Last week Meta raised the lower end of its annual capital expenditure forecast to a range of US$135 billion to US$145 billion, from an earlier outlook of US$130 billion to US$145 billion. The company has said it would issue Class C common stock in January 2027, effectively a two-for-one split, to fund acquisitions and retain top talent while maintaining CEO Mark Zuckerberg's control. Meta agreed to grant Zuckerberg Class C shares he can sell to help pay a potential California billionaire wealth tax, in exchange for a commitment to keep him in California and preserve his voting control. The fundraising underscores a shift among big technology companies increasingly tapping debt markets and raising equity to bolster AI infrastructure, having previously relied on cash.

The interest from chip suppliers adds to concerns about an increasingly circular flow of capital in the AI industry, as they help finance the expansion of one of their biggest customers. Meta has been pouring money into chips and data centres to compete better with OpenAI and Anthropic. Earlier in 2026, Alphabet increased the size of its equity offerings to US$84.75 billion. Separately on Oct 26, SpaceX said an affiliate of Apollo Global Management will buy AI chips and server hardware and lease them to the rockets-to-AI firm, in a deal with total principal payments of about US$40 billion.

Articles.Title: Meta eyes record US$95 billion equity raise to fund AI expansion - The Straits Times

stories.Headline: Ignition launches Parkes practice management AI
stories.Summary:
Ignition, a payment and billing solutions provider, announced on October 28, 2026 the launch of Parkes, an AI coworker built for accounting and bookkeeping firms so they can spend more time on clients. The product is aimed at the operating work that drives growth but often gets pushed aside. Parkes was developed by a small team inside Ignition and now runs as its own brand. Ignition describes it as available to any firm, whether or not that firm uses Ignition.

Parkes can review current proposals, service items and active agreements to find underpriced work, scoping issues and upsell opportunities. It reads each client's engagement, drafts updated proposals for review, and prepares renewals and repricing from the firm's existing terms. For collections, it compares what has been billed against what has been paid, flags overdue invoices and drafts reminders in the firm's own voice that can be reviewed in Teams or Slack and sent with one click. It also flags duplicate, missing and inactive clients, with a reason for each, and archives them once a user approves, with an option to undo.

Ignition's CEO, Greg Strickland, said in a statement that most accounting firms are short of qualified people rather than work, and that AI has not yet helped them solve that. Tom Maxwell, general manager of Parkes, said the product already understands how accounting firms operate and builds up knowledge and rules for each firm as it is connected to more tools. Maxwell has worked with Ignition customers for more than 12 years, most recently as vice president of customer experience. Ignition says firms can set guardrails deciding which actions Parkes takes automatically, which need approval, and which are turned off, and that every action is logged.

Parkes works across tools including Ignition, Slack, Microsoft Teams, QuickBooks, Xero and leading practice management solutions, with more than 30 integrations and more added regularly. It is built with the same SOC 2 security as Ignition. Setup asks users for the intended role, a start date and details about the firm, after which it drafts an onboarding pack. Ready-made playbooks, such as onboarding a new client or rolling out a price increase, are also available, and Parkes stops for approval at points the firm sets.

Articles.Title: Ignition launches Parkes practice management AI - Accounting Today

stories.Headline: Is There Momentum to Ban AI, Screens Inside Minnesota Schools?
stories.Summary:
Minnesota's school districts are facing a question about whether to restrict artificial intelligence and screens for younger students, following moves in New York City and Los Angeles. Racket reported on October 28, 2026, that the two largest districts in the country had just adopted AI moratoriums and screen limits for younger learners. Local parent groups and teachers in Minnesota say the same kind of action is needed here. The article describes a growing, bipartisan parental movement that it characterizes as building momentum statewide.

The New York City ban covers pre-K through eighth grade, while the Los Angeles moratorium spans all grade levels, and both apply to generative AI for the current school year. Chicago is mentioned as a possible next district to follow. The article also points to a classroom experiment by Minneapolis teacher Maureen Mulvaney, who removed all technology from her classroom for the 2025 school year, and reports that over 95% of surveyed students said it had a positive effect on their learning. Those survey results came in by February of this year. The article notes that the experiment is not a scalable model on its own.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said the tech industry wants people to believe that AI-powered early education is inevitable and necessary, and that the city does not see it that way. Grant Eustice, a public high school teacher and co-founder of the advocacy group MN Unplugged, compared major technology firms to Big Tobacco and Big Pharma and said he sometimes feels powerless against their influence on districts. Even so, he expects that the New York and Los Angeles actions will prompt smaller districts to follow. The article also reports that the Minneapolis Public Schools press office did not respond to an interview request.

The article ties the current situation to the period after 2020, when schools rapidly distributed devices during the pandemic. It cites National Center for Education Statistics data showing that about 45% of public schools issued take-home devices in early 2020, rising to 96% by the 2021-22 school year. It also reports that Minnesota's three largest districts, Anoka-Hennepin, Saint Paul Public Schools, and Minneapolis Public Schools, take different approaches to AI and device access. St. Paul is developing an AI policy due by the 2027-28 school year, and Anoka-Hennepin is revising its own AI policy. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Is There Momentum to Ban AI, Screens Inside Minnesota Schools? - Racket

stories.Headline: FIA to use AI to help shape future F1 regulations in new AWS partnership
stories.Summary:
The Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile (FIA) has signed a new global partnership with Amazon Web Services (AWS) that will bring artificial intelligence into how the governing body writes Formula 1 rules. Under the deal, AWS becomes the FIA's official AI and cloud computing partner across motorsport, including F1. The change will be most visible in how future regulations are drafted. The FIA already uses AWS computing power to run its aerodynamic simulations, and AWS will now give the FIA's technical and engineering staff access to AI tools for drafting rules. AWS will also become an official partner of the FIA Awards and the FIA Sustainable Innovation Series.

The FIA president, Mohammed Ben Sulayem, said technology is changing every part of the sport and that the federation must lead that change. He said the partnership would support everything from the cars of the future to grassroots clubs, and that it would make it simpler for drivers, officials and volunteers to take part. He also linked the deal to the federation's goal of doubling global motorsport participation. Kristin Shaff, AWS's global director of events, sports and entertainment, described motorsport as one of the most demanding and data-rich environments in the world. She said AWS was proud to become the FIA's official AI partner and to support its mission at every level of the sport.

The announcement came as part of a wider run of F1 news, including reports that AWS had already been a partner of the sport for some time. Coverage of the deal drew attention to the use of AI in designing new cars, a point the articles tie to the FIA's regulation work. The articles do not give a timeline for when AI-assisted rules will first take effect, nor do they set out the financial terms of the agreement. They also do not say how the AI tools will be used beyond the regulatory and simulation work described.

stories.Headline: Puno: AIDA bill eyes maximizing AI gains
stories.Summary:
The House of Representatives recently passed a bill to create the Advanced Industries Development Authority (AIDA), an agency that would govern a proposed economic zone in New Clark City. House Deputy Speaker Ronaldo Puno spoke about the measure on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, during the Daily Tribune's Straight Talk program. The bill is meant to help the country take advantage of the growing artificial intelligence market. Puno said the Philippines is well placed to do so because of its natural resources and skilled workforce.

Puno explained that the zone would be governed by AIDA and that the law is needed to define which authority oversees Clark. He noted that every economic zone in the country currently operates under its own distinct laws. According to him, a clear legal framework would help attract foreign investors, who could lose interest in an area without firm policies. He said the law would define and guarantee what the zone will look like. Puno also said the authority would be connected to the Pax Silica declaration, a non-binding agreement involving 26 countries.

Puno is the official who spoke on the bill's purpose and its intended effects. He presented the measure as a way to create a free market environment for building the ecosystem that artificial intelligence needs. His remarks were reported in the Daily Tribune article by Jerod Orcullo, published October 29, 2026.
