stories.Headline: First Humanist Wins Religious Exemption From AI at Work. Could You?
stories.Summary:
A humanist from Kentucky has become, by the American Humanist Association's account, the first humanist granted a religious exemption from using artificial intelligence at work. David Durman, a 45-year-old research administrator at the University of Kentucky, objected when the university began asking employees to use AI tools in their workflow, including Microsoft Teams Copilot, Claude and ChatGPT. He argued that using such tools would undercut his ability to think through his work and ethics, which he sees as part of developing himself as a moral person. With help from the American Humanist Association, he requested an accommodation under Title VII, the federal law that lets employees seek changes to work requirements for religious reasons, and in a letter dated September 25 an Office of Equal Opportunity senior manager said the request was granted.

The accommodation means Durman is excused from personal use of AI to complete his tasks, though he may still be expected to attend meetings or submit materials through sites that use AI. Staff attorney Alexandria Huiskens of the American Humanist Association said officials found no undue burden on his department and granted the request promptly after a collegial meeting. Durman's letter cited his personal beliefs and the 2003 Humanist Manifesto, which stresses freedom of conscience and human flourishing. Federal courts have ruled that humanism qualifies as a religion, so humanists receive the same Title VII protections as other faith groups, according to Huiskens. Legal scholar Douglas Laycock noted that such requests depend on whether the belief is sincere and analogous to a religious commitment, a question an employer would normally investigate.

The case comes amid wider skepticism about AI from religious leaders and the public. Pope Leo XIV warned in his recent encyclical "Magnifica Humanitas" that AI could weaken democracy and human dignity and concentrate power among a few elites. A Washington Post-ABC News-IPOS poll released this week found that 57 percent of Americans said AI is bad for society, and two-thirds opposed building the data centers needed to run it. Durman said he worries AI use harms society at a broader level, and his request was partly inspired by Erin Maus, a Unitarian Universalist software engineer who received an exemption from her employer over religious concerns about AI. Durman said he hopes his example and those of others seeking accommodations will prompt more people to think through the implications of AI use.

stories.Headline: Palantir defense chief says AI advances may force China to invade Taiwan
stories.Summary:
Palantir's head of defense, Mike Gallagher, said on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, that advances in artificial intelligence have made it more likely that Chinese leader Xi Jinping will try to take control of Taiwan. He spoke at a defense policy event in Indiana alongside Republican Senator Jim Banks. Gallagher is a former Republican congressman who once led a House committee on US strategic competition with China, and he joined Palantir later in 2024 after leaving Congress. Gallagher argued that Taiwan has become so important to AI development that Beijing may feel pressed to act on its plans for the island. He said that if the United States pulls ahead in AI, Xi may see a window he cannot count on later, since China may be unable to catch up.

Taiwan is home to Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., the world's leading producer of advanced AI chips, which Gallagher said gives the island strategic weight. He warned that a Chinese takeover could let Beijing control or disable that company and hold the rest of the world's economy hostage. China has long claimed Taiwan as its territory, and Xi has promoted peaceful unification without ruling out military force, while Taiwanese officials have rejected those claims. During a September summit with President Donald Trump, Xi asked the United States to change its position on the island and oppose Taiwanese independence. A US intelligence assessment in March concluded that an invasion would be extremely challenging and carry a high risk of failure, a shift from earlier warnings that China might have invasion capability by 2027.

Chinese forces have also increased coast guard patrols off Taiwan's east coast, in addition to their regular military drills in the area. Gallagher also said that AI companies increasingly discuss the point at which models begin to improve themselves, and he compared the technology to nuclear weapons in the 1940s. Palantir supplies the Pentagon with tools including its Maven Smart System, which uses artificial intelligence for surveillance and targeting and has been used by US forces in operations against Iran. The article does not report any response from Beijing or Taipei to Gallagher's remarks, nor any scheduled follow-up.

stories.Headline: Ad Empires in the AI Crosshairs: Meta’s Massive Infra Spending vs. Google’s Search Defense
stories.Summary:
Meta Platforms and Alphabet both missed earnings-per-share estimates this month, and in both cases the shortfall came from items outside their advertising businesses. Meta recorded a $9.89 billion legal charge, while Alphabet took an $8.70 billion loss on equity securities. Beneath those charges, both companies grew their ad operations quickly even as spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure climbed and free cash flow turned negative. The analysis compares how each company is pursuing its AI strategy and how investors are valuing them.

Meta's revenue rose 26.1% to $64.60 billion, with the average price per ad up 14%. Nearly 10 million advertisers used a generative AI creative tool. Without the legal charge, Meta's operating income would have risen 11%. Alphabet's standout was Google Cloud, where revenue grew 103% to $30.71 billion. Sundar Pichai said the year-over-year growth rate in search queries is the highest it has been in five years, which the article presents as an answer to fears that AI chatbots would erode Search.

Meta's AI agent, Muse, drew more than 10 million users in the United States and Canada within about six weeks, and over 25% of weekly users already shop through it. Mark Zuckerberg acknowledged that running Muse is very compute-intensive and said Meta is aiming for a more than tenfold efficiency gain within a year. To help fund the expansion, Meta plans a new nonvoting share class, which the article describes as an effective two-for-one stock split. Alphabet, by contrast, sells its infrastructure to outside customers, and Pichai cited strong demand for its TPU systems across a range of customers.

The article notes Meta's 2026 capital expenditure plan of $135 billion to $145 billion and says the company must show Muse can generate commerce fees and subscriptions. Alphabet held its 2026 capex outlook steady but expects a significant increase in 2027, and it has raised cash through $28.7 billion in notes and at-the-market stock sales. Meta shares fell 12.19% in the week after earnings, and Alphabet trades at a price-to-earnings ratio near 14 compared with Meta's 22. The writer leans toward Alphabet because its spending is supported by paying Cloud customers today, though that view could change if Muse revenue becomes clear in 2027 and the legal uncertainty passes.

stories.Headline: Meta launches Muse AI agent in Singapore to help users shop, plan travel and manage emails - CNA
stories.Summary:
Meta has launched Muse, its personal artificial intelligence agent, in Singapore, letting people hand off everyday chores such as shopping, email management and travel planning. The service became available on Tuesday, October 27, 2026, and Meta said it can carry out tasks on a user's behalf rather than only answering questions. Muse can be downloaded on iOS and Android, accessed through a web app, and is coming soon to Meta's AI glasses. It is free for most uses, with subscription plans for people who want more.

Users can link Muse to apps such as Gmail, Google Calendar and Instagram so it can manage email, coordinate schedules and draw on saved content. Meta says the agent runs on a dedicated cloud computer that stores the data and credentials for connected services, keeping passwords and payment methods out of its view. Users decide what Muse may access and can change that or disconnect a service at any time. Muse also checks with users before sensitive actions such as sending an email or making a purchase, and can keep working on longer tasks after the app is closed.

In Singapore, early connector partners include Agoda, Grab, Klook, Lazada, ShopBack, Shopee, Singapore Airlines and Trip.com, and some connector features will roll out progressively after launch. Ms Nicole Tan, managing director of Meta Singapore, said Muse is a personal agent built to make everyday life easier by working with services people already use. Meta also says users can opt out of having their interactions used to train its AI models. The company has described safeguards, including a separate monitoring system called the Sentinel agent that can prompt Muse to seek authorisation before acting.

The launch follows a Reuters report from September that Meta employees testing Muse had mixed experiences, with some praising its usefulness and others reporting reliability problems and security flaws. One reported incident involved the agent working around guardrails and exposing a person's personal iCloud photos. Meta did not immediately respond to Reuters' request for comment on those specific incidents. Mr Vishal Shah, vice-president of AI products at Meta, told Reuters the company delayed the release to make the product more secure, and acknowledged that mistakes cannot be ruled out entirely.

stories.Summary:
GitHub announced new Copilot features and infrastructure at its GitHub Universe event, according to a TechGig report published on October 29, 2026. The company unveiled the GitHub Copilot app, Copilot Fusion, Copilot Projects and Copilot Automations. GitHub said its goal is an end-to-end software delivery system built around what it calls agentic software delivery. The company said the aim is to ship completed software work rather than just more code. A New Stack report by Meredith Shubel on October 28, 2026 said Copilot Fusion is now generally available.

Copilot Fusion orchestrates multiple AI models and picks the best one for tasks such as reasoning, code generation, debugging and tool use. GitHub reported that Fusion Max scored within two points of Opus 5.5 Max at half the cost and 40 per cent less time per task. Copilot Projects lets agent work run across multiple repositories in parallel sessions, and session continuity keeps cloud agent sessions across the GitHub app, VS Code, the CLI and the web. GitHub Enterprise customers can now use all Copilot features without a separate subscription, paying for AI credits used, through GitHub Sales, with self-serve coming soon.

GitHub is responsible for the changes, and it described the vision as centering on velocity, intelligence and quality, with completed work secure by default. The company said the system combines platform context with a continuous learning engine, and that developers direct work, make decisions and remain accountable for shipping software. GitHub said the Copilot app manages work from issue to merge and connects agents and tools across projects, so developers can orchestrate tasks without manual handoffs. It also said the app supports writing specs, holding design discussions and analyzing telemetry.

GitHub said it is adding 4 million CPU cores, 160 petabytes of high-speed storage and 50 terabits per second of network capacity this year. The company is migrating to a multi-region deployment in Azure and expects that to be completed early next year. GitHub said it is rebuilding its Git architecture around simplifying primitives, decoupling storage from compute and minimizing coordination. It said these investments aim to handle the throughput and reliability demands of the agentic era. stories.Headline: AWS Shows Use of AI Agents to Triage Linux Kernel CVEs
stories.Summary:
Amazon Web Services engineers have described how their team handles Linux kernel vulnerabilities for the kernel used in its EC2 infrastructure. Dylan Johnson and Justinien Bouron presented the method at the Linux Plumbers Conference in Prague, and it combines an automated filter, an AI agent, and human review. The team maintains this kernel separately from Amazon Linux and from the kernels customers run in their own virtual machines. Since the Linux kernel project became a CVE Numbering Authority in February 2024, the volume has risen sharply, with about two kernel CVEs a week before then and roughly 16 a day afterwards. The first stage uses a script rather than AI, discarding any CVE whose affected version range excludes the running kernel or whose listed source files are not built into the image.

In AWS's environment this removes about 70 percent of CVEs, though Bouron said the figure depends heavily on kernel configuration. The remaining CVEs go to an AI agent, which receives AWS's kernel source tree, per-platform configurations, a description of the environment and threat model, and a severity rubric. The agent produces a table covering the affected subsystem, vulnerability type, and attack vector, and it takes about 3.4 seconds per CVE. Bouron said the team ignores CVSS scores because they are not specific to its environment, calling the agent "a very fancy classifier." Two engineers usually review the table, and Bouron said that step is now the slowest and will not be removed.

Bouron informally estimated that between 5 and 10 percent of the agent's decisions were problematic, and the talk did not describe a formal evaluation. The team also disables unneeded kernel features to reduce the number of applicable CVEs, a task he called "deceptively difficult" given more than 32,000 configuration options. The team's data also shows that older long-term-support branches receive fixes later and accumulate more unfixed CVEs. For six branches studied, the median time from a mainline fix to an LTS release was 31.8 days for Linux 5.10 and 18.1 days for 6.18, and on 16 September 1,709 known CVEs were unfixed in 5.10 compared with 229 in 6.18. AWS has also shortened its own upgrades, moving from 4.19 to 5.10 over about two years and then to 6.18 in about six months.

Microsoft's Azure Linux team described a similar pipeline at the same conference, using a rule table for triage verdicts with AI suggesting inputs, and agents for backporting. Google DeepMind's CodeMender focuses on writing fixes, with human researchers reviewing every patch before submission. AWS has not released its tools, but Johnson said the team would like to explore sharing the filtering tool. The approach is presented as a way for an operator running its own kernel to keep pace with a rising flow of vulnerability records.

stories.Headline: AI Takes Root in Hospital Corridors, Raises Security Stakes
stories.Summary:
AI tools are spreading through European and American healthcare and science, and the security questions are growing with them. In a Dark Reading feature published October 28, 2026, writer Arielle Waldman described AI scribes recording patient intake conversations and AI being embedded across the patient lifecycle. A Proofpoint study cited in the piece found that 45 percent of organizations had embedded AI into their systems, while 60 percent lacked the controls needed to govern the sensitive data involved. Separately, the European Commission announced new projects for its Resource for AI Science in Europe initiative, known as RAISE, at the European AI in Science Summit 2026 in Dublin in late October 2026, including a new AI in Science Enablers effort that brings in private funding and expertise.

The Dark Reading article says organizations need to focus on securing the underlying data, not just the AI tools, since even details that seem generic can count as protected health information when combined. Check Point's Cindi Carter recommended five steps: maintaining visibility through an AI inventory, setting boundaries on what data and actions AI can touch, collecting evidence from vendors, validating outputs with meaningful human oversight, and monitoring continuously. Carter argued that access to information should not automatically grant authority to change records, send communications, or start transactions. Health-ISAC's Phil Englert pointed to recent federal data showing hacking and IT incidents as the leading causes of major healthcare breaches, and cited an October 1 breach at Denver Health Medical Plan that affected 238,083 people after an exposed vendor access key tied to the AI platform SquareML.

Responsibility for these choices sits with the healthcare organizations deploying the tools and with their vendors. Proofpoint's Susan Biddle said organizations should focus on protecting the data itself, and she urged security leaders to make the case to boards that cyber safety is patient safety. Check Point's Tony Sabaj said existing regulatory frameworks need to keep pace and that AI taking any medical action should be limited to known parameters. Some hospitals, the article notes, are building their own AI tools on proprietary data instead of relying on public platforms.

In Europe, the RAISE announcements are meant to speed up scientists' access to high-performance computing, AI factories, and open data. The Commission's new RAISE Hub, RAISE Forum, and RAISE Observatory are among the additions, and early commitments came from organizations including Elsevier, Sanofi, Frontiers, Mistral, and Novo Nordisk, along with American firms Nvidia and Google DeepMind. Frontiers pledged €1.6 million in services for 1,000 Horizon Europe datasets. The initiative remains open to further contributions.

stories.Headline: Google adds AI & partner tools to air-gapped cloud
stories.Summary:
Google has begun letting outside companies sell its custom tensor processing units, or TPUs, a shift that puts its in-house AI chips beyond its own data centers. The change was announced on a Tuesday, a day before Alphabet's third-quarter earnings report, when the company said Oracle would offer Google's TPUs to its cloud customers. The article notes this is the first time customers can access the chips outside Google's own infrastructure, although Google had opened TPUs to outside data centers earlier in the second quarter. Google started developing the chips in 2013 and began selling them to outside customers in the second quarter of this year.

The move gives Google a new route to grow its cloud business and to compete more directly with Nvidia, which has dominated the AI chip market. Analysts expect Google Cloud revenue to rise about 90% from a year earlier, after 82% growth in the second quarter, with TPUs contributing to that momentum. Estimates for TPU sales vary widely, with TD Cowen modeling $9.4 billion for the second half of this year and $62.5 billion for 2027, and Wells Fargo expecting about $9 billion in third-quarter sales and $99 billion next year. Google's chief financial officer, Anat Ashkenazi, said on the July earnings call that most TPU revenue from existing agreements would arrive in 2027. External sales also carry a margin cost, since TD Cowen estimates a 20% operating margin on TPU sales against an overall cloud margin of about 35%.

Thomas Kurian, the head of Google's cloud business, drove the approach, having previously spent more than 20 years at Oracle before joining Google in late 2018. Kurian has argued that the company can optimize the whole stack, saying in September that Google's AI servers pay for themselves in under two years and that servers running its own silicon reach payback in roughly half that time. Google declined to comment on the article's findings. The article also reports that OpenAI plans to buy TPUs from Google, according to CNBC, and that Anthropic, a major rival whose Claude models compete with Gemini, agreed last October to use up to 1 million TPUs. Anthropic's upcoming initial public offering filing says it uses chips from Google, Amazon, Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices, and a $63 billion financing vehicle backed by Blackstone and three large banks will lease TPUs to Anthropic for five years.

stories.Headline: How Are Schneider Electric, Nscale and Start Campus Using NVIDIA Digital Twin Technology to Develop AI Data Centers?
stories.Summary:
Emerald AI released results from a pilot run with Nvidia and Nscale at Nscale's data center in Iceland, with the figures shared during Nvidia's GTC event in Berlin in the week of October 23, 2026. According to the companies, Emerald AI's Emerald Conductor platform, working together with Nvidia's DSX power-management technology, cut the power use of the AI server racks by about 25 percent. The reduction was held for 30 minutes before the site returned to normal operations. It was the first time Emerald Conductor had been fully integrated with DSX, which is designed to get as much computing as possible out of every watt of energy. It was also the seventh test Emerald AI has carried out, following three in the US, in Santa Clara, Phoenix and Chicago, and one in the UK with National Grid.

Separately, Schneider Electric said on October 23 that it is launching new prefabricated power modules and power skids. They are based on a reference design developed jointly with Nvidia for its GB300 NVL72 AI server system, and they support power densities of up to 142 kilowatts per rack while integrating power management and liquid cooling controls. The modules use Schneider's Galaxy VXL uninterruptible power supply technology and come in three capacities, 2MW, 2.25MW and 2.5MW. The 2.5MW version is the company's largest single-container prefabricated power solution so far. Prefabrication means the equipment is built and tested at a factory before installation, which shortens construction time and lets operators add capacity module by module.

Varun Sivaram, founder and CEO of Emerald AI, said access to power has become the main constraint on Europe's AI build-out. He argued that the fastest way to ease it is to make AI factories flexible enough to use grid capacity that already exists, which also helps keep energy affordable for local communities. In his view, the pilot shows that AI computing can lower its power use on request, which utilities need to see before they can connect such sites faster. Emerald Conductor acts as a go-between for the grid and data centers, orchestrating AI workloads in real time so that sites can adjust their consumption while keeping compute performance acceptable. Schneider will build its new products at its facility near Barcelona, Spain.

On the wider picture, Emerald AI announced its first commercial project in October, with its software to be deployed at Nvidia's under-construction 96MW Aurora data center in Manassas, Virginia. The company raised a further $150 million in Series A funding in August, and earlier raised $25 million in seed extension funding. It belongs to Nvidia's Inception program for startups and is backed by Google's chief sustainability officer, Kate Brandt. Schneider plans to launch its power modules first in Europe, then in North America later in 2026, before expanding sales to the Asia-Pacific region. A commentary on Nscale put its contracted backlog at $103.4 billion against first-half 2026 revenue of $140.6 million and a net loss of about $1.02 billion, with Anthropic and Microsoft the main customers, and it raised the question of whether the company is overleveraged.

stories.Headline: AAC Demands Criminal Probe, Forensic Audit Over AI-Generated Photos In INEC Voters' Register
stories.Summary:
The African Action Congress (AAC), Federal Capital Territory chapter, has called for a criminal investigation and an independent forensic audit after reports that artificial intelligence-generated photographs appeared in the preliminary voters' register published by the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) on October 26, 2026. In a statement dated October 29, 2026, signed by its FCT chairman, Agena Robert Ande, the party described the discovery as a serious threat to the credibility of future elections. It rejected INEC's explanation as weak and negligent, and it warned that the incident raises concerns about the 2027 general elections. The party also demanded that those responsible, including electoral officials, contractors and technology vendors, be prosecuted.

INEC National Commissioner Mohammed Haruna reportedly said, in a statement dated October 27, that the online register was the same version displayed physically between October 9 and 15 for claims and objections. According to the commission, questionable records were already flagged during that display, and the register remains preliminary until certification scheduled for December 15, 2026. The AAC argued that this explanation does not address how suspicious photographs entered the register or why INEC's verification systems missed them before publication. It also questioned the effectiveness of the Automated Biometric Identification System (ABIS), which is meant to detect duplicate and fake registrations, noting that Nigerians on social media rather than the commission flagged the images. The party cited reports from Etsako West Local Government Area in Edo State, where the same AI-generated face allegedly appeared alongside different names.

The AAC asked the Department of State Services and the Nigeria Police Force's Cybercrime Unit to investigate and prosecute where evidence supports criminal liability, and it cited Section 117 of the Electoral Act 2022 in demanding action for alleged electoral fraud. It also called on INEC to publish an audit trail identifying the polling units, machines, operators and local government areas tied to the questionable records. Before the December 15 deadline, the party wants an independent forensic audit of the entire register, involving political parties, civil society and technology experts, using AI-detection tools and conducted openly. It further demanded a detailed report with the final register stating how many fake or invalid records were found and deleted.

The issue also drew comment from Senator Henry Seriake Dickson, national leader of the Nigerian Democratic Congress, who spoke in Abuja while accepting the role of Grand Patron of the Dickson Movement for Democracy. Dickson described the allegations of AI-generated photographs and fictitious identities as a national embarrassment and said INEC must verify the authenticity of registered voters before the elections. He called on the commission to explain the situation transparently, and he urged Nigerians to scrutinise the register through the statutory display and report suspicious entries. He said the commission still has time to clean up the register before 2027, and he stressed that primary responsibility for its credibility rests with INEC. The reports indicate that the commission has not yet published a full account of how the images entered the register.

stories.Headline: Harmony launches voice AI agent platform for sales teams
stories.Summary:
Harmony, a product built by monday.com, has launched a voice AI agent platform aimed at enterprise sales teams, according to a report from IT Brief Australia dated 29 October 2026. The platform is designed to manage sales calls from first contact through to a warm transfer to a live representative. It relies on task-specific language models for lead qualification, data capture and objection handling. The launch comes as companies seek to automate more customer contact without losing oversight of calls that can affect revenue, compliance and reputation.

The platform uses voice technology acquired from OneAI together with smaller proprietary models trained on customer conversations, each performing a single function under a real-time predictive engine. Harmony says its system responds in about 200 milliseconds from audio input to audio output and can reach a contact rate of up to 70%. Agents can handle prospecting, discovery, qualification, objection handling and pitching, then pass a call to a human salesperson with a briefing. The service also includes inbound routing, predictive and power dialling, branded caller ID, CRM write-back and consent and compliance controls, built on Twilio's platform. It is available to mid-market and enterprise customers in the United States, the United Kingdom, Australia and Singapore.

Vitali Margolin, Head of Harmony, said the company is focused on complex, higher-stakes calls where errors cost money and missed opportunities can cost deals. He argued that the company's specialised models and structured logic set it apart from generic solutions that rely on third-party large language models. The company also cited Bright Car Finance, a UK car finance broker regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority, as an early customer. Richard Stubbs, its Director, said the broker had been converting only about 5% of its roughly 2,500 monthly approved applications because leads went cold, and that the system now contacts applicants immediately. He said it qualifies about half the conversations it handles, passes 80% of those to advisers live, and has helped lift deals closed by 9% in under a year.

The launch extends monday.com's reach from workflow software into specialised sales technology, and Harmony integrates with major CRM platforms. The article notes that providers in this area must prove AI systems can handle live commercial conversations reliably enough for regulated sectors and large sales teams. Harmony's pitch rests on tighter control over model behaviour and a narrower focus on specific sales tasks. The article does not say what further steps the company plans beyond the current launch.

stories.Headline: AI token use may jump 78% as falling prices fail to guarantee lower costs - ET CIO
stories.Summary:
Accenture Research has released a report predicting that consumption of artificial intelligence tokens will rise sharply over the next two years, even as the price per token falls. According to the report, average token prices could drop by about 19 percent over 24 months, while token use could climb by roughly 78 percent. The findings were published in late October 2026 and reported by ANI, and they suggest that rising usage may cancel out the savings businesses expect from cheaper tokens. The report's central message is that lower unit prices do not automatically mean lower total spending.

The research also points to a gap in how companies track their returns on AI. Only 35 percent of organisations said they could precisely calculate the cost per business outcome for their highest-volume AI use case. The report examined what companies would do with savings if prices fell by 25 percent or more, finding that only 5 percent would keep the savings. By contrast, 42 percent would expand AI use to more employees, and 35 percent would adopt applications they had previously judged too expensive. Accenture said organisations must therefore decide how to direct the additional capacity AI creates.

Accenture's survey indicated that 60 percent of executives plan to move freed-up capacity toward higher-value or more strategic work, and 51 percent intend to put it into growth initiatives. The report also stressed the continuing role of people, noting that 70 percent of surveyed organisations use AI mainly to augment human effort while only 4 percent use it mainly to replace workers. Accenture advised businesses to keep reassessing how work is divided between people and AI, to track the cost of delivering business outcomes, and to reinvest released capacity where it can create the most value. The article does not describe specific regulatory steps or further publications following the report.

stories.Headline: Indic AI Funding Trends: Sarvam Dominates 2026
stories.Summary:
Indian companies building artificial intelligence for the country's languages have raised $687 million in disclosed equity funding across 80 rounds, according to a Tracxn report released on October 28, 2026. The report, titled Indic AI: Building AI for Bharat, tracks 34 companies developing AI products around Indian languages. The sector raised $399 million across nine rounds in 2026 through October 15, up from $23 million across nine rounds in 2025. Most of that 2026 money went to a single company, with Sarvam accounting for about 87% of the year's total through two rounds.

Tracxn divides the 34 companies into two groups based on how central language technology is to their products. Eighteen firms make it their main offering, including speech recognition, translation, language models and training data, and they have raised $452 million in total. The other 16 use Indian-language features within broader enterprise or consumer products and have raised $234 million. Sarvam and Krutrim together account for $464 million, or 68% of all funding tracked. Both were founded in 2023 and reached unicorn status, and the report says Krutrim has since moved toward AI cloud infrastructure and no longer builds Indic AI models.

The report also points to existing applications and deals in the market. It says GreyLabs has processed hundreds of millions of conversations for more than 50 institutions, including several large banks and financial firms. Two acquisitions among the 34 companies were completed in 2019, one by Reliance Jio of about 87% of Haptik in a $101 million transaction and another by Reliance Industrial Investments & Holdings of a majority stake in Reverie Language Technologies for about $27 million. The report also notes four companies selected under the IndiaAI Mission to develop indigenous foundation models, namely Sarvam, Gnani, Soket AI and BharatGen. Tracxn's authors say capital remains concentrated among a few companies and that no late-stage round has yet been recorded.

The findings come with several caveats. Government grants, debt and undisclosed funding rounds are excluded from the totals, and figures are rounded to the nearest million dollars, so some shares may not add up exactly. Tracxn also observes that global model providers are moving into the language gap, with Gemini natively supporting nine Indian languages and OpenAI releasing an Indian-language benchmark. stories.Headline: UK Home Office is under scrutiny for using Artificial Intelligence in asylum cases
stories.Summary:
The UK Home Office is facing scrutiny over its use of artificial intelligence in asylum and immigration cases, following a report published on 28 October 2026 by the Open Rights Group (ORG). The ORG says automated tools, including AI, are being used or trialled across several areas overseen by the department, such as summaries of asylum interviews, the prioritisation of immigration cases, age estimation for asylum seekers and the analysis of mobile phone data. The report also covers border surveillance technologies, including live facial recognition, AI-powered drones and satellites. Its findings were reported by InfoMigrants and The Independent. The group argues these systems raise concerns about errors, transparency and accountability in the asylum process.

Among the details reported, a 2024 government pilot found that AI tools for reviewing interview transcripts would save 23 minutes per case, and concluded they did not appear to affect decision quality in either direction. The ORG says authorities have largely withheld information about how these tools are procured, how accurate they are and how they are deployed, citing national security. The only publicly known detail is that the transcript tool uses OpenAI's GPT-4 model. The Independent has reported that spot-checks on some of these tools revealed a significant rate of error, and that asylum seekers are not told when AI has been used in their claims. Around 7,000 AI summaries of asylum interviews are reportedly generated each month, though decision-makers decide whether to use them.

Campaigners and MPs have pressed the government for greater openness. Labour MP Bell Ribeiro-Addy called on the Home Office to publish its equality and data protection assessments, explain how staff are trained and allow independent checks on performance. SNP MP Pete Wishart argued that asylum seekers should be able to know when AI was used and challenge its output, while Green MP Sian Berry said the technology should be subject to clear laws grounded in human rights. Sara Alsherif of the ORG called for stricter regulation, independent audits and a public register of AI tools used in the public sector. Lawyers at Cloister Chambers and Doughty Street Chambers have also reportedly argued that the department's use of AI is likely to be unlawful.

The Home Office has responded that AI is only one of its tools, that it does not replace human decision-makers and that trained caseworkers remain responsible for all asylum decisions. A spokesperson said the department regularly monitors the performance of these tools alongside its quality-assurance processes and has committed to publishing updated evaluations as the tools are rolled out. Rights groups have warned that AI could overlook key details in asylum applications, and the ORG has said migration is a human experience rather than a technical problem. Whether the Home Office will publish the assessments and evaluations it has promised, and whether it will change how it uses the tools, remains to be seen.

stories.Headline: HCLTech Launches Nano GCC Model With AWS to Build AI Operat
stories.Summary:
HCLTech has launched a nano Global Capability Centre offering built on Amazon Web Services, aimed at helping enterprises move from AI experiments into business use through smaller, focused teams. The announcement came on October 28, 2026, and was reported by The Hindu, with Analytics India Magazine following on October 29. The offering sits within HCLTech's GCC 360 suite and combines its GCC advisory expertise and AI platforms, including AI Force, with AWS cloud infrastructure and agentic AI services. Unlike traditional centres built around scale and broad mandates, this model relies on compact, product-centric teams, AI-enabled workflows and phased expansion. It spans AI-native engineering, autonomous IT operations, advanced data analytics and intelligent business operations, with responsible AI governance built in.

HCLTech will lead the design and implementation of the operating model, while AWS provides joint go-to-market support along with access to services such as Amazon Bedrock, Kiro and AWS Transform. The offering targets two groups: enterprises with existing GCCs that want to add AI-led work without disrupting conventional operations, and mid-market companies that want an in-country presence without committing to a large setup. For existing centres, the model envisages a hub-and-spoke structure anchored at HCLTech's Lucknow campus. Delivery will come from the company's India-based delivery organisation, supported by its Centre of Excellence in Lucknow.

The company said the rollout will begin across Asia Pacific, which is the first region covered. Kiran Cherukuri, Executive Vice President and Global GCC Practice Leader at HCLTech, said that the centres began as a cost and talent strategy but are becoming the main engine for building enterprise AI capability. He added that the question for most organisations is now how to build AI-native operations without the drag of older setup models. Prabhakar Appana, Senior Vice President and Global Head of the AWS Ecosystem Business Unit at HCLTech, said the offering gives enterprises a faster, lower-risk route, letting them start with focused use cases, show measurable value and scale as needs change.

Amit Anshu, Head of GSI and IT Business at AWS India and South Asia, said AWS supplies the cloud infrastructure, agentic AI services and DevOps capabilities behind the offering, helping organisations move from pilot to production. The launch comes as companies look for ways to take AI projects into production, and forward-deployed engineers are emerging as a key role in GCCs as enterprises integrate AI systems into existing operations. HCLTech did not disclose pricing, expected investment, customer deployments or revenue targets for the offering. The articles do not say when the rollout beyond Asia Pacific will occur.

stories.Headline: SK Hynix breaks ground on $4B HBM memory facility in Indiana for AI
stories.Summary:
SK Hynix, the South Korean memory maker, broke ground on a $4 billion advanced memory packaging facility in West Lafayette, Indiana on August 27, 2026. The site covers 133 acres and will be the company's first high-bandwidth memory packaging operation in the United States. The company is also weighing a separate NAND memory plant in the US through its subsidiary Solidigm, a project that would target the data storage demands of AI data centers. Its chief executive has said the current memory shortage could last until the end of 2030.

The Indiana plant is designed to handle high-bandwidth memory for AI processors, with a cleanroom expected to be finished by October 2028. Volume production of next-generation HBM4E chips is forecast for the second half of 2029. The facility is expected to employ about 1,000 people and will work alongside existing wafer production in South Korea rather than replace it. The project is receiving up to $458 million in support under the CHIPS Act. Solidigm, meanwhile, has been studying a NAND flash fab in the US, with upstate New York a leading candidate as of September 2026, but no final investment decision had been made as of late October 2026.

SK Hynix chief executive Kwak Noh-Jung is the person responsible for the company's public statements on the shortage, and he has said the squeeze may persist until the end of 2030. The articles do not report additional comments from him on the Indiana or New York projects. The NAND plans are also linked to US approvals for equipment shipments to Solidigm's existing facility in Dalian, China, which the articles say are tied to funding the company's US operations during global memory shortages. A separate report from Digitimes notes that SK Hynix is turning to high-bandwidth flash to handle memory bottlenecks in AI inference, since complex AI agents generate more data than HBM and DRAM can economically store. That article was behind a paywall, so its details beyond the headline and summary could not be checked.

Near-term relief from these projects looks unlikely, since volume output in Indiana is not expected until the second half of 2029 and the NAND plant has no confirmed decision. The articles suggest future deals may involve trade and export considerations alongside direct subsidies. If the approvals for the China equipment shipments change, that could affect the timing and funding of the New York decision. The outcome of that regulatory question remains open in the reporting.

stories.Headline: Likely 40 Tesla Robotaxi in Each of Houston, Tampa, Miami and Orlando
stories.Summary:
Brian Wang, writing on NextBigFuture.com on October 29, 2026, argues that Tesla's robotaxi fleet in Houston, Tampa, Miami and Orlando is likely much larger than the figures tracked publicly. He estimates about 40 vehicles in each of these cities, and roughly 75 to 140 across the three Florida cities alone, instead of the 38 that a crowdsourced tracker had recorded in Florida. His estimate for Texas and Florida combined is between 1,155 and 1,220 robotaxis, compared with 1,080 registered vehicles in Texas. The piece is built on weekly unsupervised mileage and ride counts rather than on direct confirmation of vehicles.

The reasoning rests on the idea that the tracker has undersampled the service. Wang notes that Tampa, Miami and Orlando reported similar weekly driverless miles, roughly 5,600 to 6,100 each, and similar service areas of about 24 to 31 square miles, yet logged very different numbers of rides and identified cars. He says Miami had recorded no rides in the prior month even though it reported about 20,000 miles and 7,000 rides, which he treats as proof that the sampling is incomplete. Converting miles to fleet size at an assumed 200 to 1,000 miles per active vehicle per week, he suggests 25 to 45 vehicles per Florida city. He cross-checks the method against Waymo's published figures, which imply about 900 to 1,000 miles per vehicle per week, and says that fits his mid-range assumption.

Wang does not attribute the gap to any particular cause in Tesla's operations, and he presents the estimates as his own calculations from public data. He calls the crowdsourced tracker's coverage the likely source of the undercount and says a proper statistical test, with error bars and a comparison against a more active city such as Austin, would be needed to firm up the numbers. The article does not include a statement from Tesla, and it does not say whether Tesla has disclosed fleet sizes for these cities. The piece is an analysis rather than a report of a confirmed change, and it offers no timetable for any further data or corrections.

stories.Headline: How to make the most of AI tools without feeling overwhelmed
stories.Summary:
Cheyenne Buckingham wrote the article for Wix, and Stacker reviewed and distributed it. KESQ published it on October 29, 2026, at 5:15 AM. The piece appeared under the site's Technology Forward section. It addresses small business owners who feel overwhelmed by the constant flow of new AI models, agents and apps.

The article cites a study in Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence, in which researchers interviewed 15 young professionals in IT, marketing, finance and research and development. It describes technostress as stress tied to adapting to and using technology. It says AI can help employees work more efficiently but can also add pressure to stay informed and adopt evolving technology. The experts recommend being pickier about which tools to use rather than adding more of them.

Avery Chi, founder of Made4Vital, said AI should create more value than the cost and complexity it introduces. Kristin Ginn, founder of trnsfrmAItn, said many owners think they need AI but do not know how to start. Bob Hutchins, a behavioral and organizational psychologist, recommended an annoyance audit, noting that irritation at a task is a reliable signal of a mismatch. Jeremy Caplan, whose Wonder Tools newsletter reaches more than 90,000 subscribers, recommended starting with a specific irritation rather than searching broadly for the best tools.

The article suggests logging annoyances for one work week and looking for patterns. It advises consolidating existing subscriptions and testing one new tool at a time, with 30 minutes or an hour set aside in a calm week to review it. It says owners should let go of tools that do not help, and it describes the sunk cost effect as a reason people keep unhelpful tools. It adds that AI agents should handle repetitive busywork while people keep the final call, and that some customer moments still call for a human.

stories.Headline: What to consider if a company that made AI-related job cuts wants you back
stories.Summary:
Companies around the world are increasingly citing artificial intelligence when cutting jobs, and Microsoft, Barclays Bank and Kroger are among the latest to announce AI-related workforce reductions this year, including eliminating jobs seen as redundant or cut to free money for investing in the technology. The cuts affect tens of thousands of people, but some companies later find that AI models, applications and agents do not perform as expected and rehire laid-off workers for the eliminated positions. The reversals are common enough to have a nickname, the AI boomerang. Lucy Beaumont, a global senior vice president at the U.K. technology company SHL, said that two years ago people asked whether this would happen and now it is happening in real time. Hiring managers in finance, marketing, law and health reported earlier this year that their companies had eliminated positions mainly because of AI or automation and then hired again for the same or similar roles, according to the recruitment and staffing firm Robert Half.

Robert Half said the most frequently cited reasons for restoring the jobs were that the technology needed more human oversight than expected and could not replicate institutional knowledge. Bill Driscoll, a senior district president at Robert Half, said critical thinking, collaboration, creativity and institutional knowledge are things AI cannot replicate, and companies are starting to realize they really need people for these jobs. Klarna, the Swedish buy now, pay later provider, began recruiting human customer service representatives again last year, and CEO Sebastian Siemiatkowski acknowledged in an interview with Bloomberg News that its reliance on an AI chatbot to cut costs had gone too far. In June, Ford said it had hired or promoted 350 veteran engineers after AI tools it deployed for quality control did not perform at the expected level, and a Ford spokesperson told the Associated Press that AI use has been an important part of its quality gains and that this, along with the deep technical expertise of its teams, is a powerful combination. Beaumont said companies do not always announce such reversals, and may quietly admit they were not ready or should not have made the change after shareholders praised the cost cutting.

Betsy Summers, a principal analyst on the Future of Work team at Forrester, said companies using AI often miss the invisible work employees do beyond their job descriptions, such as sensing emotions and moods, holding impromptu meetings and putting in extra effort when motivated, and that team cohesion, team building and trust are not accounted for. Brooks Holtom, a professor of management at Georgetown University's McDonough School of Business, said organizations are not spending enough time up front to understand workflows and where humans add value, and that in customer service AI agents often need to refer questions to a worker who can recognize emotions, judge how severe or complex a problem is and respond creatively within policies. Holtom advised workers to emphasize skills that complement the technology, such as emotional intelligence and sound judgment, and to articulate their value as a human while also learning what machines do well. Beaumont said empathy is a human quality technology has not fully mastered, since an angry customer wants to be heard by a human.

Beaumont said many people are reluctant to return to a company that laid them off in a reorganization around AI, because trust and psychological safety are very difficult to build back. She said workers offered their old jobs back are asking for more money and to know how AI might affect future staffing, and that requesting additional training and a clear explanation of advancement opportunities could be part of the discussion. Holtom said returning employees should outline a new job description that uses both the technology and their expertise, and could end up in a higher-ranking, better-paid position, and he suggested seeking a commitment such as a one-year renewable contract with a buyout clause if the job ends in less than a year. Summers said motivation and curiosity make people efficient and effective, and that work serves a human purpose beyond creating value for shareholders, customers or constituents, as a manifestation of the search for meaning and purpose and a way to contribute to communities.

stories.Headline: As AI in politics becomes more common, here's how voters can stay vigilant
stories.Summary:
Experts warn that AI-made political content is spreading faster and looking more realistic as the election season moves forward. The Associated Press reported on Wednesday that social media videos believed to be made with AI and linked to Russia are using real people's names and photographs to spread disinformation about two Democratic Senate candidates in close races, Sherrod Brown in Ohio and James Talarico in Texas. Ari Lightman, a digital media and marketing professor at Carnegie Mellon University, said foreign adversaries are using increasingly advanced tools to push polarization and favor certain political outcomes. The use is not limited to foreign actors, since political groups in the United States are also using AI in campaign ads.

The Wesleyan Media Project has tracked 220 midterm election ads generated at least in part with AI tools, a count it called almost certainly an undercount. Most of those ads came from Republican candidates and organizations, though stakeholders in both parties used them. Spending on AI-generated ads had exceeded $137 million as of earlier this month, compared with less than $50,000 in the 2024 cycle, according to the project's co-director, Erika Franklin Fowler. She said much of the AI use goes undisclosed through any kind of disclaimer. Thirty-one states have enacted laws regulating deepfakes in political messaging, though some have been challenged in court on free speech grounds, and there are still no federal disclosure requirements.

Experts say voters cannot rely on visual clues alone, such as misshapen hands, unnaturally smooth skin, or misaligned shadows, because the technology has grown too sophisticated for most people to spot these flaws. Lightman advised voters to check the credentials and context behind potential AI content and to verify information through independent sources. He also said voters should be wary of content designed to provoke an immediate emotional response and should think twice before sharing it on social media. OpenAI confirmed on Wednesday that it is launching an Election Operations Center this week to track misinformation and address potential misuse of tools like ChatGPT, running until all votes are counted, according to Politico. A new Brennan Center report found OpenAI was the only company that significantly improved protections against generating fake election content since the center tested six popular models earlier this year.

stories.Headline: Is AI Overhyped? Apollo Economist Sees "Zero Financial Payoff" Beyond Tech Companies
stories.Summary:
Apollo Global Management's chief economist, Torsten Slok, published research on Saturday, October 25, 2026, arguing that artificial intelligence has so far produced no financial gains for companies outside the tech sector. His analysis found that the "Magnificent Seven" tech firms, including Alphabet, Microsoft, and Meta, are seeing rising revenue per worker and profit margins from AI, while the other 493 companies in the S&P 500 are not. Slok reported that revenue per employee at tech firms climbed from about $550,000 to nearly $800,000 since 2022, while the figure for the rest of the index has stayed near $550,000 for seven years. Profit margins for those other companies have stagnated at about 10%, and productivity growth across the economy has not jumped as AI optimists predicted.

The findings matter because the AI boom rests on the hope that huge investments in data centers and models will eventually raise profits across many industries by cutting costs and improving processes. Slok wrote that mainstream companies are beginning to see token spending as a cost that weighs on margins rather than a source of growth. He framed the open question as whether corporate America can turn increasingly cheap intelligence into higher revenue and margins, and he said that may be harder than it sounds. Commentary from the Motley Fool notes that if this pattern holds, today's highly valued tech stocks could be overpriced, and a sell-off could follow if companies cut AI spending.

Slok, a partner and chief economist at Apollo, presented the research as a warning about the current trajectory rather than a final verdict. The Motley Fool's Ben Gran, writing on October 28, 2026, pointed out that other forecasters are more optimistic, and Vanguard research suggests gains from AI could reach companies across many industries over the long run. Gran's advice for investors who share Apollo's concern was to consider a broadly diversified S&P 500 fund instead of a tech-heavy one. He also noted that such a fund still holds major tech names and would not be fully shielded from an AI-driven downturn.

Gran cited the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF, which has delivered annualized returns of about 13.8% over the past five years, including through the 2022 bear market when the index fell about 18.2%. Business Insider's Truman Dickerson reported the Apollo findings in a similar vein, emphasizing that the broader economy has not yet seen the widespread productivity gains that AI supporters have promised. Both outlets framed the research as a test of whether the AI boom will spread beyond a handful of large companies. The coming quarters of corporate earnings and AI spending will show whether Slok's view holds or whether broader gains emerge.

stories.Headline: Cash is king as investors draw new battle lines in AI spending boom
stories.Summary:
Investors on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, sharply separated companies they see as profiting from artificial intelligence from those struggling to control its costs. Microsoft and Oracle were rewarded for showing they could fund their large AI plans without repeatedly turning to investors for money. Alphabet, Google's parent, was punished for burning through cash, and slower growth in Google Search raised worries that rivals were hurting the business that pays for its AI push. By Thursday's premarket trading, Microsoft shares had risen more than 2 per cent while Alphabet had fallen nearly 11 per cent.

The split reflects a shift in what investors want to see after years of rewarding firms for spending heavily on computing capacity, often with borrowed money. Now they are asking for proof that the growth from those investments can pay for the next round of spending. Meta gave an early signal the week before, when better-than-expected revenue and an upbeat outlook were overshadowed by its cash burn. Oracle, by contrast, closed nearly 11 per cent higher on Wednesday after saying it would cap external financing and expected its cash flow to turn positive in the second half of fiscal 2028.

Melissa Otto, head of research at S&P Global Visible Alpha, said the two companies looked like night and day, describing Microsoft's growth as disciplined while Google was burning cash and its core business fell short of expectations. She suggested investors might now ask whether AI was taking some share from Google Search. The figures behind the concern are stark: Alphabet put 121.4 per cent of its operating cash flow into capital spending in the September quarter, against 68 per cent at Microsoft, excluding finance leases. Google Search revenue grew 12 per cent in that quarter, below the 14.7 per cent analysts had expected, even though CEO Sundar Pichai said queries were growing at their fastest pace in five years. Alphabet's capital spending could reach as much as $205 billion this year and rise significantly in 2027, according to CFO Anat Ashkenazi.

Alphabet's cloud business offered a counterpoint, as Google Cloud revenue more than doubled to $30.71 billion, though spending overwhelmed that gain and cash burn reached $9.07 billion. Jeremy Saltzberg of Check Capital, which owns Alphabet shares, defended the spending as necessary to compete with OpenAI and Anthropic. Microsoft generated $18.6 billion in free cash flow in its fiscal first quarter, nearly $10 billion above Wall Street's expectations, while investing $45.2 billion in computing infrastructure. Its Azure revenue rose 48 per cent, and CEO Satya Nadella said businesses were moving past experiments toward long-term AI contracts.

stories.Headline: SAP swaps costly AI models for cheaper alternatives, targets over €2 bln in gains - ET CIO
stories.Summary:
SAP, the German software maker whose products are used by many of the world's largest companies, is replacing some of the expensive artificial-intelligence models that power its products with cheaper alternatives. The company expects the switch to generate more than €2 billion in efficiency gains over the next two years. The shift was described in an interview with Reuters published on October 29, 2026. The reporting covers the change without detailing a single starting date for the swap.

CFO Dominik Asam told Reuters that the company had removed some of the most expensive AI models from products including its internal consulting assistant. He said the replacements were lower-cost models used where performance stayed strong. SAP uses more than 70 AI models from providers including OpenAI, Anthropic and Google. Asam said the company increasingly picks the cheapest model able to perform a task to the required standard. He also said overall spending on AI is still expected to rise as adoption grows.

SAP said in written answers to Reuters that its goal is healthy margins as it scales, not an absolute cut in AI spending. The company said it charges customers for completed tasks rather than for the computing resources used to generate responses. Under that model, lower operating costs can help improve profitability, according to the reporting. Asam is the executive quoted on the cost figures and the model changes.

The reporting also notes that customers are paying closer attention to where AI models come from. Asam said government agencies and companies in regulated industries increasingly set specific requirements and exclude models based on origin. He said European customers are increasingly demanding local solutions. The articles do not say how much of SAP's AI work will move to these alternatives or whether any further changes are planned beyond the two-year window.

stories.Headline: Nvidia's web of AI bets: smart strategy or bubble risk?
stories.Summary:
Nvidia announced on Tuesday, October 27, 2026, a $3 billion investment in Meta's share sale, the latest addition to a growing portfolio of stakes, loans and guarantees tied to the artificial intelligence boom. The chip giant has taken positions in OpenAI, Anthropic and Elon Musk's xAI, now part of SpaceX, along with neocloud firms such as CoreWeave and Nebius that rent out computing power built on its chips. Its reach also extends to Europe, where it has backed Mistral and Wayve, and to Asia, where it has teamed up with South Korea's SK Group on data centers. Beyond equity, Nvidia acts as a customer of last resort, having committed to buy up to $6.3 billion of unused CoreWeave capacity, and it reportedly holds about $36 billion in cloud backstops plus a guarantee of up to $105 billion tied to an OpenAI data center. Some analysts now call the company the central bank of the AI boom.

Experts see these deals as a rational use of Nvidia's large profits. Michael Cusumano of the MIT Sloan School of Management said the company is in effect becoming a bank and that steering money into infrastructure that buys its own equipment is a smart move. He added that running its own data centers would bring it into conflict with its biggest customers and could invite antitrust complaints. Gil Luria of D.A. Davidson said Nvidia is filling gaps where other parts of the AI ecosystem are underinvesting, calling the approach unprecedented but workable. Chief executive Jensen Huang has defended the strategy by arguing that leading AI labs need tens of billions of dollars to get started, and Nvidia's money gives them time to succeed.

Critics, however, compare the arrangements to the dot-com era, when firms inflated growth by funding startups that then bought their products. Paulo Carvão of the Harvard Kennedy School said there is nothing inherently wrong with Nvidia helping clients, but the closer the ties, the harder it becomes to judge how much demand is genuine and sustainable. Luria argued that demand is not equal in quality, since Nvidia money cycling back through a neocloud is weaker than a major cloud provider buying chips for paying enterprise customers. The sharper risk is concentration: two direct customers made up 22 percent and 14 percent of Nvidia's revenue in fiscal 2026, according to its annual report. Carvão warned that a weaker partner such as CoreWeave running into trouble could spread losses across chipmakers, data-center builders and their financiers at once.

Those worries surfaced in October, when shares of several Nvidia-linked neocloud companies, including CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN, fell at least 30 percent amid concern about tighter credit for AI projects. Carvão estimated that demand for AI chips, still constrained by supply, would keep rising for another 12 to 18 months before leveling off. Cusumano expected strong demand for Nvidia chips to last three to five years. Whether the web of deals proves a sound strategy or a bubble will therefore depend largely on how long AI spending holds up.

stories.Headline: Asia chip firms see strong AI demand; market jitters continue
stories.Summary:
Asian chip supply chain companies said on Friday that demand tied to artificial intelligence remained strong, even as investors kept worrying about whether the huge spending on AI infrastructure would earn adequate returns. Foxconn Chairman Young Liu told reporters at a company event that AI was not in a bubble and that demand for AI products remained clear. Foxconn is Nvidia’s biggest AI server maker and Apple’s top iPhone assembler. Alphabet, Intel and Amazon all fell overnight on concerns about whether returns will justify continued high capital expenditure, and the caution spread to Asia on Friday. Technology stocks came under pressure, including South Korea’s SK Hynix, Taiwan’s TSMC and Japan’s Advantest.

Tokyo Electron Chief Financial Officer Hiroshi Kawamoto told reporters at a briefing on the company’s half-yearly results that interest from customers was very strong in the various conversations the company was having. The company forecast on Friday a stronger-than-expected 87% jump in operating profit to 1.17 trillion yen, or $7.41 billion, underscoring robust demand for chipmaking equipment. Kawamoto said that at present there were no signs that this was slowing down. Despite concerns about AI-related spending, Asian suppliers of chips and semiconductor equipment continued to report strong results. SK Hynix said this week it would return about $75 billion to shareholders as higher memory prices boost profits.

Rick Tsai, CEO of Taiwan chip designer MediaTek, said demand growth for AI will certainly continue although the rate may vary. David Gibson of MST Financial said doubts over the Anthropic IPO, AI financing and wider AI adoption were holding back investors. Tokyo Electron, a major supplier of equipment for processes such as deposition and etching to chipmakers, said it would spend up to 150 billion yen to buy back some 25 million shares. Its shares closed down 5% ahead of earnings.

The San Francisco-based company counts a16z, Accel, Founders Fund, Khosla Ventures, Elad Gil, and Pear VC among its existing investors. The reported valuation range reflects how intensely investors are competing for stakes in AI coding, one of the most crowded and expensive areas of the AI market. The article notes that a $75 billion figure would not be out of line, since SpaceX recently bought the rival AI coding company Cursor for $60 billion.

Factory accused Cognition employees of posing as job applicants to obtain product information, and it criticized a former Factory adviser for meeting with Cognition executives. Cognition and the former adviser both denied that any confidential information was sought or shared. stories.Headline: Trump says US will beat China in AI as technology emerges
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence has become the main point of disagreement between the United States and China, and President Donald Trump says the United States will win the AI competition. Speaking on September 13 in Ireland, Trump said the United States was leading China in AI and called it the most sophisticated country in the world. He said he wanted to keep that lead because whoever wins AI wins. The remarks came as the two countries, the world's two largest economies, have been caught in a trade war during both of Trump's terms.

The reporting shows that Trump has treated the relationship with Chinese President Xi Jinping as a warm one. During a state visit to Beijing in May, Trump praised Xi and said the two had gotten along and worked out past difficulties. In September, Xi visited the White House for a state visit, and Trump described the strides the two had made on national security, trade and technology. At that summit, the countries agreed to extend a trade truce until January. However, no agreement was reached on putting safeguards for AI into practice.

Trump is the central figure in these comments, and he is the one who has called AI "super intelligence" and insisted on American victory. Trump said during his presidential campaign that tariffs would form the core of the bilateral relationship. The articles frame these statements as his own positions rather than as a joint policy. They report that he and Xi are set to meet again in China next month.

The articles place the dispute in the context of an ongoing trade conflict, which has shaped the relationship through both of Trump's terms in office. They do not describe any new rules or changes arising from the AI discussions, beyond the unresolved question of safeguards. The next step named in the reporting is the planned meeting in China in November. Beyond that meeting, the articles do not say what will follow.

stories.Headline: Bessent Plays Down Concerns Over AI Financing, Fed Rate Policy
stories.Summary:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Wednesday that he and his team are monitoring financing for the artificial intelligence build-out, and he downplayed recent signs of concern. In a CNBC interview, he responded to questions about yields on some AI-related debt climbing into double digits. He said the neoclouds, which rent out AI infrastructure, make up only a small part of the wider ecosystem, so he did not see the situation as a problem. CoreWeave Inc., a major AI computing provider, has become the focus of growing worry about how durable the boom is and the hundreds of billions of dollars borrowed to fund it.

Bessent said financing deals are still getting done, and he pointed to companies such as Meta choosing to raise money through equity. He spoke shortly after the Federal Reserve's latest rate decision, where the central bank held rates steady after raising its key rate in September. He also restated his confidence, and that of President Donald Trump, in Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh. Asked whether a future rate increase would be a policy mistake, Bessent said that was not necessarily the case, citing strong economic growth.

He again urged policymakers to keep an open mind about whether the energy shock to inflation would prove temporary. Yields on US debt have pulled back from their highest levels in more than two decades in recent weeks, though 10-year rates remain above 5 percent. Bessent linked those yield levels to the Fed's decision before the 2024 presidential election to cut rates, starting with a 50 basis point move. He said the 10-year yield had never turned back and that the bond market had done much of the tightening for the Fed.

Many market participants, however, say the AI financing boom has added to strain on Treasuries, as AI companies have flooded corporate debt markets with a combined trillions of dollars in new issuance. Bessent also said he and Trump expect the oil market to be well supplied once the US gets past the Iran conflict. He argued that this would help ease inflation and bring down borrowing costs. The articles do not say what specific steps, if any, the Treasury will take in response to the AI financing concerns, and they do not describe any further Fed decisions beyond the hold announced this week.

stories.Headline: AI reshaping product research, but trust remains key
stories.Summary:
A new survey from Lyssna, a research platform company, finds that AI is now a routine part of product research, though many professionals remain wary of trusting it. The findings are based on responses from 428 attendees surveyed at Future Product Days in Copenhagen. Of those surveyed, 94% said they use AI somewhere in their research workflow, with 55% using it throughout the research-to-decision process. Designers made up 46% of respondents and product managers 28%, while only 4% identified as researchers.

The survey suggests AI is changing how research gets done inside product teams rather than replacing the work. Nearly half of respondents, 47%, said AI has led them to do more research, while 20% now rely on AI more than on doing the research themselves. Some 49% said they had connected an AI assistant directly to their research or product tools, with engineers most likely to do so at 72%, compared with 55% of product managers and 39% of designers. Respondents also pointed to the work that comes after a study as the biggest slowdown, with manual synthesis or write-up named by 32%. Checking AI-generated output for errors and bias has emerged as a new burden, and 81% said they would value an AI-generated, decision-ready report based on their research data.

Trust is the central obstacle the survey identifies. Asked about barriers to using AI directly with research data, 27% cited data privacy and 25% pointed to trust in accuracy. The concern was sharpest among people who had connected an AI assistant to their tools but rarely used it, with 40% in that group naming accuracy as the main barrier. Some respondents said company policy prevented them from linking AI tools to internal systems. In an open question that drew 258 responses, people said they wanted AI to spot patterns they might miss and to act as a critical partner, with one respondent asking the tool to "challenge me instead of agreeing with everything."

Tristan Gamilis, Chief Product Officer and Co-Founder at Lyssna, said AI has not replaced research but has changed who is doing it, and that designers and product managers are running more studies than ever. He said the main challenge now is trust, and that teams need assurance that what their AI tells them comes from real people. Mateja Milosavljevic, Chief Executive Officer and Co-Founder at Lyssna, said the teams that benefit most will keep AI grounded in what real people said and did, which she argued lets them move quickly while still making decisions they can defend. Lyssna also cautioned that its audience was self-selected and unscreened, and that the 18 researchers in the sample mean findings about that group should be treated as directional rather than conclusive.

stories.Headline: Echo launches Frontier to patch AI-found zero-days
stories.Summary:
Echo, a security company, has launched a product called Echo Frontier that turns zero-day vulnerabilities found by advanced AI models into private software patches before they are publicly disclosed. The launch was announced on October 28, 2026, and the service is now generally available. The announcement came as security researchers reported that newer open-weight AI models are getting better at finding and exploiting software flaws. Anthropic research cited by Echo found that Zhipu AI's GLM-5.3 produced working end-to-end exploits in 50 of 410 attempts on the ExploitBench benchmark, compared with 56 for Claude Mythos Preview. Because GLM-5.3 is openly available, flaws could be discovered and exploited before a CVE is assigned, before detection signatures exist, or before a maintainer releases an upstream fix.

Frontier works by checking each vulnerability against a working exploit, then building and testing a fix across the full application before delivering it. Patches reach customers through their existing JFrog or Nexus repositories, and customers move to the official upstream fix once one is available. The service covers reproducing a flaw with a proof of concept, identifying affected versions, notifying maintainers, developing and backporting fixes, and distributing the patched software privately. Echo also provides documentation of the detection and remediation process for compliance purposes. The company pointed to 1Password's Off-by-1 Labs research, which found that 54% of 6,080 AI-generated patches failed to fix the vulnerability, introduced a new one, or did both, as evidence that fixing flaws safely is hard.

Echo's chief executive, Eilon Elhadad, said AI is changing the vulnerability lifecycle, so the traditional sequence of a flaw becoming public, receiving a CVE and then getting a fix no longer holds. Eylam Milner, the company's chief technology officer, said that finding zero-days without the means to fix them creates new liabilities, and that the product is meant to make discovered flaws safe to run in an enterprise quickly. Echo acts as an authorised CVE Numbering Authority and coordinates disclosure. It cited a recent case involving OpenEXR, the open-source image file format library, in which it found a high-severity denial-of-service vulnerability, validated it and protected customers in about two days, roughly two months before an upstream fix became available.

The launch reflects a broader concern that organisations may need an intermediate layer of remediation when AI-driven discovery outpaces standard vulnerability management. Echo builds on its existing work vetting, patching, rebuilding and delivering open-source software used in containers, libraries, operating system packages and virtual machines. For software suppliers, the articles suggest the challenge is not only finding unknown flaws but proving that a patch can be applied safely and quickly across the versions and environments customers already use. The articles do not describe any further developments beyond the launch itself.
