stories.Headline: DCSD discusses communication device policy, AI use
stories.Summary:
Members of the Douglas County School District are continuing to discuss a new communication device policy and the potential use of artificial intelligence in schools. During an Oct. 27 board of education meeting, Chief of Staff Steve Colella and Chief Technology Officer Mark Blair gave an update on current and potential technology uses across the district. The device policy stems from state legislation, HB25-1135, also known as Communication Devices in Schools. That law required public school districts and the Charter School Institute across Colorado to implement and post a policy on student use of communication devices on their websites by summer 2026.

To comply, the board adopted Policy JICJA, titled Student Use of Communication Devices in School, in April. The policy defines communication devices as portable technology that can access the internet, make and receive calls or messages, or create or access non-school-related content, including cell phones, smartwatches, earbuds or headphones, smart eyeglasses, cameras and recording devices, while laptops and tablets used for school purposes are excluded. All students must keep devices silenced and stored away, but elementary and middle school students cannot use them during the entire school day, while high school students cannot use them during each class period. Storage methods depend on each school's preference, such as backpacks, lockers, phone pocket charts or collection boxes, and exceptions include staff permission for instructional purposes or an urgent matter that cannot be handled through school communication options. The district will assess the efficiency and regulation of Policy JICJA during the 2028-2029 school year.

Colella said the district gathered feedback from small samples of people, and while some issues need attention, the overall response from staff, students and parents was relatively positive. Some staff see the policy as one more thing to enforce, some students are unhappy about it, and there have been reports of minor issues such as sneaky student behavior, constant phone requests and messaging apps on school computers. Others reported that students are more engaged, on-task and attentive, and that the policy seems to have fostered more peer-to-peer communication. Colella said the policy addresses students with learning needs, stating that students with a 504 plan, an Individual Education Plan, a documented health need or another state or federal law requiring a device may use it when needed, and Superintendent Erin Kane said families frustrated by a shift to paper and pencil should work directly with their special education team and school.

On AI, the district is leaning toward encouraging teachers, students and families to learn to use it safely, ethically, intelligently and with discernment. Colella said the district has tried to foster an environment where staff can explore the technology through pilot programs, but it will no longer do pilots with other tools. Blair said staff have talked with groups including Teacher Connect, the district leadership team and professional learning specialists about what is working and what supports are needed, and he said the tool can free up time to focus on kids and connections. Moving forward the district will focus on Gemini, Gemini Notebook and Gemini Classroom, with Canvas used in high schools through a Learning Tools Interoperability integration with Google, and Blair said nothing entered into Gemini is used to train its models as an education entity. The district is working toward Google Gemini certification for middle and high school staff and students by spring break 2027, while for kindergarten through fifth grade it is focusing on digital citizenship, and Colella said balanced, thoughtful conversations about AI need to continue because the district's job is to make sure kids know how to use it.

stories.Headline: Meta launches two new AI apps, including one aimed at kids
stories.Summary:
Meta launched two new AI-powered apps in the week covered by this report, as the company uses its own AI models to generate app code faster. One of them, Waddle World, is aimed at kids and gives users a virtual pet that can remember things they say and create content based on their interests. The other, Style Sketch, uses AI to suggest outfit combinations from clothes users already own. Meta describes Waddle World as a cozy, 16-bit pet care game with no streaks or scores to chase. The article notes that Waddle World is currently only available to users in the Philippines.

Style Sketch builds a virtual wardrobe by integrating with Instagram and pulling clothing items from images users have shared there. Users can also add items by hand, and the app then builds looks from those pieces. According to analyst Matt Navarra, Style Sketch is only available in Indonesia, Singapore and Thailand. The article says Waddle World collects personal data including location, contact information and user ID, according to the app's iOS page. Both launches come amid ongoing concerns about AI tools making potentially dangerous recommendations to users.

The article describes Meta as experimenting in this way because AI tools make it much easier to build and release new apps and see which ones gain traction. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said on the company's July earnings call that AI is speeding up product development, pointing to recent launches including Instagram Instants, Forum and Seller. The article lists other test apps Meta has released or is working on, including Pocket, Vibes, StoryKit and a prediction markets app called Arena. It says whether Arena reaches a full launch remains to be seen.

The writer argues that most of these experimental apps are unlikely to last long, though a few may help Meta keep people engaged on its platforms. The article also points to Meta adding parental oversight to its Meta AI app as related coverage. Against that backdrop, the writer calls Waddle World's cute design somewhat disingenuous given how the company uses such tools to gather data. stories.Headline: How AI drones are influencing the course of the Ukraine war
stories.Summary:
Yaroslav Azhnyuk, a Ukrainian tech entrepreneur, turned to drone warfare after Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022. His companies, The Fourth Law and Odd Systems, are among the leading producers of AI-powered drones in Ukraine, and dozens of Ukrainian military units already use their autonomous drone, the Lupynis-10-TFL-1. The reporting describes a broader shift in which artificial intelligence is making drones faster and more capable. Russia is also deploying AI-enabled drones against Ukraine.

The Lupynis-10-TFL-1 is a small, affordable first-person-view drone paired with an autonomous terminal guidance unit. For the last 500 meters, or 0.3 miles, of a flight, an onboard computer and AI technology take control from the human operator. The system relies on relatively simple image recognition tools rather than the large AI systems used in data centers or self-driving cars. Azhnyuk says this lets a drone navigate without a person, select a target, or fly toward one on its own. The company's testers say the drone's microcomputer runs a deep-learning network trained on hours of combat footage to recognize vehicles, armored vehicles, tanks and flying objects.

Azhnyuk argues that AI gives a smaller military an asymmetric advantage, claiming it can make a drone "10,000 times more effective." He acknowledges concern about destructive weapons but says the worry is not specific to AI, comparing it to earlier tools like fire or steel that can be used for good or bad. The company's test and integration lead, who uses the call sign Stab, says safeguards are in place so the drones will not go rogue and that humans select the targets. Azhnyuk rejects comparisons to killer robots, calling the systems "just sort of calculators," though he concedes that future drones might one day make their own targeting decisions. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that AI could lead decisions on the battlefield as soon as next year.

Azhnyuk's main argument is that Ukraine cannot afford to refuse AI in defense when adversaries are already using it for offensive decisions. He says Russian systems can decide in microseconds while human control takes minutes, hours or sometimes days, and he warns that if Ukraine loses, there would be no room to debate the ethics of AI. The company names its weapons after Ukrainian intellectuals and artists killed or persecuted by Russians, with the Lupynis drone honoring a poet who endured Soviet imprisonment. The articles do not describe any specific outcome beyond these claims or set out formal rules governing the use of such drones.

stories.Headline: FORVIA and Raiqon enter strategic AI partnership
stories.Summary:
FORVIA, a global automotive supplier, and Raiqon GmbH, a specialist in scalable AI solutions for regulated engineering environments, have entered a strategic partnership to apply artificial intelligence in automotive engineering. The announcement was issued as a press release from Nanterre, France, on Thursday, October 29, 2026. The two companies say the work centers on Requirements Engineering, a stage of product development in which technical requirements are defined, analyzed and managed. Depending on product complexity, a single development project can involve as many as 15,000 individual requirements.

The jointly developed solution automates the analysis, assessment and processing of those requirements, which the companies say will raise productivity and speed up development. It runs on Raiqon's multi-agent AI platform inside FORVIA's secure IT environment and plugs into FORVIA's existing IBM DOORS setup without disrupting established workflows. The platform pulls data from several engineering applications and is being adapted to the needs of FORVIA HELLA and Faurecia Clarion Electronics. Its tasks include analyzing requirements, spotting similarities, reusing earlier assessments, detecting inconsistencies and creating missing links automatically. By cutting manual effort, the companies say engineers can devote more time to new requirements.

FORVIA's CEO, Martin Fischer, said AI is becoming a key enabler of innovation and competitiveness in the automotive industry and linked the collaboration to the company's IGNITE transformation program. Joerg Weisgerber, Managing Director Electronics at FORVIA HELLA, said the AI-based automation is meant to make the company faster and more efficient and to let teams handle a much larger volume of requirements. Raiqon's CEO, Szabi Koppany, said the automotive industry faces growing international pressure to shorten development cycles, improve economic efficiency and manage rising complexity. He described the shared goal as improving the efficiency and quality of engineering processes and strengthening FORVIA's leadership position.

FORVIA describes itself as a global automotive technology supplier formed from the Faurecia and HELLA businesses, with more than 137,500 employees, over 12,000 R&D engineers across more than 40 countries and a patent portfolio of over 12,400. The company reported consolidated revenue of 26.2 billion euros in 2025 before IFRS 5 adjustments. stories.Headline: Early Anthropic member recalls burnout and big ambitions in the AI lab's early days
stories.Summary:
Ivan Vendrov, a former member of Anthropic's technical staff, has published a Substack post describing his time at the AI lab from late 2022 to mid-2023. In the post, he recalls an intense, safety-focused workplace where fears of AI catastrophe competed with the push to build safe AGI for commercial use. He wrote that he later felt burned out and disillusioned. The account arrives days after Anthropic filed to go public, and Anthropic declined to comment on the story.

Vendrov said he was weighing offers from OpenAI and Anthropic in 2022 when a cofounder told him over lunch that the company was already talking with regulators in Washington. A recruiter then asked whether he would pledge two-thirds of his equity to charity, and said all the cofounders had made that pledge. Vendrov said he was unsure if the offer depended on his agreement, so he said yes. Anthropic's S-1 filing describes a donation-matching program in which workers can pledge a "meaningful portion" of their equity awards, and reports that 50% of employees are included.

Vendrov described a cramped, unattractive office stocked with fresh croissants, and said a popular masseuse visited twice a week but was always fully booked when he tried to schedule. He also recalled one visit from an FBI agent, who warned that Anthropic was probably already a target of several foreign intelligence agencies. When the company hosted a sushi chef, he said a cofounder complained in Slack the next day that the event set the wrong tone. The cofounder reportedly said the company was not there to get rich and eat caviar, and suggested future dinners of rice and beans instead.

Vendrov's post describes sleepless nights, walks with other stressed colleagues, and a sense that he could not be fully honest about his feelings at work. Eight months after signing, he wrote a resignation letter, and he said he considered voicing his doubts but worried about unsettling colleagues he regarded as more capable and better intentioned than himself. Instead, he praised Anthropic as an unbelievably good organization. Vendrov has not responded to requests for comment, and he cautioned that his account is his memory of events, reconstructed from one junior employee's experience during a short period.

stories.Summary:
On October 29, 2026, Circana, a Chicago-based company that turns consumer data into growth insights, announced it had engaged Ode with Anthropic, an enterprise AI transformation company, to modernize how it produces and delivers market intelligence. The stated aim is to give Circana's clients faster, more flexible and more actionable insights. The two companies are building a governed agent platform where teams can build, test and deploy agents in one place. Each agent is measured against expert-verified cases, and work the system finds uncertain is sent to Circana specialists.

The collaboration also involves end-to-end workflows guided by experts, with data processing, trend forecasting and product classification as the first three focus areas. Ode is training Circana engineers to build and deploy agents of their own, and operators will own the goals and quality of the agents in their areas. Circana describes these as production-ready capabilities on a reusable foundation rather than standalone productivity tools. The company says this should speed up its ability to develop and deliver new solutions to clients. Circana also says it will share results and case studies as the work scales.

Stuart Aitken, Circana's president and CEO, said AI matters only if it improves clients' decisions and speed, and that the firm is turning complex manual processes into scalable workflows centered on its data and industry expertise. Michael Rosenthal, president of Operations at Circana, said removing manual steps and routing exceptions to experts allows faster, more consistent work without sacrificing the oversight clients expect. Chris Taylor, CEO of Ode, said AI works best when it gives experts more room to apply judgment and that he is pleased to work alongside Circana's analysts. The announcement notes that Circana grew from IRI and The NPD Group and has spent decades using technology and data science to help clients understand consumers.

Circana describes itself as a provider of technology, AI and data to fast-moving consumer packaged goods companies, durables manufacturers and retailers. Its platform, Liquid Data, relies on a large data set and algorithms trained on six decades of domain expertise. Ode was formally launched in 2026 through a partnership between Anthropic, Blackstone, Hellman & Friedman and a group of global investors, and it helps organizations move AI from experimentation to full deployment. It pairs Anthropic's frontier models with experienced AI engineers to find high-impact uses and build the systems that deliver them. The articles do not give financial terms of the engagement or a timeline for completion.

stories.Headline: Delta Air Lines among companies FTC investigating for potential price-setting using AI - WSB-TV
stories.Summary:
The Federal Trade Commission has opened an inquiry into nine companies, including Atlanta-based Delta Air Lines, over how they set prices for customers. The agency announced the probe on Wednesday, October 29, 2026, and it targets Delta, United Airlines, JetBlue, Lyft, Uber, DoorDash, Instacart, Target and Walmart. The announcement noted that DoorDash and Instacart had recently announced a $17 billion merger. The inquiry is aimed at learning whether these firms use personal data to set individual prices.

The FTC ordered the companies to provide detailed information about their use of personal data in setting prices and compensation. Each company has 45 days from receiving the order to respond, which means they must either provide the data or contest it in court by December 12. The agency is trying to determine whether airfares, ride share fees, food delivery costs or other services vary depending on loyalty program participation or other personal data. The FTC described these methods as "superintelligence algorithms," the federal term now used in place of the more common phrase artificial intelligence, a shift that President Donald Trump introduced at the United Nations in September. If a company refuses to comply, the commission said it would seek to compel compliance in federal court.

FTC Chairman Andrew N. Ferguson said the agency intends to examine the opaque methods some companies may use to decide what consumers pay or what gig workers earn for the same work. He said consumers should know whether their web browsing or other personal data is used to estimate the highest price they can be charged, and that workers should know whether their pay is affected in the same way. The FTC noted that a 2024 study on personalized pricing examined only middlemen consultancies, not companies like those named in this inquiry that set prices directly. Delta responded to a request for comment by pointing to an earlier statement, saying it has never used, tested or planned to use fares that target customers with individualized offers based on personal data. A Delta spokesperson said the airline has zero tolerance for discriminatory or predatory pricing and complies with applicable privacy, pricing and advertising laws.

The dispatch center serves regional fire agencies, and the renewed agreements keep those services in place. A council member also asked about the AI contract, and the reporting describes the proposal as an effort to improve policing through technology. The article notes that the public comment period included concerns about how the technology would be used and how the city would handle data. stories.Headline: Indian CEOs confident on growth, face AI ethics and talent hurdles
stories.Summary:
A KPMG survey of 125 chief executives in India found that 87 per cent are confident about their organisations' growth over the next three years, compared with 84 per cent of CEOs globally. The 2026 India CEO Outlook also found that 69 per cent of Indian CEOs expect annual earnings growth of more than 2.5 per cent over the same period. In addition, 92 per cent anticipate increasing their workforce. The results were published in a TechGig report on 29 October 2026.

On artificial intelligence, 78 per cent of the Indian CEOs treat it as a strategic investment priority, and 97 per cent said they were confident about managing AI-driven transformation. At the same time, 64 per cent named AI-related ethical concerns as an obstacle to adoption, a higher share than the 57 per cent globally. About 84 per cent believe AI can support more responsible innovation aligned with climate goals. On cybersecurity and digital resilience, 49 per cent plan to increase spending.

Workforce challenges remain, with 54 per cent of respondents naming the attraction and retention of talent as their top concern. Skills gaps followed at 53 per cent, and the need for AI upskilling was cited by 51 per cent. The survey says this points to a growing need to equip employees with new capabilities as AI reshapes job roles. On sustainability, 66 per cent of Indian CEOs have incorporated it into their core business strategy, and 68 per cent expressed confidence in achieving their net-zero ambitions by 2030.

The articles do not name any individual executive or say who commissioned the findings beyond KPMG, and they give no direct statements from respondents. The findings suggest that responsible implementation and governance are central to AI adoption strategies, according to the report. The articles do not say what steps, if any, the surveyed companies plan to take on AI ethics or talent retention. They also do not say what happens next with the survey or its findings.

Articles.Title: Indian CEOs confident on growth, face AI ethics and talent hurdles

stories.Headline: AgiBot Accelerates Deployment Stage to Unlock Full End-to-End Pipeline of Physical AI
stories.Summary:
AgiBot held its Innovation Day at the World Expo Center, where it set out a plan to move physical AI from demonstrations into real work. The company presented new models and hardware aimed at operation, motion and interaction. It also introduced a measurement standard called Worken, or Valid Intelligent Working Hour, for the actual labor output of physical AI. The event focused on deployment rather than robot stunts and group dances.

Peng Zhihui, co-founder, president and CTO of AgiBot, gave figures at the event. He said AgiBot robot revenue was close to 2 billion yuan in the first half of 2026. He said cumulative output of AgiBot general AI robots had reached 20,000 units. He said getting 10,000 units off the production line is only a manufacturing victory, while putting 10,000 units to work is the real victory for physical AI.

The company launched GO-3 Preview, an embodied foundational large model that uses a predict-first, then-act decision mechanism. It also launched the WITA-OMNI native multimodal interaction large model, which Xiong Yan described as the necessary and first entry point for robots to generate value. Xiong Yan is a partner, co-president, president of the Central R&D Department and president of the Interaction Business System. AgiBot also launched the AGILE general motion intelligence algorithm framework and the AHA3 third-generation hardware architecture.

AgiBot said GO-3 Preview has topped the RoboDojo, RoboTwin and RoboColiseum evaluation lists and will be fully open-sourced by the end of 2026. It said WITA-OMNI has a fastest response of 400 milliseconds, supports more than 20 kinds of emotional expressions and understands 73 languages. It said WITA-OMNI took first place in four lists: Daily-Omni, TimeLens-Bench, EmbSpatialBench and MMAU. The company also introduced Lingqu OS 1.0, which it calls the industry's first native operating system for embodied intelligence.

AgiBot said Lingqu OS 1.0 lets more than 100 types of peripherals in 15 categories be used as soon as they are plugged in. It said the system keeps the error of each interval under 4 microseconds when the robot sends 1,000 motion instructions per second. The company said the AHA3 architecture halves the volume of the control system and nearly doubles response speed. AgiBot also announced it will build an open source community for humanoid robots in China with the OpenAtom Open Source Foundation and donate the Lingqu OS project to the foundation.

stories.Headline: Only EU and UK users can object to Meta AI scraping terms
stories.Summary:
Meta has pushed back the start date of its new AI scraping terms to November 20, three weeks later than originally planned, after pressure from the news industry. The terms were first reported by Nieman Lab on October 15 and were originally due to take effect on October 30. Only users in the UK and the EU can object to them, while users elsewhere have no such option. The updated terms let Meta crawl websites linked to business accounts on Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp, which could include small shops, artists, and newsrooms.

Legal experts say the revised wording gives Meta wide latitude, potentially including AI uses. Before the delay, Meta removed the word "train" from its list of permitted uses and narrowed the scope to advertising and business products, where the earlier text had covered all Meta products. One legal expert said the new wording is still broad enough to drive a truck through. Meta has said the extra time lets it explain what is changing and what is not, and that site owners can still use robots.txt to signal their preferences, though Nieman Lab noted that no version of the terms mentions this.

Meta is the company responsible for the terms, and it has framed the delay as a chance to clarify them. Regulators are also involved: the European Commission welcomed the delay and says it will keep scrutinizing the terms, while the News/Media Alliance in the US urged Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg to suspend them. The British competition watchdog has asked the company to explain the terms. The right to object comes from the EU's data protection law, GDPR, and the UK has its own version, though the European Commission says GDPR covers personal data about individuals rather than companies.

For UK and EU users, 404 Media reported that objecting is possible through the Instagram privacy center on mobile by tapping the three lines on the account and selecting the object option. Two users have reportedly received emails from Meta saying their objections were approved. A reporter who tried the desktop site with a London VPN found separate objection options, but a US-based request returned an error saying the form is available only in certain regions. The terms take effect on November 20, and until then, a user's location determines how much say they have over their data.

Articles.Title: Only EU and UK users can object to Meta AI scraping terms

stories.Headline: Can AI save global health or will it deepen inequities?
stories.Summary:
Governments, philanthropies and technology companies are increasingly turning to artificial intelligence as a way to address clinician shortages and expand access to care in low-resource settings, according to a tip sheet published by the Association of Health Care Journalists on October 29, 2026 and written by Lara Salahi. The article says AI is being promoted as a scalable solution for expanding access to care, and that this comes as billions of dollars in global health funding are disappearing. It also says studies show AI research is overwhelmingly concentrated in countries with stronger health systems and fewer people living with certain diseases. That raises concerns that the next generation of AI tools could reinforce rather than reduce global health inequities.

The article describes two central problems. The first is what researchers call health data poverty, meaning AI systems are only as good as the data used to train them, so algorithms trained mostly on patients from high-income countries may perform less accurately in underrepresented populations, including many communities in low- and middle-income countries and racial and ethnic minority populations elsewhere. The second is who generates the evidence, since AI development requires data, research infrastructure, funding, technical expertise and regulatory pathways, and research suggests these resources remain concentrated in wealthier countries. That could lead to earlier validation, deployment and commercial adoption in places where the clinical need may actually be lower. The article says this does not mean AI will inevitably worsen disparities, and it points to India and China as examples of how sustained national investment in digital infrastructure and AI research can help shift innovation toward countries outside the traditional high-income research centers.

The article says reporters covering these developments should be cautious about framing AI as a simple technological fix, and it lists questions to consider about implementation, representation and accountability. These include who was included in the datasets used to develop and validate a tool, whether the technology has been independently evaluated in the populations where it is intended to be used, who owns the data collected through global health AI partnerships, whether research is led by investigators in the countries most affected by the disease or primarily by institutions in high-income countries, and whether the technology addresses a clearly identified health need or is being promoted as a substitute for investments in the workforce, public health infrastructure or health systems. The article says all of these questions get to whether AI is being developed and deployed in ways that genuinely expand access to care, or whether it risks leaving behind the very populations it promises to serve. It also lists additional resources from the World Health Organization, Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health and Harvard University, and links to a related post saying that so-called black box medical AI can deepen health disparities.

Articles.Title: Can AI save global health or will it deepen inequities?

stories.Headline: Microsoft Positioned to Sustain Elevated AI Spending Without Compromising Finances, Truist Says
stories.Summary:
Microsoft's strong balance sheet and cash flow position it to keep up heavy spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure without straining its finances, according to Truist Securities, which made the argument in a client note. The brokerage's view followed Microsoft's fiscal first-quarter earnings call on Wednesday, when Chief Financial Officer Amy Hood said the company still expects to be free cash flow positive in fiscal 2027. Microsoft reported free cash flow of $18.6 billion for the September quarter. Its shares were up 4.1% in premarket trading on Thursday and have risen 9.8% so far this year.

Hood also said Microsoft now expects capital expenditures of about $170 billion in calendar 2026, down from a previous projection of $175 billion. First-quarter capital spending came in at $45.2 billion, below the company's expectation of more than $50 billion, because some third-party capacity deliveries were pushed into the second half. Expenditures for the current three-month period are forecast to exceed $50 billion. Hood told analysts the company believes each dollar of capital spending can support more revenue and higher returns over time as it improves the efficiency of its infrastructure. Azure, Microsoft's cloud computing unit, saw revenue rise 48% to $33.17 billion in the quarter, and the company expects Azure growth of 49% to 50% in constant currency this quarter.

Truist said Microsoft's financial flexibility lets it sustain elevated investment without materially weakening its position, a point it framed as increasingly important as investors examine the returns on AI spending by large technology companies. The firm contrasted Microsoft with Alphabet, which reported negative free cash flow of $9.07 billion in its third quarter as capital expenditures more than doubled to $51.36 billion, and with Meta Platforms, which reported negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion for the September quarter. Truist also said infrastructure availability remains the main constraint on Azure growth, since customer demand continues to outpace supply. The firm raised its price target on Microsoft to $630 from $600 and kept its buy rating on the stock.

Articles.Title: Microsoft Positioned to Sustain Elevated AI Spending Without Compromising Finances, Truist Says

stories.Headline: Accelerate agentic AI with NVIDIA Nemotron models on Amazon EKS and SageMaker HyperPod EKS
stories.Summary:
Amazon Web Services published a blog post on October 29, 2026, describing how to run NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Super VL model on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), EKS Auto Mode, and Amazon SageMaker HyperPod EKS. The model is a 120-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts system that activates 12 billion parameters for each token it processes. It handles text, image, document, and video input, and produces text output. The post joins Nemotron 3.5 Super VL to other Nemotron models that AWS already offers, including Nemotron 3 Nano, Nano Omni, Super, Ultra, and Nemotron 3.5 Lightning.

The model's design aims to keep compute costs close to those of a much smaller model while still holding the full set of weights in GPU memory. It uses a hybrid architecture that mixes Mamba-2, attention, and expert layers, with a vision encoder for visual inputs and a context window of up to 1 million tokens. According to the article, NVIDIA reports scores of 63.44 percent on Hermes Bench, 87.05 percent on LangChain agent evaluations, and 80.8 percent on the CharXiv chart-reasoning benchmark. The post lists minimum GPU counts by hardware type: eight B200 or GB200 GPUs for the BF16 version, or two for the NVFP4 version; four B300 or GB300 GPUs for NVFP4 at minimum; eight H200 GPUs for BF16 or four for NVFP4; and sixteen H100 GPUs for BF16 or eight for NVFP4. The deployment pattern runs the same Kubernetes manifests across all three orchestration options, and the authors describe validating the setup on p6-b200.48xlarge and p5en.48xlarge instances.

The authors, who are AWS staff, published the post and point readers to a reference implementation in the aws-do-eks project, which includes steps for prerequisites, cluster creation, weight downloads, deployment, testing, benchmarking, and cleanup. They also suggest using NVIDIA's aiperf tool and concurrency sweeps to measure latency and throughput so that teams can plan capacity. The article presents these steps as a way for customers to start using the model in their own accounts and mentions upcoming AWS workshops on inference on EKS. It does not report any pricing, availability dates beyond the publication date, or further announcements.

Articles.Title: Accelerate agentic AI with NVIDIA Nemotron models on Amazon EKS and SageMaker HyperPod EKS

stories.Headline: Microsoft's Leadership in AI Remains 'Underappreciated,' Morgan Stanley Says
stories.Summary:
Morgan Stanley said on Thursday, October 29, 2026, that Microsoft's leadership in artificial intelligence remains underappreciated. The bank's analysts pointed to third-quarter results that showed accelerating growth and visible returns on the company's AI spending. The company reported adjusted earnings late Wednesday of $4.89 per diluted share on revenue of $92.28 billion. Analysts surveyed by FactSet had expected $4.71 per share on $90.62 billion in revenue.

The Microsoft Cloud segment drove much of the strength, with Azure growing 48 percent in constant currency from a year earlier despite delays in third-party capacity. Morgan Stanley said Microsoft 365 Commercial Cloud grew 18 percent, supported by seat volume and higher average revenue per user. The analysts described an "Enterprise AI Flywheel," in which Microsoft's positions in infrastructure, models, data and applications create demand across the whole stack. They said the platform connects models with enterprise data, orchestrates workloads and monetizes the activity that results. According to the note, these investments can support revenue growth in the high teens and earnings growth above 20 percent.

Morgan Stanley reiterated its overweight rating on the stock and raised its price target to $650 from $600. The firm's view is that Microsoft benefits as enterprise adoption and consumption of AI grow. The article's related-story links show that other brokerages, including BofA, have also written about Microsoft's AI positioning and monetization in recent months. The sidebar links do not state any additional findings about the company's future results. The report itself is a broker's analysis rather than a company statement, and the article does not describe any response from Microsoft.
