stories.Headline: Microsoft Copilot for finance: Purpose-built for the way finance teams work
stories.Summary:
Microsoft has expanded Copilot for finance professionals, announcing more than 25 new finance skills and partner-built plugins across Microsoft Copilot on October 29, 2026. The company introduced finance skills in Copilot in Excel back in June 2026, and this latest release extends them to accounting, capital markets, and broader finance work. Excel is now embedded directly in the Copilot app, so users can analyze, edit, and co-author workbooks from within Chat or Cowork. Microsoft says Work IQ grounds Copilot in organizational knowledge such as the close calendar and deal-team conversations, so it can work from more than the file in front of the user.

The new accounting capabilities, available in Frontier for Copilot in Excel and Cowork, aim to reduce repetitive manual work in three main areas. Copilot can compare balances and transactions to identify discrepancies and prepare reconciling items for review, and it can draft accruals, reclassifications, allocations, reversals, and recurring entries with checks for required inputs and balanced entries. It can also analyze performance against plan and prepare reporting that explains what changed. In a seven-day limited Insiders period, more than 8,000 unique users invoked accounting skills more than 44,000 times across more than 18,000 Copilot conversations. Finance professionals can also choose to start an audit trail that records what Copilot changed and why in their chat history.

Microsoft says Copilot is designed to support professional review rather than replace it, and that finance professionals retain control over recommendations, decisions, approvals, and actions. In Excel, Copilot can summarize recent activity, identify when and by whom specific changes were made, and selectively reverse individual edits without disrupting the rest of the workbook. The company states that Copilot processes prompts and responses within the Microsoft 365 service boundary with enterprise data protection, honors existing permissions and sensitivity labels, and does not use prompts, responses, or documents to train the underlying foundation models. Brian Jones, corporate vice president of the Excel Product Group, leads the work described in the post.

Availability varies by feature. Finance skills in Copilot in Excel and the Capital Markets and Finance plugins in Cowork are generally available, while the accounting capabilities are in Frontier, and the Dynamics 365 ERP apps plugin and partner plugins are beginning to roll out through the Microsoft plugin registry. Fabric IQ is generally available in Cowork. Third-party services may require separate licensing, subscriptions, authentication, or administrator enablement from the providers. Microsoft lists partners including Intuit QuickBooks, Xero, FactSet, Morningstar, S&P Global, and LSEG, among others, and cites early feedback from firms such as EY Ireland and Zurich Insurance North America.

Articles.Title: Microsoft Copilot for finance: Purpose-built for the way finance teams work

stories.Headline: SAG-AFTRA, WGA & AFM Warn Of "Harms" Of Unlicensed AI Training
stories.Summary:
The unions SAG-AFTRA, the Writers Guild of America East and West, and the American Federation of Musicians filed a joint amicus brief on Thursday, October 29, 2026, in a New York federal court. The filing is part of an ongoing copyright infringement case in which OpenAI faces news outlets and writers over the use of their content to train AI language models. The unions asked the judge to reject a categorical fair use exemption for AI training and to treat each case on its own terms. They say the company is taking the work of middle- and working-class people to build its technology without permission or payment.

The brief runs 34 pages and argues that a blanket exemption would allow a potentially enormous transfer of value from creators to corporations. It stresses the human element in writing, with particular attention to news, which is central to the case. The unions contend that the harms of unlicensed training reach beyond large news organizations to the many professionals who do the work. They conclude that the dispute is an ordinary copyright matter that should be decided case by case, not through a sweeping rule.

The consolidated case pits OpenAI against the New York Times, several Florida and Arkansas newspapers, The Intercept, and a group of prominent authors. Those authors include Ta-Nehisi Coates, George R.R. Martin, John Grisham, Michael Connelly, Jonathan Franzen, and Jodi Picoult, along with Sarah Silverman and the Authors Guild. Several other writers, among them David Baldacci, George Saunders, and Scott Turow, are also part of the litigation. The unions' AI positions have deep roots, since the issue was central to the 2023 strikes and resurfaced in 2026 bargaining.

The brief links the court fight to those negotiations. The writers and actors guilds secured a notice-and-bargaining right for third-party licenses of covered work used to train commercial generative AI systems. The unions argue that a ruling calling AI training categorically fair use would make those agreed terms meaningless and would harm copyright owners and the people who create the work. The case's outcome could therefore shape both the courts' approach to AI training and the labor protections negotiated in Hollywood. The articles do not say when the judge is expected to rule.

Articles.Title: SAG-AFTRA, WGA & AFM Warn Of "Harms" Of Unlicensed AI Training

stories.Headline: Fake Anthropic AI previews lure in overeager employees
stories.Summary:
A phishing campaign is luring employees with fake invitations to a private Anthropic AI preview, according to new research from the cybersecurity company Cofense, published on October 29, 2026. The attackers send what appears to be a GoTo Webinar invitation, and when recipients click the link to register, they are sent to a compromised page built to steal their Google or Microsoft login credentials. Security tools often do not block GoTo Webinar meeting emails, which helps the messages reach inboxes. The sender name is shown as "Austin from nthropic," with the first letter of the company name missing, a small inconsistency the researchers flagged as a warning sign.

The lure works by appealing to exclusivity and fear of missing out, and the email describes a select, invitation-only session on AI systems and frontier models. The link is routed through a URL shortener and a link generated by Zapier, a legitimate company, which helps it evade email filters. Recipients must pass a Cloudflare CAPTCHA page, then reach a page that imitates a Zoom invitation and asks for a work email address. A second CAPTCHA appears before the fake Google or Microsoft login page, and the researchers said these checks can also block security scanners from analyzing the attack. The Google page reportedly captured only usernames, which the researchers suspect is a misconfiguration, while the Microsoft page collected both usernames and passwords.

The researchers advised staff to check whether branding stays consistent from the email to the login page and to look for small misspellings. They also stressed that the URL and domain, not the logo or design, determine whether a login page is legitimate. Frank Dickson of Dickson Research said enterprises should verify any AI preview invitation through an account team or a known contact, treat changing branding as a red flag, and roll out phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication such as passkeys. He also argued that employees should not be the last line of defense, and that anyone who entered credentials should reset them and review account activity. Dickson further noted that attackers tend to target whatever technology is currently in the news, so similar lures using other names are likely to follow.

Articles.Title: Fake Anthropic AI previews lure in overeager employees

stories.Headline: Nvidia Finds Itself at the Center of an AI Spy Saga
stories.Summary:
On October 29, 2026, The New York Times published an investigation reporting that Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang may have been the target of Chinese espionage. According to the report, US authorities identified Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen and executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company, as a possible operative for the Chinese government, with whom Jensen Huang had developed a close relationship. Alice Huang shares no family connection with the Nvidia chief. Megaspeed buys Nvidia chips to run data centers that sell computing power to Chinese AI labs, including Alibaba's Qwen team.

US intelligence agencies had been conducting electronic surveillance of Alice Huang over allegations that she helped sell advanced Nvidia chips to China in violation of US law. During that surveillance, officials reportedly found she was also allegedly passing information to the Chinese government in Beijing. The articles do not say what information was shared or how valuable it might be, but the Times reports that the investigation and surveillance are ongoing. Jensen Huang was not warned by the US government, reportedly because doing so could have jeopardized the probe, according to people with knowledge of the matter cited by the Times.

Nvidia responded through a spokesperson, who said Jensen Huang's interactions with Alice Huang were "not unusual or unexpected" because he meets with thousands of customer executives each year. The company said customers such as Megaspeed are no different from many other regional cloud customers and do not receive sensitive trade secrets. Nvidia also said it trusts that the US government would alert it if it considered any person a threat to American industry. The Times also reports that Trump was briefed on the investigation into Alice Huang a year ago and chose not to act. The White House, the Justice Department and Megaspeed did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The story comes against a backdrop of intense competition over advanced AI chips, which have made Nvidia the world's most valuable company, with a market capitalization of $5 trillion this year. The Biden administration banned Chinese sales of a series of advanced Nvidia chips in 2022, but President Donald Trump relaxed those rules in 2025, and the US government now receives 15% of revenue from Nvidia and AMD on certain chip sales to China. Reports also show that illegal efforts to smuggle banned chips to China continue. The article notes that Trump has a friendly relationship with many Big Tech leaders, including Jensen Huang, and that this has resulted in millions in personal donations to the president. It also notes a separate FBI arrest this month of a Saudi Arabian national accused of planting a recording device in an OpenAI executive conference room.

Articles.Title: Nvidia Finds Itself at the Center of an AI Spy Saga

stories.Headline: OpenAI doubles ChatGPT Pro usage limits after backlash over planned 50% cut
stories.Summary:
OpenAI reversed a planned cut to ChatGPT Pro usage limits after customer complaints, and the change took effect immediately. The company had earlier intended to reduce the included usage allowance for existing Pro 200 subscribers after October 29, even though the monthly price of $200 would have stayed the same. Following the backlash, OpenAI decided to double the usage limits for all Pro tiers and Business Premium instead. The article does not say exactly when the earlier cut was announced. The new limits cover the $100, $200, and $500 Pro plans along with Business Premium, and they primarily affect ChatGPT Work and Codex, which share usage allowances under eligible subscriptions.

OpenAI said it would not reduce usage for Pro 200, so Work and Codex usage will remain the same for those subscribers. The company also said it will keep extended usage limits for Dots, its always-on AI assistants, for now. Dots usage will stay separate from default usage. OpenAI has not published exact numerical limits for each tier. The announcement came from Tibo, who is described as the face of ChatGPT and Codex on X, in a post on the platform.

In that post he said the company had heard customer feedback and was doubling all usage limits for the Pro 100, Pro 200, and Pro 500 tiers along with Business Premium, effective that day. He added that Work and Codex usage would stay the same for Pro 200 subscribers. The article attributes the decision to customer feedback and does not name other parties involved. The article gives no further detail on how the reversal will be implemented beyond the stated effective date, and it does not report any next steps. It also does not describe the reaction of subscribers beyond the backlash that prompted the change.

Articles.Title: OpenAI doubles ChatGPT Pro usage limits after backlash over planned 50% cut

stories.Headline: Why Is Broadcom (AVGO) Now Central To AI Funding And Infrastructure?
stories.Summary:
Broadcom (AVGO) appears in Anthropic's newly filed initial public offering plan, both as a financial backer and as a core supplier of AI chips. The filing arrives alongside Meta's record US$95 billion capital raise for AI infrastructure. Broadcom is identified as a major provider of custom accelerators powering Meta's expanded AI data center investment program. The article is a market commentary piece dated October 29, 2026, published by Simply Wall St on Yahoo Finance.

The article describes Broadcom as a designer of custom semiconductor accelerators and infrastructure software that connect directly to large-scale AI training and inference work. It says hyperscale cloud customers are tying its hardware into their data center build-outs. With a market value of about $1.6 trillion, the company ranks among the largest US chip suppliers serving these customers. The article also cites a multi-gigawatt deployment plan with Google, Anthropic, OpenAI and Meta extending through at least 2028, which underpins management's AI semiconductor revenue targets for 2027 and 2028.

The article names no executive or spokesperson from Broadcom, Anthropic or Meta. Its analysis is attributed to Simply Wall St, with the author listed as Bailey Pemberton. The piece includes a quoted passage from a Broadcom narrative describing accelerating demand for custom AI chips from hyperscale and large language model customers. The article says Simply Wall St has no position in any stock it mentions.

The article presents the Anthropic and Meta funding as a test of Broadcom's strategy of trading balance sheet flexibility for clearer chip demand. It notes that Nvidia and AMD are also providing cash to customers. It says deeper ties with hyperscalers could strengthen Broadcom's position while tying its results more closely to customer spending cycles and gross margin pressure. The article does not describe any next steps or future events beyond these ongoing investment and financing developments.

Articles.Title: Why Is Broadcom (AVGO) Now Central To AI Funding And Infrastructure?

stories.Headline: Jim Cramer says Microsoft is winning the AI spending battle — and Alphabet is paying the price
stories.Summary:
On Thursday, October 29, 2026, CNBC's Jim Cramer said that Wall Street's reaction to the latest earnings from Microsoft and Alphabet shows that investors have shifted from rewarding heavy artificial intelligence spending to favoring financial discipline and returns. Earlier this year, Microsoft's restrained spending had raised worries that it could fall behind rivals, while Alphabet was rewarded for pouring money into data centers and custom chips. Cramer's comments followed Microsoft and Alphabet reports released Wednesday night, which he said changed that picture. Cramer's Charitable Trust, the portfolio run by CNBC's Investing Club, owns shares of both companies.

Microsoft beat earnings and revenue expectations, and revenue for its Azure cloud business grew 48% from a year earlier. Its capital expenditures and finance leases totaled $45.2 billion, below Wall Street's forecasts. Cramer praised the company for pairing strong cloud growth with positive free cash flow, and he said its AI assistant for businesses, Copilot, had started slowly but was becoming a strong success. Alphabet, by contrast, missed earnings and revenue expectations, with Search and YouTube ad revenue both coming in below estimates. Although Google Cloud revenue more than doubled, its shares fell sharply in Thursday's session, which Cramer described as the stock's worst day ever.

Cramer credited Microsoft's results to CEO Satya Nadella and CFO Amy Hood, whom he called a shrewd CEO and a tight-fisted, canny finance chief who run the company like a business rather than a science project. He said Microsoft's stock is now set to soar and that it is a buy at its current level. He was far more skeptical of Alphabet, arguing that its AI investments are harder to justify as cash generation weakens. The company expects capital expenditures of $195 billion to $205 billion this year, and its free cash flow turned negative for a second straight quarter. Cramer also flagged $27.6 billion in remaining authorized stock sales as a possible drag on shares, and he said he would not buy more Alphabet while waiting for analysts to revise their estimates.

Articles.Title: Jim Cramer says Microsoft is winning the AI spending battle — and Alphabet is paying the price

stories.Headline: Renuity builds a governed AI platform on Azure and lifts sales conversion in pilot
stories.Summary:
Renuity, a full-service home remodeling business operating across 40 states, has built a governed AI platform on Microsoft Azure, according to a Microsoft customer story published on October 30, 2026. The company had been held back by fragmented systems, inconsistent data models, and technical debt left over from acquisitions, which made it hard to innovate with AI or trust the data behind it. Renuity chose Azure as an integrated, governed data plane, with Azure Machine Learning and Microsoft Foundry handling AI development and operations, and it plans to use Microsoft Fabric as the unified data layer. The platform is meant to give new AI projects a repeatable foundation so they can be delivered in weeks rather than months.

The platform standardizes infrastructure through infrastructure as code and selected Azure services, including managed identities, Microsoft Entra ID access, private networking, and policy enforcement. Governance covering data lineage, feedback loops, testing, and productionization is also standardized. Renuity identified 40 business use cases for AI and scored them on ROI, business impact, efficiency gains, partner engagement, and data readiness. The first pilots focused on the Renuity East contact center, where a new lead-scoring model called Project LQS produced a significant uplift in net-sales-per-raw-lead conversion in an A/B test. A second project, Project ACE, automated daily lead assignment, cutting the task from about three and a half hours to roughly 20 minutes.

Mayank Rathi, Renuity's Chief Technology Officer, said that the platform stopped being an IT initiative and became a business enabler once the lead-scoring results showed up, and he argued that a platform yields compounding returns while a single proof of concept yields a one-time gain. Liping Wu, Senior Director for Data Science and AI, described the approach as building shared infrastructure ahead of time so the AI team can focus on solutions rather than setup. Justin Rosenblum, Chief of Staff, reported the conversion results from the pilot, and Herculano Fernandes, Call Center Vice President, said the time saved now goes to coaching and evaluating staff. The article says the call center team is next exploring agentic, next-best-action orchestration, with people kept in the loop for critical decisions.

Articles.Title: Renuity builds a governed AI platform on Azure and lifts sales conversion in pilot

stories.Headline: [Opening Market] KOSPI Opens Above 6,000 on Semiconductor Rally
stories.Summary:
On Thursday, Oct. 29, the KOSPI opened at 6017.22, up 0.08%, after closing with a steep surge in the 6% range the previous day. Foreign investors drove early gains with net purchases in the 200 billion won range, about $149.36 million. Retail investors also bought in the 200 billion won range, while institutional investors sold in the 500 billion won range. The KOSDAQ opened down 0.45% and widened its losses, trading around the 760 mark.

SK hynix had forecast a shareholder return policy reaching 100 trillion won, about $74.68 billion, along with its highest-ever performance. SK hynix rose more than 5% at one point and passed 1.55 million won, and SK Square rose more than 5%. Samsung Electronics gained 2.07% and exceeded 245,000 won ahead of its third-quarter results and shareholder return details later that day. The won-dollar exchange rate opened at 1,339.10 won, down 4.40 won or 0.33% from the previous day, and stood at 1,339.90 won as of 10:00 a.m.

Foreign investors were described as driving the index through net buying tied to large-cap stocks. Institutional selling was interpreted as profit taking and risk management after recent surges and short-term price burdens. In the KOSDAQ, retail investors bought in the 100 billion won range while foreign and institutional investors sold in the 70 billion won and 10 billion won ranges. Editor Park Jung-hwan wrote the article.

Experts said the market settled safely at the 6,000 mark on SK hynix-led semiconductor shareholder return momentum and performance expectations. They said KOSDAQ weakness and institutional profit taking partly limited the upside. They said the key to a sustained rally is whether strength spreads beyond semiconductors and whether foreign supply continues. They added that the exchange rate stabilizing in the 1,330 won range is expected to help additional foreign inflows.

Articles.Title: [Opening Market] KOSPI Opens Above 6,000 on Semiconductor Rally - Businesskorea

stories.Headline: Bessent Dismisses AI Financing Fears Despite Credit Market Warning Signs
stories.Summary:
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent dismissed concerns about AI financing in a CNBC interview on Oct. 28, saying double-digit yields on some AI-related debt were not problematic at all. He said neocloud companies, which rent out AI computing infrastructure, are only a small part of the wider AI ecosystem. He argued that trouble at individual operators does not necessarily signal a broader market crisis. He also said another Federal Reserve rate hike would not necessarily be a policy mistake.

Credit market data nonetheless showed strain. According to Bloomberg, at least 18 speculative-grade bonds and leveraged loans tied to data centers carried double-digit yields. JPMorgan Chase and Goldman Sachs changed the terms of a $5 billion loan for Volta Infrastructure, an AI infrastructure company, and the yield exceeded 11%. Morgan Stanley said yields on top-rated data center bonds approached 7%, up from less than 5% at the start of the year. Citadel Securities warned the financial burden could spread to the major technology firms backing these companies, and the cost of credit default swap protection on Oracle hit a record high last week.

Bessent stressed that financing and dealmaking were still continuing and that capital for AI investment had not dried up. He pointed to companies raising money in equity markets, including a reported $25 billion Meta financing transaction that drew demand more than five times the amount sought. Asked whether another Fed rate hike would be a mistake, he replied, not necessarily, hours after the central bank held its benchmark rate at 3.75% to 4.00%. Traders widely expect another increase in December, after last month's hike, the first in three years. Bessent also reaffirmed confidence in Fed Chair Kevin Warsh.

On Oct. 25, xAI CEO Elon Musk warned that companies without enough revenue beyond AI data centers had effectively been shut out of financing markets. He predicted that more than 200 neocloud operators could face widespread failures or consolidation, and CoreWeave has become a focal point of market concerns. Bessent said markets were already applying considerable tightening pressure on their own, with the 10-year Treasury yield above 5%. He described Operation Economic Outcast, the U.S. campaign to isolate Iran economically, as successful and said Iran's economy could contract by as much as 25% over one year. He said he had not yet seen third-quarter GDP figures due Oct. 29 but expected strong growth, while economists forecast 3.2%, up from 2.2% in the second quarter.

Articles.Title: Bessent Dismisses AI Financing Fears Despite Credit Market Warning Signs - Businesskorea

stories.Headline: AIMATICS Expands AI Video Telematics to Freight Operators
stories.Summary:
AIMATICS, an AI-based video recognition company, said on Oct. 16 that it plans to expand its driver scoring system to freight transport operators. The system had already been used in tanker trucks and ready-mix concrete vehicles. It records risky driving behavior through video and data, issues real-time warnings and provides customized training based on individual safety scores. The company announced the expansion in a report published on Oct. 19.

The system combines real-time footage from vehicle-mounted cameras with conventional telematics data, including GPS tracking and sensor readings. Its AI cameras monitor the driver and the road ahead, issuing real-time alerts for drowsy driving, mobile phone use, distracted driving or traffic signal violations. After each trip, the system calculates safety scores and rankings for individual drivers, and managers can then identify high-risk drivers and provide customized training. In the 2024 AI Video-Based Bus Safe Driving Monitoring Project with the Korea Transportation Safety Authority, which involved 500 vehicles and 1,808 drivers from 13 bus operators, drowsy driving incidents fell 99.7%, from 1.54 to 0.005 per 1,000 kilometers driven. Other risky behaviors also declined, including distracted driving down 93.4% and traffic signal violations down 87.6%.

An AIMATICS official said freight trucks often run long distances and at night, which raises the likelihood and risks of drowsy driving. The official said digital tachographs provide driving data such as speeding and sudden deceleration, but transport operators have limited ways to monitor drivers' conditions. The company said its system could help address these monitoring gaps. It uses AIMATICS' proprietary AI engine, aimNet, which the company says has been deployed in more than 520,000 vehicles and trained on driving data equivalent to approximately 3,500 years.

The system also uses technology that alters drivers' faces and voices, so operators can manage driving records and safety scores without identifying individuals. AIMATICS said modified files cannot be restored to their original form, which reduces privacy concerns tied to in-cabin cameras. Video analysis runs directly inside the camera using on-device AI, making it independent of network connectivity. The company said the system operates on chips costing around 20,000 won without expensive GPUs, enabling low-cost deployment across thousands of commercial vehicles. AIMATICS has supplied the system for Sampyo Industry's ready-mix concrete trucks and for tanker trucks run by a global hazardous materials transportation company, and it is discussing adoption with several freight operators, including major logistics companies.

Articles.Title: AIMATICS Expands AI Video Telematics to Freight Operators - www.thelec.net

stories.Headline: Indian American AI executive leaves Meta to co-found drug discovery startup - The American Bazaar
stories.Summary:
Manohar Paluri, an Indian American technology executive who spent 14 years at Meta, has left the company to co-found Warp Sciences, a startup that uses artificial intelligence and robotics to speed up drug discovery. The San Francisco Bay Area venture announced $215 million in Series A funding on Oct. 22, led by Lightspeed Venture Partners. Other investors include IVP, Mayfield, Lux Capital, Premji Invest and Menlo Ventures. Technology executives such as LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman, Coinbase co-founder Brian Armstrong and Figma co-founder Dylan Field also took part, according to the funding announcement and published reports.

Warp Sciences is building U.S.-based laboratory infrastructure that combines artificial intelligence, robotics and chemistry to help pharmaceutical and biotechnology companies make and test molecules. The company plans to begin with lead optimization in small-molecule drug discovery, which means making and evaluating variations of promising compounds so researchers can decide which ones merit further development. Experienced chemists will work with AI tools and robotic lab equipment, and early scientists will handle customer projects while they help validate the technology. The company also plans a preclinical contract research organization to make and test molecules for customers. Warp Sciences says it will provide research infrastructure rather than develop its own drugs, and customers will keep control of their drug programs.

Paluri is a co-founder and chief technology officer of the company, which also counts CEO Kevin Weil, a former OpenAI chief product officer, and COO DJ Patil, the first U.S. chief data scientist, among its founders. Solomon Reisberg, a former Terremoto Biosciences executive, is also a co-founder. Paluri joined Facebook, now Meta, in 2012 as a computer vision researcher and rose to vice president by 2024. He announced his departure in September, saying he was leaving after 14 years at the company. Weil has argued that AI has transformed software engineering and mathematics, while the physical sciences have yet to see a comparable impact.

The company's model places laboratory work at the center of its AI strategy, with researchers setting the questions, AI helping design experiments and robots carrying them out. The resulting data is meant to inform future experiments and improve AI performance over time. With the new funding, Warp Sciences plans to build scientific research capacity in the United States and help drug developers run chemistry experiments more efficiently. The articles do not say when the first facilities will open or when customers will begin work.

Articles.Title: Indian American AI executive leaves Meta to co-found drug discovery startup - The American Bazaar

stories.Headline: Firms Face 200 AI Data Violations a Month, Security Frameworks Must Be Redesigned
stories.Summary:
Lee Gun-young, head of the Financial AI Center at EY Hanyoung, gave a keynote speech at the 31st Seoul Economic Daily Financial Strategy Forum on Nov. 29 at the Westin Josun Hotel in Jung-gu, Seoul. He said global companies record more than 200 generative AI data policy violations a month on average. Citing the 2026 Cloud and Threat Report from security firm Netskope, he said violations at Netskope client companies averaged 223 per organization each month, double the figure from a year earlier. Source code made up 42% of exposed data, followed by regulated data such as personal and financial information at 32% and intellectual property at 16%.

Lee said AI adoption at financial institutions has moved beyond the pilot stage. In the 2026 survey on AI use in financial services by the Institute of International Finance and EY, 98% of global financial institutions said they had applied AI to actual operations, and the share deploying agentic AI rose to 70% this year from 23% a year earlier. He said AI use is expanding faster than control systems are being put in place, with risks around control and visibility and around decision-making. He also said security management at Korean companies is falling short, citing Cisco's 2025 Cybersecurity Readiness Index, released in May last year, in which 83% of Korean companies said they were not confident in detecting unapproved AI tools and more than 66% said they struggled to respond to threats even while operating 10 or more security solutions.

Lee said cybersecurity management frameworks must be redesigned to cover the entire process of AI use. Companies should clarify the purpose and permitted scope of AI use, the boundaries for data and model use and the structure of accountability, and build security orchestration that integrates detection and response across multiple security systems. He urged firms to go beyond using AI safely and to create business value and reinvest it, citing Singapore's DBS Bank, which generated more than 1 billion Singapore dollars in economic value from AI last year. He said work should be redesigned so AI handles market analysis and proposes adjustments while people focus on verification and final judgment, and that productivity standards should shift from output to outcome. He also called for strategic reinvestment through partnerships with or acquisitions of outside AI companies, pointing to Ode, an AI services company set up through a partnership involving U.S. private equity firm Blackstone and AI company Anthropic.

Articles.Title: Firms Face 200 AI Data Violations a Month, Security Frameworks Must Be Redesigned - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: Comment: Is regulating AI in the NHS the right decision?
stories.Summary:
Joe McDonald, a former NHS consultant psychiatrist and member of The Access Group's health and care advisory board, has published a comment piece on 29 October 2026 arguing that AI regulation in the NHS is necessary, but only if regulators can keep pace with the technology. He opens by describing the long-running tension between regulation and innovation, which he says is being tested sharply by artificial intelligence in healthcare. He notes that a large language model can be revised very quickly and may behave differently from one hospital to another. He also points out that warnings from some experts about advanced AI threatening humanity may prove overblown, but that the technology is moving faster than those who use and oversee it.

McDonald contrasts this with the Apollo moon landing, which he says succeeded because it sat outside the rules that governed ordinary aviation and accepted risks no safety regime would have allowed. He then turns to the National Commission's recent recommendations for AI, which he praises for recognising the problem. He argues that AI cannot be regulated like a medicine or conventional device, because a drug stays the same after licensing while an AI system can change after deployment, learn from new data, and drift from its approved use. The report's central recommendation, as he describes it, is proportionate, lifecycle regulation with continuous oversight rather than a single assessment at market entry.

He calls the framework deliberately permissive, accepting that these tools are already in clinical use. McDonald does not consider the work finished. He notes there are 44 recommendations, many asking the MHRA or the department to "consider" action rather than commit to it. He says the report does not explain how any of this will be funded or who will carry it out, and warns that an under-resourced regulator is being asked to match well-funded technology.

He welcomes the clinical grounding of the work and the emphasis on keeping a human in the loop. He also suggests the Commission should collaborate more closely with AI experts and vendors if the recommendations are approved. For frontline staff, he says the practical effect is permission to keep using tools such as ambient voice technology and AI assistance, with a framework forming around them. He concludes that whether a regulator can keep pace with the technology it governs remains the open question that matters most.

Articles.Title: Comment: Is regulating AI in the NHS the right decision?

stories.Headline: Three years to the point of no return? Gates warns of losing control over AI - RBC-Ukraine
stories.Summary:
Bill Gates has warned that rapid AI development could soon let machines surpass human cognitive abilities entirely, and that humanity is nearing a point where controlling these systems becomes one of its greatest challenges. He made the remarks at a meeting of the Royal Society in London, as reported by The Observer. Gates compared the emergence of artificial intelligence to an evolutionary event that will change the very concept of intelligence on Earth. He said new systems already outperform people in many fields, and that programming skills he had cultivated since age 13 have become obsolete.

Gates outlined several risks he expects in the coming years. He said algorithms will begin to outperform humans in mathematical research, engineering and biological modeling, and that AI will gradually displace both white-collar and blue-collar workers, with humanoid robots taking over physical work. Within three to four years, he said, alignment control and the ability of algorithms to improve themselves recursively will become critically important. He also warned that AI could be out of control before the next World Cup, and he flagged cybersecurity and bioterrorism as particular concerns. According to him, AI-enabled pandemics could surpass COVID-19 in scale.

Gates argues that the current structure of capitalism encourages companies to hire robots en masse and dismiss workers without regard to the consequences. In his view, government tax revenues would fall just when authorities need large sums to support people and retrain workers. He proposes two main responses: reserving a category of professions for humans, and introducing a tax on AI tokens to fund social protection and offset lost jobs. He also urged the United States and China to cooperate on regulation, warning that an uncontrolled AI arms race threatens all of humanity.

Despite these warnings, Gates continues to direct funding through his foundation toward global health. The article reports that he plans to close the foundation by 2045, after using advanced technologies to help eliminate malaria, polio and child mortality. The article presents his warnings as part of a broader debate about how society should manage the economic and security effects of AI. The articles do not say what specific steps governments or companies will take in response.

Articles.Title: Three years to the point of no return? Gates warns of losing control over AI - RBC-Ukraine

stories.Headline: Samsung Nears 40% HBM Share, Doubles Long-Term Supply Deals
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics said on October 29, 2026, that it is pursuing a medium- to long-term growth strategy centered on next-generation high-bandwidth memory, or HBM, after becoming the first global technology company to post quarterly operating profit above 100 trillion won in the third quarter. The company is focusing on three pillars: reclaiming the top spot in the HBM market now held by SK hynix, locking in future demand through long-term agreements and infrastructure investment, and narrowing losses at its foundry business. Samsung's HBM market share rose to the high 30% range in the third quarter, up from around 20% in the first quarter and 33% in the second quarter, according to industry accounts. The gain brought Samsung close to 40%, within striking distance of SK hynix at about 50%.

Kim Jae-joon, executive vice president of the memory business at Samsung's Device Solutions division, said on a third-quarter earnings conference call that the goal of securing an HBM market share on par with the company's DRAM share in the second half appeared to have already been achieved in the third quarter. He said HBM4 revenue tripled from the previous quarter and its share of total HBM revenue expanded to around 60%. He also said Samsung has completed long-term agreements with 10 large customers and is in negotiations with another 10 major customers, with a goal of raising the share of memory volume supplied under such agreements to 60% of total capacity by 2030. The number of long-term agreement customers doubled in a single quarter from the five Samsung disclosed in late July, and the total could rise to 20 by the end of this year or early next year.

Capital expenditure this year came in higher than initially expected at 84.4 trillion won, up 60% from last year, after Samsung decided early this year to spend 110 trillion won on capital expenditure and research and development combined. Investment accelerated at new fabs in Yongin, Gwangju in Jeolla Province and Taylor, Texas, and the company decided to spend more than 10 trillion won above the original plan. Kang Seok-chae, executive vice president of Samsung's foundry business, said demand far exceeds capacity for advanced processes at 8 nanometers and below, with utilization expected to top 100% in the second half. He said Samsung plans to more than double the number of 2-nanometer order wins from last year, and the foundry division is estimated to have posted an operating loss of 1 trillion to 2 trillion won in the third quarter, while some brokerages expect a return to quarterly profit as early as the second half of next year.

Eugene Investment & Securities projects the average selling price of HBM will more than double to $3.48 per gigabit next year from $1.65 this year, while commodity DRAM is expected to reach only $2.34 next year from $1.71 this year. Demand for HBM4 is surging as it is used in the latest AI chips, including Nvidia's Vera Rubin. Beyond the fourth quarter, HBM4E will enter mass production in the first half of next year following HBM4, with volumes set to increase significantly through a ramp-up in the second half. Samsung is pursuing extensions beyond the existing maximum five-year terms with long-term agreement customers, and in foundry it will break ground on a second plant in Taylor this year and is already discussing orders ahead of building out its 1.4-nanometer process, targeted for 2029.

Articles.Title: Samsung Nears 40% HBM Share, Doubles Long-Term Supply Deals - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: AI Hacking Spreads, but 97% of Korean Firms Report Security Staff Shortages
stories.Summary:
At the 31st Seoul Economic Daily Financial Strategy Forum, held at the Westin Josun Seoul in Jung-gu, Seoul, on the 29th, speakers addressed South Korea's cybersecurity weaknesses as AI-driven hacking attacks spread. Lee Gun-young, head of EY Hanyoung's Financial AI Center, said most financial institutions complain of a shortage of AI security personnel. He said the network separation environment has left insufficient systems for financial security staff to grow or be trained. According to EY Analysis, a Cisco survey of 8,000 security executives in 30 countries found that 97% of participating South Korean companies said they lacked security personnel. Lee said domestic cybersecurity is highly vulnerable compared with major countries, calling it the result of structural limits across organization, governance, resources and systems.

Shin Jin-chang, vice chairman of the Financial Services Commission, delivered the keynote address and also pointed to the need for stronger security frameworks. He said a review of security management systems at 555 domestic financial companies found that 25% were vulnerable, and most of them were small and mid-sized financial firms. He added that some large financial firms also have weak points, so the shortcomings need to be addressed. The FSC signaled it would continue easing regulations so the industry can actively use AI. The second round of selections for easing network separation rules, provisionally postponed after recent hacking incidents in the financial sector, will resume once a supplementary review is completed.

Shin said the FSC takes seriously the criticism that the Information Security Management System is ineffective, and it will re-examine whether the certification framework and standards are appropriate. He said whether banks are allocating an appropriate share of their budgets to security is also under review. He said setting investment amounts in absolute terms could be an easy solution that does not account for side effects, and that the matter would be examined. Lee said it is important not simply to lock the door but to manage the flow so that incidents do not occur.

Articles.Title: AI Hacking Spreads, but 97% of Korean Firms Report Security Staff Shortages - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: HD Hyundai Heavy Develops AI Ship Coating Inspection System
stories.Summary:
HD Hyundai Heavy Industries developed an artificial intelligence-based inspection system for ship coating quality, the first of its kind in South Korea's shipbuilding industry, and is pushing to make it a global standard. The company announced on the 29th that it had signed a memorandum of understanding on advancing AI technology with four classification societies, Lloyd's Register, the American Bureau of Shipping, DNV and the Korean Register. The signing took place at its human resources development center in Ulsan's Dong District on Sept. 29. HD Korea Shipbuilding & Offshore Engineering and HD Hyundai Samho also joined the agreement. The system is called AI CIP, or AI Coating InsPector, and it combines vision AI and deep learning to automatically identify and analyze coating defects on ships.

HD Hyundai Heavy Industries and the AX Center of HD Korea Shipbuilding & Offshore Engineering have jointly developed the system since 2024, training the AI on coating quality data gathered from shipyards. Coating inspections on newly built ships had relied on workers' eyes and experience, so results varied with the inspector's level of skill. The company said it recently completed technical reviews with major classification societies, laying the groundwork to shift inspections from subjective judgment to an objective, data-based framework. Under the agreement, HD Hyundai Heavy Industries and HD Hyundai Samho will expand use of the system at their yards and upgrade their data collection and management systems. HD Korea Shipbuilding & Offshore Engineering will improve the program's performance and verify its compatibility with different coatings and systems.

The four classification societies will cooperate on technical reviews and on establishing standard inspection procedures to ensure the reliability of inspection results. An official at HD Hyundai Heavy Industries said introducing the AI coating inspection system had secured consistency in inspections and made quantitative quality analysis possible through accumulated data, and that the company would work with classification societies to raise confidence in the technology and broaden the scope of AI-based quality management. HD Hyundai Heavy Industries said it will continue technical cooperation with major classification societies to improve transparency in quality control procedures and build trust with shipowners. The company framed the agreement as a step toward wider AI-based quality management in its yards. The article does not say what further steps or timelines follow beyond that continued cooperation.

Articles.Title: HD Hyundai Heavy Develops AI Ship Coating Inspection System - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: AI Debt Wrecks Earnings Season for Hyperscalers
stories.Summary:
Alphabet, Google's parent company, reported third-quarter results after the market closed on October 28, 2026, and its shares fell 12.64% the next day. Nearly $500 billion in market value vanished in a single day, the second-largest such loss in New York market history after Nvidia's $593 billion drop on January 27 last year. Revenue was $127.58 billion, up 25% from a year earlier but about $600 million short of the $128.22 billion LSEG estimate. Earnings per share of $2.12 fell well below Wall Street's $3.02 estimate, and excluding valuation losses on stakes in SpaceX and Anthropic, EPS was only $2.67.

Alphabet's third-quarter capital expenditure rose to $51.36 billion, and free cash flow was negative $9.065 billion, after negative free cash flow in the second quarter for the first time since its 2004 listing. Google Cloud revenue rose 103% to $30.71 billion, and Google Services revenue rose 11% to $96.3 billion, but search revenue of about $63 billion fell short of the $65 billion estimate. Microsoft, whose fiscal 2027 first-quarter results covered July through September, reported revenue of $92.279 billion, up 19%, net profit of $36.63 billion, up 32%, and EPS of $4.89, all above LSEG estimates. Microsoft issued at least $25 billion in dollar-denominated bonds, its first bond issuance in nine years since 2017, in 10 tranches with maturities from two to 40 years, drawing more than $115 billion in orders.

Amazon reported third-quarter revenue of $201.94 billion, up 12% but below the $202.31 billion estimate, and EPS of $1.89 missed the $1.96 expectation. Its trailing 12-month free cash flow was negative $42.4 billion, widening nearly sixfold from $7.6 billion in the second quarter, after a $94.8 billion yearly surge in property and equipment purchases, and it kept its capital expenditure forecast at $220 billion. Intel's third-quarter revenue rose 21% to $16.51 billion and EPS of 52 cents beat the 41-cent estimate, but its client computing division revenue fell 5% to $8.1 billion. Intel guided fourth-quarter revenue to $15 billion to $16 billion, below the $17.1 billion LSEG estimate, and its shares traded more than 23% lower in after-hours trading.

Alphabet Chief Executive Sundar Pichai said an across-the-board approach to AI was driving the entire business. Amazon Chief Executive Andy Jassy said he expected AWS to grow more than 40% next year and in 2028. Meta shares had already tumbled 6.98% the day after its third-quarter results on October 21, with capital expenditure of $34.91 billion, negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion, and non-cancellable AI-related contracts totaling $825 billion, above the $700 billion reported in July. Market participants have been unusually sensitive to AI-related debt since October 14, when corporate bonds from CoreWeave and other neocloud companies came under concern over distress, and Bloomberg projected the PC market would contract 12% this year and another 10% next year.

Articles.Title: AI Debt Wrecks Earnings Season for Hyperscalers - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: Content And Context Matter When Your Clients Use AI
stories.Summary:
Courts have begun ruling on whether clients' use of AI chatbots to research their disputes is protected from discovery, and the question is changing how lawyers should handle client communications. According to a commentary by Nicole Black published on abovethelaw.com on October 29, 2026, several recent decisions have addressed the issue. The article says that clients often use AI tools without telling their lawyers, and that a single chatbot query could affect the outcome of a case. It also notes that courts look at the stage of litigation and whether the user was represented or appearing without counsel. Courts have reached different conclusions about whether the work-product doctrine applies to such research.

In Morgan v. V2X, Inc., a federal court in Colorado found that a pro se plaintiff had a reasonable expectation of privacy in his AI use, so work-product protection could apply despite the tool's training practices. In Assini v. Hayward, a New York Supreme Court justice reached a similar result because the responses were prepared for litigation.

The article explains that whether using a third-party AI platform waives that protection remains unsettled, with some courts treating the chats as disclosure to a third party and others treating the tools as ordinary technology. Black cites these cases to show that the answer depends on the facts. The most recent example described is Fontainebleau Florida Hotel, LLC v. Botach, decided earlier this month, in which a represented defendant researched using AI on his own initiative.

A magistrate judge in the Southern District of Florida held that using an AI tool did not automatically waive work product, and that some of the defendant's AI-assisted research could be protected. However, the court found that queries aimed at public statements or the defendant's independent activities were not covered, and it required the defendant to describe the withheld material well enough for the plaintiff to assess the claim. The article attributes this reasoning to the court and contrasts it with United States v. Heppner, where independent research not done at counsel's direction was held unprotected.

Black's practical advice is that lawyers should ask clients early whether they have discussed the dispute with an AI tool and what they shared, and make that inquiry part of intake. She recommends explaining how AI use can affect a case and asking clients to tell counsel when they interact with chatbots about the litigation. According to the article, the answers can help lawyers anticipate discovery disputes before they arise. Black concludes that transparency at the start of a case will matter more as AI becomes more common, and she writes that clients will use these tools whether lawyers like it or not.

Articles.Title: Content And Context Matter When Your Clients Use AI

stories.Headline: Google's Search and Ad Revenue Falls Short, Deepening AI Spending Doubts
stories.Summary:
Alphabet, Google's parent company, reported third-quarter results on the 28th that fell short of market expectations. Revenue for July through September reached $127.58 billion, below the $128.22 billion consensus estimate compiled by the London Stock Exchange Group. Earnings per share came in at $2.12, far below Wall Street's expected $3.02. The shortfall stemmed from weaker-than-expected advertising and search sales, while cloud revenue beat expectations at $30.7 billion.

The services segment brought in $96.3 billion, below the $98.5 billion analysts had projected. Google had guided this year's capital expenditures to between $195 billion and $205 billion, more than double last year's spending. Free cash flow was negative $9.1 billion in the third quarter, the second consecutive quarter in the red, after a negative $5.9 billion in the second quarter, its first since going public. The company also announced an $85 billion stock sale plan in June, its first new share issuance since 2005.

Analysts said the weaker-than-expected revenue and profit, along with worsening cash flow, have amplified investor concerns about the massive AI outlays. The Wall Street Journal said Google is working to develop AI models and integrate them into consumer products such as its search engine, YouTube and Gmail, but has yet to justify the enormous scale of its investment, and the same holds for search revenue. Investor disappointment mounted immediately after the report, sending Alphabet down 8.98% in after-hours trading as of 4:52 p.m. Eastern time. Google is spending more on AI than ever before in an effort to overturn the view that it is falling behind OpenAI and Anthropic in the race to develop AI models.

Articles.Title: Google's Search and Ad Revenue Falls Short, Deepening AI Spending Doubts - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: Judge Sends FTC’s Case Against Syngenta’s Key AI Rebates to a Jury - The Scoop
stories.Summary:
A federal judge has declined to throw out the Federal Trade Commission's case against Syngenta's Key AI loyalty rebate program, ruling on October 22 that a jury could find the program kept generic crop protection products out of distributor channels and kept grower prices higher than competition would have. U.S. District Judge Thomas D. Schroeder denied Syngenta's motion for summary judgment in the Middle District of North Carolina. The ruling does not find that Syngenta broke the law, since the court viewed the evidence in the light most favorable to the plaintiffs and left the disputed facts for trial. Syngenta said the court did not determine that it violated antitrust laws and that the plaintiffs keep the burden of proving their claims. The FTC leads the case, joined by 12 states, and Corteva, a co-defendant, has reached a proposed settlement that is pending court approval.

The court noted that five distributors dominating the traditional channel control at least 61% of the crop protection sales market through their integrated retail chains. Key AI required distributors to source over 90% of certain active ingredients from Syngenta, including azoxystrobin, mesotrione and metolachlor, and the thresholds left little room for generics. One distributor executive testified his company would have bought less than 50% of its azoxystrobin and mesotrione from Syngenta without the program, yet it bought between 89.6% and 100% of those products from the company. A distributor that carried its own generic line missed thresholds in 2016 and 2017, and Syngenta terminated it in 2017 until another company acquired it in 2020. Other distributors testified that cutting off access was the nuclear option and that leaving the program would be suicide for their ability to sell Syngenta products.

The judge wrote that Syngenta's own documents show it acknowledges Key AI is designed to maintain higher prices, and she cited a 2015 forecast of 50% to 60% price erosion for azoxystrobin if loyalty partners did not support the brand and generics entered. She also said that generic penetration in the market, which reached 36% at its peak, does not end the question, because a jury could find that generic entry remains substantially foreclosed. Syngenta argues that Key AI is a lawful pricing practice that sells above cost, that loyalty programs are common in the industry, and that distributors pass savings to growers. It also maintains that generic barriers to entry are low and that the termination was mutual. The court left those arguments for the jury to weigh, and the case will proceed to trial with the FTC and the states seeking to show that Key AI illegally restrained trade.

Articles.Title: Judge Sends FTC’s Case Against Syngenta’s Key AI Rebates to a Jury - The Scoop -
