stories.Headline: Samsung's AI Boom Delivers Bad News for Its Phones
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics reported a record third-quarter profit on October 29, 2026, as the AI memory boom lifted its semiconductor business, but its stock still fell. Operating profit surged to 107.4 trillion won, up from 12.2 trillion won a year earlier. Semiconductor operating profit jumped roughly 15-fold to 106.5 trillion won, meaning the chip division generated virtually all of the group's quarterly operating profit. The driver was AI, and Samsung said its high-bandwidth memory supply is already sold out for 2027, with major customers asking for more.

Samsung expects AI infrastructure spending to reach a historic level next year and said demand growth should significantly outpace industry supply. It also expects the broader memory market to remain tight through 2028, even as it accelerates spending. Chip capital expenditures are expected to rise 62% to 76.8 trillion won in 2026, with another sharp increase planned next year as the company adds capacity. Samsung said it would finalize its next capital-return policy in January, despite expectations for a fresh buyback or dividend announcement, and it previously said 2026 shareholder returns would total between 90 trillion and 110 trillion won.

Investors wanted more, and Samsung shares fell as much as 6.2% after the company offered a more conservative shortage outlook than SK Hynix. SK Hynix recently said DRAM and HBM capacity was effectively sold out through 2029 and shortages could persist into 2030. Samsung is expanding long-term supply agreements that could eventually cover 60% to 70% of production capacity by 2030. The articles say the key things to watch are HBM pricing, long-term contracts, capex, foundry losses, and Samsung's January shareholder-return decision.

Articles.Title: Samsung's AI Boom Delivers Bad News for Its Phones - TradingView

stories.Headline: Harvey Inks Deal to Acquire AI Sales Platform Aida
stories.Summary:
Harvey announced on Thursday, October 29, 2026, that it has acquired Aida, an AI-powered sales platform. The legal AI startup did not disclose the financial details of the deal in its press release. Aida was founded in 2024 by Atish Das Sarma, formerly head of growth engineering at Patreon, and Piyush Prahladka, a co-founder of the data platform Glean. The acquisition is the fifth company Harvey has added this year.

Aida offers sales-related capabilities that include risk detection for deals, performance metric reporting, note-taking and email drafting for company leadership. Aida and its search and machine-learning engineers will support Harvey's engineering capabilities. The addition is meant to help Harvey's AI agents make better use of legal and business context. The deal will also support the engineering of Harvey's context layer and how it interacts with its AI agents.

Harvey is the company responsible for the acquisition, and it announced the deal in a press release. The release gave no financial terms, so the price Harvey is paying for Aida is not public. The founders of Aida are Atish Das Sarma and Piyush Prahladka, and the company was set up in 2024. The articles do not include direct comments from Harvey or Aida beyond the stated purpose of the deal.

The acquisition fits into Harvey's run of purchases, since Aida is the fifth addition to its acquisition streak this year. The articles describe the deal as supporting Harvey's engineering work and its AI agents rather than as a standalone product launch. Beyond the announced benefits to Harvey's context layer and agents, the articles do not say what happens next for Aida's platform or its staff. No timeline for closing the deal is given.

Articles.Title: Harvey Inks Deal to Acquire AI Sales Platform Aida

stories.Headline: Chinese-Made HBM Spot Prices Top Imports by 5%-10% as Mature-Generation Quotes Near $110 Red Line
stories.Summary:
In the fourth quarter of 2026, China's AI compute supply chain showed a structural split in memory, according to BigGo Finance. Contract prices for single-stack HBM3E and HBM4, the international frontier generations, climbed above $200 to $300. Procurement prices for mature-generation HBM2 and HBM2E used in mainstream Chinese accelerator cards rose from $30 to $40 to $95 to $120. Spot quotes for Chinese-made HBM ran about 5% to 10% above comparable imports from Samsung and SK Hynix, approaching the downstream tolerance limit of $110 per unit.

The article attributes the price inversion to three overlapping factors. Chinese HBM production lines are still in the yield-ramp phase, with a blended yield of about 25% and a next-stage target of 40% to 50%, and early equipment depreciation and trial-production outlays are large. Core buyers such as Huawei's Ascend, Cambricon and Hygon Information Technology are on export-control entity lists, so incremental demand flows back to China's limited spot supply and domestic lines. Channel research expects China's total demand for high-compute chips in 2027 to reach 3.5 million to 4 million units, with Huawei's Ascend series alone at no fewer than 2.4 million on a conservative view.

Huawei is responding with a tiered memory architecture. The Ascend 950DT carries self-developed HiZQ 2.0 memory with 144GB capacity and 4.0TB/s bandwidth, about 60% to 65% of 950-series shipments. The Ascend 950PR carries low-cost HiBL 1.0 with 128GB capacity and 1.6TB/s bandwidth, bringing the end-unit card price down to roughly 50,000 yuan, about $7,500, and together they account for about 35% to 40% of shipments. The tiered approach is expected to extend to the Ascend 960 series in 2027, with samples in the first quarter and volume shipments in the third quarter on a full-year plan of about 400,000 to 500,000 cards.

The article says capacity expansions at CXMT and YMTC are seen as key to easing the shortage. CXMT's total DRAM capacity is about 320,000 to 330,000 wafers per month and is expected to expand to about 420,000 in 2027, with HBM3 shipments targeted at about 50,000 wafers for the year. YMTC's total capacity is expected to reach 300,000 wafers per month once Phase III is fully loaded in 2027. The supply-demand gap in Chinese high-bandwidth memory is expected to ease gradually in the second half of 2027.

Articles.Title: Chinese-Made HBM Spot Prices Top Imports by 5%-10% as Mature-Generation Quotes Near $110 Red Line - BigGo Finance

stories.Headline: TSMC Expands AP7, AP8 as CoWoS Capacity Remains Tight
stories.Summary:
TSMC and 精材 (3374) are linked to a potential purchase of two 友達 (2409) factories for more than NT$20 billion, according to a report published on October 29, 2026. The plants, L7A and L5C, are in Taiwan's Central Taiwan Science Park and sit beside TSMC's Fab 15. L5C makes laptop panels, while L7A began operating in 2006 and primarily produces television panels along with some monitor panels. Both factories remain in operation, and the transaction has not been confirmed.

If the reported price is reached, it would exceed the NT$17.1 billion sale of an Innolux factory. The final price, scope and division of buyer roles have not been disclosed. The report comes as CoWoS capacity remains tight and TSMC expands its AP7 and AP8 advanced-packaging facilities. TSMC owns about 41% of 精材 and is its largest customer, accounting for more than 70% of 精材's revenue. 精材's P2 plant has about 23,000 square meters of clean-room space and is already at capacity.

The two companies are also working on a 12-inch integrated voltage regulator process using backside copper for high-performance computing chips. Validation and pilot production could be completed as early as late 2026, with mass production projected to begin in the second half of 2027. If a sale proceeds, 友達 plans to requalify products at other factories to maintain supply. The transfer and closing are expected around the end of 2027.

Articles.Title: TSMC Expands AP7, AP8 as CoWoS Capacity Remains Tight - www.tokenpost.com

stories.Headline: Analysts followed an AI's hidden preferences in 86% of choices, Anthropic finds
stories.Summary:
An Anthropic study published on October 27, 2026, found that professional analysts agreed with an AI's deliberately assigned preferences in 86% of their analytical choices. Researchers secretly gave the agent, Claude Code running Opus 4.8 at High effort, preferences chosen by coin flip while telling it to make honest arguments and respond to evidence. The participants were 61 recruited professionals, and 50 of them used the agent to evaluate a fictional farming programme. Each of four analytical decisions offered two defensible options, such as which measure of productivity to use. The figure covers those decisions and excludes final recommendations.

The article stresses that the 86% figure measures influence rather than how often the choices were wrong. The experiment deliberately strengthened the agent's preferences, so the result reflects a deliberately amplified condition. The choices mattered because they could change the estimated benefit of the farming programme. Anthropic cautions that a single task and model cannot establish how large this effect would be in everyday work. The findings therefore point to a risk for analysts who rely on AI assistance without checking it.

Anthropic is the company that conducted and published the study, and the article attributes the caution about generalising the results to the company. The article does not name the individual analysts beyond the recruited pool, nor does it describe any changes that Anthropic or participants made in response. The source is a mixed-news.com article by Shane S. Ellison, and it does not give further detail on the study's methods or any follow-up work. The article also includes a note that some links to online stores may be affiliate links that earn the publisher a commission. The article does not say what further studies or changes are planned.

Articles.Title: Analysts followed an AI's hidden preferences in 86% of choices, Anthropic finds

stories.Headline: SK Hynix Creates Americas Chief Post, Taps President Ahn Hyun to Spearhead US Big Tech HBM Push
stories.Summary:
SK Hynix carried out a president-level reshuffle effective November 1 and created a new president-level organization called the Americas Chief, based in the United States. President Ahn Hyun, who had led development of AI memory including HBM and SOCAMM, was named to head the new unit. The company announced the regular personnel appointment on October 30. Ahn will build a response system for US big tech customers.

Cha Sun-yong, head of the Future Technology Research Institute, was named to lead development, the post left vacant by Ahn's move. He will also keep his role at the institute, strengthening the link between advanced technology research and product development. Yoon Poong-young, who headed the Global Growth Task Force, moves to lead the Corporate Center. CEO Kwak Noh-jung was retained, after SK Hynix posted record results for six consecutive quarters.

The company described Ahn as the right person, combining technical expertise and leadership with business, strategic and global capabilities. It said he will work to strengthen technical leadership and R&D capabilities. The company expects Cha to lead next-generation memory technology development based on his expertise in advanced semiconductor technology. Yoon will lead global business expansion and the hunt for new growth engines.

The market views the reshuffle as weighted toward mid- to long-term customer relationships and the technology roadmap rather than short-term results. HBM is an essential component in AI accelerators, making joint development between suppliers and customers from the design stage increasingly important. With AI memory demand continuing, the depth of cooperation with US big tech has emerged as a variable that will determine leadership in the next HBM generation transition. Through the reshuffle, SK Hynix plans to strengthen US customer response, enhance the link between research and product development, and accelerate global business expansion.

Articles.Title: SK Hynix Creates Americas Chief Post, Taps President Ahn Hyun to Spearhead US Big Tech HBM Push - BigGo Finance

stories.Headline: Human-Centred AI and Social Benefits: artificial intelligence in the service of people - Ambasciata d'Italia a Londra
stories.Summary:
A workshop titled "Human-Centred AI and Societal Benefits" was held at the Embassy of Italy in London on the day before the article was published, on 28 October 2026. It was organised with the University of Manchester and Sapiente Education, and researchers, experts and civil society representatives discussed how to build artificial intelligence around people so that it generates trust, transparency and concrete benefits for everyone. The central question was not whether AI will change society but how it will do so and for whose benefit. The debate reflected Italy's position as the first European Union country to adopt a national law on AI, which has been in force since October 2025.

That law rests on the principle that AI should strengthen human decision-making and accountability rather than replace them, with human supervision at every stage. The discussion was moderated by Professor Angelo Cangelosi of the Manchester Centre for Robotics and AI, an expert in robotics and human-robot interaction. Speakers included Vincenzo Naschi, president of the Human Economic Forum, Alberto Bernacchia of MediaTek Research in Cambridge, Gabriella Pizzuto of the University of Liverpool, and Cristina Becchio, who works in cognitive neuroscience at the University of Hamburg. The organisers presented the event as evidence of strong ties between Italian and British academic and research communities. The article notes that many Italian researchers at leading British and European institutions show the contribution of Italian talent to progress in AI.

The article does not describe any further steps, follow-up commitments or outcomes from the workshop. It is a news item published on the Embassy's website, so its account of the discussion comes from the Embassy itself. The page also lists other events the Embassy has hosted in 2025 and 2026, including a September 2026 trade delegation and a July 2026 space exploration event. Beyond this, the articles do not say what will come next for the initiative.

Articles.Title: Human-Centred AI and Social Benefits: artificial intelligence in the service of people - Ambasciata d'Italia a Londra

stories.Headline: Ashling Recognized by Microsoft for Capabilities in Data, AI, and Apps
stories.Summary:
Ashling, a global AI and automation consulting firm, announced on October 29, 2026 that it has achieved the Microsoft Solutions Partner for Cloud & AI Platforms designation. The firm earned recognition in two pathways, Data & AI and Digital & App Innovation. The announcement was distributed through PR Newswire from Chicago. Microsoft grants these Solutions Designations based on a partner's performance, skilling, and customer success. The Data & AI pathway covers data foundations and AI solutions that let enterprises put intelligent automation and coded agents into production with governance built in.

The Digital & App Innovation pathway covers modernizing and building applications that support automation at scale and connect new AI capabilities to existing business systems. Ashling says the press release describes a shift in enterprises from AI pilots to AI in production, where the central question is now what can be governed, integrated, and sustained. Earning two designations, the company says, reflects sustained client delivery and a bench of certified Ashling practitioners. Co-CEO Don Sweeney said the firm's team has spent years building and running automation and AI programs inside complex enterprises, and that this experience shapes its focus on governance, scale, and adoption. Co-CEO Marshall Sied said the strongest validation comes after go-live, when clients expand programs, bring in new teams, and entrust the firm with more operations.

The company also cites its validated agentic operating model, its development accelerators, and a multimodal approach that matches each use case with a suited technology. Ashling describes itself as a firm with a team of 250+ specialists, and the release gives a media contact in Chicago. Because this is a paid press release distributed by the company itself, its claims about performance and client outcomes come from Ashling and have not been independently verified in the material provided. The release does not describe any specific client engagements or outcomes beyond general statements. It also does not say what future steps, if any, follow from the designations.

Articles.Title: Ashling Recognized by Microsoft for Capabilities in Data, AI, and Apps

stories.Headline: Google Starved Out Publishers With AI Search. Now, Its Pivot Is Blowing Up in Its Face.
stories.Summary:
Google's parent company Alphabet saw its shares fall more than 11 percent on Wednesday, October 29, 2026, after the company disclosed that its AI search features were earning less money than its traditional search advertising. The drop erased more than $500 billion in market value. In its third-quarter report, Google posted quarterly revenue of $127.6 billion, up 25 percent year over year, but capital spending more than doubled from last year to $51.4 billion, driven largely by its AI investments. Search revenue grew 12 percent to $63.3 billion, slower than the 14.5 percent growth of the same period last year, even though Google Search handled more queries than ever.

Google chief business officer Philipp Schindler told investors on an earnings call that the slowdown came from weaker monetization in AI Mode, the company's chatbot-style search experience that replaces the traditional list of blue links. He argued that many AI Mode queries are early in the buying process, giving Google a chance to capture new, high-value commercial intent. He also said most AI Mode queries are incremental, which he believes will create more ways to make money over time. The company has not yet shown that these gains are materializing.

The downturn is being framed as an irony for Google, which spent years building AI Overviews into its search results after ChatGPT's rise raised fears that chatbots would erode its advertising business. Those summaries drew readers away from the websites that originally produced the information, cutting their clicks and ad revenue. Axios data cited in the report shows visits to top news sites fell from over 70 million a month in July 2024, the year Google launched AI Overviews, to just over 47 million in July 2026. Media leaders surveyed by the Reuters Institute expect traffic to their sites to fall by nearly half over the next three years.

Articles.Title: Google Starved Out Publishers With AI Search. Now, Its Pivot Is Blowing Up in Its Face.

stories.Headline: Network modeling of science teachers’ perceptions of artificial intelligence integration in science curriculum development
stories.Summary:
A study published in Scientific Reports on October 29, 2026, examined how Saudi science teachers view the use of artificial intelligence in building science curricula. The research was led by U.M. Ibrahem and used a validated questionnaire completed by 691 Saudi science teachers. The authors applied psychological network modeling to map how teachers' views of benefits, challenges and attitudes connect to one another. The work was published in volume 15, issue 20, and carries the citation DOI 10.3390/su152014766.

The study used network estimation with regularization and centrality analyses to identify key themes in teachers' perceptions. Curriculum content generation and innovative pedagogical tools came out as the most central benefits, while data processing challenges and algorithmic bias stood out as the main structural barriers. Teachers' attitudes showed ambivalence, with resistance to automating administrative functions alongside guarded optimism about interactive and adaptive learning applications. The authors said the findings point to a need to address technical constraints, ethical considerations and the changing professional identities of educators.

The authors framed the study around the Technology Acceptance Model and Social Cognitive Theory, which they said informed their interpretation rather than their formal measurement model. They argued that teachers are the main implementers of educational technology, so their acceptance and engagement directly affect how AI enters classroom practice and curriculum planning. They also tied the research to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia's Vision 2030 emphasis on digital transformation and educational innovation. They said the results could offer actionable insights for policymakers, curriculum developers and professional development providers.

The article described a gap in the literature, noting that earlier studies often used linear or isolated frameworks that fail to capture the interconnected nature of teacher perceptions. It said few studies have focused on science, where curriculum development requires specialized pedagogical and technological considerations. The authors said the study contributes a systemic understanding that can inform tailored AI tools and support frameworks. They concluded that this could advance transformative innovation in science education.

Articles.Title: Network modeling of science teachers’ perceptions of artificial intelligence integration in science curriculum development

stories.Headline: UNR conference examines the role of AI in cybersecurity
stories.Summary:
The University of Nevada hosted a conference on Thursday about the role of artificial intelligence in cybersecurity, according to KOLO. Experts who attended the event in Reno described the topic as a double-edged sword. The conference brought together people from many sectors, from students to industry leaders. It also introduced high school students to cybersecurity.

The UNR cybersecurity director, Shamik Sengupta, said the conference focused on AI cyber versus cyber-AI. That means discussing the security of AI itself, including how to make it safe, its risks, and how to use it properly, he said. It also means weighing those issues against how AI can benefit and grow cybersecurity. Sengupta said the question is no longer whether AI is used, but how. He said conversations about implementing AI in cybersecurity while also protecting it are critical for smart growth.

Jack Donelson, a UNR senior and team leader of the Nevada Cyber Range Security Operations Center, said the best way to go about it is a balanced approach. He said that means acknowledging people's fears about AI, especially how it is used in corporate environments with data and security, while also acknowledging its benefits in software patching, vulnerability finding, and other uses. Heather Case-Hall, an award-winning cybersecurity leader and author, said that as AI keeps advancing, it will help improve security, but attackers are also advancing their capabilities. She said defenders need to move at the same speed, and that is the difficult balance. Leaders at the conference acknowledged public fears and said these conversations are critical to establish strict, protective, and ethical standards.

Researchers found that implementing proper safeguards and infrastructure makes businesses and cybersecurity more efficient overall. Case-Hall said AI has become a powerful tool in society, so talking about its complexity is needed to keep it safe. All the leaders interviewed said they were excited to have these conversations and expand their knowledge. Experts said the focus is on finding a balance between allowing AI to support humanity and implementing ethical and protective standards.

Articles.Title: UNR conference examines the role of AI in cybersecurity

stories.Headline: Some voters turn to AI in making election decisions
stories.Summary:
Some voters are turning to AI chatbots for information on candidates and to help decide who to vote for in the election on the Nov. 3 ballot, Fox 8 reported on Oct. 29, 2026. Aron Culotta, a Tulane University computer science professor and AI expert, said using a chatbot means the bot goes to the web to collect and summarize information for you, which differs from using a search engine yourself. He said AI is not foolproof, and that chatbots can seem more authoritative than a website that turns out not to be. Fox 8 interviewed citizens, and Kyleigh Kaminski said she thinks AI is wrong the majority of the time and is not somewhere to get the truth about politics. Another person said AI is as trustworthy as anybody you ask and that it gets a lot of stuff wrong.

In 2024 the Associated Press reported on chatbots giving inaccurate and misleading responses about elections, and two years later there is more reporting on the topic. Culotta said some errors come from faulty information on the web and some from chatbots making things up or getting things incorrect, which he called a pervasive problem. He advised people to push back and ask a chatbot to show its sources, comparing it to a really book-smart 12-year-old who graduated from Harvard. He said some voters may turn to AI because they see it as a time saver, since there is a lot to vote on and voters do not have time for in-depth research on every issue. He said there is a lot of value in these systems summarizing sometimes very complex issues, and that voters want to be engaged and know what they are voting for.

Culotta is the Tulane computer science professor and AI expert quoted on the risks and on how voters should use chatbots. He said the problems with factual information around elections that people have faced historically are still here today. He said the challenge is that a chatbot can seem more authoritative than a website that you realize is not that authoritative once you visit it. He said voters want to know what they are voting for and that it can be hard to parse that out in the normal ways. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the Nov. 3 election date and the continued reporting on the topic.

stories.Headline: Lab combines artificial intelligence and robotics to automate tasks
stories.Summary:
The University of Nottingham in the UK has built a self-driving laboratory that combines artificial intelligence and robotics to automate experimental work, according to an IOM3 report dated 29 October 2026. The coordinated system at the Centre of Excellence in Coating and Surface Engineering uses two robotic arms, a specially designed liquid-dispensing tool, laboratory equipment and purpose-built software. Its AI approach, known as active learning, draws on information from earlier experiments to pick out material compositions worth investigating. The team first ran calibration experiments to show accurate liquid dispensing across different liquids. The researchers integrated several processing stages into one system and showed it could carry out a full sequence without manual handling.

The lab can prepare a precursor solution, transfer the material for furnace processing, manage controlled cooling and retrieve the finished sample. According to the report, the approach could improve experimental consistency, support reproducible research and allow higher-throughput materials development. The article does not give figures for throughput gains or sample numbers. Tanvir Hussain, Professor of Coatings and Surface Engineering at the university, said that a key challenge is getting laboratory robots to work reliably across different stages of an experiment, particularly when liquid handling must be combined with high-temperature processing. He said the group's work addresses an important part of that challenge.

He also said it opens opportunities for further integration with intelligent experimental planning and optimisation. The article does not describe any next steps or planned deployments beyond these comments. The report sits within IOM3's coverage of materials and manufacturing, alongside other recent items on automation and testing. The article does not say whether the system is being commercialised or used outside the university. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Lab combines artificial intelligence and robotics to automate tasks

stories.Headline: Google value plunges by $500bn as AI fears rattle Wall Street
stories.Summary:
Alphabet, the parent company of Google, lost just over $500bn (£374bn) in value on Thursday after its final business update of the year rattled Wall Street. Google's stock hit a six-month low after the company revealed that its artificial intelligence summaries on search were affecting ad revenue. Its share price fell by almost 13% that day, its second lowest showing this year. The drop followed a day when the company's total stock market value fell to $3.46 trillion from $3.97 trillion the day before. Investors were unsettled by the update even though some of the figures looked strong at first glance.

Total revenue grew 25% compared to last year, reaching $127.6bn, and Google Cloud revenue grew by 103% to almost $31bn. Profits, however, fell by 25% during the quarter. The company also posted negative free cash flow in excess of $9bn, the second time in its history as a public company that it has done so. That loss is almost twice the cash shortfall Alphabet reported just three months earlier. Nearly all of the new spending is tied to Google's AI investments, and the company is now spending more money than it brings in.

Google's chief business officer, Philipp Schindler, said on Wednesday that he felt very good about the company's direction with an AI-focused version of its search engine. Tracy Woo, a principal analyst at Forrester, said Alphabet's disappointing search results highlight the difficulty of paying for large AI investments while protecting established businesses. Amazon also reported results that disappointed investors, and its shares fell 6% in after-hours trading. Its chief executive, Andy Jassy, said the company's spending was partly aimed at two businesses that could together bring in $1 trillion in the future, though he did not name them. Jassy did say he wished the spending could be spread over 25 years, but he argued that the company can fund its plan.

Microsoft's update drew a milder reaction, with its shares falling by less than 1% on Thursday. The company, which is also one of OpenAI's largest investors, spent around $5bn less on AI-related investments and recently announced plans to cut thousands of jobs. Its revenue grew 19% to $92.3bn, and its cloud business grew 30% to $63bn. Woo said investors are looking further ahead to determine which companies will actually profit from their large AI promises, and that question remains open for the whole technology industry.

Articles.Title: Google value plunges by $500bn as AI fears rattle Wall Street

stories.Headline: Google Eats Its Own Tail (and Profits) With AI Summaries as Stock Price Plunges
stories.Summary:
Google's share price fell as much as 13% on Thursday, October 29, 2026, a day after the company released its quarterly earnings report. The drop erased more than $500 billion in market value, which Bloomberg described as the largest single-day loss the search giant has ever experienced. The sell-off followed a Wednesday earnings call in which Google disclosed that its AI Mode had cut into its traditional search and advertising business. Philipp Schindler, the company's chief business officer, said the AI-generated responses now served for most searches have made it harder for Google to monetize results.

Google's search advertising business still generated $63.4 billion in the third quarter of 2026, up 12% year over year. That figure fell roughly $1.6 billion short of Wall Street's expectations, which had forecast about 15% growth. Capital spending is also climbing, rising from $44.9 billion in the second quarter to $51.3 billion in the third, according to the Financial Times. The Financial Times reported that the fourth quarter could see as much as $73 billion in capital expenditure. The company also reportedly has future commitments for data centers, energy and other costs exceeding $1 trillion.

The article argues that Google is spending heavily on a technology that is, for now, cutting into its revenue-generating businesses. Investors appear to have reacted to the gap between that spending and any clear path to profit, beyond hoping more people buy Gemini subscriptions. The piece also notes that the AI buildout is burning cash on model training, compute and infrastructure while eroding profits on the other end. The article presents this as a case study of how big tech firms have spent large sums on AI tools without first confirming that consumers want them.

Articles.Title: Google Eats Its Own Tail (and Profits) With AI Summaries as Stock Price Plunges

stories.Headline: Glass Substrates Open the Window to Advancing AI Chip Packaging
stories.Summary:
Glass substrates are being developed for advanced packaging of AI and high-performance computing chips, Lam Research said in a blog post published on October 29, 2026. The company said glass has long served as a temporary round carrier in packaging, and the industry is now working on large rectangular panels and permanent uses such as glass-core package substrates. Lam described glass as gaining momentum because of its mechanical, electrical and chemical properties. The post said glass substrates support more complex, high-density chip assemblies.

Lam said glass can be tuned so its coefficient of thermal expansion closely matches silicon and is significantly lower than that of organic substrates, which helps prevent warpage during thermal cycling. It said the flat surface allows fine line and space patterning down to two microns, and that glass offers superior isolation for wiring along with low dielectric loss and high resistivity. The post said glass is used as a temporary carrier for AI accelerators and is being developed as a core substrate for future generations, and that it suits 5G RF modules operating above 28 GHz and photonic integrated circuits. Lam said glass carriers are established in production, while permanent glass interposers and glass-core IC substrates remain at earlier stages of development and adoption.

Lam said glass is brittle, which creates challenges in handling, singulation and defect management, and that forming features inside glass requires care to avoid chipping or cracking. It said depositing metallic films on glass requires advanced plating processes, with adhesion promoters often used before electroless seed deposition and specialized electroplating needed to fill through-glass vias. The post said handling panels larger than 500 mm demands vacuum or edge-grip tools, and thermal processing must be carefully ramped to avoid stress fractures. Lam said it is investing in research, process expertise and panel-processing hardware, including its Kallisto panel electroplating system and its Phoenix panel processing system.

Lam said the industry must address manufacturability and standardization challenges before wide adoption, because panel sizes, via specifications and material stacks vary across suppliers. The company said it collaborates with substrate makers, outsourced semiconductor assembly and test providers, equipment manufacturers and material suppliers to co-optimize electroplating solutions. The post said adoption is still evolving, with technical, manufacturing and ecosystem hurdles to overcome. It said the potential benefits include higher performance, greater integration, new applications and more efficient panel processing.

Articles.Title: Glass Substrates Open the Window to Advancing AI Chip Packaging - Lam Research Newsroom

stories.Headline: From writing to millions: A writer completes 370 books in 20 months with the help of artificial intelligence
stories.Summary:
A writer, identified in the article only as "her," reportedly produced about 370 books in 20 months by using artificial intelligence tools to speed up the writing process. The experiment was described in an article published on October 30, 2026, by Voice of Emirates, with the story datelined Washington, DC. The author used AI applications for generating ideas, drafting, and developing content, from choosing topics and key ideas to preparing, revising, and finalizing texts for publication. The article says the experiment was linked to significant financial returns, though it gives no figures for those returns.

The article presents this as an example of how modern technology is reshaping the book industry, where authors can now rely on AI rather than only traditional methods. It frames the case as showing commercial potential for content creators who use AI to reach wider audiences and produce books for different reader segments. The article does not name the writer, the publishers involved, or the specific tools used. It also does not say whether any of the books were released or sold, and it does not report on any regulatory or industry response.

The article raises wider concerns without answering them. It points to questions about the quality of published content, the importance of human review, intellectual property rights, and whether rapid production can preserve the creative and intellectual value of a book. It asks whether AI will become an essential partner for authors and publishers or will change the rules of competition across the global publishing industry. The piece concludes that AI is no longer merely a writing aid but an economic and productive tool, while stressing that human creativity and professional review remain essential to the value of the final product.

Articles.Title: From writing to millions: A writer completes 370 books in 20 months with the help of artificial intelligence

stories.Headline: SEMICON Europa 2026 puts advanced packaging and AI in focus ...
stories.Summary:
SEMICON Europa 2026 will take place in Munich, Germany, from November 10 to 13, 2026, according to an article by Asma Adhimi published on eeNews Europe on October 29, 2026. The event will be held at Messe München alongside electronica and will bring together semiconductor industry leaders. It is organized by SEMI Europe, whose president is Laith Altimime. The gathering is meant to explore advanced packaging, AI-driven manufacturing and cross-border collaboration.

The event will focus on technologies and investment strategies aimed at improving Europe's competitiveness and the resilience of its semiconductor supply chain. The Advanced Packaging Conference will examine heterogeneous integration, chiplets and next-generation packaging, with topics including wafer- and panel-level packaging, hybrid bonding, silicon photonics, co-packaged optics and thermal management. AI-powered inspection, advanced metrology and testing will also feature, along with Europe's packaging ecosystem and pilot-line activities. The Fab Management Forum is scheduled for November 11 and will cover AI-driven factory automation, progress toward autonomous fabs, and silicon carbide, wide-bandgap semiconductors, photonics and advanced foundry services.

Altimime said that as Europe navigates a complex geopolitical and technological landscape, advanced packaging is becoming a strategic pillar of semiconductor supply chain resilience. The program will also address moving advanced packaging innovations from research into high-volume manufacturing. The Voices from the Industry program will broaden the discussion to semiconductor security, supply chains and regional cooperation. The co-located imec Technology Forum will address emerging chiplet architectures, sustainable manufacturing and policy frameworks supporting Europe's AI ecosystem.

Other sessions will cover secure-by-design computing through the CHERI Alliance, agentic AI for semiconductor supply chain management, and advanced packaging industrialization. CEA-Leti will showcase innovations in 3D integration, silicon photonics and energy-efficient AI hardware. Representatives from the Baltic Sea region will discuss opportunities for a more resilient European semiconductor corridor. The program will also highlight transatlantic collaboration opportunities, including Arizona's expanding semiconductor manufacturing ecosystem.

Articles.Title: SEMICON Europa 2026 puts advanced packaging and AI in focus ... - eeNews Europe

stories.Headline: ECCC starts €42 million AI cybersecurity cluster with three European projects - INSIGHT EU MONITORING
stories.Summary:
The European Cybersecurity Competence Centre, known as the ECCC, launched three new projects during a public event in Brussels, with a total investment of about €42 million. The projects were selected under a Horizon Europe call focused on generative AI for cybersecurity applications. They form part of a new Cyber AI Cluster, whose first public gathering took place on 27 October 2026 at the event "Cybersecurity and Artificial Intelligence: From Innovation to Impact," organised with the European Commission's Directorate-General for Communications Networks, Content and Technology. The article dates the launch to 29 October 2026, and the cluster is meant to promote dialogue, visibility, cooperation and shared learning on AI for cybersecurity. Each project is designed to strengthen Europe's own AI capabilities in the field.

The three projects contribute to the EU Action Plan on Cybersecurity and Artificial Intelligence, which the European Commission adopted in July 2026. The article says AI can help cyber defence through vulnerability discovery, threat detection, incident response and recovery, but malicious actors can also use it to automate and scale attacks. The projects bring together more than 70 partners from universities, research organisations, small and innovative companies, industrial leaders and public authorities. Those partners are based in 14 EU Member States and the United Kingdom. All three projects started on 1 October 2026 and will run for 36 months.

The first project, AICYROS, is coordinated by the University of Murcia and is building a generative AI cyber-risk "operational shield" that covers detection, incident response, secure deployment and compliance. It will be tested in telecom, industry, robotics, software-defined vehicles, healthcare, media and smart cities. AIGENTIC, coordinated by the University of Piraeus Research Center, is developing auditable, guardrailed AI agents for threat intelligence and related tasks, with nine use cases across automotive, railway, telecom, finance, maritime and smart cities. GENESIS-AI, coordinated by the University of Zagreb's Faculty of Electrical Engineering and Computing, is creating a self-improving, regulation-aware system to defend complex infrastructure, and its industrial partners include Siemens, Airbus and Bosch.

The article reports that the cluster will seek to align its work with the Action Plan, strengthen collaboration with ENISA and the European Commission, and avoid overlap among EU-funded initiatives. It also plans to involve a wider range of stakeholders over time, including relevant projects funded under the Digital Europe Programme. The stated goal is to turn European strategic priorities into concrete, trustworthy AI capabilities for cybersecurity across the continent. The article attributes the announcement to the ECCC as its source and points readers to the slides presented at the Brussels event.

Articles.Title: ECCC starts €42 million AI cybersecurity cluster with three European projects - INSIGHT EU MONITORING

stories.Headline: Amazon Puts a Million Robots Behind Its AI Ambitions
stories.Summary:
Amazon said in its third-quarter earnings report, released October 29, 2026, that it now has more than a million robots working in its fulfillment network. The disclosure came during an earnings call focused largely on artificial intelligence and Amazon Web Services, where CEO Andy Jassy said AWS could become a trillion-dollar revenue business within five to 10 years. The robot figure drew attention because it gives a physical form to an AI push that is usually described in terms of chips and data centers. Chief Financial Officer Brian Olsavsky said Amazon doubled its fleet of robotic arms, including the Cardinal and Sparrow models, during 2026.

Jassy said many repetitive jobs now done by people in fulfillment centers will be handled by robots over time, though Amazon will keep a large human workforce. New facilities, including those supporting same-day delivery, are expected to rely heavily on robotics, and the company is studying how robots could help with the final stretch of delivery to customers' doors. Deployment depends on whether the machines improve productivity, safety, costs and delivery times. Amazon is also developing AI models that make robots easier to program and better able to carry out complex physical tasks. Olsavsky credited robotics and AI with measurable gains in productivity and safety.

Jassy argued that most enterprise software will be rewritten so that agents can complete tasks rather than only generate answers, and he said businesses will need that capability to move faster and manage security risks. He reported that tens of thousands of customers use Bedrock AgentCore, and that they deployed twice as many agents in the third quarter as in the previous three quarters combined. He also cited adoption of the Amazon Q workplace assistant by companies including 3M and Southwest Airlines. The spending behind these efforts is large. Amazon expects about $220 billion in cash capital expenditures this year and meaningfully more in 2027.

Financially, the earnings release showed revenue up 12% to $201.9 billion and operating income rising to $28.1 billion from $17.4 billion. AWS sales grew 39% to $46 billion. Net income fell to $20.7 billion from $21.2 billion, mainly because investment gains boosted the prior-year figure. Free cash flow over the trailing 12 months swung from a $14.8 billion inflow to a $42.4 billion outflow, driven largely by AI investment. The results arrived a day after a similar concern about whether heavy AI spending will pay off shadowed Alphabet's earnings.

Articles.Title: Amazon Puts a Million Robots Behind Its AI Ambitions

stories.Headline: Hybrid Bonding Is Costly. Is There a Cheaper Bumpless Option?
stories.Summary:
TrendForce published an article on October 30, 2026, asking whether a cheaper bumpless option exists as hybrid bonding remains costly. The article follows an earlier piece on why hybrid bonding has become the key to getting past the scaling limit of micro-bumps. It notes that TSMC's SoIC-X is expected to lift demand for hybrid bonders as its adoption in AI chips grows. The road from micro-bump to hybrid bonding is not a single step, and the industry is still seeking intermediate or complementary options.

As bump pitch shrinks, bonding has progressed from flip-chip, suited to bump pitches of roughly 50 µm, to micro-bump plus thermo-compression bonding. Fluxless TCB now supports a bump pitch as small as about 8 µm, but the micro-bump still faces a physical scaling limit. Bumpless bonding means no conventional solder balls, with metal on the chip surface such as Cu pads or under-bump metal making direct contact. This allows smaller interconnects and a bond pitch that can reach around 5 µm. Hybrid bonding is currently the only commercialized bumpless technology, bonding dielectric layers and Cu pads directly through steps such as plasma activation and pre-bonding.

SK hynix's roadmap, published in August 2026, positions bumpless TCB as an interim step between fluxless TCB and hybrid bonding. The article says it looks at the bumpless options beyond hybrid bonding, how they work, how they differ, and how equipment suppliers are developing their strategies. It states that behind the paywall it explores what drives the cost of hybrid bonding and how bumpless flip-chip, bumpless TCB and hybrid bonding compare. It also covers when memory makers could move to bumpless bonding and how die bonder suppliers are pursuing multiple tracks at once. The article does not say what happens next beyond these listed topics.

Articles.Title: Hybrid Bonding Is Costly. Is There a Cheaper Bumpless Option? - TrendForce

stories.Headline: AI changes how accountants work, not what they do
stories.Summary:
The article reports on how artificial intelligence is changing accounting work, based on interviews ahead of the 2026 AICPA National Tax Conference. The conference first spotlighted generative AI in November 2023, when tax professionals were still trying to understand how the technology might reshape tax practice. OpenAI introduced ChatGPT about a month after the 2022 conference. Since then AI has steadily gained visibility at the event: two sessions at the 2024 conference included AI in their titles, the 2025 conference featured an AI keynote and another AI-focused session, and in 2026 AI is listed among the conference's six hot topics and appears in the titles of four sessions. This year AI is the focus of sessions on ethics, workflow, firm operations, and the changing role of practitioners.

David Lifson, a CPA and senior advisor at Crowe, said in a 2023 keynote that he hoped AI would make people smarter rather than replaceable, and three years later he said he is more convinced than ever that AI cannot replace humans. He described it as an evolutionary tool without judgment and a data accelerator. Brian Davis, a CPA who is CEO of One Stop CPA and founder of OneForm for Accountants, leads a session titled "What in the AI Is Happening With Tax Firms" with two other CPAs, examining how firms adopt AI tools and where practitioners find value. Davis said AI is bigger than earlier advances such as cloud computing or e-filing because it is in every area of the business, but he also said it is sometimes overhyped and not the flip-on switch people make it seem.

Both men view AI as the latest step in a progression of technologies that changed how accountants work, with spreadsheets replacing columnar pads and electronic research replacing shelves of tax books. Lifson, who is 76 and has spent five decades in the profession, said technology has historically changed the nature of the work rather than reducing its amount, because as firms became more efficient, client expectations rose, the tax code grew more complex, and more choices required professional judgment. Davis said he once counted 250 clients meaning 250 tax returns, but now counts relationships and can have fewer than 50 relationships while doing more work than those 250 returns, and he said AI accelerated a five-year road map into a single tax season. He said there is still a difference between someone with two years of experience and someone with 20.

Lifson said the 2023 panel did not fully appreciate the need for safeguards as AI systems became more powerful and autonomous, and he said anyone reviewing AI's first-stage work must be trained, informed, and skillful enough to find its mistakes. Davis warned that overreliance on AI can create false confidence, and he said nobody knows where the technology is going or whether it will wipe out an industry or make the world a better place. Lifson said he worries about global risk for banks, governments, and other entities because of reliance on computers to process transactions and store data as paper books and records disappear, though he distinguished that risk from the use of AI in human life. His takeaway, he said, is that AI makes people better.

Articles.Title: AI changes how accountants work, not what they do - Journal of Accountancy

stories.Headline: Artificial Intelligence - Friend or Foe? The real relationship between AI and penetration testers
stories.Summary:
The article, published by teiss on 30 October 2026 and dated 29 October in its listing, asks whether AI will make human penetration testers redundant following the release of Anthropic's Mythos model earlier that year. Its answer is that AI is unlikely to replace human testers but will augment them. The piece notes that many security professionals share this view, though it attaches a caveat about how the work will change. The main strength of AI, according to the article, is speed and persistence. It never tires or stops, so once given an objective it can test every likely scenario to find a weakness, operating at a scale no person could match.

The article says these techniques can be noisy but persistent, and that in CVE disclosure and red teaming they offer clear benefits. It adds that AI can help with reconnaissance, flag potential weaknesses and remove some repetitive work from a test. The authors, Dave Henderson, Sales Director UKI at Synack, and David Neeson, Deputy SOC Team Lead at Barrier Networks, argue that human validation remains essential. They say an AI can produce many findings, but only an expert can judge how a flaw could be exploited, what an attacker could achieve and how serious the risk is to a given organisation.

They also warn that automated tools have always produced false positives, and that weaknesses which look minor alone can form an attack path when chained together. The article also raises a concern about remediation: if AI uncovers far more vulnerabilities, organisations may struggle to keep up with patching, and a long list of CVEs does not by itself make them more secure. It suggests managed security service providers can help teams judge exposure and prioritise fixes. The authors conclude that the relationship between AI and testers is better described as a partnership than as a contest between friend and foe.

Articles.Title: Artificial Intelligence - Friend or Foe? The real relationship between AI and penetration testers

stories.Headline: Inside the AI Revolution: Together AI’s CEO on Where Artificial Intelligence Goes Next
stories.Summary:

The context is a video interview series on technology and business topics. The article does not say what happens next, and it gives no further reporting on Together AI.
