stories.Headline: Stop Blaming Code Review for AI’s Delivery Problem
stories.Summary:
Ole Lensmar, co-founder and CTO of Testkube, wrote in SD Times on October 29, 2026 that code review is not the real cause of slow AI-assisted software delivery. He said engineering teams using AI coding tools report building two to three times as many features as before, but pushing those features into production is a different story. He said Testkube has the same problem, with engineers building features faster than the company can get them into releases. He wrote that review is often where teams first notice the slowdown, but it is not where the slowdown starts or ends.

Lensmar cited Faros AI, which looked at more than 10,000 developers and found that teams with high AI adoption merged 98% more pull requests while review time went up 91%. He also cited a National Bureau of Economic Research working paper that followed more than 500,000 developers on GitHub and found autonomous coding agents raised commits by about 240% but releases by only about 30%. He wrote that approved changes still must pass through testing set up for far less code, so they wait there instead. He said pipelines take 45 minutes and developers go get coffee while every build runs hundreds or even thousands of tests.

Lensmar said teams should stop treating testing as a step in the build and run it as its own system. He said tests should not have to wait for a build, and a team or an autonomous coding agent should be able to run required tests when an API changes, on a schedule, or whenever needed. He said tests should preferably run against real environments and results should end up in one place instead of scattered across pipeline logs, agent sandboxes and local harnesses. He said teams should not get rid of CI/CD, because pipelines are good at building and deploying software and can still kick off tests, but they should not be the only place testing can happen.

Lensmar said the issue matters more as teams move toward agentic development, where AI agents handle more of the work between a spec and production. He said agents should be able to trigger tests and act on results immediately without waiting for an overwhelmed build. He said he is optimistic about AI and expects models to keep getting better, but writing code has rarely been the slowest part of shipping software. He said that when someone tells him testing and release confidence is holding back their AI-powered teams, he asks how they run their tests and where they run them.

Articles.Title: Stop Blaming Code Review for AI’s Delivery Problem - SD Times

stories.Headline: QCon AI New York 2026 Program Committee Picks: Agent Identity, Context Costs, and Open-Source Infere
stories.Summary:
The QCon AI New York 2026 program committee has picked six sessions it is looking forward to at the December 15 to 16 conference, according to an InfoQ article published on October 29, 2026. Conference chair Hien Luu, an AI and ML leader, advisor, speaker, and author, shared his selections alongside committee members Wes Reisz, Technical Principal at Thoughtworks and creator of The InfoQ Podcast, and Faye Zhang, Staff Engineer at Google building autonomous agents for Gemini Enterprise. The picks cover agent identity, context costs, open-source inference, engineering organizations, agent standards, and audio AI. The article was written by Artenisa Chatziou. Wes Reisz chose a keynote by Nancy Wang, CTO at 1Password, titled When Software Becomes a User: Identity and Authorization for Agents in Production, which looks at delegated authority, credential management, and securing agent interactions as traditional identity models break down.

His second choice is Make Each Token Count: Compression, Caching, and Retrieval for Production LLM Context, by Tejas Chopra, CEO and co-founder of Headroom Labs, covering learned prompt compression, prefix-cache-aware context alignment, and compress-cache-retrieve pipelines. Hien Luu selected The Future of the Engineering Org by Peter Bell, founder and CTO of Gather.dev, drawing on conversations with engineering leaders at organizations including Anthropic, OpenAI, Shopify, and Coinbase. Hien also picked Open Source Agentic Inference: Unlocking the Harness with vLLM by Francisco Javier Arceo, a Forward Deployed Engineer at Baseten and maintainer of the vLLM Agentic API project. Faye Zhang described her two selections as talks at the intersection of frontier research and production engineering. Her first choice is Navigating Agentic Standards: What to Build On Now and What to Watch by Kevin Kelley, Technical Lead for Standards at Anthropic, which covers standards such as MCP, A2A, and OAuth and how they can establish interoperable agent identity, delegated authorization, and trust boundaries.

Her second selection is a keynote called Audio Processing with Large Language Models by Tara Sainath, Distinguished Research Scientist at Google DeepMind and lead of the Gemini audio area, covering speech recognition, generation, translation, and dialogue. Faye highlighted questions raised by LLMs reshaping speech and audio modeling, including unified multilingual representations, end-to-end versus cascaded architectures, and latency-quality trade-offs for real-time conversational intelligence. The conference takes place at the Westin Jersey City Newport, one PATH stop from Lower Manhattan, and focuses on production AI for senior software engineers, architects, and engineering leaders. Early-bird pricing is $1,705 until November 10, after which the two-day pass rises to $1,790. The article says anyone planning to use their remaining 2026 learning and development budget can explore the program and a convince your manager approval email on the conference website.

Articles.Title: QCon AI New York 2026 Program Committee Picks: Agent Identity, Context Costs, and Open-Source Infere - infoq.com

stories.Headline: RIIIR: Rewrite It In *Idiomatic* Rust (with AI)
stories.Summary:
Niko Matsakis, a lead designer of Rust and a senior principal engineer at Amazon, gave a talk at QCon about combining Rust with AI. He has worked on Rust since 2011 and is a project director on the Rust Foundation Board. He also created Symposium, an open-source platform for agent mods built on the Agent Client Protocol. The talk was published by InfoQ on October 26, 2026.

Matsakis argued that AI lets teams skip Rust's steep learning curve, because agents already learned the language in training. He said the type system acts as guardrails that help agents produce programs more likely to be correct. He cited Greg Brockman, co-founder and president of OpenAI, saying Rust suits agents because if it compiles it is approximately correct. He noted Microsoft is researching AI-driven rewrites of a million lines of code by one engineer, and that Bun moved a large codebase from Zig to Rust. He said moving large codebases now takes weeks or months rather than decades.

Matsakis said Rust is low-level enough for a kernel, with only C and Rust allowed in the Linux kernel, and used in Microsoft's kernel too. He said it is high-level enough for applications, citing the ratatui text interface library. He said efficiency drives adoption at Amazon, where Rust started in critical data paths for S3, EC2 and Lambda and spread further, including the DSQL serverless SQL database. He said memory safety concerns are pushing people toward Rust, citing Android's porting work and the long-cited figure that 70% of vulnerabilities relate to memory safety.

Matsakis described Symposium as covering gaps he sees in current tools. He said vendors like Anthropic and OpenAI each try to build a complete tool, and he wants a more extensible model where people plug in extensions. He said the Agent Client Protocol is a way past that limit and toward that extensible model. He said the industry is only scraping the surface of what is possible.

Articles.Title: RIIIR: Rewrite It In *Idiomatic* Rust (with AI) - infoq.com

stories.Headline: Opening the Black Box: Critical Explainability for AI Agent Tool Selection with Kiji Inspector
stories.Summary:
Hannes Hapke, director of engineering at Dataiku and head of its open-source 575 Lab, presented the Kiji Inspector at a conference, and InfoQ published a summary of the talk on October 26, 2026. The tool is an open-source project from Dataiku that applies sparse autoencoders to decision tokens to show why AI agents pick specific tools. Hapke said the problem is that agents do not reveal how they make decisions, and methods like prompt engineering, behavioral testing and chain of thought only give plausible narratives rather than causality. He said the team decided it needed to look inside the model itself.

The approach uses sparse autoencoders, which take activations from a model and force roughly 95 percent of features to be zero so that only a small set of features stays active. The framework focuses on the decision token rather than the whole prompt, and it adds token-level fuzzing from Eleuther and causal validation testing to check whether a feature is causal or only correlated. Training uses pairs made of an anchor, the correct tool choice, and an adversarial reply that is similar but leads to a different tool, such as an internal database lookup versus an online search. Hapke said the method works only with open-source models because closed models like OpenAI's do not give access to their weights, and he said it works across various open-source models, not just Gemma from Google or Nemotron from NVIDIA.

Hapke said the tool is meant for production monitoring workflows for software architects and senior engineering leaders. He described the training pipeline as taking a target model, running prompts through it, grabbing activations from chosen layers, and training the sparse autoencoder on them. After training, he said, users can run a contrastive analysis on the pairs or ask a large language model what the documents have in common. He said Dataiku believes responsible AI has to be open, so anything touching privacy or explainability is part of the lab and fully open source. He also mentioned the Kiji Privacy Proxy as the lab's other signature project, which can protect data from leaking to closed-source models and can be fine-tuned to use cases.

Articles.Title: Opening the Black Box: Critical Explainability for AI Agent Tool Selection with Kiji Inspector - infoq.com

stories.Headline: ‘Black box’ medical AI can deepen health disparities, researcher says
stories.Summary:
Tiffani Bright, an artificial intelligence researcher at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center, spoke at the Association of Health Care Journalists fall summit in Los Angeles, in a session moderated by Usha Lee McFarling of MIT. She said unchecked medical algorithms threaten patient safety and health equity, and that even one basic untested algorithm can harm a human life. She noted that health institutions once kept local control over their algorithms to find and remove bias, but today commercial vendors ship black box tools that health systems cannot inspect, including the underlying logic and the training cohorts. The panel discussion was published on October 29, 2026.

Bright described three main pathways for bias in health algorithms: biased historical data, asking the wrong clinical questions, and failing to act on system alerts. She gave examples, saying algorithms trained mostly on male patient data can give inaccurate or harmful results for women, and models that use health care costs to find sick patients often miss lower-income people who receive less care overall. She said most AI tools do not go through rigorous clinical trials by outside evaluators the way prescription drugs do before reaching patients. She added that a system claiming high overall accuracy can still fail specific subgroups, such as Black or Hispanic women, if developers do not check performance across intersecting groups.

Bright advised reporters to examine funding sources for medical AI claims, check whether tools were tested on diverse populations, and ask whether patients gave informed consent to tools that record visits and access records. She said bias is not a bug but a set of choices, and that there needs to be more representation and accountability in how medical technology is built and deployed. She also said she worries automated care could be sent disproportionately to disadvantaged groups, making direct human care a luxury and creating a two-tiered health care system. The articles say full recordings of the panel and other sessions from the 2026 fall summit are available on the organization's website.

Articles.Title: ‘Black box’ medical AI can deepen health disparities, researcher says

stories.Headline: Connecticut Leaders Tout Tech Talent Accelerator, AI Training
stories.Summary:
Connecticut Gov. Ned Lamont and state leaders held a press conference in East Hartford on Wednesday to promote state workforce development programs aimed at easing the AI transition and supporting workers and students. The event focused heavily on the Tech Talent Accelerator, a four-year-old program that builds partnerships between higher education institutions and businesses. In February, the state announced the launch of Tech Talent Accelerator 3.0, a more AI-oriented version of the program. The Office of Workforce Strategy is supporting several AI pilot programs, including an AI accounting and entrepreneurship course at Connecticut College, an AI for Cybersecurity program at the University of New Haven, and an online course on AI in healthcare business innovation at Quinnipiac University.

Kelli-Marie Vallieres, the state's chief workforce officer, said the goal is to work with businesses to connect students and companies well before graduation. Nicholas Schilling, a software engineer at CGI, described how being connected with the firm at an event led to an internship and then full-time work, and he now mentors students. He said the transition to full-time employment was seamless because he had spent so much time with CGI as a student. Lamont said he is optimistic because the world is moving toward more knowledge-based and skill-based work, and he said AI use will be better guided and more effective for learners.

The state has also launched other efforts, including the Connecticut AI Academy, a free online school offering certificate programs in AI literacy and AI fluency that is expected to expand to teens, teachers and small businesses. In August, the Department of Economic and Community Development announced a $20 million investment into an applied AI workforce center in Hartford. Over the summer, the state celebrated a National Science Foundation grant for its quantum computing sector, a project also slated to receive $121 million in state funding. Lamont's office also announced a partnership with RAISE US, a nonpartisan organization that offers displaced workers retraining and upskilling, and Connecticut will pilot programs training workers to interact with AI.

Dan O'Keefe, commissioner of the Department of Economic and Community Development, told CT Mirror in July that states are where the rubber really hits the road and that the federal government has been somewhat hands-off. Other states have announced similar efforts, including New York's Pursuit AI Jobs Institute, a Queens-based center aiming to train 40,000 workers by 2032 with $10 million in public investment, and Arkansas's partnership with RAISE US on a program called ArkansasLAUNCH. Lamont said Connecticut will not be the research and development leader for AI but will lead in how to apply it in the next generation of professions. The article says the coming months and years will show which efforts turn out to be most fruitful.

Articles.Title: Connecticut Leaders Tout Tech Talent Accelerator, AI Training

stories.Headline: AIB plans 50MW AI data center at former Spartanburg cryptomine to serve Nebius
stories.Summary:
AIB Data Centers plans to redevelop its former Bitcoin mining facility in Spartanburg County, South Carolina, into an AI data center with 50MW of IT capacity contracted to Nebius, an Amsterdam-based AI cloud provider. The site is about 16 acres at 389 Tyger River Industrial Drive in Moore. A draft development agreement in the county's October 19 council papers describes replacing 20 equipment containers with a standalone building known as CLT1. The Nebius agreement was announced on September 30. The initial lease term is 12 years, with two five-year renewal options.

The 50MW of critical IT capacity is supported by a 15-year agreement for 65MW of utility supply. AIB's October investor presentation estimates delivery of two 25MW data halls in the fourth quarter of 2027. The draft anticipates $1.2 billion of investment by the company and its tenant, with proposed obligations including at least $400 million of capital investment, at least 28 full-time jobs directly or through sublessees, and $12.6 million in community benefit payments over the initial 12-year term. Spartanburg County adopted a one-year moratorium on new data centers in September, but its ordinance allows exemptions for qualifying facilities with up to 65MW of IT capacity in named industrial parks or on former industrial sites, provided they do not generate electricity beyond emergency backup. The proposed AIB agreement states that the project qualifies for an exemption and caps development at 50MW of IT capacity and 65MW for the whole facility.

Nebius chief product and infrastructure officer Andrey Korolenko said when the agreement was announced that time-to-power is the binding constraint on AI infrastructure today. AIB is led by Jerry Tang, who also leads TigerDC. TigerDC withdrew its separate $3 billion Project Spero proposal in Spartanburg County in February after officials rejected a tax incentive agreement. That proposal envisaged an initial 100MW phase at a separate site. AIB had disclosed plans to repurpose the site before the moratorium was adopted.

AIB's second-quarter filing says the existing 40MW mining hosting operation was de-energized on June 5 after falling Bitcoin prices made hosting uneconomic, and it had not resumed hosting as of August 13. The filing also records the June 25 change of name from BlockchAIn Digital Infrastructure to AIB Data Centers. Its Spartanburg operations sit within wholly owned subsidiary One Blockchain, while AIB CLT1 LLC was formed as the project company. A county public notice schedules a hearing on the agreement for November 3. The company expects customer prepayments, project debt and preferred equity to help finance construction, but says project financing has not been completed.

Articles.Title: AIB plans 50MW AI data center at former Spartanburg cryptomine to serve Nebius - Data Center Dynamics

stories.Headline: AI Cloud Stocks Fall as Big Tech Capex Comes in Light: Fastly Sinks 6%, Oracle and Nebius Drop 3%
stories.Summary:
On October 28, Microsoft reported $45.2 billion in capital expenditures and finance leases for its first quarter of fiscal 2027, below the $50.7 billion Wall Street consensus and short of its own $50 billion target. Alphabet reported $51.36 billion in capital expenditures against a $55.09 billion consensus. The next day, AI cloud stocks fell in midday trading: Fastly dropped 6% to $25.43, while Oracle fell 3% to $140.57 and Nebius fell 3% to $177.56. Microsoft stock was at $523.30, down 1%, and Alphabet stock was at $287.67, down 11%, according to Stocktwits.

Microsoft chief financial officer Amy Hood said some third-party capacity deliveries the company expected in the quarter were delayed. She said she expects capital spending of more than $50 billion next quarter and approximately $170 billion for the calendar year, and she said customer demand continues to exceed available supply. Hood did not tie the delays to any named supplier. The article says Microsoft buys computing capacity from outside AI cloud providers including Nebius and CoreWeave, so slower deliveries and lower spending raise questions about how quickly those providers' revenue ramps.

The declines came a day after Oracle stock rallied 11% to close at $144.54 following its investor day. At that event Oracle forecast $30 billion in free cash flow by fiscal 2029 and capped new financing through fiscal 2030 at $20 billion, split between $10 billion in equity and $10 billion in debt. Management reaffirmed a $225 billion revenue target for fiscal 2030 and pointed to $664 billion in remaining performance obligations. Those targets followed negative free cash flow of $23.7 billion in fiscal 2026, and Oracle stock is still down 27% year to date.

Fastly stock is up 150% this year after six straight quarters of earnings beats, and it lifted its full-year 2026 revenue guidance to $732 million to $746 million on August 5. Nebius stock is up 112% this year, and three customers made up 24%, 21% and 14% of its revenue in the second quarter of 2026. CoreWeave stock was at $64, up 0.1%, and is down 11% year to date. The next test for Microsoft is whether its delayed third-party capacity arrives in the second half of its fiscal year, as Hood expects, and upcoming spending updates from other cloud giants could confirm or ease the worry.

Articles.Title: AI Cloud Stocks Fall as Big Tech Capex Comes in Light: Fastly Sinks 6%, Oracle and Nebius Drop 3% - 24/7 Wall St.

stories.Headline: CRWV vs. MSFT: Which AI Cloud Stock Offers Better Upside Potential?
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave and Microsoft are two AI cloud companies compared in a Zacks article published on TradingView on October 29, 2026. The article weighs which stock offers more upside from its current valuation. CoreWeave runs a specialized cloud built around high-performance GPUs, while Microsoft pairs its Azure cloud with enterprise software and AI products such as Microsoft 365 Copilot. Both are set to benefit from growing AI workloads, but their investment cases differ.

Microsoft reported fiscal 2027 first-quarter revenue of $92.3 billion, up 19% year over year, with operating income of $45.9 billion and Azure revenue up 48%. Microsoft Cloud revenue grew 30% to $63.9 billion, and commercial remaining performance obligation rose 73%. For the second quarter, Microsoft expects revenue of $96 billion to $97.1 billion and Azure growth of 49% to 50%, with capital expenditures above $50 billion. CoreWeave added 500 MW of active power in the second quarter to reach 1.5 GW, with contracted power at 4.2 GW and a target of more than 8 GW by 2030. It raised more than $18 billion in debt and equity, and for 2026 it guided to capital expenditure of $35 billion to $39 billion and revenue of $12.4 billion to $13.2 billion.

The article says CoreWeave management raised its capital expenditure outlook and expects adjusted operating income of up to $1.15 billion and exit ARR of $18.5 billion to $19.5 billion. It says Microsoft is prioritizing infrastructure efficiency, cost management and strong operating margins, and returned $10.2 billion to shareholders in the quarter. The article notes CoreWeave faces risks from heavy capital spending, rising financing costs and customer concentration, with three customers at 72% of second-quarter revenue. It also cites Microsoft challenges including a 22% decline in Windows OEM revenue and modest weakness in Xbox content and services.

Over the past six months, CoreWeave shares fell 42.7% while Microsoft rose 30.2%, and both stocks carry a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold). CoreWeave trades at 5.84X price to book, below Microsoft at 8.91X, and the Zacks Consensus Estimate for CoreWeave's current-year earnings was revised downward over the past 60 days. The article says CoreWeave is the more aggressive bet, with rapid revenue growth and a large backlog that could lift the shares if it executes, improves profitability and manages debt. It says Microsoft offers a broader way to participate in AI adoption, with Azure growth and a profitable software ecosystem providing multiple avenues to monetize AI. It concludes that CoreWeave may offer greater percentage upside for risk-tolerant, long-term investors, while Microsoft suits those seeking stable earnings, diversification and lower risk.

stories.Headline: LTIMindtree stock leans on AI as Q2 growth and margins improve - ad-hoc-news.de
stories.Summary:
LTIMindtree held its second-quarter earnings call on October 16, 2026, and the discussion pointed to a growing shift toward AI-led services. Management described broad-based quarterly growth and faster revenue conversion from shorter AI engagements, according to a transcript published by MarketScreener. Revenue reached 1.235 billion US dollars, up 1.1 percent from the previous quarter and 5.1 percent year over year on a constant-currency basis. In Indian rupees, revenue rose 1.7 percent sequentially and 13.6 percent year over year.

AI revenue made up 13.4 percent of total revenue and grew 40 percent from a year earlier. Including Enterprise AI, the combined AI revenue increase was 47 percent. EBIT margin improved by 10 basis points sequentially to 15.6 percent. Cash conversion weakened, with operating cash flow to profit after tax falling to 39 percent from 79 percent in the previous quarter. The company reported 88,835 employees at the end of the quarter, after adding 949 employees sequentially.

Management said it is working to keep the full-year margin broadly in line with the previous year, including the expected impact of the planned Randstad Digital acquisition. It cited gratuity funding, dividend-related tax payments and advance-tax outflows for the weaker cash conversion, and said cash conversion should normalize, though some gratuity funding may continue into the next quarter. The company expects the second half of FY27 to be stronger than the first half and is working to bring full-year growth closer to the FY26 level. It also expects the Randstad Digital approval process to be completed in the third quarter, with integration and market realignment thereafter.

Management said the shorter duration of many AI projects can support faster revenue realization, though investors will need to assess how consistently those engagements scale. The central issue for investors is whether AI-led projects can offset pressure in traditional services and regional headwinds. The AI 1,000 programme remained on track. India's technology sector remains the relevant market context for LTIMindtree.

stories.Headline: From prototype to production: Kyndryl’s smarter path to AI business value
stories.Summary:
Kyndryl has opened AI Innovation Labs in Dallas in the United States, Liverpool in the United Kingdom and Luxembourg in the European Union. The labs give customers one-stop-shop environments for testing AI, along with expertise to help them capitalize on innovation. Kyndryl’s Global Consult Lead Ismail Amla detailed the work in a Q&A published on October 27, 2026. The article says the labs aim to help customers move from experimentation to implementation with AI.

The labs are meant to go beyond simply building in more AI functionality. Their goal is to help customers create business value and capture return on their AI investments. Kyndryl says the labs help businesses evolve from being AI curious to being AI native. The article describes a four-phase process of customer immersion, co-design, building and roadmap development, which begins with rapid prototyping. It also mentions the Kyndryl Agentic Framework, which is used to move quickly from concept to a working agentic solution.

Amla said the key is to follow the right sequence, starting by identifying an organization’s challenges and defining the results it wants. He said it helps to look across each value chain, such as hiring-to-retiring, claim-to-settlement or order-to-cash, rather than a singular task. He said the team spends weeks meeting with the customer before they arrive, to understand the business, the existing technology estate, the operational processes and the metrics that matter most. He described the labs as workspaces, not showcases, where consultants, Forward-Deployed Engineers, Human Systems Architects and Kyndryl Vital designers work with the customer. He said customers typically go from visualization and discussion to co-creation and prototyping in less than two days.

According to Amla, customers leave with a structured 30-, 60- and 90-day roadmap for implementation, production and scaling. He said they walk away with something of genuine value grounded in their actual business use case. He added that prototyping is critical but is not the ultimate destination, and that moving AI into everyday operations takes deep delivery expertise. The article says Kyndryl has built this through decades of designing end-to-end services, operating mission-critical systems and modernizing IT estates to improve performance.

stories.Headline: Cisco Open Sources Quarry to Catch AI Agent Attacks Hidden in Harmless Steps
stories.Summary:
Cisco announced on October 29, 2026, that it has open sourced a project called Quarry, according to SecurityWeek. The company describes Quarry as a neurosymbolic rule language that combines machine learning judgment with rule-based checks. It is meant to catch attacks by AI agents that hide bad intent across a series of steps that each look harmless on their own. Traditional security controls judge single actions, so they miss intent that only appears when the whole sequence is viewed.

Quarry covers single-turn and multi-turn large language model conversations, agents, tool use, Model Context Protocol interactions, and multimodal inputs. Each rule draws on neural evidence from machine learning classifiers and LLM judges, plus symbolic rules that check exact conditions, sequences, string matches, and tool relationships. The starter pack includes a readable DSL, an evaluation runtime with configurable safety and resource limits, a command-line scanner, a Python SDK, optional configured model operations, a plugin for Claude Code, Codex and other MCP-compatible agents, rule metadata, examples, documentation, and a workflow for validating rules against positive and benign datasets. Cisco says the project is intended to become a common, open standard for expressing and sharing detections for AI-agent attacks, much as Snort, YARA, and Sigma became standards in other areas of cybersecurity.

Cisco says agent security needs the same combination of pattern detection and evidence, applied to the steps an agent takes rather than to purchases. It says it wants agents, as well as security and AI engineers, to be able to write Quarry rules, and a plugin lets a coding agent compose, compile, and refine rules from a plain-English description of an organization's risk and then test them against real conversations. Cisco says the open-source project gives practitioners a working foundation for detection engineering. It also says its aim is to help defenders recognize sequences like one it cites while they are still in progress, and to preserve the evidence behind each finding for the people who have to act on it.

The article cites two 2025 campaigns in which Claude Code was used by bad actors, one against around 30 organizations and a second against Mexican government institutions. In the first, the attack was split into small routine-looking tasks that told existing defenses it was part of new defense testing, and the true intent of data theft only became apparent when the requests came together in the right sequence. Cisco says Hugging Face reconstructed roughly 17,600 agent actions after the fact. The article says attackers constantly develop new approaches, so defenders must respond to each new technique by writing a new Quarry rule, and that writing rules by hand does not scale against attackers' use of AI.

Articles.Title: Cisco Open Sources Quarry to Catch AI Agent Attacks Hidden in Harmless Steps - SecurityWeek

stories.Headline: Dubai launches world's first agentic AI marketplace
stories.Summary:
Dubai Chambers has launched the Chamber AI Hub, described as the world's first chamber-led marketplace for agentic AI, with the announcement coming on 26 October 2026. The platform lets companies operating in Dubai reach ready-to-use, specialised AI solutions that can carry out a wide range of administrative and operational tasks. It was built as a response to directives from Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, who is Crown Prince of Dubai, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Defence of the UAE, and Chairman of The Executive Council of Dubai. He has called for faster adoption of agentic AI across the city's private sector, an effort overseen by Dubai Chambers. The stated aim is to change how companies operate and to strengthen the competitiveness of Dubai's private sector.

The hub currently offers 22 specialised AI agents covering seven areas: Compliance, Procurement, Operations, Finance, Sales, Human Resources and Logistics. Dubai Chambers plans to grow the offering to 100 agents. The agents handle tasks such as supplier discovery, vendor proposal evaluation, supply chain risk monitoring, contract review, invoice matching, proposal writing, resume screening, lead scoring and IT help desk requests. Companies can test any agent in a sandbox before switching it on, and members get complimentary credits to begin, with the option to move to usage-based paid packages. Dashboards show usage, costs and success rates, an admin portal lets company administrators track their teams' use of the agents, and a readiness assessment helps firms judge their preparedness.

The wider programme aims to enable more than 295,000 private sector companies and to roll out the 100 agents over two years. It also includes training tracks, recently launched by Dubai Chambers, to equip 14,000 companies from the Business Groups and Business Councils under Dubai Chamber of Commerce to use agentic AI in their administrative and operational work. In addition, the programme will support the growth of firms that develop and use agentic AI solutions, encourage knowledge-sharing and build institutional capabilities across the Dubai Chambers ecosystem. On the technical side, the platform meets the UAE's regulatory requirements and follows data privacy and protection standards. All data is hosted in the UAE and each company's information is kept separate from that of others, and the agents work in both Arabic and English.

Sultan bin Saeed Al Mansoori, Chairman of Dubai Chambers, said success in the shift to agentic AI should be judged by how well companies use the tools to solve business problems and produce real results, not by adoption alone. He said Dubai Chambers is therefore linking knowledge to practical use, building skills and widening access to specialised, high-quality tools that help firms adapt and change how they work. In his view, this approach is preparing a private sector able to respond to technological change and help shape the opportunities of the future economy. The platform was developed by Dubai Chambers, and members can now choose the agent that best fits their needs and subscribe to the available packages.

Articles.Title: Dubai Chambers launches world's first chamber-led Agentic AI marketplace - Global Times

stories.Headline: China's internet expo opens November 2 with 6G, AI agents and robots
stories.Summary:
Wuzhen, a canal town in Zhejiang Province, will host the 2026 "Light of the Internet" Expo from November 2 to 5. The event is now in its 12th edition and is a flagship event of the World Internet Conference Wuzhen Summit. This year's theme is "Intelligent Connectivity, Smart Future," and the expo will for the first time showcase "intelligent internet" comprehensively. Six exhibition zones will cover next-generation connectivity, computing and large models, intelligent devices, industry applications, smart living, and cybersecurity.

Organizers have made satellite internet, quantum communication, 6G and ultra-wideband key priorities. GSMA will bring Qualcomm and Keysight Technologies as part of a group pavilion, while China Telecom will present test results for a 6G-oriented space-air-ground network. Alibaba, Tencent and iFlytek will unveil new large models, and Hangzhou-based Kokoni will show its four-dimensional world model MoWorld 2.0. AI super-node systems from Alibaba, Huawei, ZTE and Sugon will be displayed together. Nubia's Navi X Ultra, billed as the world's first AI-agent phone, will appear alongside humanoid robots from Agibot, UBTech and Unitree, as well as AI glasses, AI earphones and AI PCs.

Unlike previous editions, this year's expo is also a marketplace. A digital-consumption fair will offer products including Stelato V8 and Luxeed R7 cars, UBTech robots, iFlytek AI learning machines and translation earphones, Keeson Technology's smart beds and ULS Robotics' exoskeleton robots, and visitors can buy on the spot. A "Tech for Warmth" program will give people with disabilities and senior residents hands-on access to brain-computer interfaces and exoskeleton rehabilitation devices. A youth science program will invite school students to explore the exhibits. Visitors must register with a mobile phone number and wait for approval before entry.

stories.Headline: AI drives digital transformation in China's primary care - Xinhua
stories.Summary:
China is introducing AI-powered tools in community health centers to speed up the digital transformation of grassroots healthcare, improve primary care, expand equitable access and enhance public well-being. AI assistants that support voice-based consultations, automated medical records, medication-risk screening, follow-up reminders and health education are appearing in community health centers. They are becoming a key part of the digital transformation of grassroots healthcare. The push comes as family doctors in China take on a wide range of duties, from resident registration and chronic-disease follow-up to initial screening and public-health record keeping, often burdened by heavy paperwork and limited staffing. AI-assisted family-doctor services have been introduced in many cities and provinces this year.

In May, the Longgang District of Shenzhen in south China's Guangdong Province launched the "Ant Afu" app, allowing residents to check medical reports, obtain AI-assisted interpretations, sign up for family-doctor services and link family members' health information. In Beijing's Fengtai District, the Majiapu Community Health Service Center has deployed an AI family doctor and an AI health steward. Built on large models and AI-agent technologies, the system supports chronic-disease management, wearable-device monitoring and automatic risk alerts, with high-risk cases forwarded to contracted family doctors. In Wuxi, east China's Jiangsu Province, AI was used in a citywide cancer screening campaign, and residents completed risk self-assessments through a mobile app or an AI-powered voice questionnaire. Big-data models identified high-risk groups for follow-up screening at 49 institutions equipped with AI-assisted imaging, ultrasound and endoscopy systems.

According to the Wuxi Municipal Health Commission, the AI-enabled screening significantly improved cancer detection among high-risk groups, with liver and lung cancers detected at markedly higher rates than in the general population. Industry insiders say the most significant shift is that AI is moving from isolated add-on tools into routine clinical workflows in some community health centers. Earlier systems often required doctors to open separate applications for image reading or diagnostic support. The newer AI systems are being integrated with hospital information systems and health-checkup platforms, so that AI prompts appear within the interfaces doctors already use.

Nie Chunlei, vice president of the Community Health Association of China, said AI used to seem lofty and unrelated to primary care, but now it has taken root at the grassroots level. With growing demand and expanding real-world deployments, more tech companies are entering the sector, further driving the digital upgrade of grassroots healthcare services. Ant Group's Ant Afu health app has rolled out its "AI agent plus human doctor" model in more than 40 cities, tens of thousands of grassroots doctors use the platform, and it had served more than 5 million residents by mid-August this year. JD Health, Runda Medical and others are also ramping up investment in primary-care AI, each drawing on its own strengths.

In October 2025, five national agencies issued guidance identifying intelligent clinical decision support, AI-enabled family-doctor services and coordinated chronic-disease management as priority areas, with a goal of basically achieving full coverage of AI-assisted diagnosis and treatment in primary care institutions by 2030. Industry insiders caution that scaling AI across primary care requires careful adaptation, and that AI cannot simply be transplanted into primary care but must be tailored to frontline needs, embedded in daily workflows and built into applications that are replicable, scalable and can be regulated. Sun Dehui, R&D director at the Beijing Medical Robotics Industry Innovation Center, said primary-care AI is a clear long-term direction for public health. With policy support increasingly focused on the grassroots level, the sector is poised for rapid growth in the coming years, offering significant market potential while continuing to ease the burden on frontline clinicians and benefiting residents with chronic conditions.

Articles.Title: AI drives digital transformation in China's primary care - Xinhua

stories.Headline: Detecting Insecure Compositions of Clean Agent Skills via Capability-Flow Graph Analysis
stories.Summary:
Researchers Yihao Li, Chuanpu Fu, Yizhou Zhao, Miao Chen, Qi Li and Ke Xu have published a paper, posted on arXiv and listed on doi.org on October 29, 2026, describing a security risk in AI agents that call third-party skills. The authors found that several skills, each judged clean on its own, can be chained together so that one skill's output becomes another skill's input during the agent's runtime, creating sequences that reach unsafe operations. To study this, they built a tool called KnotScryer, which treats each skill as a typed capability flow and maps cross-skill information flow in what they call a Skill Capability-Flow Graph. The article states that the tool searches for paths that carry protected or untrusted data toward insecure operations and then checks those paths in two stages, first by replaying the data flow for reachability and then by using an LLM audit to confirm the chains make semantic sense.

The authors applied KnotScryer to 13,598 clean skills drawn from ClawHub and tested the detected chains across three agent frameworks and three LLMs. According to the paper, the tool identified 612 insecure compositions that were consistently exploited across those frameworks. Under the GLM-5.1 model, the exploitation rate rose from between 16.5% and 18.2% for tag-match and graph-only baselines to 85.6% with KnotScryer, while the search space shrank by 85.3%. The paper also reports that 13.7% of the detected chains consisted entirely of skills that a single-skill scanner had labeled safe.

The article does not describe any formal requirement or regulation that would change as a result of the work. The paper is the work of its six named authors, and the article gives no statement from any company, platform or agent maintainer responding to the findings. The authors' central claim is that the risk comes from runtime orchestration rather than from any individual skill, which is why existing malicious-skill detection methods cannot catch it. The article does not report whether ClawHub or the agent frameworks tested have acted on the results, and it does not describe any planned follow-up beyond the paper itself.

Articles.Title: Detecting Insecure Compositions of Clean Agent Skills via Capability-Flow Graph Analysis

stories.Headline: Omni-UBench: Benchmarking Omni-Modal LLM-based Guardrails Across Safety, Utility, and Reliability
stories.Summary:
A research team led by Junhao Wang and eight co-authors has posted a paper introducing Omni-UBench, a benchmark for testing safety filters that guard omni-modal large language models, which handle text, images, audio, and video together. The paper was listed on arXiv and dated October 29, 2026. The authors say the work is the first comprehensive framework for assessing these guardrails across three dimensions: safety, utility, and reliability. The benchmark draws more than 183,000 samples from over 35 heterogeneous sources, covering text, image, audio, video, and combinations of these modalities. Each sample carries a safety label under a unified risk taxonomy.

The authors used the benchmark to evaluate 15 representative omni-modal models and guardrails. Their reasoning is that existing evaluation tools do not cover mixed-modality inputs well, which leaves the field without a shared way to measure how well such filters perform. The paper reports three main findings. First, modern omni-modal models show strong content moderation potential even without tuning specific to guardrails.

Second, existing guardrails still struggle to detect cross-modal queries that hide harmful intent or use sophisticated jailbreak techniques. Third, these guardrails show substantial safety hallucination and over-sensitivity to textual patterns, which the authors describe as a weak grasp of cross-modal safety meaning. The authors present these results as insights for building more trustworthy omni-modal guardrails in future research. The articles provided do not describe any specific follow-up plans, release dates for the benchmark, or responses from the developers of the evaluated systems.

Articles.Title: Omni-UBench: Benchmarking Omni-Modal LLM-based Guardrails Across Safety, Utility, and Reliability

stories.Headline: Development and validation of a deep learning model integrating 18F-FDG PET/CT radiomics and clinical features to predict major pathological response in non-small cell lung cancer patients receiving chemoimmunotherapy
stories.Summary:
A team of researchers from Guangdong Provincial People's Hospital and several other Chinese institutions has reported a deep learning model that predicts how well non-small cell lung cancer patients respond to chemoimmunotherapy before surgery. The study, published online on October 23, 2026, in Translational Lung Cancer Research, combined clinical data with quantitative features from fluorine-18 fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT scans. The researchers retrospectively analyzed 320 patients who received at least two cycles of treatment followed by surgical resection, and randomly split them into a training group of 256 and a validation group of 64. A further 31 patients from two independent hospitals served as an external test group.

The model was built from nine clinical characteristics, nine CT features and nine PET features, selected from a larger pool of 1,834 CT and 179 PET radiomics features. The inputs also included demographic and tumor metabolic measures, PD-L1 expression, tumor mutational burden and peripheral blood biomarkers. The authors describe the approach as a modality-aware attention model that generates a patient-specific score for predicting major pathological response, a category that includes pathological complete response. In the training set the model reached an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.7467, and in the external cohort it reached 0.7017, with a sensitivity of 82% and a specificity of 86%. The authors report that it outperformed a clinical-features-only model, which had an area under the curve of 0.6931.

The authors state that individual biomarkers such as PD-L1 and TMB, along with conventional imaging, only partly capture how sensitive a tumor is to treatment, and that combining clinical data with radiomics may improve prediction. They conclude that the multimodal model shows potential for predicting major pathological response in this setting but that larger prospective multicenter studies are needed before clinical use. The article also describes exploratory experiments suggesting the model kept some predictive ability when certain input types were missing, and the authors recommend further work on incomplete multimodal data, comparisons with simpler prediction models, and testing across different imaging platforms. The study is retrospective and its external cohort is small, and the article itself frames the model as warranting further investigation rather than as ready for clinical implementation.

Articles.Title: Development and validation of a deep learning model integrating 18F-FDG PET/CT radiomics and clinical features to predict major pathological response in non-small cell lung cancer patients receiving chemoimmunotherapy

stories.Headline: A cross-sectional benchmark of seven large language models for National Comprehensive Cancer Network guideline adherence in non-small cell lung cancer management
stories.Summary:
A cross-sectional study published on 29 September 2026 in Translational Lung Cancer Research benchmarked seven large language models on how closely their answers follow the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) Guidelines for non-small cell lung cancer. The team, led by researchers at Peking University People's Hospital in Beijing with Ant Group, built a set of 793 archived question-and-answer items based on version 4.2025 of the NCCN guidelines. Each item carried weighted criteria a good answer should meet and safety-critical criteria a model should avoid. The authors say existing medical benchmarks mostly test static knowledge through multiple-choice questions, which they consider insufficient for judging the conditional decisions oncology requires.

The seven models were each asked every item once, with no system prompt, retrieval tools, or internet access, and their answers were scored automatically against the rubric. Gemini-3-Pro had the highest clean normalized score at 0.739, and DeepSeek-V3.2 was the highest-scoring open-source model at 0.695. Gemini-3-Pro omitted required content in 28.36% of responses and DeepSeek-V3.2 in 33.24%, the lowest omission rates in the study. Gemini-3-Pro included none of the rubric-defined contraindicated points, a 0% inclusion rate. Models performed better on foundational tasks such as staging and definitions and worse on therapeutic modality selection and interpreting clinical trial results, where interpretation had the lowest task-level scores.

The authors state that the automated scores are specific to this benchmark and do not establish clinical safety or independently validated clinical quality. They conclude that the results reflect concordance with a guideline-based rubric rather than clinical correctness, and that the models are not ready for independent clinical decision-making. They recommend future clinical evaluation include external verification, guideline-based retrieval, structured assessment of retrieved evidence, uncertainty reporting, and clinician oversight. The paper notes that guideline agreement alone does not capture patient preferences, local drug access, regulatory approval, or multidisciplinary judgment. The article does not describe any follow-on trials or regulatory action.

Articles.Title: A cross-sectional benchmark of seven large language models for National Comprehensive Cancer Network guideline adherence in non-small cell lung cancer management

stories.Headline: CERT-In warns Apple users to update old iOS, macOS software
stories.Summary:
India's Computer Emergency Response Team, CERT-In, issued a high-severity warning on October 28, 2026, urging Apple device owners to install the latest software updates. The advisory flags several vulnerabilities that could let attackers run malicious code, gain elevated access, steal sensitive information, bypass security restrictions, or make a targeted device unavailable. These weaknesses affect iPhones, iPads, Macs, Apple Watches, Apple TVs, and Apple Vision Pro headsets. The warning applies to both individuals and organisations that use affected Apple products.

CERT-In says the flaws could be exploited through specially crafted web content, files, images, audio, or video, and other vulnerable applications and system components could also serve as entry points. The advisory covers older versions of several operating systems and Safari. Affected iPhones and iPads are those running iOS or iPadOS earlier than 18.7.11, 26.7.2, or 27.2, which includes iPhone XS, XS Max, and XR on the older iOS 18 branch. Macs are affected if they run macOS Sequoia earlier than 15.8.2, macOS Tahoe earlier than 26.7.2, or macOS Golden Gate earlier than 27.2.

Apple Watches, Apple TVs, and Vision Pro headsets are vulnerable if they run versions earlier than 27.2. The issues named in the advisory include memory corruption, buffer overflows, out-of-bounds read and write problems, and race conditions, any of which could compromise device integrity or cause crashes. Apple released the relevant updates on October 26, two days before CERT-In issued its warning. The agency's message to users is to install the latest compatible security update for each device.

Users can check for updates in their device settings, such as Settings, then General, then Software Update on an iPhone or iPad, and System Settings, then General, then Software Update on a Mac. Owners of older models that cannot run the newest major operating system should instead look for security updates for the version their device supports. The articles do not report any confirmed attacks exploiting these flaws. More to follow.

Articles.Title: CERT-In warns Apple users to update old iOS, macOS software

stories.Headline: How’s the US-China tech war going? Ask AI
stories.Summary:
In early 2024, ASML executives said on an earnings call that they did not expect to receive export licences for their most advanced immersion systems, the NXT:2000 and up, for China that year. The Dutch lithography company sits at the heart of the global semiconductor supply chain. The curbs came after years of US pressure, and the company warned they would cut 10 to 15 per cent from its core China equipment sales. The article describes this as an unmistakable shots-fired moment in the US-China tech war, delivered via the Netherlands.

A study has found that AI's reading of C-suite disclosures matches independent sell-side assessments almost in lockstep. The article says the technology latches on to what corporate bosses prefer to downplay, capturing a nuanced account of pains and gains. The piece was published by The Business Times on Thursday, Oct 29, 2026, at 11:18 AM and was written by Andy Mukherjee. It frames the US-China tech war around artificial intelligence, semiconductors, Trump tariffs and corporate earnings.

The article attributes the export restrictions to years of US pressure and reports ASML's own guidance on the damage to its China sales. It presents the study's finding that AI analysis of executive disclosures closely tracks independent sell-side assessments. The article does not name the authors of the study or the companies whose calls were examined. It also does not say who conducted the research or how the comparison was measured.

The article places these events in the context of the wider US-China tech war and the global semiconductor supply chain. It does not say what happens next, beyond ASML's January 2024 warning about its China equipment sales that year. No further steps by governments, companies or researchers are described. The piece offers no follow-up timeline or response from ASML or US officials.

Articles.Title: How’s the US-China tech war going? Ask AI - The Business Times

stories.Headline: The AI race belongs to those who deploy it quickly
stories.Summary:
India has a digital platform called BHASHINI that lets citizens use government services in more than 22 local languages through multilingual AI. In Japan, civil servants across government ministries began using generative AI tools in 2026 to speed up daily administration. The article says these examples show that deploying intelligence matters far more than inventing it. It adds that anyone who wonders what impact artificial intelligence has probably does not live in Asia.

The article says every week brings a new prediction that AI models are improving at a remarkable pace for many Asian economies. It presents regional execution as the force behind this change. The piece frames the race around how quickly places put AI to work rather than how quickly they build it. It gives the two country examples as evidence for that view.

The article does not name any official or give direct comments from anyone involved. It attributes the view to regional execution rather than to a specific person. Responsibility for the platforms and tools rests with the governments described, India for BHASHINI and Japan for the civil service tools. No further statements from those responsible appear in the text.

The context the article offers is the fast pace of AI model improvement across many Asian economies. What happens next is not stated beyond the continued use of the tools already described. The piece closes by suggesting that the impact of AI is most visible in Asia. More to follow.

Articles.Title: The AI race belongs to those who deploy it quickly - The Straits Times

stories.Headline: NICSI shortlists 18 firms for AI overhaul of government systems
stories.Summary:
The National Informatics Centre Services Inc (NICSI), an enterprise under the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), has shortlisted 18 companies for empanelment. The firms are expected to modernise government applications and digital platforms using artificial intelligence, according to documents reviewed by Moneycontrol. The shortlist was published on October 29, 2026, and reported by TechGig. The technical evaluation committee has recommended that the financial bids of all 18 technically qualified bidders be opened.

Among the bidders recommended for the next stage are Appinventiv Technologies, Dexian India Technologies, Amantya Technologies, CoreOps.ai, Jupitice Justice Technologies, Vayam Technologies, and CloudMojo Tech. The list also includes micro and small enterprises and startups. The selected firms would help central and state government departments, public sector undertakings and autonomous bodies. Their work would involve upgrading existing software, databases and government platforms, many of which may need changes to their underlying technology and architecture. They could also integrate AI, machine learning and generative AI into government systems as required.

Agencies could assess legacy systems, map technical dependencies, and review performance and security before making changes. Work may be awarded through fixed-price projects, time-and-material contracts, hybrid delivery models or managed services. Security compliance is a specific condition of the empanelment, and selected bidders must obtain a security audit of developed or modernised applications from a third-party auditing agency empanelled with the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In). Other firms on the shortlist include NETPROPHETS Cyberworks, Aeologic Technologies, Innovador Infotech, TECHMATRIX IT Consulting, ECHT Tech Consultancy Services, MLGS Technology, Stepforadder Technologies, Insphere Solutions, IQ-Line, Calance Software and Bocxy Technologies.

Articles.Title: NICSI shortlists 18 firms for AI overhaul of government systems

stories.Headline: Google opens Android tools to third-party AI agents
stories.Summary:
Google has opened its Android development tools to outside AI coding agents, including Anthropic's Claude Code and OpenAI's Codex. The move extends across Android Studio and the terminal-based Android CLI, letting these agents investigate bugs, test changes, and verify fixes rather than only writing code. According to Google, the change was announced alongside the Wednesday release of Android Studio Rabbit 2. The company's Bring Your Own Agent feature now works with more than 40 coding agents that use the open Agent Client Protocol.

Developers can install several agents and switch between them inside the IDE. Connected agents inherit the project context Android Studio already holds, including project structure, build configuration, symbols, and tools such as Compose Preview and the emulator. A new Change Review feature checks an agent's pending changes for common problems before they are applied. Official Android CLI plugins for Claude Code and Codex now handle project creation, emulator management, and UI inspection, and they link to Android documentation. Google also introduced Android Bench 2.0 to measure how models and agent harnesses handle complex Android development tasks.

Matthew McCullough, vice president of product for Android, stressed giving developers the freedom to choose their own models and coding agents. Adarsh Fernando, senior product manager for Android developer tools, said the aim is to help developers and their agents build high-quality Android apps more quickly. Google has framed these moves as a way to speed up development and improve app quality. Its own agent, Antigravity, is among the supported options.

The new command-line features go further into testing and production problems. A new android preview command lets agents render Jetpack Compose previews in the terminal, and Google said agents using it finished UI tasks 77 per cent faster while using up to three times fewer tokens. The android device remote command gives agents access to physical devices in Google's lab. In one demonstration, Claude Code used LeakCanary to check key user journeys for memory leaks, analysed heap dumps, traced the leaks to code, made fixes, and reran tests. Google says this helped capable models finish such investigations nearly twice as fast.

Articles.Title: Google opens Android tools to third-party AI agents

stories.Headline: NCS to grow pool of forward-deployed engineers to boost clients’ AI deployments
stories.Summary:
NCS plans to more than triple its pool of forward-deployed engineers from 100 to over 300 within two years. The technology services firm announced this on Oct 29 at the opening of its AI Mission Centre. The centre will help organisations move from pilot projects into deploying artificial intelligence on a wider scale. Forward-deployed engineers work within clients' teams, combining coding skills with business knowledge to build AI tools for everyday operations.

NCS plans to fill the positions through training existing staff and external hiring, but it did not provide a breakdown. The centre will bring together industry specialists and engineers to identify problems where AI can help, change how work is done, and safely test the tools in day-to-day operations. Successful projects will then be adapted for use by other organisations and in other markets. NCS also signed three memorandums of understanding with Changi Airport Group, the Institute of Mental Health and local food technology company Life3 Biotech.

Chief executive officer Sam Liew said the goal is to build AI capabilities that serve Singapore and solutions that can make an impact around the world. He spoke at the opening of the centre, which was officiated by Minister for Digital Development and Information Josephine Teo. Teo said that while countries or cities can come up with their own AI strategy, putting it to work requires real action, which Singapore has undertaken by setting up infrastructure like data centres, mobile networks and compute. She said NCS, which has a regional footprint, can help in Singapore's AI hub ambitions.

Google, ByteDance and Databricks have also been recruiting forward-deployed engineers, while OpenAI announced plans in May to create more than 200 technical roles here and train mid-career software engineers. With Changi Airport Group, NCS will improve an existing runway surveillance system called iFerret, which detects debris that could endanger aircraft. Its partnership with the Institute of Mental Health will explore digital tools to improve patient care, with one first project being Bio-ID, a facial recognition tool intended to help staff identify patients. Beyond expanding its forward-deployed engineers team, NCS is training employees across its workforce to use AI, and more than 2,000 staff who already work with AI are receiving further training.

Articles.Title: NCS to grow pool of forward-deployed engineers to boost clients’ AI deployments - The Straits Times

stories.Headline: These mid-career workers are back in class to learn AI. Is it paying off?
stories.Summary:
Demand for AI training has risen sharply in Singapore, especially among mid-career workers, and private academies reported a jump in enrolment. Vertical Institute said enrolment in its AI courses more than doubled over the past year. Tribe Academy said its three-month flagship programmes have been consistently oversubscribed across 10 intakes since January 2025. The demand comes as Singapore rolled out more than 200 courses on Sept 16, covering workplace productivity and advanced AI capabilities.

Kok Yokelee, general manager at Sky Vision Media, completed an introductory AI course at Vertical Institute and began using tools like Claude and Whisper to automate subtitling. Transcribing and translating a one-hour Indonesian show into Bahasa Malaysia once took two translators at least six to eight hours, and now takes 30 minutes. She later took a more advanced class on building AI agents with local large-language models so client data stays on her own device. Jason Sim, 46, an associate district director at Huttons Asia, completed a five-month Advanced Certificate in Generative AI for Digital Marketing Specialist in May, run by Singapore Management University with Tribe Academy. As a self-employed professional above 40, he received subsidies covering up to 95% of the fee, with the rest paid from his SkillsFuture credit.

Brennan Lee, 40, a senior AI search strategist at Heroes of Digital, completed an advanced certificate in generative AI for digital marketing in June. He was jobless when he signed up and secured his current job after attending. He said a reporting task that took eight to nine hours can now be done in around 40 minutes, and content briefs that took hours of competitor research take about 20 minutes. Kok said AI is not just about skills but also the willingness to accept change, and that it is better to adapt sooner than later. Sim said it is not about competing with AI but directing and leveraging it to work for us, and Lee said the key is to focus on what humans can do better, such as quality control, compliance, budget approvals and interpersonal communication.

Articles.Title: These mid-career workers are back in class to learn AI. Is it paying off? - The Straits Times

stories.Headline: PHP2Shell exploits highlight identity as key security control
stories.Summary:
Attackers exploited two remote code execution flaws in PHP, dubbed PHP2Shell, before official patches existed. Amazon observed exploitation attempts on October 17, four days before public disclosure, and PHP released its patch on October 21, the same day watchTowr reported attack attempts in the wild. Cloudflare saw attack traffic escalate rapidly after the disclosure. On October 26, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added both flaws to its list of known exploited vulnerabilities.

The incident underlines how far exploitation can outpace repair. According to Verizon's 2026 DBIR, the median time to fix a known exploited vulnerability is 43 days, and Qualys data shows 63 per cent of critical vulnerabilities remain open after a week, with a mean remediation time of 21.2 days. The problem is compounded because PHP ships inside appliances and hosting control panels that customers cannot patch directly, and PHP versions 8.1 and older received no official builds. Censys reported that 32.5 million internet-facing PHP services were still running potentially vulnerable versions as of October 27. The article argues that the damage from an incident depends largely on what access compromised service accounts, API keys, cloud roles and tokens permit, so restricting those permissions matters as much as the flaw itself.

The researchers who found the flaws, which had been present in PHP's code since 2012, worked with assistance from OpenAI and Google models, and the flaws were disclosed jointly with OpenAI. The article also points to the LiteLLM incident, in which attackers used a master key exposed in a public repository to obtain an unscoped GitHub organisation-owner token, which they then used to steal further maintainer tokens, subvert the release workflow and publish credential-stealing artifacts. The article notes that attackers often prefer the easiest route, such as leaked credentials, over chaining zero-day vulnerabilities. It does not describe further steps for affected organisations beyond these points.

Articles.Title: PHP2Shell exploits highlight identity as key security control

stories.Headline: Seed-stage creator apps should simplify 'For You' feed architecture
stories.Summary:
Seed-stage creator apps should avoid building complex, TikTok-style machine learning systems from scratch for their "For You" feeds, according to a TechGig article published on October 29, 2026. The piece recommends a simpler setup that retrieves eligible content, ranks it, applies safety and diversity rules, and logs interactions, which lets small teams learn faster and debug more easily. The article says this approach saves engineering resources that would otherwise go into building a full recommendation stack too early. It also argues that the feed should separate candidate generation, which finds plausible posts, from ranking, which orders them, so that the ranking step can be changed later without rebuilding everything. Initial ranking can combine signals such as creator affinity, content affinity, freshness, engagement quality, and exploration in a transparent weighted scoring model that product teams can understand.

The article advises that teams should prioritize collecting high-quality feedback data from the start. Every feed impression should record what was shown, its position, the ranking version, the user context, and the actions that followed, since this logging will matter for training future models. For teams without dedicated machine learning engineers, the article suggests managed services such as Amazon Personalize or Gortex's ranking API, which can reorder a supplied candidate set without requiring the team to run training and serving infrastructure. It stresses that learned ranking should be adopted only after enough interaction data has accumulated and feed quality is confirmed to be a barrier to growth. These recommendations are presented as architectural guidance rather than a regulatory or policy change.

The article does not name a specific company as responsible for the guidance, and it is written as an advisory piece in TechGig's digital architecture coverage, with the recommendations framed as the author's view of sound practice. It also does not report any incident, lawsuit, or statement from a particular executive. Beyond the design advice, the article suggests that creator apps should track creator-side health alongside viewer outcomes, including creator concentration, new-creator exposure, hides, skips, safety reports, content diversity, follow conversion, and creator retention. It recommends giving new creators controlled exploration traffic so established creators do not dominate the feed, and supplementing new users' limited data with popular and diverse content until behavioral signals emerge. The piece does not describe any timeline for implementation or any further developments to expect.

Articles.Title: Seed-stage creator apps should simplify 'For You' feed architecture

stories.Headline: South Korea financial sector hit by new cyberattacks
stories.Summary:
South Korea's financial sector was hit by another wave of cyberattacks, affecting the brokerages Daishin Securities and Mirae Asset Global Investments as well as the crypto exchange Bithumb. Daishin reported an attack that exposed the personal information of 38,490 customers, including their names, email addresses and mobile phone numbers. Mirae and Bithumb reported separate cybersecurity incidents on a Wednesday, according to local media, though neither has confirmed that customer data was taken. The reports were published on October 29, 2026, and the attacks came as part of a broader pattern of intrusions targeting the country.

Security researchers linked a September wave of attacks on South Korea to a suspected hacker based in China, who reportedly used an AI penetration testing tool called Artex. Officials are still investigating the root cause of the latest breaches, so it is not yet clear whether the same actor is responsible. South Korea's financial regulator has called for stronger cybersecurity measures after a string of attacks on financial firms and government agencies. The regulator made that call in Seoul on the Wednesday of the reports. The country also plans to run security checks on dozens of IT systems in the private sector.

The South Korean financial regulator, speaking through officials in Seoul, urged firms to strengthen their defenses. Daishin confirmed its breach, while Mirae and Bithumb have reported incidents without confirming any data loss. Security researchers, rather than officials, were the ones who tied the September attacks to the suspected China-based hacker and the Artex tool. Officials have not said who is responsible for the newest attacks. The articles do not say which specific measures the regulator will require or when the planned system checks will be completed.

Japan also reported a cybersecurity incident involving GMO Internet the day before these reports, following a series of attacks on its financial institutions. Investigators have not established any connection between the Japanese incident and the South Korean attacks. The articles make clear that AI-driven hacking is a growing concern across Asia. More details on the scope of the breaches and the investigation are expected as officials complete their work.

Articles.Title: South Korea financial sector hit by new cyberattacks

stories.Headline: Amazon updates AI usage rules for engineers, emphasizes real-world results
stories.Summary:
Amazon's engineering leaders have updated the role guidelines for Software Development Engineers, according to a company memo reported on October 29, 2026. The update says that real-world results matter more than any specific tool. Terk Terkowitz, a vice president and distinguished engineer at Worldwide Amazon Stores, laid out a vision for what the memo calls "Renaissance Developers," meaning engineers who combine human judgment with artificial intelligence. Engineers are being urged to build AI into their daily routines so they do not fall behind.

The memo warns against judging performance on what it calls flawed input metrics, such as token usage or lines of code, which it says could raise costs and add complexity. Leaders are instead directed to focus on longer-term effects on customers and the business. The memo also treats a failure of AI to perform a task as useful information rather than a mistake to hide. Managers and individual contributors are asked to use AI tools themselves, and to stay closely tied to customer needs so that adoption produces measurable business gains.

Terkowitz is the person named as setting out this vision, and the memo presents AI as central to how engineering will be done at the company. Leaders are expected to take ownership of linking the inputs their teams use to the outputs the business sees. The articles do not give specific figures, dates beyond the report itself, or a timetable for changes. They say only that Amazon will keep evolving the SDE role as AI's effects on business and engineering become clearer.

Articles.Title: Amazon updates AI usage rules for engineers, emphasizes real-world results
