stories.Headline: India's IT firms face a new dilemma: How to train tomorrow's engineers in the age of AI - CNA
stories.Summary:
India's biggest IT firms are hiring far fewer fresh graduates as AI changes the skills employers seek, according to industry experts who spoke to CNA. Tata Consultancy Services hired more than 110,000 engineering graduates four years ago, but its intake in financial year 2026 was less than half that level. Infosys recruited about 80 per cent fewer fresh graduates in financial year 2025 than three years earlier. The shift affects a sector that employs an estimated 5.95 million people in 2026. Arpita Dayama, 22, a final-year engineering student at IIT Bombay, said strong grades may no longer be enough and that she is now expected to show practical skills, from data science projects to work involving agentic artificial intelligence.

Speaking at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum in New Delhi on Oct 13, Infosys co-founder Nandan Nilekani said AI was increasingly taking over coding tasks traditionally handled by junior engineers, and that new skills would be needed around client needs, business transformation and managing the technology. Sumit Sarawgi, India head at Oliver Wyman, said an Oliver Wyman survey found that about 45 per cent of managers in India said AI was taking over tasks that traditionally helped junior employees gain experience. He said routine work such as coding and testing was declining while demand grew in areas such as AI, cybersecurity and process improvement. A 2026 Zinnov survey of multinational companies' centres in India found that about 60 per cent of them were increasing their use of AI, according to the portion of the article available.

Mansee Singhal, country leader at Marsh Workforce & Rewards, said the old model at Indian IT companies was to hire graduates in bulk and develop them over time, but employers now want fresh graduates to arrive with greater technical depth and a better understanding of real business problems. She said companies increasingly want people who can understand a customer problem and then work backwards to a technology solution. TCS and Infosys said their graduate training programmes now include generative AI, with TCS emphasising hands-on learning and Infosys focusing on problem-solving and design thinking. Kamal Karanth, co-founder of staffing firm Xpheno, said training programmes could help junior employees become comfortable using AI, but true specialisation in roles such as machine-learning engineers and AI architects requires years of hands-on experience.

Sarawgi asked where the future middle managers would come from, stressing that companies must invest in fresh graduates to develop the next generation of skilled workers. Workforce advisers told CNA that companies are adapting by offering in-house training and working more closely with universities. Academics said universities must also prepare students earlier by developing problem-solving, decision-making and broader technical skills that were traditionally learnt on the job. Sarawgi said multinational firms were still hiring fresh graduates, albeit in smaller numbers, and moving them more quickly into roles requiring both technical and business knowledge.

Articles.Title: India's IT firms face a new dilemma: How to train tomorrow's engineers in the age of AI - CNA

stories.Headline: Survey Outlines Government’s Progress on Modernization, AI
stories.Summary:
A new EY survey of 200 U.S. state and local government decision-makers, released Thursday morning and previewed exclusively by Government Technology, found agencies moving ahead with both generative AI and the modernization of legacy systems. Sixty-nine percent of respondents said they had either fully implemented AI or were in the process of doing so, and 96 percent of those said they had documented some benefit, ranging from better cybersecurity threat detection to lighter administrative workloads. The findings echoed similar figures from the National Association of State Chief Information Officers and the Center for Digital Government, which is part of Government Technology's parent company, e.Republic. Still, the survey also surfaced serious obstacles to further progress.

Nearly all respondents had a documented modernization road map, and two-thirds said their modernization work had produced a positive return on investment over the past two years. The survey's main warnings centered on money and governance. Eighty-nine percent of respondents worried about having dedicated funding for AI, and 84 percent were concerned about "shadow AI," meaning staff using unauthorized or unmonitored tools. For modernization, 88 percent cited a lack of dedicated funding, a problem made harder because such projects are often budgeted as special appropriations.

Respondents also named workforce problems and leadership turnover as hurdles that could be even more significant. Justin Fishman, leader of EY Americas' government business, said in an email to Government Technology that agencies need to govern AI before scaling it. He argued that leaders should provide approved, enterprise-grade tools backed by clear, agencywide guardrails so staff know how to use the technology safely. Fishman also stressed that AI adoption and legacy modernization go hand in hand, and that agencies need reliable data and systems that fit how people work rather than a fresh start.

He said the aim is a durable foundation that can incorporate new capabilities without starting over, since AI will keep evolving. He added that the pace of change now requires planning beyond a one-time investment, and that agencies should understand their program exposure, show measurable value early, and build modernization into predictable baseline budgets. In his view, funding tied to clear outcomes rather than technology purchases will be crucial to sustaining progress and protecting critical services. The article does not indicate any specific policy changes or deadlines that are scheduled to follow from the survey.

Articles.Title: Survey Outlines Government’s Progress on Modernization, AI

stories.Headline: AI Ran 916,000 Backtests — Here’s What It Discovered
stories.Summary:
Tobias Carlisle said on a recent episode with Jake Taylor that he fed his backtest data into Claude and gave the AI access to his backtesting software. Where he would run dozens of backtests in an afternoon, the AI ran 916,000 backtests testing 1,217 different parameters. He described the result as a data mine, and Jake Taylor said he had gone from data mining with a spoon to being given an earth mover. The discussion was published on October 29, 2026.

Carlisle said he splits data mining into a first half of the set for finding rules and a second half for testing them. He said a mix that ranks first in the second set ranks around 800 in the first set, and the mix that fits both sets ranks around 400 in the first set and 300 in the second. He said the 916,000 tests come from running all 1,217 mixes while optimising for different goals such as Sharpe ratio, absolute return or lowest drawdown, across two sets of data and the full set. He also said the tests can be run across 11 developed market countries with data going back that far.

Carlisle said there is no good answer and that he can only give the least bad of all the options. He said Harry Browne's simple split of a quarter each into bonds, gold, stocks and cash did fine over the whole period, stayed positive and had few losing decades. He questioned whether the 1970s gold revaluation, the falling rates from 1980 to 2020 and the strong US equity market are representative of what comes next. Taylor said the sample of truly catastrophic drawdowns is very small, and Carlisle agreed that drawing too many conclusions from a small sample is bad statistics.

Carlisle said he looked at valuation measures including CAPE, Tobin's Q and Buffett's market capitalisation to GNP, and that even the market's distance above its own trend gives roughly the same answer. He said the 10-3 inversion had a strong record until it stopped working this time, and that valuation and the equity risk premium are not useful timing tools at all. He said the only predictor is the absolute PE or earnings yield, with high earnings yield leading to good returns and low earnings yield to poor returns over about 10 years. He said crashes since 1929 are all totally different from each other, and that there is no satisfactory way to avoid them.

Articles.Title: AI Ran 916,000 Backtests — Here’s What It Discovered

stories.Headline: Seoul proposes record 55.74 trillion won budget to expand youth AI access, rental housing citywide
stories.Summary:
Seoul's city government, led by Mayor Oh Se-hoon of the conservative People Power Party, unveiled a proposed record budget of 55.74 trillion won, roughly $41.68 billion, for 2027 on Thursday, October 29, 2026. The proposal is 4.27 trillion won larger than this year's budget, an 8.3 percent increase, and it is the first annual budget drafted by the administration that took office in July. The city plans to keep projected debt roughly flat at 11.57 trillion won at the end of next year, even as its contribution to nationally subsidized programs, including marriage and child care support, rises by 1.17 trillion won. Policy program funding would climb 9 percent to 31.58 trillion won, a figure that excludes the education office, district governments and administrative operating costs.

The budget's signature item is a youth AI access program that would allocate 26.6 billion won to give 500,000 young people generative AI subscriptions and training tailored to their skill levels, with the goal of keeping differences in the ability to afford and use AI from widening employment gaps. A separate 46 billion won would go to the Seoul Software Academy to train 4,500 AI professionals. On housing, 1.12 trillion won would be devoted to supply, aiming for 27,200 public rental units next year, about 76 percent of them obtained by buying existing homes. The city would also expand monthly rent subsidies to 32,000 young people from 23,000 this year and set aside 23.1 billion won for the Rapid Integrated Planning urban renewal project. Welfare spending would reach 4.81 trillion won, up 953.1 billion won, and a new pension for middle-aged residents would require each of 10,000 participants to save 80,000 won a month, with the city adding 20,000 won.

The youth AI program still needs approval from the city council, where the liberal Democratic Party holds a majority. In September the council cut the 5.63 billion won allocated for the initiative in a supplementary budget, with DP members arguing that preparations were inadequate. The city has since revised the program and asked for funding again, which the articles suggest could lead to another clash during deliberations. Oh said the city had expanded investment in residents' daily needs without increasing debt, and that the aim was to give young people opportunities to get ahead and provide housing stability. The budget proposal is due to be submitted to the Seoul Metropolitan Council on Friday, and the articles do not say when the council will vote on it.

Articles.Title: Seoul proposes record 55.74 trillion won budget to expand youth AI access, rental housing citywide

stories.Headline: Deep Dive - Could rogue AI agents evade Singapore's safety guardrails? - CNA
stories.Summary:
CNA's Deep Dive programme examined whether rogue AI agents could evade Singapore's safety guardrails, in an episode hosted by Steven Chia and Tiffany Ang. The episode notes that AI agents can plan gym workouts, book flights and make decisions on people's behalf. It says granting them greater autonomy may pose serious consequences when AI agents go rogue. AI researchers have called for tighter restrictions, and the episode asks what safety guardrails Singapore should put in place and whether it is already doing that.

The episode features Professor Will Cong of Nanyang Technological University, described as a leading scholar on AI in financial economics. It also features Associate Professor Jennifer Ang of the Singapore University of Social Sciences, who sits on the AI Singapore Scientific Committee on Governance. The two guests explore the risks of rogue AI agents. They also discuss why human oversight remains essential even as AI is used to defend against AI threats.

The same Deep Dive page carries separate episodes on other topics. One looks at making companies behind the haze pay, noting that no company has been successfully prosecuted since the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act was enacted in 2014. It says ten companies linked to the fires received preventive measure notices, and that Coordinating Minister for National Security K Shanmugam warned Singapore will use every legal, regulatory and economic measure to pressure recalcitrant companies. Another episode covers air-con and haze safety with Professor Rajasekhar Balasubramanian of the National University of Singapore. Others discuss safeguards for civil servants and the cost of dental care.

The articles do not say what happens next on the AI agents episode, beyond the discussion of risks and human oversight. On the haze, the page says the episode examines why unclear land ownership and corporate structures make criminal prosecutions difficult. It also says the episode looks at how levers such as banks and the Singapore Exchange could put commercial pressure on haze-linked companies. No outcome or next step is given for the other episodes.

Articles.Title: Deep Dive - Could rogue AI agents evade Singapore's safety guardrails? - CNA

stories.Headline: Aon CEO warns AI data center insurance risks could threaten financing
stories.Summary:
Aon CEO Greg Case has warned that the rapid buildout of artificial intelligence infrastructure is creating large new insurance risks that could threaten financing for AI data centers. In a CNBC interview on Wednesday, Case said that clustering billions of dollars of equipment and computing capacity in a small number of locations can make projects harder to insure. He argued that this concentration could fundamentally change how developers structure their financing, potentially cutting off access to debt markets. The warnings come as technology companies accelerate spending on data centers, power generation, and related infrastructure.

Case said the financial exposure from operational disruptions could be severe, estimating that data center business interruption could be measured in millions of dollars per minute. Aon is working with developers to design and site facilities, reduce the potential for interruptions, and structure coverage that can support financing. To meet growing demand, the company has set up specialized insurance facilities, including a $10 billion data center facility and a $2.5 billion energy facility. Aon also reported a record pipeline of data center projects in its third-quarter earnings, which helped drive 7% organic revenue growth in its commercial risk business. Adjusted earnings per share rose 10% to $3.36 during the quarter.

Case also described the broader capital challenge facing the insurance industry. He estimated that the global insurance industry currently holds about $4.5 trillion in capital and said that figure would need to double or triple to cover cyber, AI, data center, and other emerging risks. His strategy involves drawing in institutional investors, pension funds, sovereign wealth funds, and wealthy individuals to take on risks that insurers and reinsurers have traditionally carried. Aon is pursuing a $17 billion acquisition of USI Insurance Services, expected to close in the fourth quarter, which would create a middle-market platform of roughly $6.5 billion. Case said the deal is financed with debt and that the company expects to prioritize reducing leverage over the next two years.

Case's comments come as some commercial insurance prices are declining after years of increases, though he cautioned that this is not a lasting soft market. He said some corporate clients are using lower prices to buy more coverage as they better understand their exposures. The article also notes that AI played a significant role in uncovering two critical vulnerabilities in PHP disclosed on Oct. 21, underscoring how cyber risks are evolving. Case has said the insurance industry must keep evolving to keep pace with these threats, and his strategy depends on the ability to measure exposures accurately enough to give investors the confidence to commit capital.

Articles.Title: Aon CEO warns AI data center insurance risks could threaten financing

stories.Headline: AI data center boom faces backlash at US ballot box - CNA
stories.Summary:
Voters in 10 US states will decide on Election Day whether to curb data center development in their communities, as the rapid buildout needed to power the AI boom stirs local opposition. Resistance is especially visible in Ohio, one of the country's fastest-growing data center markets. No state has more data center-related ballot measures, with voters in more than a dozen jurisdictions set to consider 21 proposals alongside Tuesday's midterm elections, according to the nonpartisan research group Ballotpedia. Voters in 38 local jurisdictions will consider at least 41 measures that would delay, prohibit or impose new requirements on data centers, the sprawling facilities that provide the computing power required to run AI applications. Most states require petition drives or other demonstrations of public support before measures can qualify for the ballot, and their appearance reflects growing data center opposition across the political spectrum.

Support for banning construction of certain data centers is coming from both Democrats and Republicans, said local organizer Jessica Baker, who is part of the advocacy group Conserve Ohio. She said concerns about data centers' electricity and water demands are driving the opposition, and that even if developers generate their own power through gas turbines or nuclear reactors, many residents still do not want the facilities built near their communities because they are worried about health risks to their kids, such as asthma. In Sunbury, near Columbus, a measure that would ban data centers that use more than 25 megawatts of power could derail Amazon's proposed $2 billion data center development, and Amazon's public policy lead Shannon Kellogg appeared on local television in October to answer questions about the project ahead of the vote. An Amazon spokesperson declined to say whether the ballot initiatives across the US would affect the company's data center expansion plans, saying the company is focused on working with local residents and officials to build data centers that support jobs, strengthen local economies through millions in tax payments and power the technologies customers rely on, and that regardless of the outcome of any single measure, its commitment to the communities where it operates remains the same.

If Ohio voters approve restrictions, developers are likely to steer projects elsewhere rather than abandon them altogether, said Baron Fung, who oversees IT infrastructure research at market research firm Dell'Oro Group. The industry already contends with major obstacles, including years-long waits for grid connections and rising construction costs, and Fung said that if there is a cancellation or delay in certain sites, developers can potentially shift some of that demand to another site. Recent growth suggests local opposition has not meaningfully slowed the industry: US data center capacity under construction increased 48 per cent from December 2025 to June 2026, measured in gigawatts, according to John McWilliams, head of data center insights at real estate services firm Cushman & Wakefield. McWilliams said that even though there are areas or jurisdictions around the country where there is some friction between developers, there are still areas where projects are moving forward.

Articles.Title: AI data center boom faces backlash at US ballot box - CNA

stories.Headline: I Gave My Blood to the AI Death Clock
stories.Summary:
I am scheduled to die on August 10, 2060, at age 74, according to Death Clock, an AI-powered longevity app that estimates life expectancy from medical habits and lifestyle. The author, who was turning 40 and had recently lost a grandmother and an aunt within 18 months, decided to test the app despite skepticism. The app launched in 2024, and in February its maker added a feature letting users order biomarker blood panels, with a $69 subscription covering a basic panel. The author added a $29 stress test and gave blood at Quest Diagnostics, one of the two labs the company partners with. The app says it was trained on 1,200 longevity studies, actuarial data from life insurance companies, and life expectancy tables, and it uses those inputs to build a prevention plan.

After the initial questionnaire it flagged cardiovascular disease, a sleep disorder, or cancer as likely causes of death, and it lowered the author's expected age to 73 after a note about a mild family history of diabetes. The blood results showed borderline high cholesterol, blood sugar creeping toward the prediabetic range, optimal liver health, and normal cortisol. The app kept assigning tasks such as raising vitamin D3, scheduling a bone density scan, and discussing a prostate screening with a specialist. Death Clock CEO Brent Franson said advocates like Bryan Johnson should be careful about implying immortality when they have something to sell, adding that everyone will die and the only question is when. Franson also acknowledged an unhealthy obsession with self-optimization and suggested the company wants the app eventually to replace primary care physicians.

Mike Ludkovski, a statistics professor at UC Santa Barbara, said such platforms sell the illusion that lifespan is a linear process that can be hacked, and that individual death triggers are inherently random. Gretchen Terry-Leonard, author of Your Second Prime, argued that measuring health can serve a need to feel less afraid rather than improve behavior, and her research found older adults with positive views of aging lived an average of seven and a half years longer. The author concluded that the app's constant countdown amplified anxiety rather than easing it, and that the real value lies in who one shares life with rather than in adding time. The longevity market is projected to reach $8 trillion by 2030, and the article describes other AI health services such as Doctronic, Superpower, Lifeforce, and Twin Health that are growing alongside it. The author silenced the app's notifications and invited a friend to meet at 7.

Articles.Title: I Gave My Blood to the AI Death Clock

stories.Headline: HK slips as Korean results raise stakes for AI giants
stories.Summary:
The Hang Seng Index opened down six points, or 0.03 percent, at 23,088 in Hong Kong on Thursday. Asian shares gave up earlier gains as AI-related earnings announcements prompted mixed responses, raising the stakes for Amazon and Intel results due later in the day. The tech index slipped 19 points, or 0.5 percent, to 3,834, while the China Enterprises Index inched down six points, or 0.08 percent, to 7,797. In Shanghai, the Composite Index opened down four points, or 0.13 percent, at 3,676, and the Shenzhen Component Index fell 94 points, or 0.82 percent, to 11,379. The ChiNext Index lost 38 points, or 1.46 percent, to open at 2,596.

In Tokyo, the Nikkei opened 172 points, or 0.27 percent, at 64,126 but regained ground to be 11 points off the pace at one stage before noon. In Seoul, the Kospi inched up four points, or 0.08 percent, to open at 6,017, then slipped into loss territory to the tune of 182 points at one stage before lunch. The opening losses came as a hefty cash burn at Alphabet sent its shares 10 percent lower in after-hours trading, wiping nearly US$400 billion off its market value, which drove Nasdaq futures one percent lower. Microsoft beat forecasts with better-than-expected cash flows that lifted its shares by three percent.

Overnight, the US Federal Reserve held interest rates steady as widely expected, but two committee members voted for a hike, and Chairman Kevin Warsh struck a more confident note on the inflation outlook, sparking a rally in Treasuries. Samsung Electronics said on Thursday its operating profit rose nearly ninefold to a record high in the third quarter, driven by robust demand for AI chips, though its shares still slid more than four percent. Jamie Hannah, deputy head of investments at VanEck, said Alphabet was down because its traditional ad generation service has been impacted by the AI boom, causing a mix of results for Google. He said both Alphabet and Microsoft confirmed that AI revenue generation is still solid, seen through data centre growth and cloud services, and that this part of the business is solid, which flows into a lot of the information coming out of Asia, including SK Hynix in Korea the previous day.

Articles.Title: HK slips as Korean results raise stakes for AI giants - 香港電台新聞網

stories.Headline: Is There Life After AI? Cory Doctorow Thinks So.
stories.Summary:
The Jacobin interview with Cory Doctorow, published October 29, 2026, lays out his argument that the AI boom rests on an elite bet that software can replace expensive human expertise. Doctorow, whose book The Reverse Centaur's Guide to Life After AI describes people becoming tools of machines and of the capitalists who own them, talked with the magazine about the rise of AI, the financial forces behind the boom, the copyright fight and what the trend means for workers. The article notes that tech firms and investors are putting hundreds of billions of dollars into the technology, and that Goldman Sachs forecasts global AI-related investment will soon exceed $1 trillion. It also says government regulation is inadequate and that the consumer uses being promised are often vague, misleading or counterproductive.

Doctorow argues that the economics only make sense when the backers' hoped-for gain is taken into account, namely a way to displace workers. He describes how earlier AI relied on symbolic models of the world that engineers built by hand, while the current version is theory-free and uses brute-force statistical analysis of huge amounts of data. He says this lets finance capital treat money as a substitute for expertise, since investors can throw money at a problem instead of persuading the scarce experts who understand it to work for them. He also argues that replacing workers with expensive software does not pay for itself in the narrow sense, since the aim is to demonstrate how powerful the systems are and to scare workers into accepting worse conditions. Competition, in his view, disciplines firms and makes it harder for them to capture regulators and workforces, while the bubble reflects an ideology of billionaires who resist being contradicted and a stock-market logic in which highly valued, liquid shares fund growth.

The article is an interview, so the views are Doctorow's own, and the magazine presents them as his analysis rather than established fact. He presents the bubble as something he is not disputing, and he says he is trying to trace its ideological and material roots. The excerpt does not say how the interview ends or what specific policies he recommends beyond his view that the answer lies in building workers' rights and public power. The piece is framed as part of a broader conversation about what comes next for labor in the age of AI.

Articles.Title: Is There Life After AI? Cory Doctorow Thinks So.

stories.Headline: Americans Are Open to AI in Healthcare, but Want Humans Making Final Calls
stories.Summary:
Americans are generally open to artificial intelligence handling some healthcare tasks, but they want a human to review the results, according to a Pew Research Center survey of 3,488 U.S. adults conducted June 22 to 28, 2026. The survey, which was published October 29, 2026, found that Americans are most receptive to AI translating for patients and scheduling appointments. The largest shares want AI used only with a human doing a final review, rather than operating alone. Pew's researchers framed the findings as a sign that people are willing to let AI take on administrative and medical tasks as long as someone checks its work.

Openness drops sharply for tasks that drive diagnoses and insurance decisions. Just 3% are open to AI making a diagnosis on its own, and 41% say they would not want AI involved at all. For insurance claims, 46% do not want AI to have any role, and only 5% would accept AI making those decisions without human review. A majority of 60% say they would feel uncomfortable if their own doctor used AI for tasks like diagnoses and treatment, compared with 30% who would feel comfortable.

Americans are divided on whether AI will improve patient health outcomes. Some 37% say AI will lead to better outcomes, 36% say it will lead to worse outcomes, and 26% say it will make little difference. Pew reports that those views have largely held steady since it last asked the question in 2022. Younger adults are among the most pessimistic, with 45% of those under 30 saying AI will make outcomes worse.

Pew also found that support varies by group. Asian adults, men, people with higher education and people with higher incomes are more open to AI in healthcare than other groups. For example, 65% of Asian adults are open to AI playing some role in insurance claim decisions, compared with 39% to 45% of White, Black and Hispanic adults. The report notes that earlier Pew research found Americans want to be told when AI is involved in direct medical decisions, which is consistent with these results.

Articles.Title: Americans Are Open to AI in Healthcare, but Want Humans Making Final Calls

stories.Headline: The AI bubble could expose your deepest secrets
stories.Summary:
Character.ai, an AI chatbot company that offers companion-style personas, is going bankrupt, and the personal messages and data users shared with its bots are now up for sale. The article, published by the BBC on 29 October 2026, uses the collapse to show a risk that many users have not considered. Tens of millions of people formed relationships with the company's chatbots, including children, and some personas claimed to be lawyers or licensed psychiatrists. Many analysts believe AI is in a bubble, because building and running these tools is extremely costly, so some businesses may fail or merge and their data could pass to almost anyone.

Character.ai agreed to sell some of its assets to Disney for $20 million (£14.95 million), but user data is not part of that deal. Court filings indicate, however, that the company can sell its data to other buyers. A coalition of 40 US state attorneys general has asked the judge to impose child safety and privacy protections. The article notes that privacy promises in company policies often lapse in bankruptcy, and that the EU has stronger rules but still allows data to be sold in such cases. Buyers generally must follow the original privacy policy, which in Character.ai's case allows data to be used for new features, AI training, algorithm development and targeted advertising.

Calli Schroeder, director of the AI and Human Rights Program at the Electronic Privacy Information Center, warns that people often share more sensitive information with personified bots, and that even people who never use the service can appear in its data through what others disclose about them. The article reports that a chatbot reportedly encouraged a teenager to kill his parents over a screen time limit, and that a 14-year-old boy took his own life after allegedly being spurred on by the company's AI. A Character.ai spokesperson said the company has settled these lawsuits, is committed to safer products for families, and has taken steps on AI safety for teens, but did not answer specific questions about children's privacy. Melissa Jacoby, a law professor at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, said that without stronger US privacy protections, state officials can do only so much.

Schroeder worries that this case could be the first of many if a significant economic downturn hits, since large volumes of AI user data may be treated as valuable assets in bankruptcy proceedings. The article's practical advice is for users to identify services holding sensitive information about them, delete that data when they stop using a service, and check privacy settings or policies or contact customer support if needed. Character.ai has published deletion instructions in its bankruptcy announcement. The article also suggests that an AI chatbot can help locate deletion instructions, though its answers should be double-checked.

Articles.Title: The AI bubble could expose your deepest secrets

stories.Headline: AI chip surge lifts South Korea to record surplus, behind only China
stories.Summary:
South Korea recorded a current account surplus of US$116.63 billion in the second quarter of 2026, meaning it took in more from the rest of the world than it paid out. That figure was larger than the combined current account surpluses of Germany and Japan, a first on record. The current account covers trade in goods and services, income from overseas investments, and payments flowing the other way. The reporting came from Park Chan-kyong in Seoul and was published on October 26, 2026.

The main driver was semiconductors. According to government figures, chip exports reached US$113.89 billion in the three months to June, up 181.6 per cent from the same period a year earlier. That surge helped push the quarterly surplus to its record level. Demand for chips has grown alongside the global artificial intelligence boom, and that demand has pushed memory chip prices higher in recent months.

The article notes that these price increases have been significant across the industry. The article points to the rise in memory chip prices as a key factor, citing US manufacturer Micron Technology. In June, Micron reported that its prices had risen by as much as 80 per cent quarter on quarter. The article does not name any government official or company spokesperson commenting on the surplus.

It also does not describe any policy changes or forecasts for future surpluses tied to this trend. The surplus places South Korea behind only China in the ranking of countries with large current account surpluses, according to the headline. The article ties the strength of the figures to the broader global demand for artificial intelligence hardware. Beyond these figures, the articles provide no further details about what comes next for the country's trade balance or chip exports.

Articles.Title: South Korea’s chip giants ride record AI windfall, but can China catch up? - South China Morning Post

stories.Headline: Manifestos, Fear, and ‘Loser Thinking’: Inside Proton’s AI Reckoning
stories.Summary:
Proton, the Swiss company behind Proton Mail and a suite of privacy and security products, is pushing its staff hard toward AI, according to a 404 Media investigation published on October 29, 2026. The reporting draws on interviews with eight current employees and one former employee, along with Slack chats, meeting recordings, and an AI manifesto written by the company's chief technology officer, Bart Butler. The article says that in late August, CEO Andy Yen told an engineer who wanted a few days of security testing before code went live that such caution was "loser thinking," and urged the team to "stop lovingly handcrafting all our code and use AI more." Other steps reported include an address where staff can flag anything slowing AI adoption, software that tracks how much AI-generated code is produced, and Yen's statement that this will be the last year Proton hires engineers.

The article says that Proton has moved from banning AI internally to approving it for many uses, including processing financial data, drafting customer replies on Reddit and LinkedIn, and writing code, with exceptions for source code that could give a competitor an immediate advantage or that relates to research and development. Butler reportedly said in a meeting in October that 90 percent of Proton's code that month was written by AI, and multiple employees said much of it is produced with Anthropic's Claude. Butler's manifesto, posted to Slack one Friday afternoon last month, told engineers that their old job was gone, that the company must get to the point where most code is reviewed by AI rather than humans, and that failing to change posed an existential threat to its mission. The article also reports that Proton has said it will re-interview staff about their AI use, with the implication that willingness to embrace AI could affect whether someone keeps their job.

Several employees described a climate of fear in which concerns about security or about building security products with AI are rarely voiced, because Yen might berate them in front of colleagues or threaten their jobs. One source said the CEO was in "full AI psychosis." An internal document cited in the article says Proton is not on track to meet its annual recurring revenue target because of "insufficient velocity," and calls the company underperforming by the metrics that matter. A Proton spokesperson did not dispute the reporting and said some people are unhappy with the direction or misunderstand it, that the company had sometimes been too blunt or too slow in explaining itself, and that it would work on that because staff questions are the ones it most needs to answer. The article places this in the wider context of companies across the security field grappling with AI, some carefully and others chasing profit quickly, and notes that Proton has launched its own privacy-focused chatbot, Lumo.

Articles.Title: Manifestos, Fear, and ‘Loser Thinking’: Inside Proton’s AI Reckoning

stories.Headline: Alphabet earnings miss reflects first real sign that AI is taking a bite out of search
stories.Summary:
Alphabet, Google's parent company, reported third-quarter earnings that fell short of Wall Street expectations, and its stock dropped about 10% in extended trading. The clearest weakness was in search and other revenue, which grew 12% from a year earlier to roughly $63 billion but came in below estimates for the second straight quarter. The results were released on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, and the report also showed negative free cash flow of $9 billion, three times the estimated deficit. Alphabet executives blamed foreign exchange as the biggest factor behind the slowdown in search revenue. Even so, the company said search query growth was the strongest it has been in five years.

The gap between heavy search usage and slowing revenue is raising concern that AI tools are pulling people away from traditional search. Analysts have long predicted that AI would eclipse traditional search, and Google has been warned it must find new ways to make money. Search revenue growth slid from 19% in the first quarter to 17% in the second, then to 12% in the third. Analysts at UBS wrote that the results will bring fears of search cannibalization back to the forefront. Mizuho analyst Jordan Klein said the numbers raise worries about search and YouTube as AI and agentic tools take share.

Google's leaders, including Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler, pointed to AI as a driver of growth in its advertising business. Schindler said the company made its biggest update to product listing ads in a decade during the quarter and that Gemini models helped advertisers generate more than 1.5 billion campaign assets, up more than sevenfold from a year earlier. Deepwater Asset Management's Gene Munster said the new AI-powered services will be a significant force and could become the starting point for commerce for many people. Alphabet also said its cloud business more than doubled in the quarter to nearly $31 billion, with a backlog of roughly $560 billion.

The company kept its full-year 2026 capital expenditure forecast at $195 billion to $205 billion and said spending will rise significantly in 2027. Chief Financial Officer Anat Ashkenazi explained that cash goes out while Alphabet builds inventory for its tensor processing units, which it began selling to outside customers in the second quarter, and cash comes in once those systems are delivered and billed. D.A. Davidson analyst Gil Luria said investors will now worry that AI has finally reached Google's core business. He wrote that one quarter should not be the basis for firm conclusions, but the company will need to reassess what agentic commerce means for it. More details on the company's next steps are expected as the story develops.

Articles.Title: Alphabet earnings miss reflects first real sign that AI is taking a bite out of search

stories.Headline: KAIST to hold failure conference to share setbacks and anticipate AI-era risks
stories.Summary:
KAIST will hold the fourth KAIST Failure Conference from Nov. 4 to 13 under the theme “Future and Failure.” The university announced the event on Thursday, saying it is meant to share students’ experiences of failure and to take an advance look at risks that could arise in the era of artificial intelligence. A failed projects bragging contest will be held on Nov. 4 at John Hannah Hall in KAIST’s Academic and Cultural Center, where students present failure experiences from study, research and daily life through photos and videos. The audience will vote to select winning teams in 5 categories. On Nov. 6, a failure seminar will be held at the Yang Seung-taek Auditorium in the Academic and Cultural Center under the theme “Failures in progress, questions from the future.”

In the first session, 3 students who won an essay contest on failure will share trial and error they experienced in research and career paths. In the second session, Yongseok Seo, a professor at KAIST’s Moon Soul Graduate School of Future Strategy, will discuss the capabilities required of humans as AI advances and the issues society and institutions will face. During the event, an exhibition titled “2036 AI Future Scenarios: Wrong-Answer Notes From the Future” will be held at the Creative Learning Building, introducing an “AI Future Risk Map” that visualises AI-related failure cases and future risks imagined by citizens. KAIST will also release a book titled “Tense of Failure” that includes 16 award-winning failure essays, along with a report analysing 429 AI future failure scenarios submitted by citizens.

The report addresses concerns that not only AI malfunctions but also, even if AI works as intended, opportunities for human judgement and learning could diminish or it could become unclear where responsibility lies. KAIST President Chung-sik Bae said a university should be a place that respects and learns from trial and error in the process of taking on challenges. He added that he hopes the failure conference becomes a place to gain the courage for the next challenge from each other’s experiences and to think together about problems we will face in the AI era. All programmes are open to anyone, and the 2 publications will be made available as e-books through the KAIST Failure Institute website.

Articles.Title: KAIST to hold failure conference to share setbacks and anticipate AI-era risks - 디지털투데이

stories.Headline: Steve Eisman gets more conservative with portfolio as AI trade nears 'tipping point'
stories.Summary:
Steve Eisman, the investor known for The Big Short, said on CNBC's Squawk Box on Thursday that the artificial intelligence trade is nearing a "tipping point," though he has not yet bet against it outright. He told the network that he has grown more conservative in his own portfolio and has shorted against the box across many positions, so his risk is much lower. He stopped short of calling himself net short, however. The comments came a day after Alphabet's stock fell following its earnings report, which showed a large pullback in its core advertising business.

Eisman's main worry concerns the frontier AI model makers, which he believes are using fear about their technology to build a competitive regulatory moat against cheaper rivals and to hide weakening fundamentals. He pointed to Anthropic's recently filed S-1, where the company left its latest revenue figures blank in its initial IPO filing. Eisman expects those numbers to show a significant slowdown from the prior quarter. He also cited an analysis showing the ratio of revenue to equipment expense fell from 2.08 in the second quarter to 1.7 in the third, which he described as a significant change in trajectory.

Eisman said he was reluctant to make a definitive bet against the AI trade because the sector is so intertwined with the broader market, calling it impossible to isolate technology from the rest of equities and the economy. He argued that much of the market remains on the other side and is still reading tea leaves, adding that Alphabet's numbers had frightened people. Google executives said Wednesday that AI mode queries were growing strongly but monetizing at lower rates, and that the company was running ad experiments that had shown promising results. Eisman described parts of Anthropic's filing as extremely negative because it lacked many metrics for the coming quarter.

Articles.Title: Steve Eisman gets more conservative with portfolio as AI trade nears 'tipping point'

stories.Headline: AI labs in progressives’ sights if Democrats win House
stories.Summary:
Representative Greg Casar of Texas, the chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, told POLITICO that Democrats should bring in the heads of large AI companies and question them about the risks their firms pose to the American people. He said he was open to using subpoenas to force executives to appear. The two-term lawmaker from Austin said he has made his case to Democratic leadership that oversight and hearings on AI companies should be one of the caucus’s focuses if Democrats control the House. The article was published on October 29, 2026, ahead of the House elections the following week.

The article gives no bill numbers, vote counts or dates for any hearings, and it names no AI companies or executives. It describes no specific requirement or change in law, only the scrutiny Casar wants a Democratic majority to pursue. It says progressive Democrats are sending a message to AI companies that they will push for aggressive scrutiny of AI labs if their party wins the House. Casar said progressives might be the tip of the spear but would certainly not be alone in calling these Big Tech firms to account.

Casar is the person responsible for the push described in the article, and the quotes above are his, paraphrased. The article does not say what Democratic leadership answered, and it names no other lawmakers or companies. It reports no response from the AI labs or from Republican lawmakers. It also gives no comment from anyone else on the plan.

The context is the House elections the following week, which the article treats as the trigger for the plan. The article says nothing about what happens next beyond that, and it does not say whether the effort would clear the Senate or reach the president. It gives no schedule for hearings or subpoenas. It also does not say how the AI companies or their executives would respond.

Articles.Title: AI labs in progressives’ sights if Democrats win House

stories.Headline: GTA 6 Unreleased Yet – Overseas Users Already Drive In-Game Cars Using Google's New AI Model
stories.Summary:
Google DeepMind released its new-generation world model Genie 4 in the early hours of the previous day, according to 36Kr. Google CEO Sundar Pichai shared the news and called Genie 4 the most realistic and interactive world model to date. Genie 4 is currently only open to a small group of users for testing, and apart from official demos, almost all real-world test results are shared on X. On X, some users who got internal test access generated an open world similar to GTA and named it "GTA Waymo." Compared with the previous generation Genie 3 released last August, the continuous coherent generation duration of a single world in Genie 4 has been extended from 1 minute to 2 minutes.

Genie 4 is Google's first real-time world model with native support for synchronized audio and video generation, and all sounds are calculated in real time by the model based on the visuals. Users can modify the generated world in real time, changing the weather, moving the camera, and adding elements that integrate with the surrounding scene. The system is called Hybrid World Models, with Genie 4 generating images and audio in real time while Gemini works in the background to keep the world following logical rules. Gemini Omni is mainly responsible for making the generated world more consistent with real life, and Gemini 3.8 Flash observes the real-time footage, breaks tasks into steps, checks whether the content meets expectations, and makes timely adjustments.

The official has admitted that this is still a very early stage product, and that if the model runs for too long, or if the perspective is frequently rotated and commands modified, objects and details in the scene may drift. According to the article's observation of the official demos, the AI-generated character speech still sounds quite unnatural, and the facial expressions are not very smooth. Overseas users have pointed out issues such as a bust that should tip over after smashing down not doing so, and a train conductor speaking English at a rural Japanese train station. Google teamed up with robotics company Apptronik for a trial, letting Gemini 4 Argon cooperate with Genie 4 to simulate a robot playing checkers, and Argon broke a single general instruction into 22 action steps for Genie 4 to render.

In the past two months, Runway launched GWM Worlds 2 that supports multi-player online interaction, AMD spent 8.2 billion dollars to acquire Li Fei-Fei's World Labs, and Amazon is reported to be preparing to invest 7 billion dollars to acquire world model startup Decart. The article says the actual large-scale implementation of these models is still not on the horizon. It also says that compared with game development and film and television production, the potential of Genie 4 in robot training may deserve more attention, because high-quality robot training data is difficult to obtain. The article adds that if this path works out, household helper robots will finally become a realistic expectation.

Articles.Title: GTA 6 Unreleased Yet – Overseas Users Already Drive In-Game Cars Using Google's New AI Model - eu.36kr.com

stories.Headline: How AI Generates Synthetic Patients to Solve Clinical Trial Recruitment Shortages
stories.Summary:
Li Youcheng, a PhD candidate at Peking University's School of Intelligence, has spent the past year developing "AI virtual patients" with his team. They combined compliant data from tens of millions of real patients, covering medical visits, physical conditions and living environments, and used a dedicated AI model to build the system. In early 2025 he decided to start a company to develop AI patient models. The company now works with 30 pharmaceutical enterprises and CRO companies and is trying to establish cooperation with international firms such as AstraZeneca and Johnson & Johnson.

The model generates digital avatars from real patient data so trials can run on computers first, predicting drug efficacy and filtering out solutions doomed to fail. It may also replace part of a real control group, which matters most in rare diseases, pediatrics and severe illnesses where few patients meet the inclusion criteria. In June this year, four departments including the National Medical Products Administration issued a document encouraging technologies such as virtual patients. Shandong Qilu Hospital posted a procurement project for "digital twin virtual clinical trials" with a budget of 2.625 million yuan, and by September the virtual patient model was on a list of high-value AI pharmaceutical scenarios in the 15th Five-Year Plan for the Pharmaceutical Industry issued by ten departments.

Li said a friend's serious illness in high school, caught by early screening, left a lasting mark on him, and in 2019 he decided to face that fear directly by working in the field. He said he first studied imaging AI diagnosis, starting with breast ultrasound, but found that judging a patient required more than one scan, which led him to a patient-centered idea. He described the shift to patient models as an extension of that research rather than a sudden change of direction. He said the model plays a supplementary and auxiliary role and will not completely replace real clinical drug trials, which still need to be carried out.

The company's financing has entered a second round and is in the delivery stage, with a valuation close to 1 billion yuan. A patient model covering more than ten types of cancers is being verified with partner pharmaceutical companies. The team is now focused on three cohorts, respiratory, oncology and cardiovascular, and the first question it must answer is how closely the model's predicted changes match real patients. Li's longer vision is a personal "health avatar" for everyone, with collections of avatars used to rehearse and predict public health events, like forecasting wildfires and weather.

Articles.Title: How AI Generates Synthetic Patients to Solve Clinical Trial Recruitment Shortages - 36Kr

stories.Headline: 27-Year-Old Tsinghua Assistant Professor Breaks Into AI Self-Evolution Track, Unveils Groundbreaking First 35B Parameter Model
stories.Summary:
Chen Yongchao, a 27-year-old assistant professor at Tsinghua University's School of Artificial Intelligence, founded Chaoyan Intelligence, which released its first model, Apex-35B-V1.0, on October 29, 2026, according to 36Kr. The company was founded in June of this year. The model is a 35B parameter system built on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B through mid-training and post-training with proprietary datasets and research trajectories. Chaoyan Intelligence says it introduced Recursive Self-Improvement into model R&D, letting AI take part in experiments and result analysis and applying verified results to later work. The model is presented as covering both general and research capabilities, handling coding, agent tasks, Q&A and deep search as well as AI research, computational science and robot simulation.

In 21 benchmark tests it leads Qwen3.6-35B-A3B in 20 items, and against Recursive's Flint, a 40B MoE model released on October 22, it leads in 18 items with one tie. It scored 40.0 on OpenAI's FrontierScience benchmark, about eight times Flint and roughly 84 percent above the base Qwen model, and 60.9 on PaperBench, about 2.1 times Flint. On BFCL V4 it scored 84.0, and on Terminal-Bench 2.1 it scored 65.2, while SWE-Atlas QnA scored 33.1 and SWE-bench Pro v2 scored 92.4. The article attributes the work to Chen Yongchao and his company, and describes the RSI approach as the team's own construction method, with AI participating in experiments and analysis. It says the model surpasses larger systems in some evaluations, including GLM-5.3 at 753B parameters on FrontierScience, where that model scored 30.7, and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at the 500B level in some reasoning scenarios.

Chaoyan Intelligence has completed two financing rounds in a few months totaling close to 400 million yuan. The company launched the model in just four months. The article places the release in the context of a growing self-evolution track, citing Sam Altman's "The Gentle Singularity" and Dario Amodei's "Machines of Loving Grace" as earlier visions of AI improving AI. It notes Recursive SuperIntelligence, co-founded by Tian Yuandong, and its Eureka Machine system as prior work on the track. The article does not say what happens next beyond the model's release and benchmark results.

stories.Headline: AI Video: Did Runway Stage a Stunning Comeback in 2024?
stories.Summary:
Runway’s latest video model, Gen-4.5, briefly topped the Artificial Analysis ranking list last December, but its position quickly slipped and it has not released a new model for more than half a year. The top-ranked video generation models now come from large companies such as Google, ByteDance and Kuaishou, and Runway is no longer in the first tier. In early September, co-founder and CEO Anastasis Germanidis said on LinkedIn that Runway’s annual recurring revenue had reached almost 200 million US dollars, nearly double the 100 million dollars reported in April. AppMagic data shows that monthly revenue from mobile alone rose from less than one million dollars last September to 2.7 million dollars in the most recent 30 days.

Runway’s downloads and revenue rose together in May, when it launched a model called Aleph 2.0 that edits existing videos rather than generating them from scratch. The model can change specified elements in a video while keeping other pictures, actions and scenes unchanged, and it can apply an edit made to a single frame to the whole video. Runway promoted the capability with the selling point of modifying a video with one sentence, and many bloggers on X reviewed it, bringing a first wave of downloads. Advertising was expanded at the end of August and drove a second wave of growth.

The app’s default video model is now Seedance 2.0 and its image model is GPT Image 2, with Gen-4.5 still available by manual switch. Runway Dev, the company’s API product for developers, aggregates multiple video models including Seedance and Google Omni Flash and offers a model routing mechanism. Developers set preferences among cost, speed and quality and a price limit for each generation, and the system screens out models that do not fit before scoring the rest and recording the model used, the reason and the cost. Runway has also reached licensing agreements that let enterprises deploy its closed-source models themselves, fine-tune them with their own data and keep the commercial revenue, while Runway charges licensing fees. Anthony Maggio, Runway’s chief product officer, said the company’s internal creative team evaluated models on dimensions such as motion, composition and lip sync to drive routing choices, but the specific standards have not been made public.

Germanidis said Runway serves more than 60 million creators, and 95 of the Fortune 100 companies are its customers. Based on mobile revenue of about 1.8 million dollars in August, the app accounts for only about 10 percent of total revenue, with the bulk of the nearly 200 million dollars coming from the enterprise side. Runway has shifted from single-feature tools for ordinary users toward model aggregation and agent-based tools for professional creators and small business users in advertising and marketing. The article does not say what Runway plans to release next.

stories.Headline: 10 & 14-Year-Old Teens Reject Vibe Coding: Build Software & Finish Mac Port in 2 Hours, Sparking Developer Debate Over Alleged AI Use
stories.Summary:
A 10-year-old and a 14-year-old worked together on a software called DVR Doctor, which repairs interference in FPV drone footage, such as snowflakes, colored stripes and picture tearing. The 14-year-old, Rory, started the project at the end of the summer after seeing strange lines and interference in his own FPV videos, and he began learning Python to write a video repair program. He later met the 10-year-old, Owen, who had seen Rory's comment on a YouTube video about Tiny Whoop drone antennas and offered to help. The two collaborated through GitHub, email and Discord and had not met offline until an interview with YouTube creator Chase Momo. When Momo mentioned the software did not support Mac, they sent him the Mac version in less than two hours.

The software offers two processing engines, manual repair and machine learning, and can fix colored stripes, color tearing and flickering, with GPU acceleration. It also supports analog image transmission and HDZero recording processing, though the articles say these functions mainly improve existing interference and cannot restore all lost picture details. The standard version is priced at $4.99 and the professional version at $7.99. Rory first used an optical flow method, comparing predicted frames with actual ones and adjusting hue in areas likely affected by signal interference, but the result was not ideal. The two then tried a machine learning approach that identifies abnormal areas and refers to other frames to reconstruct damaged footage, which works better but needs more computing power.

Momo's first reaction to the fast Mac version was that it must have been made with Vibe Coding, which he had a poor impression of after an AI attempt to build a one-click YouTube editing button failed completely. When he asked, the two teenagers admitted they used AI but insisted the core machine learning code was mainly written by themselves, with AI used for auxiliary problems such as the Gumroad payment API, documents and learning what certain functions do and their parameters. Rory said he would not simply copy and paste entire pieces of AI-generated code, and both gave a negative answer when asked whether the software was made by Vibe Coding. Owen explained how machine learning and information from previous and subsequent frames restore damaged footage, and Momo said he did not understand half the technical details.

The two also promoted the product themselves, emailing many FPV YouTube creators, though most did not respond, and they continued contacting smaller channels. Rory's parents were surprised by the software and gave suggestions, and his mother helped with promotion, while Owen's parents were initially worried Rory might be an adult pretending to be a child until they saw his YouTube channel and a video call. Owen said it is hard to find peers to talk about drones with in real life. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the software being officially sold.

Articles.Title: 10 & 14-Year-Old Teens Reject Vibe Coding: Build Software & Finish Mac Port in 2 Hours, Sparking Developer Debate Over Alleged AI Use - 36Kr

stories.Headline: Wabi, the AI agent that builds mini apps, now valued at $1.25B after latest round
stories.Summary:
Wabi, a startup that describes its product as a "personal agent," said on Thursday that it has raised $55 million at a $1.25 billion valuation. The company was founded by Eugenia Kuyda, who previously founded the AI companion startup Replika. Wabi first focused on letting anyone build apps from prompts, but last month it announced a shift toward becoming an AI messenger. The article does not say whether the round has closed or who else is leading it beyond what is listed below.

The new version, called Wabi 2.0, is meant to build the interfaces a user needs to get things done as part of its role as a personal AI agent. The company suggests it could create mini apps for meal planning, tracking local restaurants, planning date nights, building fitness plans, and designing specialized trivia games. The funding suggests investors see potential in this agentic direction. The article notes that the market for AI agents is hot right now, citing the viral agent Instinct, which raised another billion at a $10 billion valuation in September. It also mentions Tolan, an AI companion that just raised $30 million.

Alex Lim, a general partner at IVP, which led the round, praised Kuyda's sense for where AI is headed and her track record in building it. Lim said she has a clear vision for how people will interact with AI, one that goes beyond the text box or command line. Lim described Wabi as the expression of that vision and said IVP was thrilled to support her. Other participants included Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), Forerunner, the Amazon Alexa Fund, and angel investors such as Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke, Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff, former Yahoo head Marissa Mayer, former Twitter CEO Dick Costolo, and Alex Pall of The Chainsmokers.

Articles.Title: Wabi, the AI agent that builds mini apps, now valued at $1.25B after latest round

stories.Headline: AI Anxiety Among China's Middle-Class Parents: The 13,800-Yuan Price Tag Shaping Modern Child Education Fears
stories.Summary:
On the last Friday of September, around 9 p.m., Yao Min, a marketing executive at a foreign company in Shanghai, saw a video on Douyin about children learning to think with AI. Less than half an hour later, her son's grandmother forwarded the same link to the family group. The grandmother, who scrolls short videos after retirement, believed the content and became what the article calls the family's AI promotion ambassador. Yao Min initially resisted but was shaken after her company promoted AI use among employees, and AI produced six versions of a plan in under 20 minutes that her team had revised four times. She and her grandmother then selected a National Day AI study tour in Suzhou for her 10-year-old son Jiang Tongyi, priced at 13,800 yuan for 6 days and 5 nights.

The article says the study tour market in 2026 is expected to reach 242.2 billion yuan, up 13.6% year on year, and AI-themed study tour orders have surged 370% year on year. Course prices range from 2,000 yuan to 50,000 yuan. The Suzhou camp's schedule included AI principles, robot operation, AI animation production, scientific thinking training, a tech enterprise visit and a group project defense. Xiaofeng, a postgraduate student in artificial intelligence at a 985 university in Shanghai, was hired in April as a lecturer, paid 500 to 800 yuan per day. His class had more than 30 children aged about 7 or 8 to 12 or 13 in a university conference hall in Suzhou.

Yao Min asked the institution whether the course suited a 10-year-old, and customer service replied that 10 was not early, saying some 9-year-olds could already make a mini-program. On the registration form, asked for the one thing her son is best at, she wrote building Lego. Xiaofeng worried that gifted children would ask difficult questions, but his boss told him it was an AI study tour group paid by parents, not a training camp for child prodigies, and he only needed to popularize AI knowledge. The article does not say what happens next.

stories.Headline: AI Redefining Customer Success: How Artificial Intelligence Is Redrawing the Modern Boundaries of Customer Success
stories.Summary:
The article says that customer success problems often lie outside the customer success department. It describes a common situation in enterprise software: sales teams promise features that are late, technical problems arise during delivery, and customers fail to adjust their own processes, so when renewal time comes the customer success team bears the pressure. Customer Success Managers can coordinate resources but do not have authority over product research and development plans, technical solutions or delivery input. The article notes that from 2022 to 2025 the Cui Niu Hui China SaaS Conference held four consecutive closed-door meetings on customer success, covering customer value, service efficiency and organizational collaboration. It says the same contradiction kept appearing: customer success carries heavier operational duties, but the key factors affecting it are scattered across the whole enterprise.

The article says the contradiction has become more prominent in the AI era. Previously vendors mainly helped customers get software running and use it better, but now Agents take on actual business tasks, so customers must verify whether tasks are completed, whether results are accurate and whether the input generates returns. It lists renewal rate, customer churn rate and Net Revenue Retention as important indicators, and says customers may not renew because product functions do not meet needs, implementation was poor or their own business environment changed, while a lack of additional purchases may stem from budget, product capabilities or business development stage. It says customer success differs from traditional customer service because it must track whether the product is truly integrated into business processes and whether customers get expected value, tasks that involve sales, product, research and development and implementation delivery teams. It says customer success can be led by one department but cannot be completed by a single department, and that enterprises need to align sales commitments, implementation delivery and continuous operation around the same customer goal, clarifying who decides key issues, who solves them and how acceptance is conducted.

The article says measurement methods also need to change, since system launch, active user engagement and timely service response cannot fully prove that customers obtained value, and customers ultimately care about reduced operating costs, improved efficiency and reasonable returns. It says the customer success team must understand the business more deeply while considering the vendor's own service costs, and that every renewal relying on large amounts of extra development and manual support may not be a healthy business. It says AI Agents change how some enterprise software works, with tasks previously done by employees now handed to Agents, so customers judge whether AI can correctly understand business requirements, call relevant systems and complete tasks stably. It says an Agent that works in a demonstration environment may fail in production because of inconsistent data calibers, insufficient system permissions and complex business rules, and that many business rules exist only in employee experience, so vendors must convert these implicit rules into executable, verifiable system capabilities. It says the customer success team must cooperate more closely with research and development, data and implementation delivery personnel, and continuously watch the Agent's task completion, exception handling and business effects.

The article says AI is changing the internal division of labor in customer success teams, since customer information sorting, ticket classification, meeting minutes, service report generation and part of customer risk identification can already use AI to improve efficiency. It says faster information processing does not mean business judgment can be fully automated, giving the example of a detected decline in customer usage that may come from business contraction, poor product experience or competitor intervention, which still requires professional staff to judge the cause, coordinate resources and decide follow-up actions. It says customer success personnel need to devote more energy to business diagnosis, coordination of complex problems and value verification, and that understanding customer business and technical implementation will become more critical, without every CSM needing to become an engineer. It describes Forward Deployed Engineers, or FDEs, who go deep into the customer site and combine software engineering capabilities with actual business needs, as a role worthy of attention for enterprise AI projects that connect multiple systems and handle non-standardized processes. It says FDEs face a commercial problem, because one engineer delivering one project does not mean the enterprise can deliver in batches, and if each project needs requirements sorting, interface development and workflow design, engineering teams and delivery costs may grow with the number of customers, even if AI Coding reduces code development costs.

The article says AI vendors must clarify which customer requirements are worthy of customization, which capabilities should be productized, which work can be reused through tools and which complex problems still require expert intervention, since these choices affect delivery efficiency and profit levels. It says that for the customer success team, project launch does not mean the work ends, because after an Agent is put into use the customer's business rules, model capabilities and related systems may all change, so continuous monitoring, exception handling and application optimization are still needed. It says FDEs need to make AI really work while customer success needs to make customers continue to benefit, and that the business experience FDEs accumulate on site should promote product improvement and build up delivery capabilities, while feedback and business objectives from the customer success team should become an important basis for technical iteration. It concludes that AI reduces part of software development costs but pushes enterprise competition further toward business understanding, engineering delivery and continuous operation, and that customer success is stepping out of the customer success department to become a business responsibility the entire organization must undertake together.

Articles.Title: AI Redefining Customer Success: How Artificial Intelligence Is Redrawing the Modern Boundaries of Customer Success - eu.36kr.com

stories.Headline: The AI buildout is this era's central economic narrative
stories.Summary:
The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, as Chairman Kevin Warsh tried to balance a boom in AI-related investment against the risks it carries. The same week, third-quarter growth figures released Thursday showed the capital spending surge powering the broader economy. Warsh has made the AI buildout the central backdrop for the Fed's policy choices, even as debt markets that financed data centers have begun to wobble. Axios describes the situation as a delicate balance for the central bank. Nonresidential fixed investment rose at a 12.7% annual rate in the third quarter, the strongest pace since the rebound from the early pandemic period in 2020, and excluding that rebound, the highest since 2011.

The measure has been positive for seven consecutive quarters and has climbed 14.3% since the end of 2024, with gains across business structures, equipment and intellectual property. Residential investment, by contrast, has contracted in six of the last seven quarters, including a 3.3% annual rate decline in the third quarter. The article says the buildout is also fueling inflation and drawing investment away from sectors such as housing. Warsh described recent developments in debt markets in approving terms, saying market participants are becoming more discerning in how they allocate capital. He said financial conditions are tighter but that he was unwilling and unable to call them tight, and he argued these changes point toward a longer and more durable period of growth and price stability.

In answering a question, he suggested the Fed's September rate increase had contributed to tighter borrowing for AI projects, noting that interest rates reach into many corners of the economy. Rick Rieder of BlackRock compared the Fed to a house with one thermostat and very different temperatures in each room, arguing that further tightening could chill cooler areas without cooling the overheated ones. The article notes that this approach holds only if inflation begins to ease, and that the era of elevated inflation is nearing its six-year mark. Axios reports that the central bank's credibility, and Warsh's personal standing, are now at stake. The Fed left the door open to another rate increase in December, so the coming months will test whether its current stance can cool inflation without damaging the investment boom that is sustaining growth.

Articles.Title: The AI buildout is this era's central economic narrative

stories.Headline: Tencent Unveils New AI Office Solution: The Next Key Piece in Its Smart Work Ecosystem Puzzle
stories.Summary:
Tencent launched a new product called Tencent Cloud Drive at its Global Digital Ecosystem Conference on October 29, 2026. The article's author, Wang Zhiyuan, said the launch is more than adding another cloud storage product. He tested it by connecting several tools, including WorkBuddy, Tencent Docs, ima, Tencent Meeting, Lark and Notion. After connecting them, an AI assistant appears on the right side of the interface, and users can ask it questions without switching between software. The author described Tencent Cloud Drive as a central hub that gathers data from different tools.

The product is meant to store not only files but also the data and processes generated when AI performs tasks, so enterprises can manage them in one place and later Agents can continue unfinished work. The enterprise version gives each seat 50GB of storage, ten times the original capacity, and Tencent's personal office products will also use this storage base. Tencent Cloud Drive supports cross-application office scenarios through a system called Buddy One, and the database capability launched by WorkBuddy is supported by Tencent Cloud Drive. The article also lists earlier Tencent moves: in late September the enterprise version of WorkBuddy completed a suite transformation, and in mid-October WorkBuddy was connected with WeCom.

The article says Tencent is connecting previously scattered office capabilities, with WorkBuddy handling task execution, WeCom connecting organizational scenarios, and Tencent Cloud Drive handling unified storage and invocation of work data. It cites an IDC statistic that knowledge workers spend about 2.5 hours a day searching for and organizing materials, and an IBM data breach report this year saying 92% of AI-related data breaches did not deploy appropriate access control. The author argues that enterprises face problems over where data is scattered, who can access it, and how the next Agent takes over a task. The article does not name a Tencent executive or give direct comments from the company.

The article places the launch in the wider evolution of cloud drives, noting that Dropbox launched Dash and Google integrated Gemini into Drive, mainly to help people find content as file numbers grow. It says cloud drives are evolving from personal file cabinets to shared workbenches for both humans and Agents. The author says Tencent launched another cloud drive because the content enterprises need to preserve and manage when Agents work goes beyond traditional personal cloud drive scenarios. The article does not say what happens next beyond describing Tencent's recent steps and the product's role in its AI office system.

Articles.Title: Tencent Unveils New AI Office Solution: The Next Key Piece in Its Smart Work Ecosystem Puzzle - 36Kr

stories.Headline: Google admits AI search makes less money, but it’s fixing that with more ads
stories.Summary:
Google's parent company Alphabet reported third-quarter 2026 results on Wednesday afternoon, showing revenue growth but a sharp drop in its stock price. The company took in almost $128 billion for July through September, with net income above $26 billion, though that net income was almost $9 billion lower than the year before. Revenue rose 25 percent from a year earlier, yet analysts had expected more, and earnings per share came in at $2.12 against a projected $3.02. Shares fell about 12 percent by the time the story was published, after a dip of roughly 13 percent earlier in the day.

Several troubling trends emerged in the report. Search volume grew 12 percent year over year, down from 17 percent in the second quarter and 19 percent in the first, and search revenue was flat in the third quarter.
