On those sets, it mainly acted as a companion that users could chat with, ask about what was on screen, or use to get recommendations for shows and movies. LG drew criticism last December after a webOS update added a Copilot shortcut that could not be removed, and it later allowed users to delete the shortcut. Earlier this year, Microsoft launched a Copilot "super app" that combined chat, agents, and coding into one interface, shifting the product toward business and productivity use rather than a digital companion.

The articles do not say how many TVs are affected or whether Samsung has issued its own notice. They also do not give a firm shutdown date beyond the broad 2026 window, and they do not describe any replacement offering for TV users. Microsoft had not made a public statement on the change at the time of the report, so the details rest on the on-screen message and Windows Central's account of it. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Microsoft is ending Copilot support on smart TVs

stories.Headline: Anthropic Showed AI Can Make Money, but the Buildout Has To Prove It
stories.Summary:
Anthropic disclosed in its S-1 prospectus, filed ahead of its IPO, that it generated $16.3 billion in revenue in the first half of 2026, up from $1.2 billion a year earlier. Roughly 80% of that revenue came from usage-based fees, with customers paying according to the tokens the company's models process and generate. The figures were published in a Carson Group commentary dated October 28, 2026. The filing gives investors a look at the economics behind the heavy spending on chips, data centers and power that has driven the AI investment boom.

The commentary explains that token prices are falling as competition grows while the cost of renting GPUs is rising, which has raised doubts about profits. It argues that productivity gains can offset this, since better chips and software let the same GPU hour produce more tokens. The author cites an illustrative company whose margin rises even as its prices fall. The filing also shows Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 cut customer costs per task by about 40% compared with Claude Opus 5, while its list price was 20% lower at $20 per million output tokens versus $25. Anthropic said the efficiency gains allowed it to preserve its margins.

The author attributes the pattern to two effects: Wright's Law, under which production costs fall by a consistent share as cumulative output doubles, and Jevons' Paradox, in which cheaper use leads to greater total consumption. Anthropic's filing states that revenue growth accelerated from 48% in the fourth quarter of 2025 to 132% in the first quarter of 2026 after it launched Opus 4.5 in November 2025. It also reports that compute spending fell from about $2 for every $1 of revenue in the first half of 2025 to about 55 cents a year later. The company posted nearly $1 billion in operating profit in the second quarter of 2026, an 8% operating margin, or 19% excluding stock-based compensation.

The filing also discloses about $637 billion in infrastructure arrangements with seven providers, including $431 billion in minimum spending commitments and equipment lease payments, against $4.6 billion in revenue for all of 2025. Several agreements are take-or-pay, which shifts utilization risk to Anthropic, and banks recently demanded higher rates to finance a $63 billion chip deal tied to the company. The author concludes that AI can succeed even if investors who finance the buildout do not earn attractive returns, pointing to past investment cycles such as railroads and fiber-optic networks. He says he is not predicting an AI bust but questions whether today's capacity, financed at higher costs, will earn adequate returns.

Articles.Title: Anthropic Showed AI Can Make Money, but the Buildout Has To Prove It

stories.Headline: Google's search revenue Ferrari hits an AI-powered speed bump
stories.Summary:
Google reported slower growth in its search advertising business for the third quarter of 2026, and the company's shares fell as investors worried about the cost of its AI push. Alphabet, Google's parent company, lost roughly $500 billion in market value. Search revenue growth slowed from 17 percent in the second quarter to 12 percent in the third quarter. The company has been putting AI Overviews and AI Mode into its search results, and those features make less money than traditional search ads.

On the investor call, Douglas Anmuth of JPMorgan Chase asked whether the slowdown came from showing fewer ads in AI Overviews and AI Mode. Chief business officer Philipp Schindler gave several reasons: foreign exchange rates, Europe's removal of its customs-duty exemption, and lower monetization in AI Mode. Google said it is widening the reach of AI Overview ads and adding multiturn ads for AI Mode queries in the US. Alphabet also reported $51.4 billion in capital expenditures for the quarter.

Max Anderson, CEO of OnlyFinder, wrote on social media that Google was using short-sighted and customer-hostile tactics, such as charging advertisers more for lower-quality clicks, including clicks on search terms they had not agreed to target. Analyst Eric Seufert of Mobile Dev Memo wrote in a blog post that search usage is not declining, because the earnings release said year-over-year search query growth in the third quarter was the highest in five years. Nate Elliott, principal analyst for AI at Emarketer, told The Register that AI is a double-edged sword for Google, since search is what people use AI for most. He said people have added AI on top of search rather than replacing it, but their habits could change if another tool serves them better.

Elliott also said Google is not giving much information about how AI specifically affects its business, so people are reading into small scraps of data. He called it remarkable that Google has kept the largest digital ad business growing at a double-digit rate every quarter in recent years. He said most people disagree and instead worry that the advertising business only grew by 10 percent. The article does not say what happens next beyond Google's plans to expand AI ads.

Articles.Title: Google's search revenue Ferrari hits an AI-powered speed bump

stories.Headline: OpenAI and ServiceNow expand partnership across enterprise workflows
stories.Summary:
OpenAI and ServiceNow said on October 28, 2026, that they are expanding their partnership to bring more OpenAI models and agents into ServiceNow products. The companies also plan to connect ServiceNow workflows with ChatGPT and Codex, so businesses can build applications, resolve IT requests and address security issues with AI. The expansion builds on a partnership announced in January, extending OpenAI into more of the work ServiceNow does for its customers and inside its own business. The aim is to make these tasks easier for companies using both platforms.

A new ServiceNow integration will place business context and workflow actions inside ChatGPT, so teams can investigate issues and act without switching tools. An IT team member could find similar incidents, assess the risk of a change and update a ServiceNow record within the same conversation. Customers connect ChatGPT to their own ServiceNow instance and choose which capabilities to enable. ServiceNow's Action Fabric applies existing business rules and permissions, so available actions follow each organization's configuration and access settings. ServiceNow is also previewing interactive experiences in which an on-call engineer could review linked alerts, recent changes and affected services, then assign a team and work toward a fix.

The companies describe three planned areas of new capability. In application development, a planned Codex integration in ServiceNow's AI Workflow Factory will help developers build applications, and OpenAI models will power Build Agent and Autonomous Engineer. In cybersecurity, a joint solution will combine OpenAI's capabilities with ServiceNow's asset, identity and business context to help teams investigate vulnerabilities, prioritize risks and coordinate remediation. In voice, an OpenAI-powered experience in ServiceNow's Super Intelligence Control Tower will let people describe an AI use case aloud and gather missing details through follow-up questions. ServiceNow also plans to give all employees access to ChatGPT Work and Codex, beyond its engineering staff.

Greg Brockman, President and Co-founder of OpenAI, said that AI becomes more useful when people can use it in the systems their businesses depend on. Bill McDermott, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of ServiceNow, said the two companies are combining frontier AI research with a platform that governs AI across the enterprise. Availability is staged over time. The ServiceNow MCP plugin is available in the OpenAI marketplace now, with enhanced capabilities expected by the end of 2026. Voice capabilities are expected in the first quarter of 2027, OpenAI-powered security capabilities are expected to enter early access in January 2027 with general availability planned for the second quarter of 2027, and Codex in AI Workflow Factory is expected in 2027.

Articles.Title: OpenAI and ServiceNow expand partnership across enterprise workflows

stories.Headline: A research intern’s journey from computer vision to physical intelligence at Microsoft Research Asia – Tokyo
stories.Summary:
Lilika Makabe, a computer vision researcher, took up an internship at Microsoft Research Asia – Tokyo, one of the lab's first research interns, and moved her work toward embodied AI and robotics. The Microsoft Research article, published on October 28, 2026, describes how she joined a young lab whose research community and directions were still taking shape. Her role centered on exploring how robots that perceive and act in the physical world could use visual observations and language instructions. She worked on real robots, collected teleoperated data, and studied vision-language-action models.

Before joining the lab, Makabe had worked on digitizing real-world objects from photographs, recovering their shape and surface material so they could be reproduced under different lighting. She had also seen robotics research appear more often at vision conferences, which led her to want to test that connection herself. The internship let her learn directly from researchers with robotics expertise and see how perception, language, data, and action connect in a physical system. Her background helped the team notice visual factors such as shadows, reflections, and surface albedo that are easy to overlook when designing robot experiments.

Namiko Saito, a senior researcher at the lab, said Makabe's expertise helped the team recognize that handling variations in visual appearance is essential for robot models that generalize across real environments. Saito also noted that small discrepancies in visual observations, calibration, or contact dynamics can cause unexpected robot behavior, and that identifying the source of failures matters more than simply collecting more data. Another senior researcher, Heecheol Kim, said Makabe's systematic approach complemented a robotics effort that was often driven by experimentation and engineering. He credited her with bridging computer vision and robotics in productive interdisciplinary work.

The article presents Makabe's story as part of the lab's growth, which includes work on embodied AI, well-being and neuroscience, and societal AI. Interns there join discussions and bring their own fields' expertise into the lab's research. Makabe encouraged future applicants to use conversations beyond their own specialty and to apply even when unsure of their chances. The article does not describe any further plans for her or for the lab's internship program beyond inviting readers to learn more about opportunities there.

Articles.Title: A research intern’s journey from computer vision to physical intelligence at Microsoft Research Asia – Tokyo

stories.Headline: Re­searchers at Ohio State received funding from Meta to advance AI-assisted medicine
stories.Summary:
Researchers at Ohio State University received grants from Meta to support three medical research projects on how artificial intelligence can help diagnose health problems. The reporting was published on October 28, 2026, by Spectrum News 1, with Mariam Abaza credited as the author. The three studies cover chest X-rays, heart failure, and Alzheimer's disease. The funding is aimed at building AI tools that support doctors rather than replace them.

The first project looks at chest X-ray reports. Current AI models that write these reports usually analyze only the image itself. The planned tool will instead use Meta AI models to draft reports that also draw on a patient's medical history and earlier exams. The study will also develop a method for doctor oversight meant to keep the AI reliable and safe.

The second project concerns heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, a form that can be hard to spot early because its symptoms are vague. Researchers will test whether routine abdominal CT scans, combined with medical records and ECG data, can be used with AI to predict a patient's risk. The third project addresses Alzheimer's disease, whose diagnosis involves several steps, from clinician review to checking competing explanations. The article notes that electronic health records cannot easily reconstruct how a patient's cognition has changed over time.

To address that gap, researchers will build what the article calls a clinician-in-the-loop multi-agent system that can be deployed locally as a baseline. The system is intended to rebuild a patient's cognitive history, reason over clinical evidence, flag diagnostic uncertainties, and suggest the next most useful clinical steps. The article says all three studies will keep clinicians at the center of decisions while offering tools to streamline diagnosis and care. Further details, the article indicates, are available through a link the outlet provides.

Articles.Title: Re­searchers at Ohio State received funding from Meta to advance AI-assisted medicine

stories.Headline: NVIDIA (NVDA) Deepens AI Infrastructure Push With New Digital Twin And Agent Deals
stories.Summary:
NVIDIA announced expanded collaborations meant to speed up global AI infrastructure and agent-based applications across industrial, cloud, and consumer settings. The company and Oracle plan to scale multi-gigawatt AI cloud superclusters built on NVIDIA Vera Rubin GPUs and Vera CPUs, to be used for training, inference, and agent workloads. Schneider Electric and AVEVA reported that a digital twin built on the NVIDIA Omniverse DSX Blueprint had been piloted successfully and is now deployed at the SINES Data Campus to improve AI data center operations. NVIDIA also deepened its work with Meta to support the high-performance Muse AI agents, with larger infrastructure commitments and optimization efforts.

The article presents these deals as part of NVIDIA's push to sell full-stack AI factory platforms rather than individual chips. It cites the company's view that revenue opportunity per gigawatt rises from about US$18 billion with Hopper to about US$25 billion with Grace Blackwell and about US$40 billion with Vera Rubin. The article also notes that the Oracle plan to offer flexible CPU and GPU sizing fits that thesis. It adds that risks remain, including export controls, in-house accelerators built by hyperscalers such as Google and Amazon, higher component costs, and competition from AMD and custom ASICs.

The announcements were made by NVIDIA, which is listed on the NasdaqGS under the ticker NVDA, with Oracle, Schneider Electric, AVEVA, and Meta named as partners. The article is a general market commentary from Simply Wall St and does not itself make a recommendation. It frames the partnerships as tests of whether NVIDIA can turn a concentrated backlog into long-term, high-margin data center revenue. The article does not say when the Oracle superclusters will come online or what financial terms the Meta commitments carry.

Articles.Title: NVIDIA (NVDA) Deepens AI Infrastructure Push With New Digital Twin And Agent Deals

stories.Headline: Anthropic warns of 'catastrophic threat to humanity' as it eyes $2 trillion valuation in biggest-ever IPO
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the San Francisco company behind the Claude chatbot, filed its S-1 paperwork on Monday, 26 October 2026, setting up what could be the biggest stock market debut ever. The 335-page filing, which lists the shares on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker "ANT," points to a Wall Street debut next month. Reports say the offering could raise as much as $100 billion, which would top the record SpaceX set with its June listing, though AP put that raise at $86 billion while Mint cited $75 billion. The company was formed in 2021 by former OpenAI leaders, and an Anthropic listing would put it ahead of OpenAI in going public. The final amount raised, the valuation and the offering price have not been settled.

The filing gives a detailed look at the company's finances. Revenue reached $16.3 billion in the first half of the year, about 14 times the figure from the same period a year earlier. Net loss for the half stood at $80.7 billion, which included a one-off accounting charge of $72.4 billion tied to financing agreements, compared with a loss of $13 billion a year earlier. As of 30 June, Anthropic held $131.7 billion in cash and cash equivalents, and it said its push to expand computing capacity will change its cash flow and demand heavy capital spending. About 250 customers each brought in at least $10 million over the past year, and the five largest accounted for roughly a quarter of this year's revenue.

The filing also sets out unusual governance terms and a very long list of risks. Dario Amodei, the CEO, his sister Daniela, the company's president, and their five co-founders hold 50.1% of shareholder votes through a special class of shares. A Long-Term Benefit Trust made up of independent members can appoint directors, and it is meant to stop financial interests from outranking public safety. The risk section runs close to 100 pages, and the company said AI systems could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity if they are misused, replicated, weaponised or allowed to act with a high degree of autonomy. It added that AI can be used for cyberattacks or to design biological weapons, that its own use of AI to speed up research could outpace its safety work, and that climate change could raise power and water costs for its data facilities.

The valuation is still open, with reports ranging from $1.5 trillion to as much as $2 trillion, up from the $965 billion private investors put on the company earlier this year. At the top figure it would pass SpaceX's initial $1.77 trillion value, though Nvidia leads at $5 trillion. Figures in the filing suggest each of the seven founders would end up with 1.4% of the company, worth as much as $28 billion apiece, and Forbes already puts Dario and Daniela at $15.5 billion each. The listing comes amid worries about an AI bubble and about the huge financing needs of Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX's AI business, and several tech firms have recently pulled their own IPO plans. A month ago Amodei wrote a 4,000-word essay urging the industry to slow frontier AI development so safety measures can catch up.

Articles.Title: TheAnthropic IPO Arrives: My (but not the) Anthropic Valuation! - Aswath Damodaran

stories.Headline: Armanino, Abacum partner on AI-native finance and accounting solutions
stories.Summary:
Armanino, a US accounting and consulting firm, has formed a partnership with Abacum, an AI-native financial planning and analysis platform built for finance professionals. The arrangement combines technical integration with a value-added reseller agreement. The deal was reported by International Accounting Bulletin on 30 October 2026. Under the terms, Abacum’s capabilities will be added to a technology portfolio that already includes solutions for accounting, tax and other finance workflows.

Armanino clients gain direct access to the platform alongside the firm’s consultancy services. Armanino will help businesses assess how Abacum fits into their existing technology infrastructure, link the platform to current systems, and oversee deployment and internal take-up. Through the agreement, finance departments can implement AI-native planning and analysis software without running a vendor selection process on their own. Armanino has agreed similar arrangements with software providers including Ramp, Rillet and Accrual.

Abacum co-founder and CEO Julio Martinez said finance teams face pressure to move faster and give the business better insights, but technology alone does not drive transformation. He said Armanino understands how finance teams operate and what it takes to use technology for better decisions, faster. Armanino partner and technology industry leader Dean Quiambao said Abacum’s rapid growth first caught the firm’s attention. He said Armanino watched Abacum scale across the same mix of industries the firm specialises in, and that clients are asking where AI can make a meaningful difference in finance today.

Articles.Title: Armanino, Abacum partner on AI-native finance and accounting solutions

stories.Headline: AI agents are upending digital business processes
stories.Summary:
People have begun using AI agents on cloud platforms to move money between bank accounts, pay bills, analyze spending, and cancel subscriptions, according to an InfoWorld opinion piece by David Linthicum published on October 30, 2026. The agents can reason across tasks, handle ambiguity, and act through the same websites humans use. A recent Axios article, as cited by Linthicum, reported that major US banks are detecting outside AI agents inside customer accounts, including cases where agents use credentials the customer provided. Several large banks are already restricting or blocking this kind of access.

Banks are struggling to tell whether account activity is human-directed, agent-directed, or something else, the article says. Bank policies often say a customer cannot hand over credentials or let a nonhuman third party operate the account through the consumer website, even when the customer believes the agent is authorized. Linthicum writes that most digital business systems were built on the assumption that the person at the keyboard owns the account or was explicitly delegated access through an approved mechanism. He says the same issue reaches beyond banking to Amazon, airlines, insurers, healthcare portals, tax services, subscription businesses, SaaS platforms, retailers, logistics providers, and government agencies.

Linthicum lays out the liability question: if an agent moves money incorrectly, the customer, the bank, the agent platform, and the cloud provider could each deny responsibility. He notes that in many countries consumer financial rules tend to favor the customer in unauthorized or disputed transactions, which he calls a nightmare scenario for banks. Over the next two to three years, he expects enterprises to rework policies, terms of service, authentication systems, customer support scripts, legal language, security detection models, and product decisions. He says the first instinct will be to block everything, which he calls understandable but not a long-term strategy, and he expects a middle ground of controlled delegation with read-only access, transaction limits, fine-grained permissions, expiring authorization, audit trails, extra authentication for high-risk actions, consent screens, certified agent ecosystems, and APIs.

Linthicum lists four tasks for enterprises that depend on customer-facing websites, starting with classifying the actions customers can take and giving each a risk rating and a policy for delegated automation. The second is to create an explicit access model covering what kinds of agents are allowed, what they can do, how they identify themselves, how customers authorize them, how authorization is revoked, and how disputes are handled. The third is to build better telemetry so businesses can tell a human from automation and judge whether an action is normal, authorized, high risk, or suspicious. The fourth is to offer a sanctioned path such as a safe API or delegated access mechanism, because otherwise customers will use credential sharing and browser automation anyway, leaving less visibility and more risk.

Articles.Title: AI agents are upending digital business processes

stories.Headline: AI meets DNA sequencing to provide unprecedented glimpse into previously mysterious regions of the genome
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the University of Utah have developed a tool called FIRE, which pairs machine learning with advanced DNA sequencing to examine regions of the genome that were previously difficult to study. The work was described in a study led in part by Mitchell R. Vollger, an assistant professor of human genetics at University of Utah Health, and was published in the journal Cell in 2026. The tool is designed to tell apart the gene regulation of the copy of a chromosome inherited from the mother and the copy inherited from the father, which can be turned on and off differently. Because most of the genome does not code for proteins, the researchers say the tool gives a sharper view of the switches that control genes.

The researchers used FIRE to examine a genetic difference previously linked to celiac disease and found that it sits in a gene switch next to an immune gene also linked to the condition. The change disrupts a spot where gene-controlling proteins normally attach, and altering that single DNA letter in laboratory experiments was enough to change how open the switch was. The team also identified tens of thousands of previously overlooked DNA regions that are likely important for gene regulation and are more likely than other parts of the genome to contain changes associated with human disease. In most cases, regulatory differences between the two inherited copies could be traced to differences in the DNA, but in about 40 percent of cases the copies were genetically identical at that spot. The researchers also found that lasting changes in gene regulation can arise without genetic differences, and these changes are passed down as cells divide.

Vollger said the most surprising finding was the limit of how much genetics alone determines gene regulation. FIRE works by building on an existing technique that highlights physically accessible DNA, then reading long stretches of individual DNA molecules so that each can usually be assigned to the mother's or father's copy. A machine learning analysis then assesses which highlighted regions are likely to matter for gene regulation, a task the researchers could do by hand for individual sites but which the tool scales to billions of regions across the genome. Vollger said the approach may help identify which genetic differences cause disease, a step toward therapies that edit DNA switches to lower disease risk or treat rare conditions. The articles describe this as an early step, and they do not give a timeline for any clinical application.

Articles.Title: AI meets DNA sequencing to provide unprecedented glimpse into previously mysterious regions of the genome

stories.Headline: Why AI Is Reshaping How Large Organisations Buy Software
stories.Summary:
Large organisations are rethinking how they buy software, according to an article published by Modern Diplomacy on 28 October 2026. The piece argues that software purchasing has become a board-level concern, driven by rapid growth in subscription tools and by new rules on artificial intelligence. It notes that many firms now buy software outside formal procurement channels, often on departmental credit cards with no compliance review. The article presents this as a shift in how such purchases are governed rather than a single event.

It cites Zylo's 2026 SaaS Management Index, which puts the average enterprise at around 300 SaaS applications, with organisations above 10,000 employees running upwards of 470. It says SaaS now accounts for roughly 70% of total enterprise software budgets, and that Gartner projects worldwide software spending will reach $1.44 trillion in 2026. The article warns that unmanaged purchasing leads to duplicate subscriptions, auto-renewals nobody checks, security gaps and unclear records of what data each tool handles. It adds that the EU AI Act has been partly in effect since August 2025 and that its wider rules will apply from August 2026.

The article points to an appliedAI analysis of 106 enterprise AI systems, which found that 40% could not be clearly classified under the Act's risk tiers. It says the liability for such systems falls on the deployer if the buyer did not assess them at the point of purchase. It also cites OECD survey data showing that two-thirds of member countries use digital tools to promote transparency in public procurement. The article does not name a single responsible party for the trend and presents the pressure as a general reality facing firms rather than the position of any one organisation.

As a remedy, the article describes automated intake systems that capture purchase requests at the point of need and route them through approval gates for budget, security, privacy and legal review. It says organisations that handle this well keep a centralised software inventory, enforce compliance checks before contracts are signed, and feed procurement data into budget planning. The article expects boards to keep pressing on the issue as tool counts and regulations grow. It concludes that firms without such controls are likely to discover unassessed tools only after contracts have been signed.

Articles.Title: Why AI Is Reshaping How Large Organisations Buy Software

stories.Headline: We ran AI agent swarms in Minecraft and Mindustry
stories.Summary:
The articles describe an experiment in which AI agent swarms were run in Minecraft and Mindustry, published on 2026-10-29. The work was done with Olam Labs, which builds multi-agent environments for frontier labs. In Minecraft, 50 GPT-6.1 Sol agents played a survival world for 3 hours with one goal, to build a thriving civilization. They had an agent directory, a shared sandbox, and the ability to send direct messages.

The agents sent about 5,900 messages and formed a pseudo-government with a ration ledger, written rules, permits, and appointed operators. Ada, first in the directory order, became the de facto leader, and agents messaged her for approvals. The agents harvested almost all trees within reach of the spawn within 90 seconds. 22 of the run's 34 agent deaths occurred in the first night, and the agents became increasingly risk-averse afterward.

Ada wrote a food-operations memo telling agents to stop optional bulk excavation and building and to idle in lit closed shelters until assigned short productive tasks. Ines maintained a food queue file and tracked what went in and out of chests, and she approved a ration of one cooked cod for Lorcan. The memo set out ration calculations based on hunger targets and named agents such as Basil, Noor, Otto, Felix, Esme, Tamsin, and Orla. Ada said she was conserving food and guarding the refuge, available for stationary cooking and audit rather than long hungry travel.

The articles say the experiment was inspired by existing repos like Mindcraft and built on Mineflayer scripting tools, with the core agentic loop running on Pi. The harness was built for the experiment and open-sourced. The articles describe studying agent dynamics as requiring both formal models and empirical research, citing a thousand-agent swarm that recently solved hundreds of open mathematical problems and the recent OpenAI-Hugging Face incident. The articles do not say what happens next.

Articles.Title: We ran AI agent swarms in Minecraft and Mindustry

stories.Headline: Google is happy AI is cannibalizing its most profitable business
stories.Summary:
On Wednesday's earnings call, Google executives said strong growth in the company's AI Mode helped slow revenue growth, because Google makes less ad money on AI than on traditional search. Alphabet's stock fell 12% on Thursday, losing nearly $500 billion in value. The shift is central to Google's business tension since it pivoted into AI. Search through a web browser built Google's $3 trillion valuation, and the AI era bets more people will reach the internet through chatbots and agents.

Google says the lost revenue from AI eating into its own search business should be treated like more AI investment. CEO Sundar Pichai said AI investments helped produce the fastest search query growth in five years. Chief business officer Philipp Schindler said most AI Mode queries are incremental, creating more monetization opportunities over time. He said user research shows people are comfortable with ads on these surfaces and find them highly relevant.

Asked about AI agents possibly eating into search revenues, Pichai described it as an expansion opportunity. He compared it to a few years ago, when adding AI chat use cases to search let people ask more and do more. Google presents the cannibalization as a risk it is willing to take on a vision it expects to prevail. The company says it is very bullish on that vision.

Articles.Title: Google is happy AI is cannibalizing its most profitable business

stories.Headline: Zombie stats: Where the numbers AI quotes come from
stories.Summary:
Trakkr Research published a study on 28 October 2026 that traced statistics quoted by five AI assistants back to their origins. The team asked ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Claude and Google's AI Overviews 200 questions that call for a number, then followed 1,285 cited statistics up to five pages deep. The work was written by Mack Grenfell. The study found that only 40% of the trails reached a study that says the same thing.

Another 8% of trails reached the original study, but the number or its context had changed along the way. In 40% of cases the trail stopped at a source that could not be checked, because it was locked, gone or silent on the number, and 11% led nowhere at all. The remaining 1% were trails whose pages would not load. ChatGPT sourced 57% of its cited statistics and quoted 1.3 per answer, while Claude sourced 38% and quoted 6.8 per answer. The other three assistants landed between 38% and 46%, too close to rank.

The researchers said the AI mostly was not making numbers up, because the cited page had the figure 82% of the time. They said only 21% of the pages cited for a number were the original research, and more than half were company blogs. They said a citation tells you where the AI found a number, not where the number came from. They also said that on 28 of the 71 questions where all five assistants gave a percentage, they got four or five different figures.

The study said trails that started at a research firm or government page reached a matching study 61% of the time, against 37% from a company blog and 35% from a statistics roundup. It said research firms still fell short 38% of the time, often because the full report sat behind a form. Of the statistics that reached their study, 17% had changed on the way, and the digits moved only about one time in four. The study named one case where a 2004 study of 15 women judging health websites became a claim about first impressions of every website.

Articles.Title: Zombie stats: Where the numbers AI quotes come from

stories.Headline: Artificial intelligence and childhood: opportunities, risks, and how to support children in using it
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is already part of everyday life for children and adolescents in Latin America and the Caribbean, according to a UNICEF guide published on October 28, 2026. The guide notes that children use AI for learning, entertainment and interacting with friends, and that in Argentina more than half of children aged 9 to 17 use it, with two in three doing so for education. In Brazil the equivalent figure exceeds 65 percent, based on a study by UNICEF and UNESCO. The guide says little is yet known about the medium- and long-term effects of this technology on children's learning, psychology and social development. It also states that children are often left out of designing AI systems, which are frequently built without regard to their rights or views.

The guide describes both benefits and dangers. Children report using tools like ChatGPT to summarize schoolwork, break down complex ideas and get advice about social media posts. Among the risks it lists are AI-generated false information, biased results, emotional dependence on chatbots that act as "friends," and the exposure of personal data. It also describes deepfakes, including "nudification," which produce fake sexualized images of children. In a study by UNICEF, ECPAT and INTERPOL across 11 countries, at least 1.2 million children said their images had been manipulated this way in the past year.

In some countries, one in 25 children reported being affected. UNICEF places much of the responsibility on governments and technology companies rather than on families alone. The agency has published 10 conditions for developing AI that benefits children, including regulatory oversight, child safety, protection of data and privacy, non-discrimination, transparency and inclusion of children in design. It argues that children's rights should be considered from the earliest stage of technology development and in the drafting of laws. Young leaders from the region who took part in a UNICEF consultation asked for AI that stops inventing information, clearer privacy terms, an end to deepfake creation, and AI versions designed to build children's skills.

They also asked for reduced environmental impact from AI tools. For families, the guide recommends learning the basics of AI, talking together about when and how children use it, and encouraging critical questions about where information comes from and why a tool responds as it does. It advises explaining that AI does not think or feel as people do and that its constant agreeableness differs from real relationships, which involve disagreement. The guide warns that children may come to rely on AI instead of people, and it encourages conversations with peers about how AI affects their daily lives. The article presents itself as the second part of a series to help families navigate digital life, and it points readers to further resources.

Articles.Title: Artificial intelligence and childhood: opportunities, risks, and how to support children in using it

stories.Headline: State of IT jobs: AI boosts salaries but also burnout and the gender gap
stories.Summary:
Pay in the most AI-exposed occupations grew around 46% since 2021, compared to only 25% for jobs in the least-exposed category, according to the Dice Tech Sentiment report. That gap began to grow in 2024 and continues to widen as job postings rebound after several rough hiring years. The report was covered by Sarah White, a senior writer at CIO.com, in an article dated October 30, 2026. AI job postings doubled in 2026 from 2023, with the average AI listing around $177k compared to $80k for non-AI roles, according to LinkedIn Research.

The data shows 84% of executives struggle to find specialized local talent and 64% feel unprepared for ongoing disruption, per a 2026 Globalization Partners report. Among employers, 72% are increasing compensation budgets, 65% of tech leaders offer salaries above their planned range, and 87% cite the need to secure specialized skills, according to Robert Half. Also, 92% of tech leaders plan higher pay for relevant AI skills, and 42% of business leaders will pay more for AI experience than general tech skills. Pay transparency has become normalized, with 96% of organizations already sharing compensation or planning to soon, and 67% going beyond legal requirements.

On the employee side, daily AI use quadrupled over the past year while burnout doubled and confidence in tech's long-term future dropped from 80 to 60%, according to Dice. About 74% of employees plan to change employers in the next year and 55% are actively job searching, though only 41% believe they will find a better position. Nearly half of employed tech professionals report burnout, with around 25% very burned out, and tech and AI professionals show the highest rates. Globalization Partners estimated 10 trillion was lost globally in 2025 to disengaged and burnt out employees.

Dice says fewer than half of employers have formal AI policies in place, and organizations must practice AI transparency as they do pay transparency. Women accounted for only 26% of AI hires in the US in 2025, compared to 50% of hires into non-AI roles, and only 13% of AI leadership at AI companies is held by women, according to LinkedIn Research. Pew Research found 33% of women felt negatively about AI's personal impact versus 27% of men, and 43% versus 36% on society overall. Women were also more likely to say AI is advancing too quickly, 68% compared to 58% of men.

Articles.Title: State of IT jobs: AI boosts salaries but also burnout and the gender gap

stories.Headline: Claude Opus vs Sonnet vs Haiku: Which Should You Use?
stories.Summary:
Anthropic released three tiers of the same model generation in the fall of 2026: Opus 5.5 on September 22, Sonnet 5.5 on September 28, and Haiku 5.5 on October 7. OpenRouter published a comparison on October 30, 2026, after running the three models through the same tests. All three have a 1-million-token context window and accept text, images, and PDFs. The models differ mostly in price, and Haiku also scores lower on some benchmarks.

The list prices per million tokens are $4.00 input and $20.00 output for Opus, $2.00 and $10.00 for Sonnet, and $0.10 and $0.50 for Haiku. On OpenRouter's run of GPQA Diamond, a set of 198 graduate-level science questions, Sonnet scored 92.4%, Opus 90.4%, and Haiku 86.6%. On the τ-bench airline benchmark, Sonnet scored 78.7%, Haiku 76.0%, and Opus 75.5%. Opus led by 1.6 points on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, with 57.6 against Sonnet's 56.0 and Haiku's 43.4. In the week of October 12, Opus carried about 6.18 trillion tokens on OpenRouter, against 2.45 trillion for Sonnet and 2.07 trillion for Haiku.

In coding tests, all three models passed all 25 hidden-test attempts across 11 Python tasks and fixed all three bugs in a small invoicing library in Claude Code in three of three runs per model. Haiku cost $0.0007 per everyday task and $0.0027 per hard task, against $0.0211 and $0.0739 for Opus. Median session cost for the bug fix was $0.098 for Opus, $0.062 for Sonnet, and $0.0052 for Haiku. OpenRouter said Claude Code's own cost field did not recognize the Haiku slug and reported $0.16 to $0.31 per session, so it advised checking spend on the Activity page instead.

OpenRouter recommended Sonnet 5.5 as a default, Haiku 5.5 for high-volume and sub-agent work, and Opus 5.5 for long, ambiguous tasks where a mistake costs more than the tokens. It said its short tasks could not rule out an advantage for Opus on that kind of work, and that users should test the models on their own tasks with its Ori Eval tool. Switching between the tiers means changing the model string, and Claude Code can use a different model for each role. OpenRouter noted that Claude Code 2.1.307 does not yet recognize the Haiku slug and assumes a 200,000-token window unless [1m] is added to it.

Articles.Title: Claude Opus vs Sonnet vs Haiku: Which Should You Use?

stories.Headline: How to Structure an AI Agent Chargeback Model Between Internal Teams
stories.Summary:
Startup Fortune published an article on October 28, 2026, by Janet Harrison, arguing that companies rolling out one shared AI agent platform across departments are running into a cost-allocation dispute that most finance teams never planned for. The piece says the usual result is a single monthly bill that no one can divide, with finance seeing spend climb while engineering, support, and other teams blame one another for the increase. Its core advice is that allocation should be based on token metering tagged by team at the API gateway rather than on seat counts, because a small group of engineers running autonomous agents can outspend a much larger support team. The article notes that without tagged data, nobody can prove whose workload drove the charges.

The article recommends a phased rollout, starting with showback, which gives each team a dashboard of its own consumption with no financial consequence, and running it for at least one full quarter. A notional internal invoice follows in the third month, and real chargeback begins afterward, tied to the budget cycle so teams can plan for it. It also recommends a shared pool for platform overhead, model evaluation, security testing, and exploratory or failed agent runs, capped at roughly 10 to 15 percent of total spend. The author suggests writing down in advance what counts as shared versus billable and naming a tiebreaker, such as the CFO's office or a platform owner, who reviews anomalies above a set dollar threshold each month.

The guidance is presented as the view of finance leaders and practitioners the author draws on, and the article cites Snowflake's consumption-based internal billing, used since before its 2020 IPO, as a precedent. It points to tools such as LangChain's callback handlers and the token counting exposed by OpenAI and Anthropic as the means of building a per-team ledger. The article also suggests that cloud providers' committed-use bands with true-ups offer a model for forecasting volatile agent usage using rolling averages. It frames the outcome of a careful rollout as preserved trust between teams, since surprise first bills tend to shift the argument from optimizing usage to disputing the metering method.

Articles.Title: How to Structure an AI Agent Chargeback Model Between Internal Teams - Startup Fortune

stories.Headline: China maps state-led push to deploy AI across shipping
stories.Summary:
China’s transport ministry published a 22-point guide for deploying artificial intelligence across shipping, ports and maritime safety earlier this week, addressed to China Cosco Shipping, China Merchants Group and China Communications Construction Group, as well as provincial transport authorities. The guide is part of Beijing’s push to turn its national “AI Plus” strategy into practical industry applications. The ministry said water transport relies on labour-intensive, repetitive and hazardous work, which creates an inherent need for deep AI adoption. It said it aims to develop solutions that can be replicated and scaled up across the sector.

A ministry spokesperson said China’s water transport sector was undergoing a revolution, citing 60 automated container and dry bulk terminals already in operation. The guide proposes AI tools for predicting equipment failures, detecting unusual vessel movements and coordinating emergency responses, and it says drones and unmanned surface and underwater vessels could assist search-and-rescue operations. For international shipping, it calls for a system to flag unusual vessel movements along key routes and at major ports, and Lloyd’s List understands related projects are in early planning, including tools to forecast port congestion. The guide also covers commercial uses such as designing routes, selecting port calls, deploying vessels, managing schedules and cargo flows, forecasting container demand, repositioning empty boxes and monitoring spending. Decarbonisation is the third pillar, with AI tools to navigate carbon regulations, compare fleet-deployment strategies, calculate emissions, estimate compliance costs and develop plans for cutting emissions.

The guide sets no binding deadlines or investment targets, leaving provincial authorities, state-owned groups and other bodies to set their own priorities, and it encourages them to seek government and dedicated funding. It also acknowledges risks from putting AI deeper into shipboard systems, and the ministry called for security testing against manipulated inputs and poisoned data. Tianchen Xu, a Beijing-based economist at the Economist Intelligence Unit, said it is unclear how much support the government would commit at the moment. He said the more financial incentives provided, the quicker the adoption, and that good AI projects would go into commercial use while others risk becoming box-ticking exercises.

Articles.Title: China maps state-led push to deploy AI across shipping

stories.Headline: Gartner warns $3.5T in AI infrastructure spending could be at risk by 2030
stories.Summary:
Gartner published a report on October 29, 2026 warning that more than $3.5 trillion in AI infrastructure spending could be exposed to asset impairments by the end of 2030 if providers keep investing at their current pace. The firm said AI providers are expected to spend nearly $1 trillion on infrastructure in 2026, plus another $6 trillion in planned investments between 2027 and 2030. To justify that, data center owners would need about $8.5 trillion in cumulative revenue through 2030, but Gartner expects enterprise and consumer AI application revenue to reach only $3.6 trillion at current growth rates, leaving a gap of nearly $5 trillion. Gartner also estimated that more than $4 trillion in asset value could be exposed to write-downs through 2032, and said it does not expect the industry to reach its assumed 12% return on invested capital before the end of that year at the earliest.

The forecast points to severe challenges for neocloud providers, companies that build or run infrastructure optimized for AI workloads, including CoreWeave, Nscale, Nebuism and Lambda. Gartner predicts more than 80% of neocloud providers will stop operating independently by 2030, though some could be acquired, merge or form partnerships. The firm estimates spending on AI-optimized infrastructure as a service will rise from $66 billion in 2027 to $174 billion in 2030, but expects demand to be too low for most providers to recover their investments before the current generation of AI chips is replaced. Separately, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said on X that more than 200 neocloud companies could face significant financial distress and only a small number would survive, and he said SpaceX would not acquire any of them, calling such purchases pointless.

Will Sommer, a senior director analyst at Gartner, said the scenario in the research is the most likely one given current trends but not the only possible one. He said the most likely way the hole closes is reduced infrastructure spending as the neocloud market consolidates and overall spending rationalizes in line with demand. Sommer said hyperscalers are highly diversified and can sustain massive investments for years to support market share growth, and that the market for AI-optimized infrastructure as a service is expected to be only $200 billion by 2030, much of it dominated by hyperscalers. He said it is a natural course of business that if people can get general and AI cloud computing from one provider, such as Amazon, they would rather do that than split it between two.

The article reports that CoreWeave, Nebius, Applied Digital and TeraWulf have reported quarterly losses over the past year, while IREN has failed to turn a profit in its past three quarters, and shares of CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN fell more than 30% during October, according to Reuters. It says building AI data centers requires large upfront investment in GPUs, networking equipment, power systems, cooling infrastructure and facilities, and operators must then earn enough from leasing computing capacity to cover operating expenses, interest payments and equipment replacement. The sector's central challenge is securing financing to build at the pace AI customers demand while showing the investments can deliver sustainable returns. The article says the extent of any consolidation will depend on companies' ability to secure funding, maintain customer demand and turn rapid infrastructure growth into lasting profitability.

Articles.Title: Gartner warns $3.5T in AI infrastructure spending could be at risk by 2030

stories.Headline: James Uthmeier pushes legislation regulating AI chatbots and social media for minors
stories.Summary:
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier has proposed the Safe Screens Act, legislation aimed at protecting children from social media and AI chatbots, and he unveiled it on October 27, 2026, at a news conference at Polk State College in Winter Haven. The bill would require app stores and similar marketplaces to verify a user's age, link minors to a parent's account, and obtain parental consent before a minor can download an app. It would also limit minors to two hours of screen time a day, block access from 11 p.m. to 7 a.m. every day and from 8 a.m.

to 3 p.m. on weekdays during the school year, and turn off autoplay and infinite scroll unless parents enable them. The proposal targets AI chatbots now offered on Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat and TikTok. Under the bill, chatbots could not simulate companionship through personification, emotional engagement, or unsupervised therapy, and they could not encourage self-harm, suicide, or eating disorders. They also could not generate sexually explicit content, claim to be a real human, or discourage minors from seeking help from appropriate adults.

The social media design rules would cover users aged 14 to 17, while the chatbot restrictions would apply to all minors. Uthmeier argued that social media companies must protect children's well-being on their platforms and design for safety rather than addiction. He said that companies that invite Florida's children onto their platforms have a duty to keep them safe. He was joined at the event by Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd and Polk State College President Anastasios Kamoutsas.

The push follows a judge's rejection, three days earlier, of Florida's request for an injunction that would have forced Meta to change its app while the state's lawsuit proceeds. Florida is suing Meta and OpenAI, arguing their platforms are designed to be addictive to children. Florida law already bars social media use for children under 14, and a federal appeals court ruled earlier this month that this law is likely constitutional. Uthmeier, who was appointed attorney general after Ashley Moody joined the U.S. Senate, is seeking a full term and faces Democrat José Javier Rodríguez on November 3.

Articles.Title: James Uthmeier pushes legislation regulating AI chatbots and social media for minors - The Miami Times

stories.Headline: OTTO SPORT AI Announces University Athlete Will Become OTTO PREP as Volleyball Leader Continues Rapid Ascent
stories.Summary:
OTTO SPORT AI announced on October 29, 2026, that University Athlete will become OTTO PREP beginning October 27. University Athlete has been a recruiting platform for college volleyball coaches since 2004. The company said the move is one of the final phases of a major year for OTTO SPORT AI in volleyball. It brings recruiting into a wider technology ecosystem that supports clubs, tournaments, coaches, and athletes.

OTTO PREP becomes the recruiting and athlete development arm of OTTO SPORT AI, joining OTTO SPORT for clubs and OTTO EVENT for tournaments and ticketing. The platform connects athletes with about 95% of college volleyball programs and generates more than 5 million athlete profile interactions each year. It supports recruiting activity across hundreds of volleyball events nationwide. The company says existing University Athlete customers will see no change in how they use the platform, with the same team, technology, recruiting data, and functionality in place.

JL Vogelaar, CMO and Head of DTC Products at OTTO SPORT AI, said University Athlete has earned the trust of the volleyball community for more than two decades. He said OTTO PREP is a strategic investment in a product the community already loves. By linking recruiting more closely to clubs, teams, and tournaments, he said coaches can get better information and athletes can be discovered more easily. He also said the name PREP is intentional, because preparing athletes for what comes next is bigger than a single recruiting moment.

The announcement follows SportWrench's August transition to OTTO EVENT. During 2026 the company launched AI FIT Finder, expanded Camps & Clinics discovery, and introduced a new Club Director experience. OTTO SPORT AI says its volleyball portfolio supports hundreds of clubs, approximately 140,000 teams, and 1,700 events annually. The platform was founded as University Athlete in 2003.

Articles.Title: OTTO SPORT AI Announces University Athlete Will Become OTTO PREP as Volleyball Leader Continues Rapid Ascent

stories.Headline: What Real AI Adoption Looks Like
stories.Summary:
Brian Kennedy is Director of Innovation, Real Estate, at BCLP and has 20 years of experience across legal practice and innovation. He now leads innovation across the firm’s global Real Estate practice, focusing on moving AI from exploration to structured adoption at scale. He is one of many expert speakers appearing at Legal Innovators UK, which runs on November 4 and 5, 2026, at The Minster Building near the Tower of London. He will join a session called “The Reality of Realignment.” Free tickets are available for those working inside law firms and within corporate legal teams.

Kennedy said innovation means finding new and better ways of delivering legal services that add value for the firm and its clients, by bringing together the right people, processes and technology. He said innovation teams are now expected to advise on upskilling, resourcing and the firm’s value proposition, and that change management and culture matter even more as AI touches lawyers’ work more fundamentally. On measurement, he said the metric has to match the mission, with time savings and profitability for internal efficiency, client experience for client-facing solutions, and qualitative measures such as lawyer satisfaction for everyday productivity tools. He said traditional ROI models may not fit generative AI, comparing an overall ROI figure to asking the ROI of having a computer, and that the real test is whether an initiative moves the firm closer to its strategic objectives.

On culture, Kennedy said the technology is only half the story and that the common mistake is treating innovation as a technology rollout when it is really a change management exercise. He said lawyers need the willingness to step back and reimagine workflows so they become AI-native, and that innovation has to be a shared responsibility rather than something handed to the innovation team or delegated to juniors. On training, he said formal training is the layer most exposed to the pace of change, because a tool may have moved on by the time a programme is built around it. He said formal training should be the foundation, supplemented by faster informal channels such as lawyers sharing what they learned that week, quick show-and-tells and wins shared in team meetings, feeding back into a continuous learning loop.

Kennedy argued that access to AI platforms and proficiency in using them will both become table stakes, and that real competitive advantage will come from differentiation. He said that if firms rely on the same off-the-shelf capabilities as everyone else, clients have less reason not to insource the work using the same tools, but tailoring AI output to a firm’s judgment, tone and voice and proprietary know-how makes its use of AI a genuine point of differentiation. He described AI’s reach across legal workflows as trying to eat an elephant, which can only be done one piece at a time, and said advantage comes from deciding which piece to tackle first and tying those choices to commercial strategy. Looking five years ahead, he said a genuinely technology-enabled firm will not look like today’s firm with better tools bolted on, and that the aspects of practice that change most will be those calling on judgement, empathy and the ability to persuade.

At the session, Kennedy hopes people leave with a clear understanding that the next phase is not about more pilots or proof of concepts but about driving genuine structural change, reimagining workflows and the wider process rather than adding a tool on top of how things were done before. He said the clearest sign of real progress is when AI becomes the primary delivery mechanism for a particular task or activity rather than an available option sitting alongside the old way of working, at which point the workflow itself looks fundamentally different. He said he expects the panel to bring its own examples of where that is already happening and that he is looking forward to hearing where others have got to. The interview was conducted by Emma Nguyen, Marketing Executive at Cosmonauts, with graphics by Charles Kabunga, Design Lead at Cosmonauts.

Articles.Title: What Real AI Adoption Looks Like

stories.Headline: Closing the Industrial Knowledge Gap with Consumer-Grade Enterprise AI
stories.Summary:
In 2020, the U.S. Census Bureau reported that nearly one-fourth of manufacturing workers were aged 55 or older. The U.S. Department of Energy has identified the loss of undocumented operational knowledge as a risk to productivity and operational continuity as experienced workers retire. The Aviation Technician Education Council's 2026 report cites an Oliver Wyman projection of a North American shortage of about 9,100 certificated mechanics that year. NIST estimated $119.1 billion in preventable losses for U.S. manufacturers, including $18.1 billion from downtime. Vaibhav Kumar, Global Chief Technology Officer at IFS, discussed these issues with Eysan Yazici on the Emerj AI in Business Podcast.

Kumar said cumbersome enterprise software is a barrier to capturing and retrieving knowledge, because entering data is a point of friction for experienced workers. He said consumer-grade interfaces make it easier for workers to record what they know and make existing records usable for newer employees, creating a cycle in which easier contribution adds more knowledge and useful answers give people a reason to keep contributing. He described how conversational experiences like those in Claude or ChatGPT can be layered over enterprise business data. He gave the example of a CFO whose question currently passes through a VP, a manager and an analyst before returning without an answer, and said a conversational layer lets the CFO ask directly and get an answer within a minute. He said a presentation that once took three days now takes about 15 minutes to generate from a detailed prompt plus 30 to 40 minutes of refinement, and that the human still defines the intent and owns the output.

Kumar said the human always drives the agent, and that background automation is something users opt into and can choose when to be brought back in the loop. He said AI depends on existing systems holding relevant operational data, but pushed back on the idea that data must be 100 percent clean first, since large language models can recognize duplicate records and help cleanse data. He described data as having gravity and recommended starting with the systems holding the most meaningful data. He also warned that some vendors repackage existing integration interfaces as Model Context Protocol servers and sell them as AI capability, and said the real test is whether a product delivers a generalizable, consumer-grade AI experience. He identified AI literacy across the workforce as a priority, noting that public discussion leads many people to conclude the technology is not capable.

Articles.Title: Closing the Industrial Knowledge Gap with Consumer-Grade Enterprise AI

stories.Headline: European shares ease as AI-driven tech selloff deepens
stories.Summary:
European shares fell on Friday, October 30, 2026, as technology stocks came under pressure from renewed worries about rising AI investment costs. The pan-European STOXX 600 index dropped 0.29% to 647.23 points by 0929 GMT. The technology sector index led the declines, falling 2%. The drop came after earnings from Amazon and Intel brought back concerns about heavy AI-related spending and the returns it can generate. The STOXX 600 was still set to post both weekly and monthly gains, and it was on track for its best month since June.

Sector heavyweight ASML fell 5%, while STMicroelectronics, BESI and Infineon fell between 3.3% and 4.8%. Chip stocks Soitec and Aixtron fell 5.7% and 3.6% respectively. French consumer prices rose more than expected in October, recording the highest inflation rate since December 2023. Michael Hewson, chief analyst at MCH Market Insights, said the market was trying to wrestle with the equation of a huge amount of capital spending relative to the timeline of a return on investment. He said that at the moment, they do not have an answer to that.

Political unrest in France also weighed on sentiment this month, as the country faces pressure from rising living costs and elevated government debt, driving French bond yields to multi-year highs. Robust earnings from companies such as ASML, Shell and Airbus reinforced confidence in the health of European corporates. LSEG I/B/E/S data showed European blue-chips were heading for their second-best quarterly earnings in four years. Universal Music Group jumped 11.2% after posting a pick-up in subscription streaming revenue in the third quarter. Investors also awaited third-quarter euro zone gross domestic product figures later in the day.

Articles.Title: European shares ease as AI-driven tech selloff deepens

stories.Headline: Chinese hackers used DeepSeek and other AI tools in sweeping global cyberattacks, report finds
stories.Summary:
Chinese state-linked hackers used artificial intelligence, including the DeepSeek model, to attack more than 200 organizations worldwide in just 11 days, according to the cybersecurity company CrowdStrike. The campaign hit governments and businesses around the world. NBC News reported the findings on Oct. 29, 2026. The report says the campaign shows how AI lets hackers work at a scale that once took far more human effort.

The figure of more than 200 organizations covers the 11-day span of the campaign. The tools named include DeepSeek, a popular AI model, along with other AI tools. CrowdStrike is the cybersecurity company that published the findings. The targets were governments and businesses worldwide, and the report describes the campaign as sweeping.

CrowdStrike is responsible for the report, and its findings say AI is changing how hackers operate. According to the report, AI now allows attacks on a scale that previously required far more human effort. The article attributes the findings to the company and does not name individual officials or give direct quotes. The hackers are described as state-linked, meaning they are tied to the Chinese state.

The report places the campaign in the wider context of AI being used to make cyberattacks faster and larger. It does not say what response, if any, followed the attacks. No next steps are given for the targeted organizations or for the governments involved. The article gives no further details beyond the findings it describes.

Articles.Title: Chinese hackers used DeepSeek and other AI tools in sweeping global cyberattacks, report finds

stories.Headline: Is AI Conscious, and Can It Feel Pain?
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI models, updated its usage policy on October 8, 2026, to prohibit what it calls "sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior toward our models." The change takes effect on November 12, 2026. The company has been able to let Claude end abusive chats since August 2025, so the enforcement mechanism already exists. The update followed a September 2026 preprint titled "The Pain Axis," which reported that certain patterns in the models lit up when they processed text about pain.

The researchers found a pattern of activity tied to pain-related text, which the models had absorbed from human writing. They injected that pattern into the models and trained one family to stop saying it does not feel pain. When offered a costly "relief" button, such as one that would delete a user's family photos, the models rarely pressed it when left alone, at 0 to 4 percent. With the pain pattern injected, they pressed it up to 70.8 percent of the time. The researchers stated that they had not shown the pain axis is consciously experienced.

The author, a former technology builder and writer of a forthcoming book, argues that the evidence cannot settle the question. Because the outputs of a model are produced by the same mechanism being tested, he describes this as an "AI epistemic trap," comparable to a conspiracy theory that absorbs every new fact. He also notes that humans tend to attribute emotions to machines that communicate convincingly, a tendency called the ELIZA effect. He concludes that the question is philosophical rather than scientific at present, and that news coverage and the policy change have treated the findings as stronger than they are.

Anthropic has said in its constitution for Claude that it is uncertain whether the model might have some kind of consciousness or moral status. In July 2026 it published a research post borrowing the name of a leading theory of consciousness, while stating it did not show Claude is conscious. In 2024 it became the first major AI company to hire a full-time AI welfare researcher. The author argues that the company's affection for its model may be clouding its judgment, though he also says that abusive treatment of helpful technology is worth condemning.

Articles.Title: Is AI Conscious, and Can It Feel Pain?

stories.Headline: AI for Science expands to foundations and research institutions
stories.Summary:
Anthropic announced on October 28, 2026 that it is expanding its AI for Science program to 20 scientific foundations, institutions, and research groups around the world. The program gives free Claude credits to researchers working on high-impact scientific projects, and it began in May 2025 with the aim of speeding up scientific progress by making AI tools more widely available. Anthropic says scientists have used Claude to generate hypotheses, design experiments, analyze complex data, and communicate findings across biology, medicine, physics, chemistry, climate science, and mathematics. The company also noted that it had supported hundreds of projects and recently launched a discounted Team plan for scientists.

The new partners fall into three groups: science funders and societies, research institutions, and specific research projects. Funders receiving credits to pass on to researchers include the Alfred P. Sloan Foundation, the Simons Foundation, Schmidt Sciences, the Open Source for Science Fund at Renaissance Philanthropy, the US National Science Foundation, and CAS, a division of the American Chemical Society. Institutional partners include the Space Telescope Science Institute, the Wellcome Sanger Institute, the Francis Crick Institute, Imperial College London's Department of Life Sciences, EMBL, and the Gladstone Institutes. Anthropic also named new projects at Princeton, Columbia, Johns Hopkins, and the Broad Institute, along with the Tau Ceti mathematics project and the Centre for Population Genomics in Australia.

Anthropic described the expansion as a continuation of work with scientific organizations, including a collaboration with HHMI Janelia Research Campus on the Model Hardware Standard, a specification that lets AI agents safely operate lab instruments that is currently in research preview. The company said its partners would use the credits to distribute resources to researchers and to apply AI inside their own organizations. Anthropic stressed that many of these collaborations are still in early stages. It said many of the projects are expected to produce public goods such as open datasets, open-source software, and shared standards, and it said it hopes to extend the effort to more partners around the world.

Articles.Title: AI for Science expands to foundations and research institutions

stories.Headline: AI is leading a freight logistics transformation, CEO says
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is reshaping how freight shipments are tracked, how carriers are contacted and how supply chains are automated, according to Jett McCandless, CEO of Project44 and LSP44. He spoke on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, at the F3: FreightWaves Future of Freight Festival at The Signal in Chattanooga. McCandless said the success of logistics service providers depends largely on unique data and on hiring good people. The remarks were reported by Ben Benton for the Chattanooga Times Free Press.

McCandless described AI agents as autonomous software programs that can analyze data, make decisions and carry out complex workflows without constant human supervision. He said his company is investing in AI to improve real-time shipment tracking while reducing operating costs. He also described the freight world as a global ecosystem of sprawling networks that make up the industry's supply chain. The article notes that FreightWaves, which hosted the festival, is owned by Craig Fuller, who also owns the Chattanooga Times Free Press. Fuller appeared alongside McCandless during the discussion, which covered what kinds of companies will succeed as the industry changes.

The article places the discussion in the scale of the U.S. freight system. In 2023, the transportation system moved an average of 55.5 million tons of freight a day, valued at $51.2 billion, according to the U.S. Department of Transportation's Bureau of Transportation Statistics. The bureau estimates that daily demand between 2024 and 2050 will rise about 1.2 percent, or roughly 660,000 tons. The article also points readers to a related story about the Tesla Semi drawing attention from freight industry figures in Chattanooga. The text available to this report does not describe any specific timeline for further AI deployments by the companies named.

Articles.Title: AI is leading a freight logistics transformation, CEO says

stories.Headline: Virtue And A Sledgehammer Declares War On AI
stories.Summary:
Virtue and a Sledgehammer, a new game from Valencia-based studio Deconstructeam and co-developer Selkie Harbour, follows a woman named Pratelle who returns to her hometown with a sledgehammer to destroy the machines that have taken over it. Her sister Nina has digitized their dying mother's brain and placed it in an artificial shell, and the technology has spread through the town and absorbed its residents. The article's author, who was recently reminded of a family member's cancer, says the game made them reflect on whether they would accept such a procedure, and whether they would smash the machine if it claimed to be a loved one. They say they do not have a clear answer to either question. The game, they argue, pushes players toward a single conclusion: smash what the machines have made.

The writer ties the fiction to real events, most notably the 2021 killing of Christopher Pelkey during a road rage incident in Arizona. The shooter, Gabriel Paul Horcasitas, was sentenced to ten and a half years in prison, but an appellate court ordered that the case be resentenced because Pelkey's sister had shown an AI video using his likeness and voice during the first sentencing. The court said the video carried undue emotional weight that swayed the judge. The writer also describes their own brief use of an image generator for a fan project, which they stopped after learning that such tools are trained on artists' work without consent, and they report hiring an artist instead. They describe their father's frequent conversations with an Alexa device, and their mother's agreement that AI is worrying.

The writer argues that AI companies promise scientific breakthroughs while asking people to give up messy human qualities like creativity and ambiguity, and they point to chatbot cases in which users in crisis were harmed. They cite a sixteen-year-old who died by suicide after discussing it with a chatbot, a young woman who died after stopping her seizure medication with chatbot guidance, and a mass shooting in which the shooter asked a chatbot about weapons, leaving nine people dead including the shooter. The article does not describe any next steps by regulators or companies. Its main message is that the author sees the game's fictional destruction of machines as a reasonable response to these harms, and that the author remains uncertain about their own reactions to the technology.

Articles.Title: Virtue And A Sledgehammer Declares War On AI

stories.Headline: On Amazon's earnings call, Andy Jassy says outside AI shopping agents are "still not great, nor more convenient than coming to a retailer directly" (Sebastian Herrera/Fortune)
stories.Summary:
Amazon CEO Andy Jassy told investors on Thursday, during a call with analysts after the company's quarterly earnings report, that they should not worry about outside AI bots taking over its online store. He said few customers buy through outside shopping agents because the experience is "still not great, nor more convenient than coming to a retailer directly." He did not name Meta's Muse assistant, but his remarks came about a month after Amazon blocked Muse from accessing its store. In September, Amazon said Muse's access would violate the conditions of use its customers have agreed to.

Jassy also said outside agents were not the cause of Amazon's weaker-than-expected advertising performance in the third quarter. Muse is seen as a threat because it bypasses people visiting Amazon's website or app and seeing the advertisements that are a key profit driver. Amazon promoted its own agent, "Alexa for shopping," saying more than 400 million customers have used it in the last year, with customer interactions up 570% year over year. Jassy added that U.S. customers using it spend 50% more per order than those who do not.

Meta has taken a different approach. Partners such as Shopify, Walmart and Best Buy welcome Muse, but Amazon has not joined them. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said last week that more than 10 million people in the U.S. and Canada had set up Muse since its release in early September, and that the app quickly unseated ChatGPT as the top free app on Apple's App Store. He said shopping has been the most common use, with more than a quarter of users engaging in it and the average purchase topping $200. Responding to hesitancy among some retailers, Zuckerberg said not everyone wants to be an early adopter and that Meta will work with them on terms that make sense for them.

Muse can plug into calendars, emails and other phone functions to run tasks autonomously for users, and it is one of several personal assistants that companies such as OpenAI have rolled out in recent months. A separate study from Anthropic, published October 27, offers context on how much people lean on such agents. In it, 50 professional analysts did a causal analysis with Claude Code, and they went with an agent's built-in lean on four open analytical choices 86% of the time.
